$comment: Content layer for the exercise library. Merge these fields into exercise-library.json by matching on 'id'. Contains: the full field spec, muscle taxonomy for anatomy diagrams, and 14 fully-written entries to use as the quality template for the rest.

content_schema.summary: one sentence, shown under the title in search results
content_schema.description: 2-3 sentences: what it trains and why you'd program it
content_schema.setup: array of numbered setup steps before the first rep
content_schema.execution: array of numbered steps for one rep
content_schema.cues: short coaching cues, the things a good coach says mid-set
content_schema.rom_notes: what full range of motion actually means here
content_schema.safety_notes: bailout procedure, spotter needs, when to stop
content_schema.grip_variations: array of grip/stance options and what each shifts emphasis to
content_schema.tracking_type: weight_reps | bodyweight_reps | weighted_bodyweight_reps | time | distance_time | reps_only - drives your logging UI
content_schema.log_per_side: true if unilateral and each side is logged separately
content_schema.substitutes: array of exercise ids with the same pattern

media.muscle_map_front: array of muscle ids to highlight on the front anatomy diagram
media.muscle_map_back: array of muscle ids to highlight on the back diagram

muscle_taxonomy.$comment: Use these ids everywhere. The 'view' field tells your anatomy diagram which body view to highlight on. 'group' is for filtering ('show me back exercises').

content.summary: The primary barbell lower-body strength lift, loading the quads and glutes through a deep knee and hip bend.
content.description: The back squat is the highest-yield lower body strength exercise for most people, training the quads, glutes and adductors under heavy load while demanding bracing from the entire trunk. It carries over well to almost every other lower-body movement, which is why it anchors most strength programs. It also has the steepest technique requirement of the common squat variations.
setup: Set the bar in the rack at roughly mid-chest height.
Step under and place the bar on the upper traps (high bar) or across the rear delts (low bar).
Grip just outside shoulder width, pull the elbows down and squeeze the upper back tight.
Take a big breath, brace, and stand the bar out of the rack.
Walk back two or three steps, feet shoulder width, toes turned out 15-30 degrees.
execution: Take a deep breath into the belly and brace as if about to be punched.
Break at the hips and knees together, sitting down between your feet.
Descend under control until the hip crease passes below the top of the knee.
Drive the floor away, keeping the bar over mid-foot and the chest angle constant.
Stand fully, exhale at the top, then re-brace for the next rep.
cues: Spread the floor with your feet
Knees track over the middle toes
Brace before you descend, not on the way up

common_mistakes.mistake: Knees cave inward on the ascent
common_mistakes.fix: Lighten the load and actively push the knees out; add hip abduction work.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hips shoot up first, turning it into a good morning
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce weight and drive the chest up out of the hole; check quad strength.

common_mistakes.mistake: Heels lifting off the floor
common_mistakes.fix: Usually ankle mobility. Widen the stance slightly or use lifting shoes.

common_mistakes.mistake: Losing the brace at the bottom
common_mistakes.fix: Hold the breath through the turnaround; exhale only at the top.

common_mistakes.mistake: Lower back rounding at depth (butt wink)
common_mistakes.fix: Squat to the depth you can hold neutral, then build range over time.

content.breathing: Inhale and brace at the top, hold through the descent and the drive out of the bottom, exhale once past the sticking point.
content.rom_notes: Full range is hip crease below the top of the kneecap. Going deeper is fine if you can keep a neutral spine; going higher is a partial and should be logged as such.
content.safety_notes: Always squat in a rack with the safety pins set just below your bottom position. To bail, drop the bar backwards while stepping forward. Learn to bail with an empty bar before going heavy.

grip_variations.name: High bar
grip_variations.effect: More upright torso, more quad emphasis.

grip_variations.name: Low bar
grip_variations.effect: More forward lean, more glute and hip emphasis, usually heavier.

grip_variations.name: Wide stance
grip_variations.effect: More adductor and glute involvement.

grip_variations.name: Narrow stance
grip_variations.effect: More quad, requires more ankle mobility.

content.summary: A full-body pull from the floor, training the posterior chain under the heaviest loads you'll handle.
content.description: The deadlift trains the glutes, hamstrings and spinal erectors, along with the grip and upper back that hold the bar in position. It's the lift where most people can move the most weight, which also makes it the one where technique breakdown carries the highest cost. Programmed sparingly for most lifters because of how long it takes to recover from.
setup: Stand with mid-foot under the bar, feet about hip width.
Hinge and grip the bar just outside your shins, double overhand or mixed.
Drop the hips until the shins touch the bar, shoulders slightly ahead of it.
Pull the chest up and set a flat, neutral back.
Take the slack out of the bar until you hear or feel it click.
execution: Breathe in, brace hard against the belt line.
Push the floor away with the legs, keeping the bar dragging up the shins.
Once past the knees, drive the hips forward to lock out.
Stand tall with the shoulders back but not hyperextended.
Lower by hinging first, then bending the knees once the bar passes them.
cues: Chest up, lats tight, bar close

common_mistakes.mistake: Hips rise before the bar leaves the floor
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce load and set the hips slightly higher at the start so the position doesn't change.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bar drifting away from the shins
common_mistakes.fix: Engage the lats — think about tucking your armpits over the bar.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rounding the lower back
common_mistakes.fix: Drop the weight substantially. This is the single highest-risk fault in the lift.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hyperextending at lockout
common_mistakes.fix: Finish with glutes squeezed and ribs down, standing tall rather than leaning back.

common_mistakes.mistake: Yanking the bar off the floor
common_mistakes.fix: Pull the slack out first, then apply force gradually.

content.breathing: Big breath and brace before each rep. Reset the breath on the floor between reps rather than breathing at the top.
content.rom_notes: Full range is bar from the floor to full hip and knee lockout. Rack pulls and block pulls are partial-range variants and should be logged as separate exercises.
content.safety_notes: Stop the set the moment your back position changes — one bad rep is worth more than the extra rep. Never bounce reps off the floor unless deliberately programmed. No spotter can help you on a deadlift; just set the bar down.

grip_variations.name: Double overhand
grip_variations.effect: Safest for the biceps, grip usually limits the load.

grip_variations.name: Mixed grip
grip_variations.effect: Allows heavier loads, small biceps tear risk on the supinated arm.

grip_variations.name: Hook grip
grip_variations.effect: Secure and symmetrical, painful to learn.

grip_variations.name: Straps
grip_variations.effect: Removes grip as the limiter, useful for volume work.

content.summary: The benchmark upper-body pressing lift, training chest, triceps and front delts.
content.description: The barbell bench press allows heavier loading than any other horizontal press, making it the standard for upper body pushing strength. It trains the pecs through a large range with significant triceps and front delt contribution. Bar path and shoulder position matter more than most people assume, both for performance and for keeping shoulders healthy long term.
setup: Lie back with eyes roughly under the bar.
Set the feet flat and drive them into the floor.
Pull the shoulder blades back and down, creating a slight arch in the upper back.
Grip roughly 1.5x shoulder width, wrists stacked over the elbows.
Unrack by pulling the bar out rather than pressing it up, keeping the blades set.
execution: Take a breath and brace.
Lower the bar under control to the lower chest or sternum.
Touch lightly — no bouncing — keeping the elbows at roughly 45-70 degrees from the torso.
Press up and slightly back toward the shoulders.
Lock out without letting the shoulder blades come unglued.
cues: Shoulder blades in your back pockets
Leg drive without lifting the hips
Press yourself away from the bar

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows flared to 90 degrees
common_mistakes.fix: Tuck to 45-70 degrees — the flared position is the main driver of shoulder pain in benching.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bouncing the bar off the chest
common_mistakes.fix: Pause briefly on the chest; reduce load if you can't control it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hips lifting off the bench
common_mistakes.fix: Use leg drive to push into the bench, not upward.

common_mistakes.mistake: Shoulder blades losing position mid-set
common_mistakes.fix: Reset the setup; unrack by pulling the bar rather than pressing.

common_mistakes.mistake: Uneven bar path or one side lagging
common_mistakes.fix: Drop to dumbbells for a block to address the imbalance.

content.breathing: Inhale on the way down, hold through the press, exhale at lockout. On heavy singles, hold through the whole rep.
content.rom_notes: Full range is bar to chest contact and full elbow lockout. Board presses and pin presses are partial variants — log separately.
content.safety_notes: Use a spotter or set the safety pins at chest height. Never use collarless plates as a bail-out method. If alone with no rack safeties, use dumbbells instead.

grip_variations.name: Standard (1.5x shoulder)
grip_variations.effect: Balanced chest and triceps.

grip_variations.name: Close grip
grip_variations.effect: More triceps, less shoulder stress.

grip_variations.name: Wide grip
grip_variations.effect: More chest, shorter range, more shoulder stress.

content.summary: Standing barbell press from shoulders to overhead, training delts and triceps with heavy trunk bracing.
content.description: The overhead press builds shoulder strength through the full overhead range while demanding a rigid trunk to prevent the ribcage flaring. It's the most honest upper body lift — there's very little way to cheat it once you're standing. Loads progress slowly compared to bench, which frustrates people who don't expect it.
setup: Set the bar at upper-chest height in the rack.
Grip just outside shoulder width, elbows slightly in front of the bar.
Unrack onto the front delts, bar resting on the shoulders.
Step back, feet hip width, glutes and abs squeezed tight.
execution: Breathe in and brace hard; squeeze the glutes to stop the lower back arching.
Pull the head back slightly to clear a path for the bar.
Press straight up, moving the head back through as the bar passes the forehead.
Lock out with the bar over the mid-foot, biceps near the ears.
Lower under control to the shoulders and re-brace.
cues: Squeeze the glutes — don't lean back
Head through the window at the top

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaning back to turn it into an incline press
common_mistakes.fix: Squeeze the glutes and abs; reduce the load.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bar pressed forward, finishing in front of the body
common_mistakes.fix: Move the head back out of the way and press vertically.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using leg drive on a strict press
common_mistakes.fix: If you need leg drive, log it as a push press instead.

common_mistakes.mistake: Wrists bent back under the bar
common_mistakes.fix: Stack the wrist over the forearm; the bar should sit in the heel of the palm.

content.breathing: Inhale and brace at the shoulders, hold through the press, exhale at lockout.
content.rom_notes: Full range is bar touching the shoulders to full elbow lockout with the head through. Stopping short at the top is a partial.
content.safety_notes: Set rack safeties at shoulder height when pressing heavy. If you fail a rep, lower it to the shoulders under control rather than dropping it forward.

grip_variations.name: Standard barbell
grip_variations.effect: Heaviest loading, fixed hand path.

grip_variations.name: Dumbbell
grip_variations.effect: Freer shoulder path, often kinder to cranky shoulders.

grip_variations.name: Neutral grip
grip_variations.effect: Reduces impingement risk for many people.

content.summary: Bodyweight vertical pull from a dead hang, the benchmark for relative upper-body pulling strength.
content.description: The pull-up trains the lats through their full range with heavy involvement from the biceps and mid-back. Because load is bodyweight, progression comes from adding reps first and then external weight. It's one of the few exercises where getting lighter genuinely improves performance.
setup: Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder width, palms facing away.
Hang with arms fully extended, shoulders active rather than shrugged to the ears.
Squeeze the glutes and brace the core so the body doesn't swing.
execution: Start by pulling the shoulder blades down and back.
Drive the elbows down toward the ribs, leading with the chest.
Pull until the chin clears the bar or the chest approaches it.
Lower under control to a full dead hang.
Reset the shoulders before the next rep.
cues: Pull the elbows to your pockets
Squeeze the glutes to stop swinging

common_mistakes.mistake: Kipping or swinging to generate momentum
common_mistakes.fix: Use an assisted machine or bands so you can do strict reps.

common_mistakes.mistake: Partial range, not reaching a full hang
common_mistakes.fix: Count only reps from full extension; drop the rep target if needed.

common_mistakes.mistake: Shoulders shrugging up at the bottom
common_mistakes.fix: Practise scapular pull-ups to learn the depression.

common_mistakes.mistake: Chin craning over the bar
common_mistakes.fix: Lead with the chest instead of reaching with the head.

content.breathing: Exhale on the way up, inhale on the way down. On heavy weighted sets, brace and hold through the rep.
content.rom_notes: Full range is dead hang with elbows locked, to chin clearly above the bar. Anything less is a partial.
content.safety_notes: Build up gradually if you have elbow or shoulder history — the dead hang position loads both. Don't drop off the bar from height; lower under control.

grip_variations.name: Pronated (overhand)
grip_variations.effect: Most lat-dominant, hardest version.

grip_variations.name: Supinated (chin-up)
grip_variations.effect: More biceps, usually easier.

grip_variations.name: Neutral
grip_variations.effect: Kindest on the elbows and shoulders.

grip_variations.name: Wide
grip_variations.effect: More lat, shorter range, more shoulder stress.

content.summary: A hip hinge with soft knees that loads the hamstrings and glutes through a long stretch.
content.description: The Romanian deadlift is the primary hamstring builder for most programs, training the muscle in a lengthened position where it responds well. Unlike a conventional deadlift it starts at the top and never touches the floor, keeping constant tension. Range of motion is limited by hamstring flexibility, not by the floor.
setup: Take the bar from a rack at hip height, or stand up a deadlift first.
Feet hip width, bar against the thighs, grip just outside the legs.
Set a soft bend in the knees and lock it there for the whole set.
Pull the shoulders back and set the lats to hold the bar close.
execution: Breathe in and brace.
Push the hips backwards, letting the torso lean forward as a counterweight.
Keep the bar dragging down the thighs, back flat throughout.
Stop when you feel a strong hamstring stretch or the back is about to round — usually mid-shin.
Drive the hips forward to stand, squeezing the glutes at the top.
cues: Push the hips back to the wall behind you
Bar stays glued to your legs
Knees stay soft, not bending further
Stretch, don't reach for the floor

common_mistakes.mistake: Turning it into a squat by bending the knees
common_mistakes.fix: Lock the knee angle at the start and keep it there.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rounding the lower back to reach lower
common_mistakes.fix: Stop at the point where you can hold neutral — that's your range.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bar drifting away from the legs
common_mistakes.fix: Set the lats and think about squeezing the bar into your thighs.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hyperextending at the top
common_mistakes.fix: Finish standing tall with glutes squeezed and ribs down.

content.breathing: Inhale at the top, brace, hold through the descent and the lift, exhale at the top.
content.rom_notes: Range is individual and defined by hamstring flexibility, not by touching the floor. Log the same range each session so progress is comparable.
content.safety_notes: Stop the set as soon as the back rounds. This is a stretch-loaded position, so the eccentric causes significant soreness when new — start light.

grip_variations.name: Barbell
grip_variations.effect: Heaviest loading.

grip_variations.name: Dumbbell
grip_variations.effect: Easier to keep close, better for beginners.

grip_variations.name: Single-leg
grip_variations.effect: Adds balance demand, exposes side-to-side differences.

content.summary: Bent-over horizontal pull that builds mid-back thickness under heavy load.
content.description: The barbell row trains the lats, rhomboids and mid traps while the spinal erectors work isometrically to hold the bent-over position. It allows more load than most rowing variations, at the cost of significant lower back fatigue. Torso angle determines emphasis — more horizontal hits the mid-back, more upright shifts toward the lats.
setup: Stand with the bar over mid-foot, feet hip width.
Hinge at the hips until the torso is 15-45 degrees above horizontal.
Grip just outside shoulder width, overhand.
Set a flat back and brace hard before the first rep.
execution: Pull the bar toward the lower ribs or upper stomach.
Drive the elbows back and squeeze the shoulder blades together.
Pause briefly at the top without letting the torso rise.
Lower under control to full arm extension.
Keep the torso angle identical for every rep.
cues: Squeeze the blades at the top

common_mistakes.mistake: Torso rising with each rep until it's a shrug
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce load; film a set from the side to check.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using hip momentum to swing the weight up
common_mistakes.fix: Try a chest-supported row for a block to relearn strict pulling.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rounding the lower back
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce load; if it still happens, switch to a chest-supported variation.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pulling to the chest with flared elbows
common_mistakes.fix: Aim for the lower ribs and keep elbows closer to the body.

content.breathing: Inhale at the bottom, exhale as you pull, keeping the trunk braced throughout.
content.rom_notes: Full range is arms fully extended at the bottom to bar contact (or near contact) with the torso at the top.
content.safety_notes: This loads the lower back isometrically for the whole set — avoid stacking it in the same session as heavy deadlifts if you're new. Set the bar down between sets rather than holding it.

grip_variations.name: Overhand
grip_variations.effect: More mid-back and rear delt.

grip_variations.name: Underhand
grip_variations.effect: More lat and biceps, allows heavier loads.

grip_variations.name: Pendlay (from the floor each rep)
grip_variations.effect: Removes the eccentric, more explosive, less back fatigue over the set.

content.summary: Machine-based lower body press that loads the quads and glutes with the back fully supported.
content.description: The leg press lets you train the quads and glutes heavily without loading the spine or requiring squat technique, which makes it valuable for beginners, high-volume work, and anyone with back issues. Foot position on the platform shifts emphasis noticeably. It's also one of the safest places to train close to failure.
setup: Sit with the back and hips flat against the pad.
Place feet shoulder width on the platform, mid-foot pressure.
Release the safety handles and take the weight.
Keep hands on the handles, head against the pad.
execution: Lower the platform under control until the knees reach roughly 90 degrees or slightly past.
Stop before the lower back starts to lift off the pad.
Press through the whole foot to return, without locking the knees out hard.
Keep constant tension by stopping just short of full extension.
cues: Don't let the hips curl off the pad

common_mistakes.mistake: Lower back rounding off the pad at the bottom
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the depth — this is where leg press back injuries come from.

common_mistakes.mistake: Slamming the knees into lockout
common_mistakes.fix: Stop just short of full extension.

common_mistakes.mistake: Heels lifting off the platform
common_mistakes.fix: Move the feet slightly higher on the platform.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hands on the knees to push
common_mistakes.fix: Keep hands on the handles; reduce the weight.

content.breathing: Inhale on the way down, exhale on the press.
content.rom_notes: Depth is limited by the point where your pelvis starts to tuck. That point is your full range — going deeper is not more range, it's spinal flexion under load.
content.safety_notes: Always engage the safety catches before getting out. Never place hands on the knees. If the weight stalls, use the handles to guide it back to the catches rather than trying to grind.

grip_variations.name: Feet high on platform
grip_variations.effect: More glutes and hamstrings.

grip_variations.name: Feet low on platform
grip_variations.effect: More quads, more knee flexion.

grip_variations.name: Wide stance
grip_variations.effect: More adductors and glutes.

grip_variations.name: Narrow stance
grip_variations.effect: More outer quad.

content.summary: Seated machine isolation for the quadriceps, particularly the rectus femoris.
content.description: The leg extension isolates the quads with no contribution from other muscle groups, which makes it useful for adding quad volume without additional systemic fatigue. It's also the most practical way to train the rectus femoris, which is under-loaded in squats. Open-chain loading means it's often restricted after knee injury.
setup: Adjust the seat so the knee joint lines up with the machine's pivot point.
Set the ankle pad just above the top of the foot.
Sit back fully against the pad and hold the handles.
execution: Extend the knees until the legs are nearly straight.
Pause briefly at the top and squeeze the quads.
Lower under control, resisting the weight all the way down.
Stop just short of the weight stack touching to keep tension.

common_mistakes.mistake: Swinging the weight up with momentum
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the load and slow the tempo.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hips lifting off the seat
common_mistakes.fix: Hold the handles and reduce the weight.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bouncing at the bottom
common_mistakes.fix: Stop just short of the stack touching.

common_mistakes.mistake: Knee not aligned with the pivot
common_mistakes.fix: Adjust the seat — misalignment is what makes this machine feel bad on the knees.

content.breathing: Exhale as you extend, inhale as you lower.
content.rom_notes: Full range is roughly 90 degrees of knee flexion to near-full extension. Some machines allow deeper starting flexion — keep it consistent between sessions.
content.safety_notes: This is open-chain knee loading, commonly restricted after ACL reconstruction or with patellofemoral pain. Reduce range or load rather than pushing through knee pain.

grip_variations.name: Toes pointed up (neutral)
grip_variations.effect: Standard quad emphasis.

grip_variations.name: Toes turned out
grip_variations.effect: Slight shift toward the inner quad.

grip_variations.name: Single leg
grip_variations.effect: Exposes and addresses side-to-side differences.

content.summary: Isolation for the side delts, the main driver of shoulder width.
content.description: The lateral raise is the only common exercise that meaningfully isolates the lateral deltoid, which is why it appears in nearly every hypertrophy program. It's almost always done too heavy — the muscle is small and responds to controlled tension rather than load. Best performed for higher reps with strict form.
setup: Stand with dumbbells at your sides, palms facing in.
Soft bend in the elbows, locked there for the set.
Slight forward lean at the hips, ribs down.
execution: Raise the arms out to the sides, leading with the elbows.
Stop at roughly shoulder height — no higher.
Pause briefly at the top.
Lower slowly under control, resisting the whole way.
cues: Lead with the elbows, not the hands
Pour the water out slightly at the top
Slow negatives — this is where the work is

common_mistakes.mistake: Swinging with the hips and momentum
common_mistakes.fix: Halve the weight. Almost everyone goes too heavy here.

common_mistakes.mistake: Shrugging the traps to raise the weight
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the shoulders down; lighten the load.

common_mistakes.mistake: Raising above shoulder height
common_mistakes.fix: Stop at shoulder level — above that the traps take over and impingement risk rises.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dropping the weight on the eccentric
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds to lower.

content.breathing: Exhale as you raise, inhale as you lower.
content.rom_notes: Arms at the sides to roughly shoulder height. Going higher shifts the work to the traps rather than extending the useful range.
content.safety_notes: If you have shoulder impingement history, stop below shoulder height or use a cable at a slight angle in front of the body.

grip_variations.name: Dumbbell
grip_variations.effect: Standard; tension peaks at the top.

grip_variations.name: Cable
grip_variations.effect: More constant tension through the range.

grip_variations.name: Leaning away on a cable
grip_variations.effect: Increases stretch and tension at the bottom.

grip_variations.name: Thumbs slightly up
grip_variations.effect: Reduces impingement for sensitive shoulders.

content.summary: Rear-foot-elevated single-leg squat, brutal for quads and glutes with minimal spinal load.
content.description: The Bulgarian split squat trains one leg at a time through a long range, exposing and correcting side-to-side differences that bilateral work hides. Because the load is comparatively light, it builds substantial leg strength with very little spinal loading — useful for anyone managing back issues. Widely disliked for good reason.
setup: Stand roughly two feet in front of a bench.
Place the top of the rear foot on the bench, laces down.
Adjust the front foot until the front shin is roughly vertical at the bottom.
Hold dumbbells at your sides or a barbell on the back.
execution: Lower straight down by bending the front knee and hip.
Descend until the front thigh is roughly parallel or the rear knee nears the floor.
Keep most of the weight through the front foot.
Drive through the front heel and mid-foot to stand.
Complete all reps on one side before switching.
cues: Slight forward lean for more glute, upright for more quad
Rear leg is a kickstand, not a pusher

common_mistakes.mistake: Front foot too close to the bench
common_mistakes.fix: Step further forward until the shin can stay near vertical.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pushing off the rear leg
common_mistakes.fix: Think of the back leg as balance only.

common_mistakes.mistake: Losing balance every rep
common_mistakes.fix: Hold a rack upright with one hand while you learn the pattern.

common_mistakes.mistake: Front knee caving inward
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce load and actively track the knee over the middle toes.

content.breathing: Inhale on the descent, exhale on the drive up.
content.rom_notes: Full range is front thigh to at least parallel. Depth is often limited by hip mobility and rear leg comfort rather than strength.
content.safety_notes: Very stretch-loaded for the rear hip flexor and quad — expect significant soreness the first few sessions. Use a pad under the rear foot if the bench is uncomfortable.

grip_variations.name: Dumbbells at sides
grip_variations.effect: Easiest to bail out of, grip may limit.

grip_variations.name: Front rack / goblet
grip_variations.effect: More upright, more quad, more core demand.

grip_variations.name: Barbell on back
grip_variations.effect: Heaviest loading, hardest to balance.

content.summary: Isometric core hold resisting spinal extension.
content.description: The plank trains the deep core and abs to resist the lower back arching, which is the core's main job during heavy lifting. It's a time-based isometric rather than a rep exercise, and progression comes from adding load or leverage rather than adding minutes. Holding for very long durations stops being productive fairly quickly.
setup: Lie face down, elbows under the shoulders, forearms flat.
Tuck the toes under.
Lift the hips so the body forms a straight line from head to heels.
execution: Squeeze the glutes and tuck the ribs down toward the hips.
Brace the abs as if about to be punched.
Hold the position, breathing normally.
End the set when the hips start to sag or pike.
cues: Push the floor away with the forearms
Straight line from head to heels

common_mistakes.mistake: Hips sagging, lower back arching
common_mistakes.fix: End the set — this is the failure point, not something to push through.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hips piked too high
common_mistakes.fix: Lower the hips into line; it's easier in the piked position and does less.

common_mistakes.mistake: Holding for minutes on end
common_mistakes.fix: Add load or leverage instead. Past about 60 seconds you're training endurance, not core strength.

common_mistakes.mistake: Holding the breath
common_mistakes.fix: Breathe shallowly while keeping the brace.

content.breathing: Breathe continuously and shallowly while maintaining the brace. Do not hold your breath.
content.rom_notes: No range of motion. Quality is defined by position: neutral spine, ribs down, glutes engaged.
content.safety_notes: Stop when position degrades rather than chasing time. If you feel it in the lower back rather than the abs, the hips are sagging.

grip_variations.name: Forearm plank
grip_variations.effect: Standard.

grip_variations.name: High plank
grip_variations.effect: More shoulder and triceps involvement, loads the wrists.

grip_variations.name: Weighted plank
grip_variations.effect: Plate on the upper back — the correct way to progress.

grip_variations.name: Long-lever plank
grip_variations.effect: Elbows further forward, much harder without added weight.

content.summary: Explosive hip hinge that trains the glutes and hamstrings ballistically while building conditioning.
content.description: The kettlebell swing is a hinge, not a squat, and not a front raise — the bell travels because the hips snap, not because the arms lift. It develops explosive hip extension and doubles as effective conditioning at higher rep ranges. It's the most commonly performed with the wrong pattern of any exercise in this library.
setup: Place the kettlebell about a foot in front of you.
Hinge at the hips and grip the handle with both hands.
Set a flat back, shoulders pulled down, lats engaged.
Hike the bell back between the legs like a rugby pass.
execution: Snap the hips forward explosively to drive the bell up.
Let the bell float to roughly chest height — the arms stay relaxed.
Stand tall at the top with glutes squeezed hard.
Let the bell fall, hinging as it passes the hips.
Load the hips again and repeat without pausing.
cues: Attack the zipper with the bell

common_mistakes.mistake: Squatting the swing instead of hinging
common_mistakes.fix: Practise the hinge pattern unloaded against a wall first.

common_mistakes.mistake: Lifting the bell with the arms
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the arms relaxed — they're ropes attaching the bell to your body.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rounding the back at the bottom
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the weight and keep the chest up during the backswing.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaning back at the top
common_mistakes.fix: Finish standing tall with ribs down and glutes squeezed.

content.breathing: Sharp exhale at the top of each swing, inhale on the backswing.
content.rom_notes: Russian swing goes to roughly chest height; American swing goes overhead and adds shoulder demand. Log them as separate exercises.
content.safety_notes: Ballistic and hard to abort mid-rep. Not appropriate for acute lower back issues. Always swing in clear space and set the bell down in front of you rather than dropping it.

grip_variations.name: Two-handed
grip_variations.effect: Standard, heaviest loading.

grip_variations.name: Single-arm
grip_variations.effect: Adds anti-rotation demand.

grip_variations.name: Hand-to-hand
grip_variations.effect: Adds coordination and grip demand.

content.summary: Cable isolation for the triceps with constant tension through the range.
content.description: The pushdown isolates all three heads of the triceps with the elbows fixed at the sides, and the cable keeps tension constant throughout. It's easy to load progressively and easy to take close to failure safely, which makes it a staple of arm training. Attachment choice makes a modest difference to which head gets emphasised.
setup: Set the cable at the top of the tower with a straight bar or rope.
Stand close, feet hip width, slight forward lean.
Grip the attachment and pin the elbows to your sides.
execution: Extend the elbows until the arms are straight.
Squeeze the triceps briefly at the bottom.
Return under control until the forearms are roughly parallel to the floor.
Keep the elbows pinned in place for every rep.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows drifting forward or flaring out
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the weight and pin the elbows.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaning into the weight to push it down
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the load; keep the torso still.

common_mistakes.mistake: Cutting the range short at the top
common_mistakes.fix: Let the forearms come to at least parallel.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the shoulders to press down
common_mistakes.fix: Think of the elbow as a hinge that's the only moving joint.

content.breathing: Exhale as you extend, inhale on the return.
content.rom_notes: Forearms at least to parallel at the top, full elbow extension at the bottom.
content.safety_notes: Very low risk. If you have elbow tendinopathy, reduce range at the bottom and avoid locking out hard.

grip_variations.name: Straight bar
grip_variations.effect: Heaviest loading, standard.

grip_variations.name: Rope
grip_variations.effect: Allows spreading at the bottom for a stronger contraction.

grip_variations.name: V-bar
grip_variations.effect: Comfortable for most wrists.

grip_variations.name: Reverse grip
grip_variations.effect: Slight shift toward the medial head.

grip_variations.name: Single arm
grip_variations.effect: Addresses side-to-side differences.

content.summary: Back squat with the bar carried lower on the shoulders, shifting work toward the hips and allowing heavier loads.
content.description: The low bar squat places the bar on a shelf across the rear delts rather than the traps, which shortens the moment arm at the hip and lengthens it at the knee. The result is a more forward torso, more glute and hamstring involvement, and usually 5-10% more weight than the same lifter's high bar squat. It demands more shoulder and wrist mobility than any other squat variation, which is the main reason people can't perform it.
setup: Set the bar at mid-chest height and grip as narrow as your shoulders allow.
Pull the shoulder blades together hard to create a muscular shelf across the rear delts.
Duck under and place the bar on that shelf, below the spine of the scapula.
Keep the wrists straight and the bar supported by the back, not the hands.
Brace, stand it out, and walk back with feet slightly wider than for a high bar squat.
execution: Take a big breath and brace hard against the belt line.
Break at the hips first, sitting back before sitting down.
Let the torso lean forward more than a high bar squat — the bar must stay over mid-foot.
Descend to just below parallel, keeping the shins relatively vertical.
Drive the hips up and forward, keeping the chest angle constant until past the sticking point.
cues: Squeeze the blades together to build the shelf
Bar stays over mid-foot the whole way

common_mistakes.mistake: Bar slides down the back mid-set
common_mistakes.fix: The shelf has come loose. Re-rack and reset the upper back — squeeze the blades harder before you unrack.

common_mistakes.mistake: Wrists bent back taking the bar's weight
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the wrists straight and let the back carry the bar. Widen the grip or use thumbless if mobility limits you.

common_mistakes.mistake: Squatting it like a high bar with an upright torso
common_mistakes.fix: The bar drifts behind mid-foot and you stall. Deliberately push the hips back further on the descent.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hips rising faster than the chest out of the hole
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the load and drive with the chest and hips together; add pause squats to fix the position.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbow and shoulder pain from the rack position
common_mistakes.fix: Widen the grip, keep elbows under the bar rather than lifted behind it, and work on shoulder external rotation.

content.breathing: Inhale and brace at the top, hold through the descent and the drive, exhale only once past the sticking point.
content.rom_notes: Full range is hip crease below the top of the kneecap. Low bar naturally reaches depth with less knee travel than high bar — depth is judged at the hip, not by how far the knees go forward.
content.safety_notes: Squat in a rack with safeties set just below your bottom position. Bail by dropping the bar backwards while stepping forward. The shelf position makes bailing slightly harder than high bar, so practise it light.

grip_variations.name: Narrow grip
grip_variations.effect: Tightest shelf, hardest on the shoulders and wrists.

grip_variations.name: Wide grip
grip_variations.effect: Kinder to the shoulders, looser shelf that needs more upper back tension.

grip_variations.name: Thumbless
grip_variations.effect: Keeps the wrist stacked when mobility is limited.

content.summary: Barbell squat with the bar racked on the front delts, forcing an upright torso and heavy quad and core demand.
content.description: The front squat loads the quads harder than any other barbell squat because the front rack keeps the torso vertical and the knees travelling forward. It also punishes any loss of upper back position — if you round, the bar falls off the front, which makes it a self-limiting lift. Most people are held back by wrist and shoulder mobility long before their legs give out.
setup: Set the bar at upper-chest height and grip just outside shoulder width.
Step in close and drive the elbows up and through until the upper arms are parallel to the floor.
Let the bar rest on the front delts, sitting in the shelf they form — the fingers only steady it.
Brace hard, stand the bar out, and take two steps back.
Feet shoulder width, toes turned out slightly.
execution: Take a big breath into the belly and brace.
Descend straight down, keeping the torso as vertical as you can.
Let the knees travel forward over the toes — this is intended here, not a fault.
Reach depth with the elbows still high and the upper back tight.
Drive up, leading with the elbows to stop the chest folding forward.
cues: Sit straight down between your feet
Bar rides the shoulders, not the hands
Lead out of the hole with the elbows

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows drop and the bar rolls onto the wrists
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the load and drill holding the rack position for time. Dropping elbows is what makes people quit this lift.

common_mistakes.mistake: Trying to grip the bar full-hand without the wrist mobility
common_mistakes.fix: Switch to a two- or three-finger grip, straps, or the cross-arm rack. The hands only balance the bar.

common_mistakes.mistake: Chest folds forward at the bottom and the bar dumps
common_mistakes.fix: Upper back gave out. Add front rack holds and reduce load until you can hold position at depth.

common_mistakes.mistake: Heels lifting off the floor
common_mistakes.fix: Ankle mobility. Widen the stance slightly, work on dorsiflexion, or squat in lifting shoes.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bar sitting on the collarbones rather than the delts
common_mistakes.fix: Push the shoulders forward and up to build the shelf — the bar should never rest on bone.

content.breathing: Inhale and brace at the top, hold through the whole rep, exhale at lockout. Do not exhale at the bottom — losing the brace collapses the rack.
content.rom_notes: Full range is hip crease below the top of the kneecap with the elbows still up. Most people can squat deeper front-loaded than back-loaded, so don't cut the range to match your back squat.
content.safety_notes: Safeties set just below your bottom position. To bail, simply open the hands and let the bar fall forward as you step back — this is the safest bailout of any barbell squat, which is why it suits training alone.

grip_variations.name: Clean grip (fingers under the bar)
grip_variations.effect: Standard, most secure, needs wrist and lat mobility.

grip_variations.name: Cross-arm
grip_variations.effect: No wrist demand, but harder to keep elbows up and harder to bail cleanly.

grip_variations.name: Straps
grip_variations.effect: Removes the wrist limit entirely, keeps elbows high.

content.summary: Squat to a set box height, teaching consistent depth and heavy hip loading with a pause at the bottom.
content.description: The box squat removes the stretch reflex by pausing on a box, so every rep starts from a dead stop and the hips do more of the work. It fixes depth exactly, which makes it valuable for anyone whose squat depth wanders between reps, and it lets you sit back further than a free squat without falling over. Because the eccentric is controlled and the bottom is supported, it's also easier on the knees than most squat variations.
setup: Set a box or bench so the top puts you at or just below parallel when seated.
Position the box far enough back that you can sit without stepping backwards.
Unrack as you would for a back squat and walk back until the box is directly behind you.
Set a slightly wider stance than usual, toes turned out.
execution: Breathe in, brace, and push the hips back to start the descent.
Sit back and down, keeping the shins near vertical.
Settle onto the box under control — touch it, don't drop onto it.
Stay tight and braced while seated; do not relax or rock.
Drive the floor away and stand, keeping the chest up.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dropping onto the box and bouncing off it
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the load and control the last few inches. Collapsing onto a box compresses the spine — this is the injury risk of the exercise.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rocking backwards then forwards to build momentum
common_mistakes.fix: Pause fully still for a count, then stand. If you can't, the box is too low or the weight is too heavy.

common_mistakes.mistake: Releasing the brace while seated
common_mistakes.fix: Hold the breath through the pause; only exhale standing.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using a high box to claim a heavier squat
common_mistakes.fix: Set the box at your actual target depth and log the height alongside the weight.

common_mistakes.mistake: Shins sliding forward so it becomes a normal squat to a box
common_mistakes.fix: Push the hips back first; think about reaching for the box with your backside.

content.breathing: Inhale and brace at the top, hold through the descent, the pause and the drive, exhale once standing.
content.rom_notes: Range is defined by the box height, which should be recorded — a box squat to a 40cm box and one to a 30cm box are different exercises. Parallel or just below is the usual target.
content.safety_notes: Use a solid box that cannot tip or slide, and set rack safeties as normal. Never relax the spine while seated under load; the moment you soften, the load lands on a passive spine.

grip_variations.name: Low bar
grip_variations.effect: More hip, matches the sit-back pattern best.

grip_variations.name: High bar
grip_variations.effect: More upright and more quad, needs a slightly narrower stance.

grip_variations.name: Wide stance
grip_variations.effect: More glute and adductor, the classic powerlifting setup.

content.summary: Squat with a cambered, padded bar that sits on the shoulders with handles in front — no shoulder mobility needed.
content.description: The safety squat bar puts the weight slightly forward and higher than a straight bar, so it pushes you toward folding at the chest and the upper back has to fight for the whole set. It removes the shoulder and wrist demand entirely, which makes it the standard substitute for anyone with a cranky shoulder, elbow or wrist who still wants to squat heavy. Expect to handle roughly 10% less than your back squat.
setup: Set the bar at mid-chest height and duck under so the yoke sits on the traps and the pads on the shoulders.
Take the handles in front, elbows down, and pull them lightly toward you to lock the bar in place.
Brace hard, stand the bar out and walk back — it will feel top-heavy compared to a straight bar.
Feet shoulder width, toes slightly out.
execution: Big breath, brace, and actively push the upper back into the bar.
Descend under control, resisting the bar's pull to fold you forward.
Squat to depth keeping the torso as upright as you can hold.
Drive up, leading with the chest and keeping the upper back rigid.
Stand fully before re-bracing for the next rep.
cues: Push your back into the bar
Upper back does as much work as the legs

common_mistakes.mistake: Letting the bar pull the chest down into a good morning
common_mistakes.fix: This is the defining fault of the SSB. Cut the load and actively drive the upper back up into the bar.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pulling hard on the handles to stay upright
common_mistakes.fix: Use a light hold — if you're hanging off the handles the upper back is not doing its job. Some lifters let go and hold the rack instead.

common_mistakes.mistake: Expecting back squat numbers
common_mistakes.fix: Log it as its own lift. Ten percent below your back squat is normal and not a step backwards.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bar sitting too far back on the neck
common_mistakes.fix: Set it so the yoke sits on the traps with the pads on the shoulders, and re-rack if it creeps during the set.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows flared out wide
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the elbows down and close; flaring rotates the bar forward and adds to the fold.

content.breathing: Inhale and brace at the top, hold through the whole rep, exhale at lockout.
content.rom_notes: Full range is hip crease below the top of the kneecap, same as any squat. The forward bar position often lets people reach depth more comfortably than a straight bar.
content.safety_notes: Set rack safeties as normal. Bailing is harder than a straight bar because the pads sit on you, so err toward leaving a rep in the tank rather than grinding.

grip_variations.name: Handles held
grip_variations.effect: Standard, most control over the bar.

grip_variations.name: Hands on the rack uprights
grip_variations.effect: Forces the upper back to hold position, used as a strength drill.

grip_variations.name: Wide stance
grip_variations.effect: More hip and adductor, slightly less forward fold.

content.summary: Squat holding a single dumbbell or kettlebell at the chest, where the weight acts as a counterbalance.
content.description: The goblet squat is the fastest way to teach someone to squat well, because the front-loaded weight forces an upright torso and stops you falling backwards as you reach depth. It doubles as a genuine training exercise for higher reps, limited only by how much weight you can hold at your chest. Most people squat deeper and with better position holding a goblet than they do with a bar on their back.
setup: Hold a dumbbell vertically by one end, or a kettlebell by the horns, against your sternum.
Keep the elbows tucked in under the weight, not flared out.
Stand with feet shoulder width, toes turned out slightly.
Pull the shoulders down and brace the trunk.
execution: Breathe in and brace.
Sit straight down between your feet, keeping the chest tall.
Descend until the elbows track inside the knees, or as deep as you can hold position.
Pause briefly at the bottom without relaxing.
Drive through the whole foot to stand, keeping the weight glued to the chest.
cues: Elbows inside the knees at the bottom
Chest tall, sit between your feet

common_mistakes.mistake: Weight drifting away from the chest as you descend
common_mistakes.fix: Squeeze it into the sternum. Once it drifts, it becomes a front raise and pulls you forward.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows flared out to the sides
common_mistakes.fix: Tuck them under the weight — flared elbows put the load on the shoulders instead of the trunk.

common_mistakes.mistake: Heels lifting at the bottom
common_mistakes.fix: Widen the stance a little or turn the toes out more; work on ankle mobility over time.

common_mistakes.mistake: Going heavy enough that the arms fail before the legs
common_mistakes.fix: That's the ceiling of this exercise — move to a front squat or hack squat when you outgrow it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rounding the lower back at the very bottom
common_mistakes.fix: Stop at the depth you can hold neutral and build range gradually.

content.breathing: Inhale at the top, brace, hold through the descent and drive, exhale at the top.
content.rom_notes: Full range is as deep as you can go with a neutral spine — usually well below parallel. The upright torso makes deep positions accessible to most people here.
content.safety_notes: Very low risk. If you lose it, simply drop the weight in front of you and step back. Watch that the dumbbell doesn't slide out of the hands as they sweat on high-rep sets.

grip_variations.name: Dumbbell held vertically
grip_variations.effect: Standard, easiest to hold.

grip_variations.name: Kettlebell by the horns
grip_variations.effect: Sits closer to the chest, more comfortable at heavier loads.

grip_variations.name: Wide stance
grip_variations.effect: More adductor and glute, easier to reach depth.

grip_variations.name: Heels elevated
grip_variations.effect: More quad and a more upright torso, helps limited ankle mobility.

content.summary: Squat holding a dumbbell in each hand at the sides, limited by grip rather than leg strength.
content.description: The dumbbell squat is the simplest loaded squat there is — pick up two dumbbells and squat. It suits home gyms and high-rep leg work, but the load hangs at the sides rather than sitting on the trunk, so the torso leans further forward and grip usually gives out before the legs do. Think of it as a volume tool rather than a way to build maximum leg strength.
setup: Take a dumbbell in each hand and stand with them hanging at your sides.
Feet shoulder width, toes turned out slightly.
Pull the shoulders back and down so the weight doesn't round you forward.
Brace the trunk before the first rep.
execution: Breathe in and brace.
Sit down and slightly back, letting the dumbbells travel just outside the legs.
Descend to parallel or below, keeping the chest up against the forward pull.
Drive through the whole foot to stand.
Keep the arms passive throughout — they only hold the weight.
cues: Shoulders back, don't let the weight round you

common_mistakes.mistake: Torso folding forward as the dumbbells pull down
common_mistakes.fix: Set the shoulders back and reduce the load; if it keeps happening switch to a goblet squat where the weight counterbalances instead.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dumbbells banging into the knees or thighs
common_mistakes.fix: Widen the stance slightly and let them pass outside the legs.

common_mistakes.mistake: Grip failing well before the legs
common_mistakes.fix: Use straps, or move to a goblet or barbell variation — this is the natural ceiling of the exercise.

common_mistakes.mistake: Shrugging the shoulders to hold the weight
common_mistakes.fix: Let the arms hang. Shrugging fatigues the traps for no benefit and pulls you out of position.

common_mistakes.mistake: Cutting depth because the weight feels awkward
common_mistakes.fix: Lighten it and squat the full range; the point of this variation is reps, not load.

content.breathing: Inhale at the top, brace, exhale on the way up.
content.rom_notes: Full range is thighs to at least parallel. Depth is often limited by the dumbbells contacting the floor before you do — use taller dumbbells or stand on low blocks if so.
content.safety_notes: Low risk and easy to bail: just set the dumbbells down. On high-rep sets watch for the grip slipping as the hands sweat.

grip_variations.name: Dumbbells at the sides
grip_variations.effect: Standard, most weight, most grip demand.

grip_variations.name: Straps
grip_variations.effect: Removes the grip limit so the legs can be trained properly.

grip_variations.name: Heels elevated
grip_variations.effect: More upright torso and more quad.

content.summary: Squat on a fixed bar path, which removes the balance demand and lets you place the feet forward.
content.description: The Smith machine fixes the bar in a vertical or near-vertical track, so you don't have to balance the load and can put your feet further forward than a free squat allows. That foot position lets you load the quads hard with very little forward lean, and it makes taking a set close to failure safe on your own. The trade-off is that the fixed path doesn't adapt to your body, so it suits some people far better than others.
setup: Set the bar at upper-chest height and place it across the traps as for a back squat.
Walk the feet forward of the bar — roughly 20-30cm — so your body leans back slightly against it.
Set the feet shoulder width, toes slightly out.
Brace, stand up, and rotate the wrists to release the hooks.
execution: Breathe in and brace.
Lower under control, letting the knees bend deeply with the torso staying near vertical.
Descend until the thighs are at or below parallel.
Drive through mid-foot to stand, stopping just short of a hard knee lockout.
Rotate the wrists to re-hook the bar only once you're standing at the top.
cues: Feet forward, lean back into the bar

common_mistakes.mistake: Standing with the feet directly under the bar as in a free squat
common_mistakes.fix: Walk them forward. Feet under the bar on a fixed path forces the knees into an uncomfortable shear position.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to check which way the hooks rotate
common_mistakes.fix: Test the rotation with an empty bar before loading. This is where most Smith machine accidents come from.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming Smith numbers carry over to a free barbell squat
common_mistakes.fix: Log it as its own exercise — the fixed path removes stabiliser work and typically flatters the load.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bouncing out of the bottom against the fixed track
common_mistakes.fix: Control the descent and pause briefly; the machine will happily let you bounce into a bad position.

common_mistakes.mistake: Setting the safety stops too low to be useful
common_mistakes.fix: Set them just below your bottom position so a failed rep parks safely.

content.breathing: Inhale on the way down, hold through the bottom, exhale on the way up.
content.rom_notes: Full range is thighs at or below parallel. Foot position sets the emphasis — further forward is more quad-dominant with less hip travel.
content.safety_notes: Always set the safety stops and know the hook direction before loading. The machine cannot be bailed like a free bar; you must be able to re-hook or park it on the stops.

grip_variations.name: Feet forward
grip_variations.effect: Upright torso, quad-dominant, easy on the lower back.

grip_variations.name: Feet under the bar
grip_variations.effect: Closer to a free squat but with awkward shear — generally avoided.

grip_variations.name: Wide stance
grip_variations.effect: More adductor and glute.

grip_variations.name: Heels elevated
grip_variations.effect: Even more quad emphasis and deeper knee flexion.

content.summary: Plate-loaded sled squat with the back supported on a pad, loading the quads through a deep knee bend.
content.description: The hack squat holds your torso against a pad on a fixed angled track, so the lower back is supported and the legs get all the work. It allows very deep knee flexion under load, which makes it one of the best quad builders available, and the support means you can train close to failure without a spotter. Foot placement on the platform shifts the emphasis noticeably between quads and glutes.
setup: Set the shoulder pads so you can stand tall with the back and hips flat against the pad.
Place the feet shoulder width in the middle of the platform.
Take the handles and stand up to release the safety catches.
Brace the trunk before lowering.
execution: Lower under control, letting the knees bend deeply.
Descend until the thighs pass parallel, or to the point just before the hips start to curl off the pad.
Keep the whole foot in contact with the platform.
Press back up through mid-foot without slamming into lockout.
Stop just short of full extension to keep tension on the quads.
cues: Back and hips glued to the pad
Whole foot pressing, not just the toes

common_mistakes.mistake: Hips curling off the pad at the bottom
common_mistakes.fix: Stop the descent just above that point — beyond it the lower back is loaded in flexion, which is where hack squat back injuries come from.

common_mistakes.mistake: Feet placed high on the platform, turning it into a leg press
common_mistakes.fix: Move them to the middle. High feet reduce the knee flexion that makes this exercise worth doing.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rising onto the toes at the bottom
common_mistakes.fix: Move the feet slightly higher and keep pressure through the heel and mid-foot.

common_mistakes.mistake: Knees caving inward under load
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the weight and actively press the knees out over the middle toes.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to re-engage the safety catches before stepping out
common_mistakes.fix: Rotate the handles and confirm the sled is parked before you release it.

content.breathing: Inhale on the descent, exhale on the press.
content.rom_notes: Full range is as deep as you can go before the pelvis tucks away from the pad. That point is your range — going further is spinal flexion under load, not extra depth.
content.safety_notes: Always engage the catches before getting out. Don't place your hands on your knees. If a rep stalls, guide the sled back onto the catches rather than grinding it.

grip_variations.name: Feet mid-platform
grip_variations.effect: Balanced quad emphasis, standard.

grip_variations.name: Feet low
grip_variations.effect: More knee flexion, strongly quad-dominant, harder on the knees.

grip_variations.name: Feet high
grip_variations.effect: More glute and hamstring, less knee travel.

grip_variations.name: Wide stance
grip_variations.effect: More adductor and glute.

content.summary: Machine squat on an arcing path that keeps resistance high through the bottom of the range.
content.description: The pendulum squat swings on an arc rather than a straight track, which keeps the load challenging in the deep position where a normal squat gets easiest. The hips are free to travel back as the machine rotates, so it tends to feel far kinder on the knees and lower back than a hack squat while still loading the quads heavily. It's a specialist machine, but where one exists it's among the best quad exercises in a gym.
setup: Set the shoulder pads so you stand tall with the back flat against the pad.
Place the feet in the middle of the platform, shoulder width, toes slightly out.
Take the handles and release the safety catch.
Brace the trunk before the first rep.
execution: Lower slowly, letting the machine's arc carry the hips back as the knees bend.
Descend as deep as you can while keeping the hips against the pad.
Pause briefly in the bottom — this is where the machine loads hardest.
Press back up through the whole foot.
Stop just short of full lockout to keep tension.
cues: Let the arc take you back
Deep and slow — the bottom is the point

common_mistakes.mistake: Rushing the bottom where the resistance peaks
common_mistakes.fix: Slow the eccentric and pause. Rushing skips the exact part of the range this machine exists for.

common_mistakes.mistake: Feet too low on the platform
common_mistakes.fix: Move them up slightly — feet too low forces the knees far past the toes and loads the joint uncomfortably.

common_mistakes.mistake: Cutting depth because the load feels heavy down there
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the weight and use the full range; heavy partials on this machine waste its advantage.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pushing through the toes
common_mistakes.fix: Keep pressure spread through the whole foot; heels stay down.

common_mistakes.mistake: Letting the hips lift off the pad at depth
common_mistakes.fix: Stop the descent at the point where the hips stay in contact.

content.breathing: Inhale on the descent, exhale on the press.
content.rom_notes: Full range is as deep as the machine and your hips allow with the back on the pad. Because resistance rises as you descend, partial reps here are worth far less than on a straight-track machine.
content.safety_notes: Engage the catch before stepping out. If a rep stalls, the arc means the sled will settle back rather than trap you, but still park it deliberately rather than dropping it.

grip_variations.name: Feet mid-platform
grip_variations.effect: Balanced, standard.

grip_variations.name: Feet slightly higher
grip_variations.effect: More glute and hamstring, less knee travel.

grip_variations.name: Wide stance
grip_variations.effect: More adductor involvement.

grip_variations.name: Narrow stance
grip_variations.effect: More outer quad, more knee flexion.

content.summary: Squat with the load hung from a hip belt, so the legs work hard with nothing carried on the spine.
content.description: The belt squat attaches the weight to a belt around the hips, which means the legs are loaded while the spine carries nothing at all. That makes it the most useful squat variation for anyone managing a back injury, and a good way to add leg volume in a week that already has heavy spinal loading. Because your hands are free, the position is easy to hold and easy to bail out of.
setup: Fit the belt around the hips, sitting low on the pelvis rather than the waist.
Stand on the platform or blocks so the weight can travel below your feet.
Attach the belt to the machine or loading pin and take up the slack.
Set the feet shoulder width, toes slightly out, and hold the uprights lightly for balance.
execution: Brace the trunk and unload the safety support.
Sit down between the feet, letting the hips travel back and down.
Descend to parallel or below, keeping the torso tall — there's no bar pulling you forward.
Drive through the whole foot to stand.
Squeeze the glutes at the top without leaning back.
cues: Belt low on the hips, not the waist
Stand tall — nothing is pushing you forward

common_mistakes.mistake: Belt riding up onto the waist
common_mistakes.fix: Reset it low across the pelvis. High on the waist it digs into the ribs and compresses the trunk, defeating the point of the exercise.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pulling on the handles or uprights to help stand
common_mistakes.fix: Hold lightly with fingertips only — if you need to pull, reduce the load.

common_mistakes.mistake: Standing too far forward or back on the platform
common_mistakes.fix: Position so the load hangs straight down between the feet; off-centre and it drags you out of position.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaning back at the top to finish the rep
common_mistakes.fix: Stand tall with ribs down; the belt pulls the hips back, so leaning back is unnecessary.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating it as a lighter squat
common_mistakes.fix: Loads are often higher than expected because the trunk isn't the limit — start conservative and build.

content.breathing: Inhale on the descent, exhale on the drive up. No heavy breath-hold is needed since the spine isn't loaded.
content.rom_notes: Full range is thighs to at least parallel, usually deeper. Depth is limited by the platform gap and your own mobility rather than by the load.
content.safety_notes: The safest loaded squat variation to train near failure — if a rep fails, stand the weight down or sit onto the support. Check the belt fastening before every set.

grip_variations.name: Standard stance
grip_variations.effect: Balanced quad and glute.

grip_variations.name: Wide stance
grip_variations.effect: More adductor and glute.

grip_variations.name: Feet elevated on blocks
grip_variations.effect: Deeper range and more stretch under load.

grip_variations.name: Paused at depth
grip_variations.effect: Removes the stretch reflex, harder at the same weight.

content.summary: Leg press performed one leg at a time, exposing and correcting side-to-side differences with the back supported.
content.description: The single-leg press gives you the loading and back support of a normal leg press while forcing each leg to work on its own, which is the only way to find out whether one side has been carrying the other. It's the standard rehab and rebalancing tool after a knee or hip injury because the load is controllable to the kilo and there's no balance demand to complicate it. Expect the weaker side to manage noticeably less than half of your two-legged load.
setup: Sit with the back and hips flat against the pad.
Place one foot in the centre of the platform, directly in line with that hip.
Rest the other foot on the floor or the frame, out of the way of the sled.
Release the safety handles and take the weight on the working leg.
execution: Lower the platform under control until the knee reaches roughly 90 degrees or slightly past.
Stop before the hip on that side starts to lift or rotate off the pad.
Press through the whole foot to return, without locking the knee out hard.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch and match the weaker side's reps.
Keep the hips square to the pad for every rep.
cues: Foot in line with the hip, not the middle of the platform
Match the reps to the weaker side

common_mistakes.mistake: Placing the foot in the centre of the platform instead of in line with the hip
common_mistakes.fix: Line the foot up with the working hip. Centring it forces the pelvis to rotate to reach, which is where the back gets loaded.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hip lifting or twisting off the pad at the bottom
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the depth to the point where the pelvis stays flat, and lower the weight.

common_mistakes.mistake: Loading the stronger side heavier so the numbers look better
common_mistakes.fix: Use the same weight both sides and let the weaker side set the reps — the imbalance is the thing you're here to fix.

common_mistakes.mistake: Resting the free foot on the moving platform
common_mistakes.fix: Keep it on the floor or the frame. On the platform it quietly assists and defeats the exercise.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pushing through the toes and lifting the heel
common_mistakes.fix: Move the foot slightly higher on the platform and press through the whole foot.

content.breathing: Inhale on the way down, exhale on the press. No heavy breath-hold needed at these loads.
content.rom_notes: Depth is limited by the point where the pelvis starts to tuck or rotate. Record the same depth each session so side-to-side comparisons are meaningful.
content.safety_notes: Engage the safety catches before getting in or out. Never put hands on the knee to help. If a rep stalls, guide the sled to the catches rather than grinding it.

grip_variations.name: Foot mid-platform
grip_variations.effect: Balanced quad and glute.

grip_variations.name: Foot high
grip_variations.effect: More glute and hamstring, less knee flexion.

grip_variations.name: Foot low
grip_variations.effect: More quad, more knee travel.

grip_variations.name: Toes slightly out
grip_variations.effect: Often more comfortable for the hip at depth.

content.summary: Unloaded squat used to learn the pattern, warm up, or train legs with no equipment at all.
content.description: The bodyweight squat is where the pattern gets learned and where most people's squat faults are cheapest to fix. It's also a genuine training exercise at higher reps for beginners and a reliable warm-up before loaded squatting. Because there's no external load, depth and control are the only variables you have, so both matter more here than anywhere else.
setup: Stand with feet shoulder width, toes turned out 15-30 degrees.
Arms out in front or hands at the chest as a counterbalance.
Pull the shoulders back and brace the trunk lightly.
Set the weight through the middle of the foot.
execution: Break at the hips and knees together and sit down between your feet.
Descend as deep as you can while keeping the heels down and the back neutral.
Keep the chest up and the knees tracking over the middle toes.
Pause briefly at the bottom rather than bouncing.
Stand up fully and squeeze the glutes at the top.
cues: Sit between your feet, not behind them
Heels stay glued to the floor
Knees out over the middle toes

common_mistakes.mistake: Heels lifting as you reach depth
common_mistakes.fix: Ankle mobility. Turn the toes out a little more, or squat with the heels on a 2cm plate while you work on it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Knees caving inward on the way up
common_mistakes.fix: Slow down and actively push the knees out; if it persists, add glute medius work such as banded walks.

common_mistakes.mistake: Half-depth reps done quickly for a number
common_mistakes.fix: Slow the tempo and go to full depth — with no load, range is the only thing making this hard.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bouncing out of the bottom
common_mistakes.fix: Add a one-second pause at depth; bouncing teaches a pattern you don't want under a barbell.

common_mistakes.mistake: Looking down and rounding the upper back
common_mistakes.fix: Fix the eyes on a point a couple of metres ahead on the floor and keep the chest tall.

content.breathing: Inhale on the way down, exhale on the way up. For high-rep sets, breathe continuously rather than holding.
content.rom_notes: Full range is as deep as you can hold a neutral spine and flat heels — usually well below parallel once mobility allows. Partial reps here have very little training value.
content.safety_notes: Effectively no risk. If depth causes knee or hip pinching, reduce range and work on mobility rather than pushing through it.

grip_variations.name: Arms forward
grip_variations.effect: Counterbalance, helps beginners reach depth.

grip_variations.name: Hands behind head
grip_variations.effect: Harder to counterbalance, more upper back demand.

grip_variations.name: Heels elevated
grip_variations.effect: More quad and a more upright torso, bypasses ankle restriction.

grip_variations.name: Tempo or paused
grip_variations.effect: Adds difficulty without adding load.

content.summary: Isometric hold at squat depth with the back against a wall, training the quads under time rather than reps.
content.description: The wall sit loads the quads isometrically with no equipment, no spinal load and no technique to learn, which makes it useful for beginners, for finishing a leg session, and in early rehab when moving through range is uncomfortable. Progression comes from holding lower, holding longer, or adding weight on the lap rather than from adding reps. It burns badly and produces very little soreness the next day.
setup: Stand with your back flat against a wall.
Walk the feet forward until they're roughly two foot-lengths from the wall, hip width apart.
Slide down until the thighs are parallel to the floor and the knees are over the ankles.
Rest the arms at your sides or fold them across the chest.
execution: Press the whole back and shoulders into the wall.
Keep the shins vertical and the weight through the heels and mid-foot.
Hold the position, breathing normally throughout.
End the set when the hips start to creep upward, not when it starts to burn.
cues: Whole back pressed into the wall

common_mistakes.mistake: Sitting above parallel to make the hold easier
common_mistakes.fix: Set the thighs level with the floor. A high wall sit is nearly free and does almost nothing for the quads.

common_mistakes.mistake: Sliding gradually upward as fatigue builds
common_mistakes.fix: End the set at the point you start to rise, and log that time rather than a longer number at a worse position.

common_mistakes.mistake: Resting the hands on the thighs to take load off
common_mistakes.fix: Arms at the sides or folded across the chest.

common_mistakes.mistake: Knees pushed forward past the toes
common_mistakes.fix: Walk the feet further from the wall until the shins are vertical.

common_mistakes.mistake: Holding the breath through the burn
common_mistakes.fix: Breathe steadily — this is an endurance hold, not a braced lift.

content.breathing: Breathe continuously and steadily throughout. There is no reason to hold the breath here.
content.rom_notes: No range of motion. Quality is defined by position: thighs parallel, shins vertical, back flat against the wall. Record the depth if you vary it.
content.safety_notes: Very low risk. If you feel it sharply at the front of the knee rather than in the quads, walk the feet further out so the shins are vertical.

grip_variations.name: Standard hold
grip_variations.effect: Both legs, thighs parallel.

grip_variations.name: Weighted
grip_variations.effect: Plate held on the lap — the cleanest way to progress.

grip_variations.name: Single leg
grip_variations.effect: Far harder, exposes side-to-side differences.

grip_variations.name: Heels raised
grip_variations.effect: Shifts more work to the quads and adds calf demand.

content.summary: Full-depth single-leg squat with the other leg held out in front, demanding strength, balance and ankle mobility together.
content.description: The pistol squat asks one leg to lower and raise the whole body through a full range while the trunk and hip stabilisers stop you toppling, which is why most people who are strong enough still can't do one. Ankle dorsiflexion is usually the limiting factor rather than leg strength. It's an excellent test of single-leg capability but a slow way to build it — use loaded single-leg work for that and treat the pistol as the goal.
setup: Stand on one leg with the other extended in front, knee straight.
Hold the arms out in front as a counterbalance.
Set the standing foot flat with the weight through the middle.
Brace the trunk before starting the descent.
execution: Lower slowly, pushing the hips back and letting the knee travel forward.
Keep the free leg off the floor and roughly parallel to it.
Descend until the hamstring meets the calf, or as low as you can control.
Pause briefly, then drive through the whole foot to stand.
Complete all reps on one side before switching.
cues: Slow all the way down — this is a control exercise
Reach the arms forward to balance

common_mistakes.mistake: Heel lifting at the bottom
common_mistakes.fix: Ankle mobility is the usual limiter. Practise holding a rack upright, or squat to a box, while you work on dorsiflexion.

common_mistakes.mistake: Collapsing into the bottom rather than lowering
common_mistakes.fix: Slow the eccentric to five seconds. Dropping in and bouncing out is how knees get hurt on this.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rounding the back hard to counterbalance
common_mistakes.fix: Reach the arms further forward, or hold a light plate out in front — the counterweight makes it easier, not harder.

common_mistakes.mistake: Standing knee twisting inward on the way up
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce range and add glute medius work; a rotating knee under bodyweight is a warning.

common_mistakes.mistake: Only training the strong side because the other can't do a full rep
common_mistakes.fix: Use a box or assisted version on the weaker side and match the volume.

content.breathing: Inhale on the descent, exhale on the way up. Keep a light brace throughout for balance.
content.rom_notes: Full range is the hamstring touching the calf with the free leg clear of the floor. Squatting to a box is a legitimate partial version — log the box height.
content.safety_notes: The failure mode is falling, so train it in clear space with something to grab. Stop the set when the descent stops being controlled rather than grinding out a last rep.

grip_variations.name: Arms forward
grip_variations.effect: Standard counterbalance.

grip_variations.name: Holding a light plate
grip_variations.effect: Counterweight makes balance far easier — the usual way in.

grip_variations.name: To a box
grip_variations.effect: Sets the depth and removes the hardest part; the standard progression.

grip_variations.name: Heel elevated
grip_variations.effect: Bypasses ankle mobility so leg strength can be trained.

content.summary: Deadlift from a wide stance with the hands inside the knees, shortening the range and shifting work to the hips and quads.
content.description: The sumo deadlift widens the stance until the hips can start much closer to the bar, which shortens the pull by several inches and lets the torso stay far more upright than a conventional deadlift. That means less shear on the lower back and more demand on the glutes, adductors and quads. It suits lifters with long torsos and good hip mobility, and it is not an easier lift so much as a different one — the weight often feels immovable for the first inch.
setup: Take a wide stance with the toes turned out 30-45 degrees, shins close to the plates.
Push the knees out over the toes and drop the hips down toward the bar.
Reach down between the knees and grip the bar about shoulder width.
Pull the chest up, set a flat back, and drop the hips until the arms are vertical.
Take the slack out of the bar until it clicks.
execution: Breathe in and brace hard.
Push the floor apart with the feet rather than pulling with the back.
Keep the hips low and the chest high as the bar breaks the floor.
Drive the hips forward once the bar passes the knees.
Lock out standing tall, then reverse the path under control.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hips set too high at the start
common_mistakes.fix: Drop them until the arms hang vertical. High hips turn a sumo pull into a stiff-leg deadlift from a wide stance.

common_mistakes.mistake: Knees collapsing inward off the floor
common_mistakes.fix: Actively push the knees out over the toes throughout; reduce the load until you can hold it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bar drifting away from the shins
common_mistakes.fix: Set the lats before pulling and keep the bar in contact with the legs the whole way up.

common_mistakes.mistake: Yanking the bar to break it off the floor
