common_mistakes.fix: Take the slack out first and build force gradually — sumo has no run-up and jerking it just wastes position.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stance so wide the hips can't open
common_mistakes.fix: Narrow it until you can reach depth comfortably; extreme width looks the part but usually costs leverage.

content.breathing: Big breath and brace before each rep, held through the pull. Reset the breath with the bar on the floor between reps.
content.rom_notes: Full range is the bar from the floor to full hip and knee lockout. The range is genuinely shorter than a conventional pull — that's the point of the stance, not a shortcut.
content.safety_notes: Stop the set the moment the back position changes. No spotter can help on a deadlift; if a rep stalls, set it down. The wide stance loads the adductors hard, so build up slowly if you're new to it.

grip_variations.name: Double overhand
grip_variations.effect: Safest, grip usually limits the load.

grip_variations.name: Mixed grip
grip_variations.effect: Heavier loads, small biceps tear risk on the supinated arm.

grip_variations.name: Hook grip
grip_variations.effect: Secure and symmetrical, painful to learn.

grip_variations.name: Straps
grip_variations.effect: Removes grip as the limiter for volume work.

content.summary: Deadlift from inside a hexagonal bar with neutral handles, easier to learn and kinder to the lower back.
content.description: Standing inside the bar puts the load in line with your centre of mass instead of in front of it, which lets the torso stay more upright and shifts work toward the quads. The neutral handles are more comfortable on the shoulders and grip than a straight bar. For most people who want the training effect of a deadlift without the technical cost, this is the version to use.
setup: Step into the middle of the bar with feet hip width, weight through mid-foot.
Hinge and drop the hips until you can grip both handles.
Set the chest up and the back flat, shoulders over or slightly behind the handles.
Take the slack out of the bar before pulling.
execution: Breathe in and brace.
Push the floor away with the legs, keeping the chest up.
Stand tall, driving the hips through at the top.
Lower by hinging at the hips first, then bending the knees.
Reset the position on the floor between reps rather than bouncing.
cues: Stand in the middle of the frame

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the high handles and comparing to a straight-bar deadlift
common_mistakes.fix: High handles shorten the range considerably. Pick one handle height and log it — they're effectively two different lifts.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hips shooting up first so it becomes a stiff-leg pull
common_mistakes.fix: Start with the hips slightly higher and hold that angle; the trap bar is meant to let you use the legs.

common_mistakes.mistake: Standing off-centre in the frame
common_mistakes.fix: Check both handles are level under your hands before pulling — off-centre loads one side and twists the trunk.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bouncing reps off the floor
common_mistakes.fix: Set the bar down and reset each rep. The frame makes bouncing easy and it's the fastest way to lose back position.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rounding the upper back as the load gets heavy
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the weight and pull the chest tall before every rep.

content.breathing: Breathe in and brace before each rep, hold through the pull, exhale at the top. Reset on the floor.
content.rom_notes: Full range is from the floor (or the chosen handle height) to full hip and knee lockout. Record which handle height you used — high and low handles are not comparable.
content.safety_notes: Stop the set the moment your back rounds. If a rep fails, simply set it down — the frame surrounds you, so make sure your feet are clear when you do.

grip_variations.name: Low handles
grip_variations.effect: Full range, more hamstring and glute.

grip_variations.name: High handles
grip_variations.effect: Shorter range, heavier loads, good for beginners or long-limbed lifters.

grip_variations.name: Straps
grip_variations.effect: Removes grip as the limiter on high-volume sets.

content.summary: Romanian deadlift with dumbbells, easier to keep close to the body and simpler to learn than the barbell version.
content.description: The dumbbell RDL trains the same hip hinge as the barbell version but the weights hang either side of the legs rather than in front of them, so the load stays closer to your centre of mass and the pattern is easier to feel. It suits beginners learning to hinge and anyone training at home. Grip becomes the limit before the hamstrings do at higher loads, which is the main reason to move to a barbell eventually.
setup: Hold a dumbbell in each hand in front of the thighs, palms facing you.
Feet hip width, weight through mid-foot.
Put a soft bend in the knees and keep it fixed for the whole set.
Pull the shoulders back and set the lats to hold the weights close.
execution: Breathe in and brace.
Push the hips backwards, letting the torso lean forward as a counterweight.
Slide the dumbbells down the front of the thighs, keeping them in contact.
Stop when you feel a strong hamstring stretch or the back is about to round.
Drive the hips forward to stand, squeezing the glutes at the top.
cues: Hips back to the wall behind you
Dumbbells brush the thighs the whole way
Knees stay soft, not bending further
Feel the hamstrings, not the lower back

common_mistakes.mistake: Dumbbells drifting forward away from the legs
common_mistakes.fix: Set the lats and keep them touching the thighs; forward drift moves the load onto the lower back.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bending the knees further as you descend, turning it into a squat
common_mistakes.fix: Lock the knee angle at the start and keep it there for every rep.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rounding the back to lower the weights further
common_mistakes.fix: Stop at the point where you can hold neutral — that's your range, regardless of how far the dumbbells are from the floor.

common_mistakes.mistake: Grip failing before the hamstrings do
common_mistakes.fix: Use straps, or switch to a barbell where the load is shared across a longer bar.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hyperextending the back at the top
common_mistakes.fix: Finish standing tall with ribs down and glutes squeezed, not leaning back.

content.breathing: Inhale at the top, brace, hold through the descent and the lift, exhale at the top.
content.rom_notes: Range is set by hamstring flexibility, not by the dumbbells reaching the floor. Keep it consistent between sessions so the load comparison means something.
content.safety_notes: Stop the set as soon as the back rounds. This is a stretch-loaded exercise and causes significant soreness when new, so start light and build over several weeks.

grip_variations.name: Dumbbells in front of the thighs
grip_variations.effect: Standard, closest to a barbell RDL.

grip_variations.name: Dumbbells at the sides
grip_variations.effect: Slightly easier on the lower back, less hamstring stretch.

grip_variations.name: Straps
grip_variations.effect: Removes the grip limit so the hamstrings set the ceiling.

grip_variations.name: Elevated on a low platform
grip_variations.effect: Adds range for those with good flexibility.

content.summary: Hip hinge balanced on one leg, training the hamstrings and glutes while exposing side-to-side differences.
content.description: The single-leg RDL loads one hamstring and glute at a time while the standing hip works hard to stop the pelvis rotating, which makes it as much a stability exercise as a strength one. It reveals imbalances that a two-legged hinge hides completely. Loads stay modest because balance usually gives out before the muscle does, so treat it as quality work rather than a place to chase weight.
setup: Hold a dumbbell in the hand opposite the standing leg, or one in each hand.
Stand on one leg with a soft bend in that knee.
Set the shoulders back and brace the trunk.
Let the free leg hang directly behind you, ready to counterbalance.
execution: Push the standing hip backwards and let the torso tip forward.
Let the free leg travel back in a straight line, staying in line with the torso.
Keep the hips square to the floor — do not let the free hip open upward.
Descend until you feel a strong stretch in the standing hamstring.
Drive the hip forward to stand, and complete all reps before switching sides.
cues: Hips stay level, like headlights pointing at the floor
Free leg and torso move as one line
Reach the hip back, not the hand down

common_mistakes.mistake: Free hip rotating open toward the ceiling
common_mistakes.fix: Turn the free foot toward the floor and think about keeping both hip bones level; reduce the weight until you can.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reaching for the floor with the hand instead of hinging
common_mistakes.fix: The hand goes down because the hip goes back, not the other way round. Cue the hip first.

common_mistakes.mistake: Standing knee locking straight
common_mistakes.fix: Keep a soft bend throughout — a locked knee shifts the load off the hamstring and stresses the joint.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rushing reps and using balance saves as momentum
common_mistakes.fix: Slow to a three-second descent; if you still wobble, touch the free toe down between reps.

common_mistakes.mistake: Loading heavy so balance becomes the limiting factor
common_mistakes.fix: Use a lighter weight and a longer range, or hold a rack lightly with one hand to remove the balance element.

content.breathing: Inhale at the top, brace, exhale as you stand. Keep the brace light so balance isn't compromised.
content.rom_notes: Range is set by hamstring flexibility and by the point where the hips start to rotate — whichever comes first. Log both sides separately.
content.safety_notes: The failure mode is losing balance, so train near a rack you can grab. Stop the set when the hips start rotating rather than pushing for extra reps.

grip_variations.name: Contralateral (opposite hand)
grip_variations.effect: Standard, most anti-rotation demand.

grip_variations.name: Ipsilateral (same-side hand)
grip_variations.effect: Easier to balance, less rotational challenge.

grip_variations.name: Two dumbbells
grip_variations.effect: Most load, least rotational demand.

grip_variations.name: Kickstand (rear toe lightly down)
grip_variations.effect: Removes most of the balance demand so the hamstring can be loaded properly.

content.summary: Deadlift from the floor with near-straight legs, loading the hamstrings through the longest range of any hinge.
content.description: The stiff-leg deadlift keeps the knees almost locked so the hamstrings take the whole job of raising the torso, and because it starts and finishes on the floor it covers more range than a Romanian deadlift. That extra range under stretch is what makes it effective and also what makes it demanding — it is the hinge most likely to punish a lapse in back position. Loads should be well below your conventional deadlift.
setup: Stand with the bar over mid-foot, feet hip width.
Grip just outside the legs with almost straight knees.
Pull the chest up and set a flat back — the hips will be high.
Set the lats to hold the bar against the legs before pulling.
execution: Breathe in and brace hard.
Raise the torso by driving the hips forward, keeping the knees fixed.
Keep the bar dragging up the legs the whole way.
Stand tall with the glutes squeezed, ribs down.
Lower under control along the same path, touching the floor lightly before the next rep.
cues: Flat back or end the set

common_mistakes.mistake: Confusing it with an RDL and bending the knees
common_mistakes.fix: The knees stay near-locked here and it starts from the floor. If the knees bend, log it as an RDL instead.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rounding the lower back to reach the bar on the floor
common_mistakes.fix: Elevate the bar on blocks until your flexibility allows a flat back at the bottom. Rounding under load is the real risk of this lift.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using conventional deadlift loads
common_mistakes.fix: Start at roughly half and build. The straight legs remove your strongest joint from the pull.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bar drifting forward off the legs
common_mistakes.fix: Engage the lats and keep it in contact — forward drift here loads a straight spine at its longest lever.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hyperextending at the top to feel a finish
common_mistakes.fix: Stand tall with the ribs down; there's nothing to gain past neutral.

content.breathing: Big breath and brace before each rep, held through the lift, reset with the bar on the floor.
content.rom_notes: Full range is the bar from the floor to a tall standing position with the knees near-straight. If you can't reach the floor with a flat back, raise the bar on blocks and record that height.
content.safety_notes: Stop the moment the back position changes — this variation offers the least margin of any hinge. Not appropriate as a heavy max-effort lift; keep it in the moderate-load, controlled-tempo range.

grip_variations.name: Double overhand
grip_variations.effect: Standard, grip often limits.

grip_variations.name: Straps
grip_variations.effect: Lets the hamstrings be the limit rather than the hands.

grip_variations.name: Deficit (standing on a plate)
grip_variations.effect: Even more range; only for those who can hold a flat back at full depth.

grip_variations.name: From blocks
grip_variations.effect: Shortens the range for those with limited flexibility.

content.summary: Deadlift performed standing on a raised platform, adding range at the bottom to attack the first inch off the floor.
content.description: Standing on a two to four inch platform forces the hips lower and the knees more bent at the start, which makes the initial pull considerably harder and builds strength exactly where most deadlifts fail. It's an assistance lift rather than a test of strength — the extra range means less weight for the same effort. It demands the back position you already have; it will not build one.
setup: Stand on a stable platform of 2-4 inches, bar over mid-foot as usual.
Hinge and grip just outside the shins.
Drop the hips further than a floor pull until the shins touch the bar.
Pull the chest up and set a flat back — check this carefully, the extra depth makes it harder to hold.
Take the slack out of the bar.
execution: Breathe in and brace hard.
Push the floor away, keeping the chest up as the bar leaves the platform.
Keep the bar dragging up the shins through the extended range.
Drive the hips through to lock out standing tall.
Lower under control and reset fully on the platform between reps.
cues: Push the floor away, don't pull with the back
Bar close through the extra range

common_mistakes.mistake: Deficit too high for your mobility
common_mistakes.fix: Start at two inches. If you can't reach a flat back at the bottom, the deficit is too big and you're training rounding.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using normal deadlift loads
common_mistakes.fix: Expect 10-20% less. The extra range is the training stimulus, not the weight.

common_mistakes.mistake: Back rounding at the bottom where the range is new
common_mistakes.fix: End the set. This variation puts the spine at its most flexed under load, so there is no acceptable rounded rep.

common_mistakes.mistake: Plates catching the edge of the platform
common_mistakes.fix: Use a platform narrower than the bar path, or set the bar so the plates clear it entirely.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating it as a max-effort lift
common_mistakes.fix: Keep it in the moderate range as assistance work; test your max on a floor pull.

content.breathing: Big breath and brace before each rep, held through the pull, reset on the platform between reps.
content.rom_notes: Range is the floor pull plus the deficit height. Always record the deficit — a 2-inch and a 4-inch deficit deadlift are different exercises and not comparable.
content.safety_notes: Use a solid platform that cannot shift or tip. Stop the set at the first change in back position. Not a lift to attempt when tired or at the end of a heavy pulling session.

grip_variations.name: Double overhand
grip_variations.effect: Safest, grip usually limits before the back.

grip_variations.name: Mixed grip
grip_variations.effect: Allows heavier loads, small biceps tear risk.

grip_variations.name: Hook grip
grip_variations.effect: Secure and symmetrical.

grip_variations.name: Straps
grip_variations.effect: Lets you train the range without the grip failing first.

content.summary: Partial deadlift starting with the bar raised on pins or blocks, overloading the top half of the pull.
content.description: The rack pull starts the bar somewhere between mid-shin and above the knee, which removes the hardest part of a deadlift and lets you handle more weight through the lockout. It builds the upper back, traps and glutes at loads a full pull can't reach, and it's a useful way to keep training the pattern when the floor position aggravates something. It's assistance work, not a deadlift substitute — the number it produces means nothing without the pin height beside it.
setup: Set the pins or blocks so the bar starts at the height you intend to train — record it.
Stand with mid-foot under the bar, feet hip width.
Hinge and grip just outside the shins, shoulders slightly ahead of the bar.
Pull the chest up, set the lats and get a flat back before pulling.
execution: Breathe in and brace hard.
Push the floor away and drag the bar up the thighs.
Drive the hips forward to lock out standing tall.
Lower under control back to the pins — do not drop it.
Let the bar settle fully on the pins before the next rep.
cues: Finish with the glutes, not the lower back
Set it down, don't drop it

common_mistakes.mistake: Not recording the pin height
common_mistakes.fix: Log it every time. A rack pull from below the knee and one from above are different exercises with wildly different loads.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rounding the upper back because the start is easier
common_mistakes.fix: Set the same flat back you would for a floor pull; the shorter range tempts people to skip the setup.

common_mistakes.mistake: Loading far beyond what the back position can hold
common_mistakes.fix: Cap it at a weight you can lock out with a neutral spine and a controlled lower.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dropping the bar onto the pins each rep
common_mistakes.fix: Lower it under control. Dropping loses the eccentric and hammers the bar and rack.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaning back hard at lockout
common_mistakes.fix: Stand tall with ribs down and glutes squeezed — leaning back adds nothing but spinal extension under load.

content.breathing: Big breath and brace before each rep, hold through the pull, exhale at lockout, reset on the pins.
content.rom_notes: Range runs from the pin height to full lockout, so the pin height defines the exercise. Below-knee, at-knee and above-knee rack pulls should each be logged separately.
content.safety_notes: Set the pins level on both sides and check the bar sits flat before loading. Stop the set at the first change in back position — the heavy loads here leave little margin.

grip_variations.name: Double overhand
grip_variations.effect: Grip limits first; good for building it.

grip_variations.name: Mixed grip
grip_variations.effect: Heavier loads, small biceps tear risk on the supinated arm.

grip_variations.name: Straps
grip_variations.effect: Standard here, since the point is loading the back rather than the hands.

content.summary: Hip hinge with the bar on the back, loading the hamstrings and spinal erectors through a long lever.
content.description: The good morning puts the load on your shoulders and asks the hips to raise it, which makes the spinal erectors work isometrically at the longest lever of any common hinge. It builds the exact position that fails in a heavy squat or deadlift, which is why it's a staple of powerlifting assistance work. It is also the lift most often ruined by ego — the weights that work here are far lighter than people expect.
setup: Set the bar on the upper back as for a high bar squat and squeeze the upper back tight.
Unrack and step back, feet hip to shoulder width.
Put a soft bend in the knees and fix it there.
Brace hard before the first rep.
execution: Push the hips straight back, letting the torso tip forward.
Keep the back flat and the bar pressed into the traps.
Descend until the torso is near parallel, or until the hamstrings stop you.
Drive the hips forward to stand tall.
Re-brace fully between reps.
cues: Squeeze the bar into your back
Stop where the back can stay flat

common_mistakes.mistake: Loading it like a squat
common_mistakes.fix: Start with an empty bar and build over weeks. A third of your squat is a lot of weight here.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rounding the lower back to reach a lower position
common_mistakes.fix: End the range where neutral ends. Depth beyond that is spinal flexion under a bar on your back.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bending the knees more as it gets hard, turning it into a squat
common_mistakes.fix: Fix the knee angle at the start and hold it; film a set from the side to check.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bar creeping up onto the neck
common_mistakes.fix: Re-rack and reset it on the traps with the upper back squeezed tight.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bouncing out of the bottom
common_mistakes.fix: Pause briefly at the bottom of each rep; the stretch reflex hides a position you can't actually control.

content.breathing: Inhale and brace at the top, hold through the whole rep, exhale once standing.
content.rom_notes: Range is limited by hamstring flexibility and by where your back stops being neutral, usually short of horizontal. Keep it identical between sessions.
content.safety_notes: Use a rack with safeties set at the depth you'll reach, so a failed rep can be dumped forward onto them. Stop the set at the first sign of rounding — this is the highest-leverage position for the spine in the gym.

grip_variations.name: High bar
grip_variations.effect: Standard, shortest lever.

grip_variations.name: Low bar
grip_variations.effect: Longer lever, harder at the same weight.

grip_variations.name: Safety squat bar
grip_variations.effect: Kinder on the shoulders, pushes you forward more.

grip_variations.name: Seated
grip_variations.effect: Removes the hamstrings so the erectors do nearly all of it.

content.summary: Barbell hip extension with the upper back on a bench, the heaviest way to load the glutes directly.
content.description: The hip thrust loads hip extension at the point where the glutes are shortest and working hardest, which is exactly where squats and deadlifts are easiest. That makes it the most direct glute exercise available and one where the loads climb quickly. Because the spine isn't loaded and the range is short, it's also easy to train hard on without much systemic fatigue.
setup: Sit on the floor with your upper back against a bench, the bench edge just under the shoulder blades.
Roll the loaded bar over your hips and set a pad where it crosses the hip bones.
Plant the feet flat, shoulder width, so the shins are vertical at the top of the rep.
Tuck the chin slightly and brace the trunk.
execution: Drive through the heels and push the hips up.
Extend until the torso and thighs form a straight line — no higher.
Squeeze the glutes hard and hold for a moment at the top.
Lower under control until the hips are just off the floor.
Keep the ribs down and the chin tucked throughout.
cues: Ribs down — extend the hips, not the back
Chin tucked, eyes on your knees
Squeeze and pause at the top

common_mistakes.mistake: Arching the lower back instead of extending the hips
common_mistakes.fix: Tuck the ribs down and finish with a glute squeeze. Feeling this in the lower back means the hips stopped moving and the spine took over.

common_mistakes.mistake: Feet too close so the quads take over
common_mistakes.fix: Walk the feet out until the shins are vertical at lockout.

common_mistakes.mistake: Feet too far away so it becomes a hamstring exercise
common_mistakes.fix: Bring them in until the shins are vertical at the top; cramping hamstrings are the giveaway.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bench too high, so the shoulders slide up during the set
common_mistakes.fix: Use a bench around 40cm and set the edge just below the shoulder blades.

common_mistakes.mistake: Looking up at the ceiling
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the chin tucked and the eyes forward or on the knees — extending the neck pulls the whole spine into extension.

content.breathing: Inhale at the bottom, exhale as you drive up and squeeze. Keep the ribs down rather than taking a big chest breath.
content.rom_notes: Full range is hips just off the floor to a straight line from knees to shoulders. Pushing past that line is lumbar extension, not extra range.
content.safety_notes: Always use a pad — an unpadded bar on the hip bones is genuinely painful and shortens sets for the wrong reason. Make sure the bench cannot slide backwards before loading.

grip_variations.name: Feet shoulder width
grip_variations.effect: Standard, balanced glute emphasis.

grip_variations.name: Feet wider, toes out
grip_variations.effect: More glute medius and adductor.

grip_variations.name: Feet elevated
grip_variations.effect: Longer range and more hamstring involvement.

grip_variations.name: Single leg
grip_variations.effect: Exposes side-to-side differences, no bar needed.

content.summary: Hip thrust on a dedicated machine, with the setup handled for you and the load easy to change.
content.description: The hip thrust machine removes the awkward part of the barbell version — rolling a loaded bar onto your hips and finding a bench that doesn't slide — while keeping the same loading pattern on the glutes. Because changing weight takes seconds, it suits drop sets and high-volume glute work far better than the barbell. The fixed path means the setup positions matter: get the pad and seat wrong and you'll feel it everywhere but the glutes.
setup: Set the back pad so its top edge sits just below your shoulder blades.
Adjust the seat so the lap pad crosses the hip bones, not the stomach.
Plant the feet so the shins are vertical when the hips are fully extended.
Pull the lap pad down and brace before the first rep.
execution: Drive through the heels and extend the hips.
Finish with the torso and thighs in a straight line.
Squeeze the glutes and pause briefly at the top.
Lower under control until you feel the glutes stretch, without letting the weight rest.
Keep the ribs down and the chin tucked for every rep.
cues: Pad on the hip bones, not the belly

common_mistakes.mistake: Lap pad sitting on the stomach
common_mistakes.fix: Raise the seat until it crosses the hip bones — on the stomach it's uncomfortable and the load never reaches the hips properly.

common_mistakes.mistake: Half reps because the weight is easy to add
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the load and extend fully every rep; the machine makes it easy to go heavy and short.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bouncing off the bottom of the stack
common_mistakes.fix: Stop just short of the plates touching and reverse under control.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pushing through the toes
common_mistakes.fix: Move the feet slightly forward and drive through the heels.

common_mistakes.mistake: Arching the lower back at lockout
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the ribs down and finish with a glute squeeze rather than reaching for extra height.

content.breathing: Inhale at the bottom, exhale as you drive up and squeeze.
content.rom_notes: Full range is a deep hip flexion start to a straight line at the top. Machines vary in where they let you start, so keep the seat setting consistent and note it.
content.safety_notes: Very low risk. Check the lap pad is locked before loading heavy, and don't let the stack slam at the bottom.

grip_variations.name: Feet shoulder width
grip_variations.effect: Standard.

grip_variations.name: Feet wide, toes out
grip_variations.effect: More glute medius.

grip_variations.name: Feet higher on the platform
grip_variations.effect: More hamstring involvement.

grip_variations.name: Single leg
grip_variations.effect: Halves the load and exposes imbalances.

content.summary: Floor-based hip extension with no equipment, used to learn the pattern or train glutes anywhere.
content.description: The glute bridge is the hip thrust's simpler relative: the same hip extension, performed from the floor, with a much shorter range. It's the standard starting point for learning to extend the hips without arching the back, and it works as a warm-up before heavy hinging. Progress by adding a plate across the hips, going single leg, or moving to a hip thrust once bodyweight stops being a challenge.
setup: Lie on your back with the knees bent and feet flat, heels close to your backside.
Set the feet hip width, arms at your sides.
Tuck the ribs down and flatten the lower back into the floor.
Brace the trunk lightly before the first rep.
execution: Push through the heels and lift the hips.
Rise until the knees, hips and shoulders form a straight line.
Squeeze the glutes hard and hold for a moment.
Lower under control until the hips just touch the floor.
Keep the ribs down for the whole set.
cues: Push the floor away with the heels

common_mistakes.mistake: Arching the lower back to get higher
common_mistakes.fix: Stop at the straight line. Extra height comes from the spine, not the hips, and it's why people feel this in their back.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pushing through the toes
common_mistakes.fix: Lift the toes slightly inside your shoes so the drive comes through the heels.

common_mistakes.mistake: Feet too far from the body
common_mistakes.fix: Walk the heels in until they're close to your backside — far out turns it into a hamstring exercise and often cramps.

common_mistakes.mistake: Racing through reps without squeezing
common_mistakes.fix: Pause a full second at the top of every rep; the contraction is the whole point at bodyweight.

common_mistakes.mistake: Staying at bodyweight long after it's easy
common_mistakes.fix: Add a plate across the hips, go single leg, or move to a hip thrust.

content.breathing: Exhale as you lift and squeeze, inhale as you lower.
content.rom_notes: Full range is hips on the floor to a straight line from knees to shoulders. The range is naturally short — going higher means arching, not more range.
content.safety_notes: Effectively no risk. If you feel it in the lower back rather than the glutes, you're arching at the top; reduce the height and tuck the ribs.

grip_variations.name: Bodyweight, both legs
grip_variations.effect: Standard starting point.

grip_variations.name: Plate on the hips
grip_variations.effect: The simplest way to add load.

grip_variations.name: Single leg
grip_variations.effect: Roughly doubles the load and exposes imbalances.

grip_variations.name: Feet elevated
grip_variations.effect: Longer range, more hamstring.

content.summary: Hip hinge on a 45-degree bench, training the glutes, hamstrings and spinal erectors with the feet fixed.
content.description: Despite the name, the 45-degree back extension is a hip exercise — the pad supports the thighs and the hips do the work while the spine stays neutral. It builds the whole posterior chain with almost no spinal compression, which makes it one of the best ways to add posterior chain volume without adding fatigue. Rounding deliberately to train the erectors is a different exercise and should be logged separately.
setup: Set the pad so its top edge sits just below the hip bones, leaving the hips free to hinge.
Set the foot plate so the ankles are secure and the knees are almost straight.
Cross the arms on the chest or hold a plate against it.
Set a neutral spine and brace before the first rep.
execution: Hinge at the hips and lower the torso under control.
Descend until you feel a strong hamstring stretch, keeping the back flat.
Raise by squeezing the glutes and driving the hips into the pad.
Stop when the body forms a straight line — do not arch past it.
Keep the neck in line with the spine throughout.
cues: Hinge at the hips, not the waist
Flat back all the way down
Squeeze the glutes to come up

common_mistakes.mistake: Pad set too high, blocking the hips
common_mistakes.fix: Lower it until the top edge is below the hip bones. Too high and the spine has to do the bending instead.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hyperextending hard at the top
common_mistakes.fix: Finish in a straight line. Swinging past it repeatedly under load is what gives this exercise its bad reputation.

common_mistakes.mistake: Holding the weight up behind the head
common_mistakes.fix: Hold it against the chest, or at the chin at most — behind the head it loads the neck and lengthens the lever unhelpfully.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rounding down and then yanking up
common_mistakes.fix: Choose one version: neutral-spine hip hinge (this exercise) or a deliberate rounded extension, and keep it consistent.

common_mistakes.mistake: Adding weight before the bodyweight version is smooth
common_mistakes.fix: Get 15 clean bodyweight reps first; this is a small muscle group working at a long lever.

content.breathing: Inhale on the way down, exhale as you rise and squeeze.
content.rom_notes: Full range is a deep hip hinge to a straight line. Going past straight is lumbar extension under load, not extra range.
content.safety_notes: Low risk when the pad is set correctly. If you feel it sharply in the lower back rather than the glutes and hamstrings, the pad is too high or you're rounding.

grip_variations.name: Bodyweight, arms crossed
grip_variations.effect: Standard.

grip_variations.name: Plate on the chest
grip_variations.effect: The clean way to add load.

grip_variations.name: Toes turned out
grip_variations.effect: More glute emphasis.

grip_variations.name: Toes straight, knees soft
grip_variations.effect: More hamstring emphasis.

content.summary: Bodyweight hamstring curl performed on a glute-ham developer, combining knee flexion with hip extension.
content.description: The glute-ham raise trains the hamstrings at both ends — bending the knee and extending the hip — which almost nothing else does in one movement. It's brutally hard the first time and most people can only manage the lowering portion, which is fine, because the eccentric is where the protective benefit for the hamstrings comes from. Widely used in sport for exactly that reason.
setup: Set the foot plate so the knees sit just behind the pad when kneeling.
Place the feet against the plate and the thighs on the pad.
Kneel upright with the body in a straight line from knees to head.
Cross the arms on the chest and brace the trunk.
execution: Lower the torso forward under control by straightening the knees.
Keep the hips extended so the body stays in a straight line — no piking.
Descend as far as you can control, ideally until near horizontal.
Pull yourself back by curling the knees, keeping the line intact.
Use the hands on the pad only if you have to.
cues: One straight line from knees to head
Hips stay open — no bending at the waist
Curl yourself back with the hamstrings

common_mistakes.mistake: Breaking at the hips to make the lower easier
common_mistakes.fix: Squeeze the glutes to hold the line. Piking shortens the lever and removes most of the hamstring load.

common_mistakes.mistake: Falling rather than lowering
common_mistakes.fix: Take at least three seconds. If you can't, use a band or push off the hands and build the eccentric first.

common_mistakes.mistake: Knee position too far forward on the pad
common_mistakes.fix: Set the knees just behind the pad edge so the thighs are supported and the knees can move freely.

common_mistakes.mistake: Doing high volume the first session
common_mistakes.fix: Three sets of three eccentrics is plenty to start. This causes some of the worst soreness in the gym.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pushing hard off the hands the whole way up
common_mistakes.fix: Use the hands as the minimum assistance needed, and reduce it session by session.

content.breathing: Inhale as you lower, exhale as you pull back up. Keep a light brace to hold the line.
content.rom_notes: Full range is upright kneeling to near-horizontal and back. Assisted or partial reps are legitimate — record the assistance used so progress is visible.
content.safety_notes: Keep the hands ready to catch yourself on the pad in front. Because the eccentric is so much stronger than the concentric, start with very low volume to avoid a week of severe soreness.

grip_variations.name: Arms crossed on chest
grip_variations.effect: Standard.

grip_variations.name: Hands ready in front
grip_variations.effect: Lets you push off at the bottom; the usual way in.

grip_variations.name: Band assisted
grip_variations.effect: Reduces effective bodyweight so full reps are possible.

grip_variations.name: Plate held on chest
grip_variations.effect: Progression once bodyweight reps are easy.

content.summary: Kneeling eccentric hamstring curl with the ankles held, one of the strongest protective exercises for the hamstrings.
content.description: The Nordic curl anchors the ankles and asks the hamstrings to control the whole body lowering forward from kneeling. It produces very high eccentric hamstring force with no equipment beyond something to hold your feet, and it has more evidence behind it for reducing hamstring injuries than any other exercise. Almost nobody can do a full controlled rep at first, and that's expected.
setup: Kneel on a pad with the ankles held by a partner, a loaded barbell or a strap.
Set the body in a straight line from knees to head.
Cross the arms on the chest or hold them ready in front of you.
Squeeze the glutes to lock the hips open.
execution: Lower forward as slowly as you can, resisting with the hamstrings.
Keep the hips extended — the body falls as one straight piece.
Catch yourself on the hands when you can no longer control the descent.
Push off the floor just enough to return, or pull back with the hamstrings if you can.
Reset the line before the next rep.
cues: Fight it the whole way down
Push back with the minimum help

common_mistakes.mistake: Bending at the hips so the backside sticks out
common_mistakes.fix: Squeeze the glutes and hold the line. Piking is the body's way of avoiding the hard part.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dropping most of the way and catching late
common_mistakes.fix: Only count the range you actually control, and use a band to extend it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Doing sets of ten in the first session
common_mistakes.fix: Start with three sets of three. This reliably produces days of severe soreness if you overdo it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Ankles not properly secured
common_mistakes.fix: Use a loaded barbell, a partner, or a proper strap — a foot slipping mid-rep drops you onto your face.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rushing back up by pushing hard with the arms
common_mistakes.fix: Use the least push that gets you up; that assistance is what you're trying to reduce over time.

content.breathing: Inhale before lowering, exhale on the way back up. Hold a light brace to keep the line.
content.rom_notes: Full range is upright kneeling to the chest near the floor with control. Most people train a partial eccentric at first — record the angle or the assistance so progress shows.
content.safety_notes: Always kneel on a pad and keep the hands ready to catch. Build volume very gradually: the eccentric load here is extreme relative to what the hamstrings are used to.

grip_variations.name: Arms crossed
grip_variations.effect: Hardest, no assistance available.

grip_variations.name: Hands ready in front
grip_variations.effect: Standard, lets you catch and push back.

grip_variations.name: Band assisted
grip_variations.effect: Takes weight off so more of the range is controlled.

grip_variations.name: Slow eccentric only
grip_variations.effect: The usual starting version — lower slowly, then push back up.

content.summary: Machine hip extension performed lying face down, loading the glutes and lower back with traction rather than compression.
content.description: The reverse hyper fixes the torso and swings the legs, so the hips extend against load while the spine is pulled long rather than compressed. That combination makes it popular for training the posterior chain on days when the back is sore, and as accessory work after heavy pulling. Its weakness is that the pendulum invites swinging, which turns a strength exercise into a game of momentum.
setup: Lie face down with the hips at the edge of the pad and the torso fully supported.
Grip the handles and pull the chest into the pad.
Hook the legs into the strap or pendulum with the knees slightly bent.
Brace the trunk before the first rep.
execution: Raise the legs by squeezing the glutes until the body is roughly straight.
Pause briefly at the top rather than swinging through it.
Lower under control, resisting the pendulum on the way down.
Let the legs hang fully at the bottom without bouncing into the next rep.
Keep the chest pinned to the pad throughout.
cues: Squeeze the glutes to raise the legs
Control the swing, don't ride it
Chest stays glued to the pad

common_mistakes.mistake: Riding the pendulum's momentum for reps
common_mistakes.fix: Pause at the top and at the bottom. If the machine is doing the work, the weight is too heavy or the tempo too fast.

common_mistakes.mistake: Swinging up far past straight into hard extension
common_mistakes.fix: Stop at roughly a straight line; higher is lumbar extension under a swinging load.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hips positioned too far onto the pad
common_mistakes.fix: Slide down until the hip crease is at the pad edge so the hips can actually move.

common_mistakes.mistake: Letting go of the handles or a loose chest
common_mistakes.fix: Pull the chest into the pad — a loose torso means the load pulls on the lower back rather than being held by it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating it as a heavy strength lift
common_mistakes.fix: Keep it in the moderate range with control; the swinging load makes heavy grinding sets a poor idea.

content.breathing: Exhale as the legs rise, inhale as they lower.
content.rom_notes: Full range is legs hanging to roughly a straight line with the torso. The pendulum will happily carry you past that — stop yourself there.
content.safety_notes: Check the strap or pendulum is secure before each set. Not appropriate during an acute lower-back flare-up despite its reputation, since the load still swings.

grip_variations.name: Feet together
grip_variations.effect: Standard.

grip_variations.name: Feet apart, toes out
grip_variations.effect: More glute emphasis.

grip_variations.name: Knees bent
grip_variations.effect: Shortens the lever, easier on the hamstrings.

grip_variations.name: Single leg
grip_variations.effect: Exposes imbalances and halves the load.

content.summary: Cable hinge that teaches the hip pattern with the resistance pulling backwards instead of down.
content.description: The pull-through applies resistance horizontally through a rope between the legs, so the hips get loaded without the spine carrying anything. That makes it the clearest way to teach someone what a hinge feels like, and a genuinely useful glute exercise in its own right because tension peaks at lockout where the glutes are shortest. It's the standard regression whenever a deadlift or RDL is aggravating a back.
setup: Set a rope attachment on the lowest cable setting.
Face away from the stack, straddle the cable and take the rope between your legs.
Walk forward until there's tension with the weight off the stack.
Feet slightly wider than shoulder width, soft knees, arms hanging straight.
execution: Push the hips back and let the rope pull your hands between your legs.
Keep the back flat and the knees fixed as you hinge.
Descend until you feel a strong hamstring stretch.
Drive the hips forward to stand tall, squeezing the glutes at the top.
Keep the arms straight and passive throughout.
cues: Hips back, arms are just ropes
Let the cable pull you into the stretch
Knees stay soft, not bending further

common_mistakes.mistake: Squatting down instead of hinging back
common_mistakes.fix: Fix the knee angle and push the hips back toward the stack. If the knees bend more, it's become a squat.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pulling the rope up with the arms
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the arms straight and passive — they only connect you to the cable, they don't lift anything.

common_mistakes.mistake: Standing too close to the stack
common_mistakes.fix: Walk forward until the weight is off the stack at the top; too close and there's no tension where it matters.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaning back at the top
common_mistakes.fix: Finish standing tall with ribs down; leaning back turns a glute squeeze into lumbar extension.

common_mistakes.mistake: Going heavy enough to be dragged backwards
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the load — this exercise is about the pattern and the squeeze, not the number.

content.breathing: Inhale as you hinge back, exhale as you stand and squeeze.
content.rom_notes: Range is set by hamstring flexibility, same as an RDL. Full lockout at the top matters most here, since that's where the cable's tension peaks.
content.safety_notes: The lowest-risk hinge in the gym — nothing is loading the spine and a failed rep simply means the stack returns. Watch that the rope doesn't catch on clothing.

grip_variations.name: Rope between the legs
grip_variations.effect: Standard.

grip_variations.name: Wider stance
grip_variations.effect: More adductor and glute, easier to reach depth.

grip_variations.name: Single leg
grip_variations.effect: Adds balance and anti-rotation demand.

grip_variations.name: Band instead of cable
grip_variations.effect: Same pattern with no machine; tension rises toward lockout.

content.summary: Lunging forward step after step, alternating legs while carrying the load and moving continuously.
content.description: The walking lunge trains each leg through a deep range while the trunk and hips work to keep you upright between steps, which adds a balance and conditioning cost that stationary lunges don't have. It's an efficient way to accumulate single-leg volume and it exposes side-to-side differences quickly once fatigue arrives. Because you're moving under load, technique degrades late in a set faster than in almost any other leg exercise.
setup: Take a dumbbell in each hand and stand tall with them at your sides.
Choose a clear stretch of floor at least ten metres long.
Set the shoulders back and brace the trunk.
Look forward, not down.
execution: Step forward far enough that both knees can reach roughly 90 degrees.
Lower straight down until the back knee is just above the floor.
Drive through the front heel and mid-foot to stand.
Bring the back foot through into the next step without pausing.
Alternate legs continuously and count reps per leg.

common_mistakes.mistake: Steps too short so the front knee shoots far past the toes
common_mistakes.fix: Lengthen the stride until the front shin is close to vertical at the bottom; short steps are what make people's knees ache after lunges.

common_mistakes.mistake: Torso bobbing forward and back between steps
common_mistakes.fix: Slow down and keep the chest tall throughout; the bob usually means the step length is inconsistent.

common_mistakes.mistake: Crashing the back knee into the floor
common_mistakes.fix: Stop an inch short. Control the descent rather than using the floor to find the bottom.

common_mistakes.mistake: Losing the line and drifting sideways as you go
common_mistakes.fix: Step slightly wider — feet on a tightrope makes balance far harder than it needs to be.

common_mistakes.mistake: Grip failing before the legs on longer sets
common_mistakes.fix: Use straps, or switch to a front-racked or barbell variation.

content.breathing: Inhale on the way down, exhale on the drive up. Breathe every step rather than holding through a long set.
content.rom_notes: Full range is back knee to just above the floor with the front thigh at parallel or below. Count reps per leg, and keep the distance or step count consistent between sessions.
content.safety_notes: Needs clear floor space and room to set the dumbbells down. Stop the set when the steps stop being controlled — fatigue here shows up as a wobbling knee, which is the point to end on.

grip_variations.name: Dumbbells at the sides
grip_variations.effect: Standard, easiest to bail out of.

grip_variations.name: Front rack / goblet
grip_variations.effect: More upright torso, more quad and core.

grip_variations.name: Barbell on the back
grip_variations.effect: Heaviest, hardest to balance, least forgiving.

grip_variations.name: Bodyweight
grip_variations.effect: Good for learning the step length and for conditioning.

content.summary: Lunge stepping backwards instead of forwards, which is far kinder on the knees than the forward version.
content.description: Stepping back rather than forward means you never have to decelerate your bodyweight onto a bent front knee, so the reverse lunge loads the front leg's glutes and quads with much less stress on the joint. It's the lunge to teach first and the one to keep using if knees are a problem. The front foot stays planted throughout, which also makes it easier to balance than a walking lunge.
setup: Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides, or one at the chest.
Stand tall with feet hip width and the trunk braced.
Pick a clear space behind you.
Set the weight over the leg that will stay planted.
execution: Step one foot straight back, landing on the ball of that foot.
Lower until the back knee is just above the floor and the front thigh is at parallel.
Keep most of the weight through the front foot.
Drive through the front heel to bring the back foot home.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch.
cues: Weight stays on the front foot

common_mistakes.mistake: Stepping back too short so the front knee jams forward
common_mistakes.fix: Take a longer step until the front shin is near vertical at the bottom.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pushing off the back foot to stand
common_mistakes.fix: Think of the back leg as balance only; if you need it to stand, reduce the weight.

common_mistakes.mistake: Chest collapsing forward at the bottom
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the load and hold the trunk tall; a goblet hold makes this easier to feel.

common_mistakes.mistake: Front knee drifting inward on the way up
common_mistakes.fix: Slow down, track the knee over the middle toes and add glute medius work if it persists.

common_mistakes.mistake: Alternating legs when you meant to work one side
common_mistakes.fix: Complete all reps on one leg before switching — alternating gives each side a rest and changes the exercise.

content.breathing: Inhale as you step back and lower, exhale as you drive up.
content.rom_notes: Full range is front thigh to parallel with the back knee just off the floor. Log reps per leg.
content.safety_notes: One of the safest loaded single-leg exercises. Make sure there's clear space behind you and that you can set the dumbbells down if balance goes.

grip_variations.name: Dumbbells at the sides
grip_variations.effect: Standard, most load.

grip_variations.name: Goblet hold
grip_variations.effect: Counterbalance keeps the torso upright, best for learning.

grip_variations.name: Deficit (front foot on a plate)
grip_variations.effect: Longer range and more glute stretch.

grip_variations.name: Barbell front rack
grip_variations.effect: More core demand and a very upright torso.

content.summary: Lunge stepping forwards and returning to the start, with a braking demand on the front leg.
content.description: The forward lunge asks the front leg to absorb your bodyweight as you step out, then push you back to standing, which makes it the most knee-intensive of the lunge family and also the most athletic. That braking quality is useful for sport, but it's the reason this variation aggravates knees that the reverse lunge leaves alone. Step length matters more here than in any other lunge.
setup: Hold dumbbells at your sides and stand tall, feet hip width.
Brace the trunk and set the shoulders back.
Choose a clear space in front of you.
Pick your step length before the first rep and keep it consistent.
execution: Step forward and land through the whole front foot, not the toes.
Absorb the step by bending both knees and lowering straight down.
Stop with the back knee just above the floor.
Push back off the front foot to return to standing.
Complete all reps on one leg or alternate, but stay consistent.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stepping short so the knee travels far over the toes on landing
common_mistakes.fix: Lengthen the step. The short-step forward lunge is the specific version that makes knees sore.

common_mistakes.mistake: Landing hard on the heel or the toes
common_mistakes.fix: Land flat through the whole foot and absorb with the hip and knee together.

common_mistakes.mistake: Falling forward into the rep rather than controlling it
common_mistakes.fix: Slow the step down and reduce the weight until you can land quietly.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using momentum from the bounce back to standing
common_mistakes.fix: Pause at the bottom for a beat before pushing back.

common_mistakes.mistake: Choosing this over a reverse lunge with sore knees
common_mistakes.fix: Switch to reverse lunges — same muscles, no braking, and usually pain-free.

content.breathing: Inhale as you step and lower, exhale as you push back to standing.
content.rom_notes: Full range is front thigh to parallel with the back knee just off the floor. Step length defines the exercise — keep it fixed between sessions or the loading changes.
content.safety_notes: The knee_shear component means this is a poor choice during patellar or knee pain. Land under control and stop the set when the landings stop being quiet.

grip_variations.name: Dumbbells at the sides
grip_variations.effect: Standard.

grip_variations.name: Goblet hold
grip_variations.effect: Counterbalance, more upright, easier to control the landing.

grip_variations.name: Barbell on the back
grip_variations.effect: Heaviest, and the least forgiving on the landing.

grip_variations.name: Bodyweight
grip_variations.effect: Best for learning the step and for conditioning circuits.

content.summary: Stationary lunge with both feet planted, the simplest way to load one leg at a time.
content.description: The split squat holds a fixed stance and moves straight up and down, which removes the stepping and balance demands of other lunges and leaves just the leg work. That makes it the easiest single-leg exercise to load heavily and the best place to start for anyone new to unilateral training. Once the stance is set correctly it's almost impossible to do badly.
setup: Take a long step forward into a split stance, roughly your own leg length.
Set the back heel up so the weight is on the ball of that foot.
Adjust until the front shin is near vertical when you're at the bottom.
Hold dumbbells at your sides and brace the trunk.
execution: Lower straight down by bending both knees.
Descend until the back knee is just above the floor.
Keep most of the weight through the front foot.
Drive through the front heel and mid-foot to stand.
Complete all reps on one side before switching.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stance too short so both knees travel forward
common_mistakes.fix: Step out further until the front shin can stay vertical at the bottom.

common_mistakes.mistake: Travelling forward and back instead of straight down
common_mistakes.fix: Fix your eyes on a point ahead and think about dropping the back knee to the floor.

common_mistakes.mistake: Back heel flat on the floor
common_mistakes.fix: Keep it lifted so the back leg can't contribute to the drive; that's what keeps the load on the front leg.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pushing off the back toe to stand
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the load and think of the back foot as a kickstand for balance only.

common_mistakes.mistake: Different stance lengths on each side
common_mistakes.fix: Mark or count the step length so both sides are trained through the same range.

content.breathing: Inhale on the descent, exhale on the drive up.
content.rom_notes: Full range is back knee just above the floor with the front thigh at or below parallel. Stance length sets the range — keep it consistent.
content.safety_notes: Very low risk and easy to bail from — just stand up or set the dumbbells down. Expect soreness in the rear hip flexor when new to it.

grip_variations.name: Dumbbells at the sides
grip_variations.effect: Standard, easiest to bail.

grip_variations.name: Goblet hold
grip_variations.effect: More upright, more core, best for learning.

grip_variations.name: Front foot elevated
grip_variations.effect: Longer range and more glute stretch.

grip_variations.name: Barbell on the back
grip_variations.effect: Heaviest loading, more balance demand.

content.summary: Stepping onto a box with one leg, training single-leg strength through a range you set with the box height.
content.description: The step-up loads one leg concentrically from a deep position, and because you choose the box height you can dial the difficulty precisely — which makes it excellent for building back up after a knee problem. It also transfers directly to stairs and hills. The catch is that it's the easiest single-leg exercise to cheat, because the trailing leg can quietly do half the work.
setup: Set a box or bench at a height that puts the working thigh at roughly parallel when your foot is on it.
Hold dumbbells at your sides.
Place the whole working foot on the box, close to the near edge.
Stand tall and brace before the first rep.
execution: Drive through the working foot to stand up on the box.
Keep the trailing leg passive — do not push off the floor with it.
Stand fully upright on the box without slamming the trailing foot down.
Lower back down under control, touching the floor lightly with the trailing foot.
Complete all reps on one side before switching.
cues: Push the box away with the working foot

common_mistakes.mistake: Pushing off the floor with the trailing leg
common_mistakes.fix: Lift the trailing toes slightly before you drive; if you can't stand without them, lower the box.

common_mistakes.mistake: Box so high the hip has to hike to get the foot up
common_mistakes.fix: Lower it until the thigh is around parallel; higher boxes look impressive and train the hip flexor.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dropping off the box on the way down
common_mistakes.fix: Lower under control — the eccentric is half the exercise and the part that builds knee tolerance.

common_mistakes.mistake: Only the toes or ball of the foot on the box
common_mistakes.fix: Place the whole foot on so you can drive through the heel.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bouncing straight into the next rep on floor contact
common_mistakes.fix: Touch, settle, then drive again.

content.breathing: Exhale as you drive up, inhale as you lower.
content.rom_notes: Range is set by the box height, so record it — a step-up to a 30cm box and a 45cm box are different exercises.
content.safety_notes: Use a stable box that cannot tip or slide. Keep the dumbbells clear of the box edge on the way down, and don't set a height you can't step off safely.

grip_variations.name: Dumbbells at the sides
grip_variations.effect: Standard.

grip_variations.name: Goblet hold
grip_variations.effect: More upright torso, more core demand.

grip_variations.name: Lateral step-up
grip_variations.effect: Stepping up sideways, more glute medius.

grip_variations.name: Slow eccentric
grip_variations.effect: Lower over four seconds — excellent for knee tolerance.

content.summary: Stepping sideways into a single-leg squat, one of the few exercises that loads the adductors through range.
content.description: The lateral lunge moves in the frontal plane, which almost nothing else in a gym does. One leg bends and takes the load while the other stays straight and stretches the adductors, building strength in a direction that squats and lunges never touch. It's valuable for anyone playing a sport with cutting or side-stepping, and it's a genuinely useful groin-strain preventer.
setup: Stand tall holding a dumbbell at the chest or one in each hand.
Feet together, toes pointing forward.
Brace the trunk and set the shoulders back.
Clear enough space to take a wide step to the side.
execution: Step wide to one side, keeping both feet flat and pointing forward.
Sit the hips back and down over the stepping leg, bending that knee.
Keep the trailing leg straight and feel the stretch through its inner thigh.
Descend until the working thigh is near parallel or the stretch limits you.
Push off the working leg to return to standing, and complete all reps on that side.
cues: Sit back into the hip, don't just bend the knee
Both feet stay flat and forward

common_mistakes.mistake: Bending both knees so it becomes a wide squat
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the trailing leg locked straight — that's what creates the adductor stretch this exercise exists for.

common_mistakes.mistake: Turning the working foot out to reach further
common_mistakes.fix: Keep both feet pointing forward; rotating turns it into a lunge and removes the frontal-plane work.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bending at the waist instead of sitting the hips back
common_mistakes.fix: Push the hips back as if reaching for a chair behind that leg, keeping the chest tall.

common_mistakes.mistake: Going deep on the first session
common_mistakes.fix: Build the range over several weeks — the adductors are easy to strain in a loaded stretch they're not used to.

common_mistakes.mistake: Trailing foot rolling onto its edge
common_mistakes.fix: Keep it flat; if it lifts, your step was too wide for your current mobility.

content.breathing: Inhale as you step and lower, exhale as you push back to standing.
content.rom_notes: Range is limited by adductor flexibility on the straight leg, not by the working knee. Expect it to increase over weeks; keep the step width consistent within a session.
content.safety_notes: The loaded stretch on the inner thigh is the risk here, so warm up and progress the depth slowly. Stop the set if you feel a sharp pull in the groin rather than a stretch.

grip_variations.name: Goblet hold
grip_variations.effect: Standard, counterbalances the sit-back.

grip_variations.name: Dumbbells at the sides
grip_variations.effect: More load, harder to keep the chest up.

grip_variations.name: Cossack squat (staying low, shifting side to side)
grip_variations.effect: More range and mobility work, less loading.

grip_variations.name: Bodyweight
grip_variations.effect: Best for learning the pattern and building range.

content.summary: Lunge stepping diagonally behind the standing leg, biasing the glute medius and outer hip.
content.description: The curtsy lunge crosses the working leg behind, which puts the hip into adduction and makes the glute medius work hard to control it. That's the point — it loads the outer hip in a position ordinary lunges never reach. It also adds a rotational demand through the pelvis, so it needs lighter loads and more control than a straight-line lunge.
setup: Stand tall with a dumbbell at the chest or one in each hand.
Feet hip width, trunk braced.
Set the weight over the leg that will stay planted.
Clear space behind and to the side.
execution: Step one foot diagonally backwards, crossing behind the standing leg.
Lower until the back knee is just above the floor.
Keep the hips as square to the front as you can.
Drive through the front heel to return to standing.
Complete all reps on one side before switching.
cues: Front knee tracks over the toes
Control it — this isn't a heavy lift

common_mistakes.mistake: Front knee collapsing inward as you cross behind
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the load and actively press the knee out; the crossed position already biases the knee inward.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pelvis rotating to follow the stepping leg
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the hip bones pointing forward. Rotating under load is the flagged risk of this variation.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stepping too far across
common_mistakes.fix: A shallow diagonal is enough; a deep cross twists the standing knee and ankle.

common_mistakes.mistake: Loading it like a reverse lunge
common_mistakes.fix: Use noticeably lighter weight — the position is less stable and the target muscle is smaller.

common_mistakes.mistake: Ankle rolling on the standing foot
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the standing foot flat and the weight through mid-foot; reduce the step depth if it persists.

content.breathing: Inhale as you step and lower, exhale as you drive back up.
content.rom_notes: Full range is the back knee just above the floor with the hips still square. Depth is limited by hip control rather than leg strength.
content.safety_notes: The rotational element means this is a poor choice with an unstable knee or an acute ankle sprain. Keep the loads moderate and stop when the hips start rotating.

grip_variations.name: Goblet hold
grip_variations.effect: Standard, counterbalances well.

grip_variations.name: Dumbbells at the sides
grip_variations.effect: More load, more balance demand.

grip_variations.name: Bodyweight
grip_variations.effect: Best for learning the crossing pattern.

grip_variations.name: Deficit (standing foot on a plate)
grip_variations.effect: More range and glute medius stretch.

content.summary: Split squat on a fixed bar path, removing the balance demand so the working leg can be loaded properly.
content.description: Running a split squat on the Smith machine takes balance out of the equation entirely, which for most people is the thing that limits single-leg loading long before their legs do. The fixed path means you can position the feet for pure quad or pure glute emphasis and hold it exactly. It's the most practical way to train single-leg strength heavily without a decade of balance practice.
setup: Set the bar at upper-chest height and place it across the traps.
Step into a split stance with the front foot forward of the bar, back heel up.
Check the bar travels straight down through your split stance without dragging you forward or back.
Brace, stand up and rotate the wrists to unhook.
execution: Lower straight down by bending both knees.
Descend until the back knee is just above the floor.
Keep most of the weight through the front foot.
Drive through the front heel and mid-foot to stand.
Complete all reps on one side, re-hook the bar, then switch.
cues: Front foot forward of the bar

common_mistakes.mistake: Front foot placed directly under the bar
common_mistakes.fix: Step it forward. Under the bar, the fixed path forces the knee into an awkward angle for the whole set.

common_mistakes.mistake: Not checking the bar path against your stance before loading
common_mistakes.fix: Run a rep with the empty bar first — if it drags you forward or back, move the feet, not your torso.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting which way the hooks rotate before a heavy set
common_mistakes.fix: Test it empty. On a split stance you cannot easily reposition to re-rack if you get it wrong.

common_mistakes.mistake: Back heel flat on the floor
common_mistakes.fix: Keep it lifted so the back leg can't push; that's what keeps the load on the front leg.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming the load carries over to a free split squat
common_mistakes.fix: Log it separately — no balance demand usually means noticeably heavier numbers here.

content.breathing: Inhale on the descent, exhale on the drive up.
content.rom_notes: Full range is back knee just above the floor with the front thigh at or below parallel. Foot position and the bar's fixed path together define the range — set both the same each session.
content.safety_notes: Set the safety stops at a height that catches the bar just below your bottom position. Know the hook direction before loading; a split stance is a poor position to be stuck in.

grip_variations.name: Front foot well forward
grip_variations.effect: More glute and hamstring, more upright shin.

grip_variations.name: Front foot closer
grip_variations.effect: More quad, more knee travel.

grip_variations.name: Front foot elevated
grip_variations.effect: Longer range and more stretch under load.

grip_variations.name: Rear foot on a bench
grip_variations.effect: Becomes a Smith Bulgarian split squat — harder and longer range.

content.summary: Barbell press on an inclined bench, shifting emphasis toward the upper chest and front delts.
content.description: Tilting the bench upward changes the angle of the press so the upper chest fibres and front delts take more of the work than in a flat bench. It's the standard way to add upper chest development, which is the region most people find lags. Bench angle is the whole variable: too steep and it quietly becomes a shoulder press.
setup: Set the bench between 15 and 30 degrees — steeper than that shifts the work to the shoulders.
Lie back with the eyes roughly under the bar and feet flat on the floor.
Pull the shoulder blades back and down into the bench.
Grip slightly narrower than your flat bench and unrack by pulling the bar out.
execution: Take a breath and brace.
Lower the bar under control to the upper chest, just below the collarbones.
Keep the elbows at roughly 45-60 degrees from the torso.
Touch lightly, then press up and slightly back over the shoulders.
Lock out without letting the shoulder blades come unglued.
cues: Bar to the upper chest, not the throat

common_mistakes.mistake: Bench angle set too steep
common_mistakes.fix: Drop it to 15-30 degrees. Past about 45 the front delts take over and it stops being a chest exercise.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bar drifting up toward the neck
common_mistakes.fix: Touch the upper chest below the collarbones; a bar path toward the throat is both weaker and unnerving.

common_mistakes.mistake: Shoulders rolling forward off the bench at the top
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the blades retracted throughout; reaching at lockout is where the shoulder gets loaded badly.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the same weight as your flat bench
common_mistakes.fix: Expect meaningfully less — the shorter, steeper path takes the strongest part of the pec out of it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Feet up on the bench
common_mistakes.fix: Keep them flat on the floor; on an incline you need the base more than on a flat bench.

content.breathing: Inhale on the way down, hold through the press, exhale at lockout.
content.rom_notes: Full range is bar to upper chest contact and full elbow lockout. Record the bench angle — 15 and 30 degrees are different exercises in practice.
content.safety_notes: Use a spotter or set safeties at chest height. Bailing on an incline is harder than a flat bench because the bar tends to roll toward your face — never train it to failure alone without pins.

grip_variations.name: Standard grip
grip_variations.effect: Balanced upper chest and triceps.

grip_variations.name: Close grip
grip_variations.effect: More triceps, less shoulder stress.

grip_variations.name: Dumbbells
grip_variations.effect: Freer path, better for shoulders, easier to bail.

grip_variations.name: Low incline (15 degrees)
grip_variations.effect: Closest to a flat bench with a slight upper-chest bias.

content.summary: Barbell press on a declined bench, emphasising the lower chest through a shorter range.
content.description: The decline bench tips your head below your hips, which changes the press angle to favour the lower chest fibres and shortens the range compared with a flat bench. Most people can handle more weight here than on any other press. It's a niche exercise — useful for lower chest work and often more comfortable for cranky shoulders, but awkward to get into and out of under load.
setup: Set the bench to a modest decline, around 15-30 degrees.
Hook the legs securely under the pads before lying back.
Set the shoulder blades back and down into the bench.
Grip roughly 1.5x shoulder width and have a spotter hand the bar out if possible.
execution: Take a breath and brace.
Lower the bar under control to the lower chest, just below the nipple line.
Keep the elbows tucked at roughly 45 degrees.
Touch lightly, then press straight up over the lower chest.
Lock out with the shoulder blades still pinned.
cues: Legs locked in before you lie back

common_mistakes.mistake: Getting under a loaded bar without a spotter
common_mistakes.fix: Have someone hand it out. Head-down with a bar on your chest is the worst position in the gym to be stuck in.

common_mistakes.mistake: Legs not properly hooked before lying back
common_mistakes.fix: Lock them in first and test that you're secure before taking the bar.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bar path drifting back toward the face
common_mistakes.fix: Press straight up over the lower chest; the decline angle makes a backward path especially dangerous.

common_mistakes.mistake: Sitting up quickly at the end of a heavy set
common_mistakes.fix: Rack the bar, then come up slowly — the head-down position makes people light-headed.

common_mistakes.mistake: Comparing the load to your flat bench
common_mistakes.fix: The range is shorter, so the number is higher. Log it as its own lift.

content.breathing: Inhale on the way down, hold through the press, exhale at lockout. Avoid long breath-holds given the head-down position.
content.rom_notes: Full range is bar to lower chest contact and full lockout. The range is genuinely shorter than a flat bench — that's the angle, not a partial rep.
content.safety_notes: Use a spotter for anything heavy, and never train to failure alone. The inverted position raises blood pressure in the head, so skip this variation entirely if you have blood pressure or eye conditions, and get up slowly afterwards.

grip_variations.name: Standard grip
grip_variations.effect: Balanced lower chest and triceps.

grip_variations.name: Close grip
grip_variations.effect: More triceps.

grip_variations.name: Dumbbells
grip_variations.effect: Much easier to bail out of, and a longer range.

grip_variations.name: Dip
grip_variations.effect: Trains the same region without the inverted position.

content.summary: A narrow-grip bench press that shifts the work onto the triceps.
content.description: Bringing the hands to roughly shoulder width lengthens the range at the elbow and shortens it at the shoulder, so the triceps take a much larger share of the load than in a standard bench. It is the most direct way to add loaded triceps strength that carries straight back to lockout on the competition bench, and the tucked elbow position is usually kinder to the shoulder than a wide grip.
setup: Lie back with the eyes under the bar and the feet flat on the floor.
Grip at roughly shoulder width — index fingers on the smooth ring is a common landmark.
Set the shoulder blades back and down and hold that position.
Check the wrists sit stacked over the forearms, not bent back.
Unrack by pulling the bar out over the shoulders rather than pressing it up.
execution: Breathe in and brace the trunk.
Lower the bar to the lower chest with the elbows tucked to roughly 30 degrees.
Keep the forearms vertical as seen from the side through the whole descent.
Touch the chest lightly, then drive the bar back up over the shoulders.
Lock the elbows out fully at the top without letting the blades unset.
cues: Drive the bar off the sternum

common_mistakes.mistake: Hands set narrower than shoulder width
common_mistakes.fix: Widen back to shoulder width — a very narrow grip loads the wrist into extension and gives no extra triceps work.

common_mistakes.mistake: Wrists bending backwards under the load
common_mistakes.fix: Set the bar lower in the palm against the heel of the hand and squeeze the grip hard so the wrist stays stacked.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows drifting out to a flared bench position
common_mistakes.fix: Tuck to about 30 degrees and film a set from the side — flaring turns this back into a normal bench press.

common_mistakes.mistake: Loading it like a standard bench
common_mistakes.fix: Start around 80 percent of your bench working weight; the shorter shoulder lever means it will always be the lighter lift.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bar drifting toward the neck on the descent
common_mistakes.fix: Aim for the bottom of the sternum and keep the forearms vertical rather than angled back.

content.breathing: Inhale at the top, brace and hold through the descent and press, exhale once the elbows lock.
content.rom_notes: Full range is bar to chest contact and complete elbow lockout. Board and pin variants stop short deliberately — log those as separate movements.
content.safety_notes: Use a spotter or set the rack safeties at chest height. The narrow grip loads the wrists, so wrist wraps help on heavy sets. Stop the set if the elbow joint gives a sharp point of pain rather than a general ache.

grip_variations.name: Shoulder width
grip_variations.effect: The standard — most triceps work with a wrist position most people tolerate.

grip_variations.name: Thumb-width inside shoulders
grip_variations.effect: Slightly more triceps, noticeably more wrist stress.

grip_variations.name: Football or swiss bar neutral grip
grip_variations.effect: Same triceps emphasis with the wrists and shoulders in a more comfortable position.

content.summary: A bench press from the floor that stops the range at the triceps lockout portion.
content.description: Pressing while lying on the floor means the upper arms hit the ground before the shoulder reaches full extension, cutting off the deepest and most stressful part of the range. That makes it a useful press for anyone whose shoulder complains at the bottom of a bench, and a targeted way to train the mid-range and lockout where most bench presses stall. The dead-stop pause between reps also removes any stretch reflex.
setup: Lie on the floor under the rack with the bar over the shoulders, or have a partner hand it off.
Bend the knees with the feet flat, or leave the legs straight for a stricter version.
Set the shoulder blades back and down against the floor.
Grip at your usual bench width with the wrists stacked.
Unrack by pulling the bar out over the chest rather than pressing it away.
execution: Breathe in and brace before the bar moves.
Lower the bar under control with the elbows tucked to roughly 45 degrees.
Let the back of the upper arms touch the floor and pause there for a full beat.
Press from a dead stop without bouncing the triceps off the ground.
Lock out over the shoulders, keeping the blades pinned to the floor.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bouncing the upper arms off the floor
common_mistakes.fix: Add a deliberate one second pause with the triceps resting on the ground and drop the load until you can hold it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Flaring the elbows because the range is short
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the same 45 degree tuck you use on the bench — the shorter range does not make a flared shoulder position safe.

common_mistakes.mistake: Arching the low back to add leg drive
common_mistakes.fix: Straighten the legs or plant the feet wide and flat, and press the ribs down toward the floor.

common_mistakes.mistake: Expecting the same numbers as a full bench
common_mistakes.fix: Treat it as its own lift with its own log — the missing bottom range changes the weight in both directions depending on where you are weak.
