common_mistakes.mistake: Rolling the bar into position alone with heavy weight
common_mistakes.fix: Set the rack safeties low and press out from the pins, or use dumbbells so each side can be set independently.

content.breathing: Inhale before lowering, hold the brace through the pause, exhale after the elbows lock.
content.rom_notes: Range is deliberately partial and ends where the upper arm meets the floor. Depth varies with arm length, so keep the same surface between sessions for the log to mean anything.
content.safety_notes: Set the rack safeties just above chest height, or use dumbbells if pressing alone. Never roll a loaded barbell over the face or throat to get it into position.

grip_variations.name: Standard bench width
grip_variations.effect: Balanced chest and triceps in the top half of the range.

grip_variations.name: Close grip
grip_variations.effect: Shifts almost all of the work to the triceps and lockout.

grip_variations.name: Neutral grip dumbbells
grip_variations.effect: Easiest on the shoulder and lets each arm work independently.

content.summary: A flat press with two independent dumbbells, allowing a deeper and more natural path.
content.description: Two separate weights force each side to hold its own line, which exposes and slowly corrects strength differences a barbell lets you hide. The hands are free to rotate and travel inward at the top, so the chest works through a longer arc than a fixed bar allows, and the shoulder can sit in whatever position is comfortable. The trade-off is that getting heavy dumbbells into place is its own skill.
setup: Sit on the end of the bench with a dumbbell resting on each thigh.
Kick one knee up at a time and lie back with the weights, letting the legs bring them to the shoulders.
Set the shoulder blades back and down and plant both feet flat.
Press the dumbbells up over the chest with the palms facing forward or slightly inward.
Take a breath and check both arms are level before the first rep.
execution: Lower both dumbbells together toward the outside of the chest.
Keep the elbows at roughly 45 degrees from the torso, not flared to the sides.
Stop when the upper arms reach about chest level and you feel a stretch without shoulder strain.
Press back up and slightly inward, bringing the weights toward each other.
Stop just short of the dumbbells touching so tension stays on the chest.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dropping too deep and hanging on the shoulder joint
common_mistakes.fix: Stop when the upper arms are level with the torso; going lower loads the front of the shoulder capsule with no extra chest work.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows flared straight out to the sides
common_mistakes.fix: Angle them back to roughly 45 degrees so the forearm stays under the weight and the shoulder is not pinned at end range.

common_mistakes.mistake: Clanging the dumbbells together at the top
common_mistakes.fix: Stop a hand's width apart — the bang is just a rest, and the collision can drift a weight off line.

common_mistakes.mistake: Muscling the dumbbells up from the floor
common_mistakes.fix: Sit them on the thighs and kick one knee at a time to roll them into position, and reverse the same way to put them down.

common_mistakes.mistake: One side pressing faster than the other
common_mistakes.fix: Slow the tempo and match the weaker arm, or start each set with the weaker side setting the pace.

content.breathing: Inhale as the weights come down, hold the brace at the bottom, exhale on the way up.
content.rom_notes: Full range is upper arms to roughly torso level and near lockout at the top. The extra depth over a barbell is a benefit only while the shoulder stays comfortable.
content.safety_notes: There is no rack to bail into, so learn the knee-kick entry and exit before going heavy. If a rep fails, let the dumbbells travel out to the sides rather than dropping them onto the chest.

grip_variations.name: Palms forward
grip_variations.effect: Closest to a barbell press, most chest involvement.

grip_variations.name: Neutral, palms facing each other
grip_variations.effect: Much easier on the shoulder, shifts some work to the triceps.

grip_variations.name: Rotating from neutral to forward
grip_variations.effect: Comfortable at the bottom, full chest contraction at the top.

content.summary: A dumbbell press on an inclined bench, biased toward the upper chest.
content.description: Tilting the bench raises the pressing angle so the clavicular fibres of the chest take the lead, with the front delt sharing more of the load than on a flat press. Dumbbells suit this angle particularly well because the hands can rotate and come together at the top, giving the upper chest a contraction a barbell cannot reach. Bench angle matters: past about 45 degrees this quietly becomes a shoulder press.
setup: Set the bench between 30 and 45 degrees — 30 is plenty for most people.
Sit with a dumbbell on each thigh and lie back, kicking the weights up one knee at a time.
Pull the shoulder blades back and down into the pad.
Plant both feet flat and keep the hips on the seat.
Press the weights to arms length over the upper chest before starting.
execution: Lower both dumbbells toward the upper chest and shoulders.
Keep the elbows at roughly 45 degrees, tracking under the wrists.
Stop when the upper arms reach torso level and the chest feels a stretch.
Drive back up and slightly inward over the collarbones.
Stop short of the weights touching and hold the top for a beat.
cues: Press toward the ceiling, not the face
Squeeze the top of the chest

common_mistakes.mistake: Bench set too steep
common_mistakes.fix: Drop to 30 degrees; anything past 45 turns the movement into a shoulder press and the upper chest stops leading.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hips lifting off the seat to help the press
common_mistakes.fix: Lighten the load and keep the glutes on the bench — lifting the hips flattens the angle and removes the point of the exercise.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows flared level with the shoulders
common_mistakes.fix: Tuck to about 45 degrees so the front of the shoulder is not pinned at end range under load.

common_mistakes.mistake: Chin tucking and head lifting off the pad
common_mistakes.fix: Rest the head on the bench and look straight up — craning the neck to watch the weights strains the cervical spine.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the same weight as the flat press
common_mistakes.fix: Expect roughly 10 to 20 percent less on the incline and log it as its own lift.

content.breathing: Inhale on the descent, hold the brace through the bottom, exhale as the arms straighten.
content.rom_notes: Full range is upper arms to torso level and near lockout overhead of the chest. Record the bench angle with the set — the same weight at 30 and 45 degrees are not comparable.
content.safety_notes: Learn the knee-kick entry before loading heavy; there is no rack to catch a failed rep. If a rep stalls, guide the dumbbells out to the sides rather than forward over the face.

grip_variations.name: Palms forward
grip_variations.effect: Maximum upper chest involvement.

grip_variations.name: Neutral grip
grip_variations.effect: Kinder to the shoulder, more triceps and front delt.

grip_variations.name: Rotating grip
grip_variations.effect: Neutral at the bottom for comfort, turned in at the top for a stronger contraction.

content.summary: A guided chest press on a selectorised machine, easy to learn and safe to fail on.
content.description: The machine fixes the path, so the only decisions left are seat height and how hard you push. That makes it the fastest horizontal press to teach, the safest one to take close to failure without a spotter, and a reliable fallback when the shoulder does not like a free-weight bar path. The stabilising work is largely removed, which is a drawback for transfer and an advantage when you want the chest to be the limiting factor.
setup: Set the seat so the handles sit level with the middle of the chest, not the shoulders.
Sit back with the whole spine against the pad and both feet flat.
Set the start depth so the hands begin just outside the chest, not behind the torso.
Take the handles with the wrists stacked over the forearms.
Pull the shoulder blades back into the pad before the first rep.
execution: Breathe in and press the handles forward.
Keep the elbows tracking at roughly 45 degrees rather than flaring level with the shoulders.
Extend until the elbows are nearly straight without locking hard.
Return under control until the hands are level with the chest.
Pause briefly at the stretch, then press again without letting the weight stack rest.
cues: Chest against the pad, back against the seat
Push the handles apart as well as forward
Stop the stack short of touching

common_mistakes.mistake: Seat set too low so the press runs upward
common_mistakes.fix: Raise the seat until the handles line up with mid chest — pressing from a low seat turns it into a shoulder exercise.

common_mistakes.mistake: Letting the weight stack slam down each rep
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds on the return and stop a centimetre short of the stack; the negative is where most of the growth stimulus sits.

common_mistakes.mistake: Shoulders rolling forward at the end of the press
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the blades pinned to the back pad and let the arms finish the movement rather than the shoulder girdle.

common_mistakes.mistake: Start position set so deep the shoulders are pulled behind the torso
common_mistakes.fix: Move the start lever forward a notch so the hands begin level with the chest, not behind it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bracing the feet on the frame and pushing with the legs
common_mistakes.fix: Plant the feet flat on the floor and lower the load until the chest can move it alone.

content.breathing: Inhale as the handles come back, exhale through the press.
content.rom_notes: Full range is hands level with the chest to near lockout. The machine's own stops define the depth, so set the start lever rather than reaching further back.
content.safety_notes: This is one of the few presses you can safely take to failure alone, since releasing the handles ends the set. Check the seat and start-lever pins are fully engaged before loading.

grip_variations.name: Horizontal handles
grip_variations.effect: Palms forward, most chest emphasis.

grip_variations.name: Vertical or neutral handles
grip_variations.effect: Easier on the shoulder, more triceps.

grip_variations.name: One arm at a time
grip_variations.effect: Longer range across the body and exposes side-to-side differences.

content.summary: A bench press on a fixed vertical bar path, with catch hooks at every height.
content.description: The Smith machine locks the bar into a single line, removing the balance demand and letting the chest work without the stabilisers becoming the limit. Hooks along the rails mean a failed rep is a wrist flick away from safe, which makes it the natural choice for pressing hard while training alone. The fixed path is also its weakness: the bar cannot travel back over the shoulders, so body position on the bench has to do that job instead.
setup: Slide the bench under the bar and lie down, then check the bar lands on the lower chest, not the throat.
Shift the bench up or down until that line is right before adding plates.
Set the shoulder blades back and down and plant both feet flat.
Grip at roughly 1.5 times shoulder width with the wrists stacked.
Unhook by rotating the bar and take a breath before the first rep.
execution: Lower the bar under control to the lower chest.
Keep the elbows at roughly 45 degrees from the torso.
Touch lightly without letting the bar rest on the ribs.
Press straight up along the rails until the elbows lock.
Keep the blades set throughout and rehook only at the end of the set.
cues: Bench position sets the bar path

common_mistakes.mistake: Bench placed so the bar lands on the neck or upper chest
common_mistakes.fix: Move the bench a few centimetres toward the feet and test the line with an empty bar before loading it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating the Smith number as a bench press number
common_mistakes.fix: Log it separately — the machine carries part of the load and the counterweight varies between brands, so the two are not comparable.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows flared to 90 degrees because the bar cannot drift
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the same 45 degree tuck; the fixed path does not protect the shoulder from a flared position.

common_mistakes.mistake: Arching hard to reach a bar path the machine will not allow
common_mistakes.fix: Adjust the bench position instead of the spine — a big arch on a vertical bar path just loads the low back.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to check the hooks are clear before unracking
common_mistakes.fix: Rotate the bar fully to the free position and press once against the rails to confirm before starting.

content.breathing: Inhale on the way down, hold the brace at the chest, exhale at lockout.
content.rom_notes: Full range is bar to chest contact and full elbow lockout. The fixed vertical path is shorter than a free bar's arc, so expect the numbers to sit differently.
content.safety_notes: Learn the hook rotation before going heavy — a failed rep is only safe if you can flick the bar into the catches. Set the lowest safety stop just below chest height when training alone.

grip_variations.name: Standard width
grip_variations.effect: Balanced chest and triceps.

grip_variations.name: Close grip
grip_variations.effect: Shifts the work to the triceps and shortens the shoulder range.

grip_variations.name: Wide grip
grip_variations.effect: More chest, shorter range, more shoulder stress on a fixed path.

content.summary: The base bodyweight horizontal press, training chest, triceps and trunk together.
content.description: A push-up is a moving plank with a press attached: the chest and triceps drive the arms while the trunk has to stop the hips sagging or piking. It needs no equipment, scales in both directions by changing the angle or adding load, and teaches the shoulder position that every other press depends on. Most people can do more reps than they can do well, so quality is the thing worth tracking here.
setup: Place the hands slightly wider than the shoulders, level with the mid chest.
Set the feet together or hip width — wider is more stable.
Push the floor away so the upper back is broad rather than pinched.
Squeeze the glutes and brace the trunk so the body makes one straight line.
Tuck the chin slightly so the neck follows the spine.
execution: Breathe in and bend the elbows, keeping them at roughly 45 degrees from the ribs.
Lower until the chest is a fist's height from the floor.
Keep the hips level with the shoulders the whole way down.
Press the floor away and drive back to straight arms.
Finish each rep with the shoulder blades spread rather than pinched together.
cues: One line from head to heels
Screw the hands into the floor
Push the floor away at the top

common_mistakes.mistake: Hips sagging toward the floor
common_mistakes.fix: Squeeze the glutes and brace before the first rep, and move to an incline push-up until you can hold the line for a full set.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hips piking up into an inverted V
common_mistakes.fix: Bring the shoulders forward over the hands and think of the whole body moving as one plank.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows flared straight out to the sides
common_mistakes.fix: Draw them back toward the ribs at about 45 degrees so the shoulder is not pinned at end range.

common_mistakes.mistake: Head dropping to the floor ahead of the chest
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the chin lightly tucked and judge depth by the chest — a nodding head hides a half rep.

common_mistakes.mistake: Only lowering halfway to make the reps count
common_mistakes.fix: Lower to a fist's height from the floor every rep and drop the reps rather than the range.

content.breathing: Inhale on the way down, exhale through the press. Keep the trunk braced throughout rather than releasing at the bottom.
content.rom_notes: Full range is chest to roughly a fist's height from the floor and full elbow lockout. Hands on parallettes or dumbbells allow a deeper stretch — log those as deficit push-ups.
content.safety_notes: Loaded wrist extension is the usual complaint; use push-up handles or dumbbells to keep the wrists neutral if that bothers you. Stop the set when the hips start to sag rather than pushing on with a broken line.

grip_variations.name: Shoulder width plus a hand
grip_variations.effect: The standard, balanced chest and triceps.

grip_variations.name: Narrow or diamond
grip_variations.effect: Much more triceps, shorter range for the chest.

grip_variations.name: Hands on parallettes
grip_variations.effect: Neutral wrists and a deeper range at the bottom.

content.summary: A push-up with the hands raised, reducing the load so the line can be held.
content.description: Raising the hands onto a bench, box or bar takes a share of the bodyweight off the arms, which turns an impossible push-up into a set that can be done properly. The higher the hands, the easier the rep, so it is a scale rather than a single exercise: work down from a waist-high bar to a low box, then to the floor. It is also a useful way to hold volume in a chest session when the shoulder is irritated.
setup: Choose a stable surface — a bench, a box, or a bar set in a rack.
Place the hands slightly wider than the shoulders on the edge.
Walk the feet back until the body makes one straight line.
Squeeze the glutes and brace the trunk.
Set the shoulders down away from the ears before the first rep.
execution: Breathe in and bend the elbows to roughly 45 degrees from the ribs.
Lower until the chest touches or nearly touches the surface.
Keep the hips in line with the shoulders throughout.
Press away and return to straight arms.
Spread the shoulder blades at the top rather than pinching them.
cues: Lower the surface as you get stronger

common_mistakes.mistake: Hips dropping because the surface feels easy
common_mistakes.fix: Brace and squeeze the glutes for every rep — the whole point of the incline is that the line can be held.

common_mistakes.mistake: Standing too upright with the feet under the hands
common_mistakes.fix: Walk the feet back until the body is at a clear angle; feet close in removes most of the load.

common_mistakes.mistake: Staying on the same height for months
common_mistakes.fix: Once you can do 15 clean reps, drop to a lower surface and rebuild the reps from there.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using a bench that slides on the floor
common_mistakes.fix: Use a fixed box or a bar locked in a rack, and test the surface with bodyweight before starting the set.

common_mistakes.mistake: Cutting the depth short of the surface
common_mistakes.fix: Touch the chest lightly to the edge each rep and reduce the count rather than the range.

content.breathing: Inhale on the descent, exhale as the arms straighten, keeping the trunk braced across the whole set.
content.rom_notes: Full range is chest to the surface and full elbow lockout. Record the surface height with the set, since the same rep count at two heights is not the same work.
content.safety_notes: Make sure the surface cannot slide or tip before loading it with bodyweight. If the wrists complain, grip a bar or handles instead of a flat edge.

grip_variations.name: Shoulder width plus a hand
grip_variations.effect: The standard, balanced chest and triceps.

grip_variations.name: Narrow
grip_variations.effect: More triceps, less chest.

grip_variations.name: Hands on a bar in a rack
grip_variations.effect: Neutral wrists and easy to adjust height between sets.

content.summary: A push-up from raised hands, letting the chest travel below the hands.
content.description: Putting the hands on parallettes, dumbbells or low blocks lets the chest sink past hand level, adding range at the end where the chest is most stretched. That extra stretch under load is a strong growth stimulus and it makes a bodyweight movement harder without adding a single kilo. It also puts the shoulder into more extension than a floor push-up, so it is worth earning rather than jumping straight to.
setup: Set two parallettes, hex dumbbells or low blocks slightly wider than the shoulders.
Check both are stable and level before taking any weight on them.
Take the handles with the wrists neutral and the hands level with mid chest.
Walk the feet back into one straight line from heels to head.
Brace the trunk and squeeze the glutes.
execution: Breathe in and bend the elbows to roughly 45 degrees from the ribs.
Lower until the chest passes below hand level and you feel a stretch across the chest.
Stop at the point where the stretch is strong but the front of the shoulder is quiet.
Hold there for a beat rather than bouncing out of the bottom.
Press back to straight arms with the hips still level.
cues: Sink the chest between the hands

common_mistakes.mistake: Chasing depth until the shoulders roll forward
common_mistakes.fix: Stop at the depth where the chest stretches and the front of the shoulder stays quiet, and raise the blocks less rather than more.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bouncing out of the bottom position
common_mistakes.fix: Pause for a full second at the deepest point; the stretch is the reason for the exercise and a bounce skips it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hips sagging as the range gets longer
common_mistakes.fix: Drop back to floor push-ups until you can hold a straight line for the full set, then add the deficit again.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using round dumbbells that can roll
common_mistakes.fix: Use hex dumbbells, parallettes or fixed blocks, and load a hand onto each before committing bodyweight.

common_mistakes.mistake: Blocks set too high too soon
common_mistakes.fix: Start with a hand's height of deficit and add height over weeks as the shoulder tolerates the range.

content.breathing: Inhale as the chest lowers, hold the brace through the pause, exhale on the press.
content.rom_notes: Range runs from full lockout to the chest below hand level. Log the block height with the set — a deeper deficit is a different exercise, not more reps of the same one.
content.safety_notes: This is the most shoulder-demanding push-up variation, so build up the deficit gradually. If the front of the shoulder pinches at the bottom, reduce the depth or return to floor push-ups.

grip_variations.name: Parallettes, neutral grip
grip_variations.effect: Kindest on the wrists and shoulders for a given depth.

grip_variations.name: Hex dumbbells
grip_variations.effect: Same effect as parallettes and available in most gyms.

grip_variations.name: Rings
grip_variations.effect: Adds a rotation and stability demand on top of the deficit.

content.summary: A bodyweight press between parallel bars, biased to the lower chest and triceps.
content.description: Supporting the whole bodyweight on two bars and lowering under control is one of the hardest horizontal presses available without a barbell, and it loads the lower chest through a range no bench angle reaches. Leaning the torso forward emphasises the chest, staying upright shifts the work to the triceps. The bottom position puts the shoulder into deep extension, which is exactly why it builds so much and why depth needs to be earned.
setup: Choose parallel bars roughly shoulder width apart — much wider is hard on the shoulder.
Jump or step up to a supported position with the arms locked.
Push the floor away so the shoulders sit down, not shrugged up by the ears.
Cross the ankles behind and squeeze the glutes so the body does not swing.
Lean the torso slightly forward for chest, or hold it upright for triceps.
execution: Breathe in and bend the elbows, letting them travel back rather than out.
Lower under control until the upper arms are roughly parallel to the floor.
Keep the forward lean constant through the descent.
Stop at the depth where the chest stretches and the shoulder stays quiet.
Press back up to locked elbows without shrugging at the top.
cues: Shoulders down away from the ears
Lean forward for chest, upright for triceps
Control the bottom, don't drop into it

common_mistakes.mistake: Dropping far below parallel to chase depth
common_mistakes.fix: Stop when the upper arms reach parallel; below that the load moves off the muscle and onto the front of the shoulder capsule.

common_mistakes.mistake: Shoulders shrugging up at the top of each rep
common_mistakes.fix: Actively push the bars down and hold the shoulders away from the ears through the whole set.

common_mistakes.mistake: Swinging the legs to generate momentum
common_mistakes.fix: Cross the ankles, squeeze the glutes and keep the body still — if you need the swing, use the assisted machine instead.

common_mistakes.mistake: Free-falling into the bottom position
common_mistakes.fix: Take two to three seconds on the descent; an uncontrolled drop into deep shoulder extension is the most common way people hurt themselves here.

common_mistakes.mistake: Adding weight before the bodyweight reps are clean
common_mistakes.fix: Build to around 10 controlled bodyweight reps to full depth before hanging a belt on.

content.breathing: Inhale on the way down, hold the brace at the bottom, exhale on the press up.
content.rom_notes: Full range is locked elbows to upper arms roughly parallel with the floor. Deeper is not better here — depth past parallel is where most shoulder complaints come from.
content.safety_notes: Deep shoulder extension under bodyweight is demanding, so warm the shoulders up first and build the range over weeks. Use the assisted machine or bands if you cannot control the descent. Stop if the front of the shoulder pinches at the bottom.

grip_variations.name: Shoulder width parallel bars
grip_variations.effect: The standard, balanced and easiest on the shoulder.

grip_variations.name: Wide bars with a forward lean
grip_variations.effect: More lower chest, considerably more shoulder stress.

grip_variations.name: Rings
grip_variations.effect: The hands can rotate, easier on the joint but far harder to stabilise.

content.summary: A dip machine that carries part of your bodyweight so the reps can be built up.
content.description: A counterweighted platform holds the knees or feet and pushes upward, cancelling out whatever share of bodyweight you select. That turns the dip from something you can either do or not do into something adjustable, so the pattern can be trained with real volume long before a full bodyweight dip is possible. As the assistance comes down over weeks the movement stays identical, which makes it the cleanest on-ramp to the bar version.
setup: Set the assistance weight — more weight on the stack means more help, the reverse of every other machine.
Step onto the platform and take the handles with the arms locked out.
Kneel or stand on the pad depending on the machine and let it take the load.
Push the handles down so the shoulders sit away from the ears.
Lean the torso slightly forward for chest, or hold it upright for triceps.
execution: Breathe in and bend the elbows, keeping them travelling back rather than out.
Lower until the upper arms are roughly parallel to the floor.
Hold the same torso angle the whole way down.
Press back up to locked elbows.
Keep the shoulders pushed down at the top instead of letting them shrug.
cues: Shoulders down, away from the ears

common_mistakes.mistake: Reading the stack backwards and loading it like a normal machine
common_mistakes.fix: Remember the number is assistance — going up makes it easier, so progress by taking weight off across the weeks.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bouncing off the pad at the bottom to get the next rep
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds on the descent and pause at parallel; the pad is there to hold you, not to spring you back up.

common_mistakes.mistake: Shoulders shrugging toward the ears at the top
common_mistakes.fix: Push the handles down actively and hold the shoulders low through the whole set.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dropping well below parallel because the machine makes it easy
common_mistakes.fix: Stop at upper arms parallel — the assistance does not protect the front of the shoulder from deep extension.

common_mistakes.mistake: Staying on the same assistance level for months
common_mistakes.fix: Once you hit 12 clean reps, drop one plate of assistance and rebuild the reps from there.

content.breathing: Inhale on the way down, exhale on the press up, keeping the trunk braced through the bottom.
content.rom_notes: Full range is locked elbows to upper arms roughly parallel with the floor. Log the assistance weight with every set — the same reps at less assistance is the progression.
content.safety_notes: Check the knee or foot pad is locked at the height you set before putting weight on it. Mount and dismount with the arms locked rather than stepping off mid rep.

grip_variations.name: Standard parallel handles
grip_variations.effect: Balanced chest and triceps.

grip_variations.name: Wide handles with a forward lean
grip_variations.effect: More chest, more shoulder stress.

grip_variations.name: Upright torso, narrow handles
grip_variations.effect: Shifts the work almost entirely to the triceps.

content.summary: An overhead press driven off a short leg dip, moving far more weight than a strict press.
content.description: A shallow dip and hard drive from the legs gives the bar upward speed before the arms take over, so loads well beyond a strict press can be handled overhead. That makes it a bridge between pure pressing strength and the explosive hip extension used in the Olympic lifts. The dip is small and vertical — the moment it becomes a squat or the torso tips forward, the bar leaves its line and the lift falls apart.
setup: Set the rack so the bar sits at roughly collarbone height and unrack it into a front rack position.
Rest the bar on the front delts with the elbows slightly ahead of the bar.
Take a stance about hip width with the feet flat.
Brace the trunk hard and set the ribs down over the hips.
Take two steps back and check the bar is settled before the first rep.
execution: Dip by bending the knees a few inches, keeping the torso vertical.
Reverse instantly and drive through the legs — no pause at the bottom of the dip.
Let the leg drive throw the bar upward and punch the arms through as it slows.
Lock out overhead with the bar over the middle of the foot and the head through the arms.
Lower under control back to the front rack and reset the brace before the next rep.
cues: Punch the head through at lockout
Bar over the middle of the foot

common_mistakes.mistake: Dipping too deep and turning it into a squat
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the dip to a few inches — a deep dip is slow, and speed off the bottom is the whole mechanism of the lift.

common_mistakes.mistake: Torso tipping forward during the dip
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the chest up and the weight through the mid foot; a forward lean throws the bar out in front where the shoulder cannot recover it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pausing at the bottom of the dip
common_mistakes.fix: Reverse the instant the dip stops so the bar keeps the elastic energy — a pause turns it back into a strict press with sloppy legs.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pressing with the arms before the legs finish
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the arms passive until the hips and knees are fully extended, then punch through.

common_mistakes.mistake: Catching the bar hard on the collarbones on the way down
common_mistakes.fix: Absorb the return by bending the knees slightly as the bar lands on the front rack.

content.breathing: Take a big breath and brace at the front rack, hold it through the dip and drive, exhale at lockout. Reset the breath for every rep.
content.rom_notes: Full range is bar from the front rack to full overhead lockout with the head through the arms. The dip is part of the setup, not the range — it is not a squat rep.
content.safety_notes: Heavy overhead work with a braced valsalva raises blood pressure sharply; skip it if that is a concern for you. Press inside a rack or in clear space where the bar can be dumped forward safely, and never press overhead with people directly behind you.

grip_variations.name: Shoulder width, full grip
grip_variations.effect: The standard, strongest lockout position.

grip_variations.name: Fingertip front rack
grip_variations.effect: Lets the elbows sit higher, better bar shelf, harder on wrist mobility.

grip_variations.name: Dumbbells or kettlebells
grip_variations.effect: Each side works independently and the load can be dropped safely if a rep fails.

content.summary: A standing overhead press with two dumbbells, one per hand.
content.description: Two independent weights let the arms find their own path overhead, which usually suits the shoulder better than a fixed bar and stops the stronger side carrying the weaker one. Standing means the trunk has to resist the load leaning you backwards, so the abs and low back work alongside the delts. It is the most broadly useful overhead press: available anywhere, easy to bail out of, and honest about side-to-side differences.
setup: Clean or curl the dumbbells to shoulder height with the palms facing forward.
Stand with the feet about hip width and the knees soft.
Squeeze the glutes and brace the trunk so the ribs sit down over the hips.
Set the elbows slightly in front of the torso rather than flared straight out.
Take a breath before the first rep.
execution: Press both dumbbells up and slightly inward toward each other.
Keep the wrists stacked over the elbows through the whole path.
Lock out overhead with the weights roughly over the ears, not in front of the face.
Lower under control to shoulder height with the elbows tracking down.
Reset the brace at the bottom before the next rep.
cues: Stack the wrists over the elbows
Finish with the weights over the ears

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaning back to turn it into an incline press
common_mistakes.fix: Squeeze the glutes and brace the trunk before pressing; if the low back still arches, the load is too heavy for a standing press.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows flared straight out to the sides
common_mistakes.fix: Bring them forward to roughly 30 degrees ahead of the torso — the flared position pinches the shoulder at the top of the range.

common_mistakes.mistake: Locking out with the weights in front of the face
common_mistakes.fix: Finish with the arms beside the ears so the load sits over the shoulder joint rather than hanging in front of it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Only pressing to the top half of the range
common_mistakes.fix: Lower until the upper arms are roughly parallel to the floor each rep and cut the weight rather than the depth.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hauling heavy dumbbells up to the shoulders with the arms
common_mistakes.fix: Use a knee kick or a light hang clean to get them into position so the set starts with the shoulders fresh.

content.breathing: Inhale at the shoulders, brace and hold through the press, exhale at lockout.
content.rom_notes: Full range is upper arms parallel to the floor at the bottom to full elbow lockout overhead. Going deeper than parallel adds shoulder stress without more delt work.
content.safety_notes: If a rep fails, let the dumbbells travel out to the sides rather than forward or back over the head. Overhead pressing needs enough shoulder and thoracic range to lock out without arching the low back — press seated or on an incline if you cannot.

grip_variations.name: Palms forward
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most front and side delt involvement.

grip_variations.name: Neutral, palms facing each other
grip_variations.effect: Kinder to the shoulder, slightly more triceps.

grip_variations.name: Rotating from neutral to forward
grip_variations.effect: Comfortable start, full delt contraction at the top.

content.summary: A dumbbell overhead press from a supported seat, removing the trunk from the equation.
content.description: Sitting against an upright pad takes the balance and bracing demand out of the press, so the shoulders become the limiting factor rather than the low back. That usually means more weight and cleaner reps than standing, and it removes the temptation to lean back under load. The cost is that nothing transfers to holding a heavy weight overhead on your feet, so it is a hypertrophy tool more than a strength one.
setup: Set the bench upright, or one notch back from vertical if that suits your shoulder better.
Sit with the dumbbells on the thighs and kick them up one knee at a time.
Press the whole back into the pad and plant both feet flat.
Start with the weights at shoulder height, palms forward, elbows slightly ahead of the torso.
Brace the trunk so the low back stays against the pad.
execution: Press both dumbbells up and slightly inward.
Keep the wrists stacked over the elbows.
Lock out overhead without letting the shoulders shrug up to the ears.
Lower under control to shoulder height.
Stop at the bottom with the upper arms roughly parallel to the floor.

common_mistakes.mistake: Low back arching off the pad
common_mistakes.fix: Brace the trunk and keep the ribs down; if the back still lifts, drop the weight or set the seat back one notch.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows flared level with the shoulders
common_mistakes.fix: Keep them roughly 30 degrees ahead of the torso so the shoulder is not pinned at end range under load.

common_mistakes.mistake: Shrugging the shoulders up at lockout
common_mistakes.fix: Finish with the shoulders pulled down away from the ears and let the arms do the last few inches.

common_mistakes.mistake: Clanging the dumbbells together overhead
common_mistakes.fix: Stop a hand's width apart at the top — the collision can knock a weight off its line.

common_mistakes.mistake: Backrest set well past vertical
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the pad upright or one notch back; reclining further quietly turns the movement into an incline chest press.

content.breathing: Inhale at the bottom, hold the brace through the press, exhale at lockout.
content.rom_notes: Full range is upper arms parallel to the floor at the bottom to full lockout. Record the backrest angle — a reclined seat is a different exercise.
content.safety_notes: Learn the knee-kick entry so the shoulders are not spent before the set starts. If a rep fails, guide the dumbbells out to the sides rather than back behind the head.

grip_variations.name: Palms forward
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most delt involvement.

grip_variations.name: Neutral grip
grip_variations.effect: Easier on the shoulder, more triceps and front delt.

grip_variations.name: Slightly reclined seat
grip_variations.effect: More comfortable at the bottom, brings the upper chest in to help.

content.summary: A dumbbell press that rotates from palms-in to palms-forward on the way up.
content.description: Starting with the palms facing you and turning them out as the weights rise adds a rotation to the press, which keeps tension on the front delt across a longer arc than a straight press. The rotation is the point and also the catch: turning the arm out while the elbow is rising is the position most likely to irritate a shoulder, so it suits people whose shoulders are already comfortable overhead. Loads are lighter than a plain press.
setup: Sit upright on a bench with back support and both feet flat.
Kick the dumbbells up to shoulder height one knee at a time.
Start with the palms facing you and the elbows tucked in front of the chest.
Hold the weights close, roughly at collarbone height.
Brace the trunk and keep the back against the pad.
execution: Begin pressing up while rotating the palms outward.
Time it so the palms face forward around the halfway point, with the elbows out to the sides.
Continue pressing to lockout overhead without shrugging.
Reverse the path exactly — lower and rotate the palms back toward you.
Finish each rep back at the start with the palms facing in.
cues: Turn as you press, not after

common_mistakes.mistake: Pressing first and rotating at the top
common_mistakes.fix: Blend the two — the rotation should be complete by the midpoint, since twisting at lockout puts the shoulder at end range under load.

common_mistakes.mistake: Loading it like a normal dumbbell press
common_mistakes.fix: Start around 60 to 70 percent of your seated press weight; the rotation and the long range make it a much harder lift.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows flaring wide at the start
common_mistakes.fix: Keep them tucked in front of the chest at the bottom so the rotation has somewhere to travel.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rushing the reps so the rotation becomes a flick
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds up and three down; the exercise only earns its place if the rotation is controlled.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pushing through a pinch at the top of the shoulder
common_mistakes.fix: Swap to a neutral or standard press — this variation is the least forgiving of an irritated shoulder and there is nothing unique to lose.

content.breathing: Inhale at the bottom, hold the brace through the press and rotation, exhale at lockout.
content.rom_notes: Full range is palms-in at collarbone height to full lockout overhead with the palms forward. The rotation is part of the range, so a rep without it does not count as one.
content.safety_notes: Rotating the arm outward as the elbow rises is the most impingement-prone part of any press. Warm the shoulders up first, keep the load moderate, and switch to a neutral-grip press if anything pinches.

grip_variations.name: Full rotation, palms in to forward
grip_variations.effect: The standard, longest arc of front delt tension.

grip_variations.name: Half rotation to neutral
grip_variations.effect: Most of the benefit with much less shoulder stress.

grip_variations.name: Standing
grip_variations.effect: Adds a trunk bracing demand and forces lighter loads.

content.summary: A guided overhead press with a fixed path and a seat back.
content.description: The machine fixes the path and the seat takes the trunk out of it, leaving the delts as the only thing that decides whether the rep happens. That makes it the easiest overhead press to learn, the safest to push close to failure without a spotter, and a reliable way to keep pressing volume when balance or a cranky low back rules out the standing versions. Handle height is the one setting that matters and the one most people get wrong.
setup: Set the seat so the handles start at roughly shoulder height, not above the ears.
Sit with the whole back against the pad and both feet flat on the floor.
Take the handles with the wrists stacked over the forearms.
Pull the shoulders down away from the ears before the first rep.
Brace the trunk so the low back stays in contact with the pad.
execution: Breathe in and press the handles overhead.
Extend until the elbows are nearly straight without locking hard.
Keep the shoulders down rather than letting them shrug at the top.
Lower under control until the hands return to shoulder height.
Pause briefly at the bottom without letting the weight stack rest.

common_mistakes.mistake: Seat set too low so the handles start above the ears
common_mistakes.fix: Raise the seat until the handles line up with the shoulders — starting higher shortens the range and jams the joint at the bottom.

common_mistakes.mistake: Letting the weight stack slam down between reps
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds on the descent and stop just short of the stack touching.

common_mistakes.mistake: Low back arching away from the pad
common_mistakes.fix: Plant the feet, brace the trunk and lower the load until the back can stay flat through the set.

common_mistakes.mistake: Shrugging the shoulders at the top of every rep
common_mistakes.fix: Hold the shoulders pulled down and let the elbows finish the movement.

common_mistakes.mistake: Gripping the handles so hard the forearms fail first
common_mistakes.fix: Hold firmly but not maximally — the handles are guided, so the grip does not need to stabilise anything.

content.breathing: Inhale as the handles come down, exhale through the press.
content.rom_notes: Full range is hands at shoulder height to near lockout overhead. The machine's stops define the bottom, so set the seat rather than reaching lower.
content.safety_notes: One of the few presses you can safely take to failure alone, since letting go ends the set. Check the seat pin is fully engaged before loading, and skip it if pressing overhead pinches — the fixed path cannot adjust to your shoulder.

grip_variations.name: Palms forward handles
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most side delt involvement.

grip_variations.name: Neutral handles
grip_variations.effect: Kinder to the shoulder, more front delt and triceps.

grip_variations.name: One arm at a time
grip_variations.effect: Exposes side-to-side differences and lets the trunk resist the load.

content.summary: A single-arm press on an angled bar, halfway between overhead and horizontal.
content.description: One end of a barbell sits in a floor pivot while you press the other end up and away, so the path runs on a diagonal rather than straight overhead. That angle asks far less of shoulder mobility than a true overhead press, which makes it the most reliable pressing option for a shoulder that does not like being loaded at full lockout. Pressing one side at a time also makes the trunk resist rotation on every rep.
setup: Set one end of a barbell into a landmine pivot or wedge it into a corner with a towel.
Load the free end and stand facing it in a split stance or half kneeling.
Take the end of the bar in one hand at shoulder height with the palm facing in.
Square the hips and shoulders to the bar and brace the trunk.
Let the free arm hang or rest on the hip rather than counterbalancing.
execution: Breathe in and press the bar up and away on its natural arc.
Keep the elbow travelling under the hand rather than flaring out.
Extend until the arm is straight, following the angle of the bar rather than pressing vertical.
Resist the pull that wants to rotate the torso toward the working side.
Lower under control back to shoulder height and reset before the next rep.
cues: Press up and away, not straight up

common_mistakes.mistake: Torso rotating open toward the pressing arm
common_mistakes.fix: Brace the trunk and keep both hips and shoulders facing the pivot — resisting that rotation is half the exercise.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaning back to press the bar more vertically
common_mistakes.fix: Follow the bar's own arc up and away; the diagonal path is the reason this suits a stiff or sore shoulder.

common_mistakes.mistake: Free arm pushing off the thigh to help
common_mistakes.fix: Let it hang at the side so the working shoulder gets the full load and both sides can be compared honestly.

common_mistakes.mistake: Not securing the far end of the bar
common_mistakes.fix: Use a proper landmine pivot, or wedge the end into a corner with a towel and a plate behind it so it cannot skid out.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting the bar itself is part of the load
common_mistakes.fix: Log the plate weight and the bar you used, since a 20 kg bar in a pivot carries roughly half its weight to your hand.

content.breathing: Inhale at the shoulder, brace through the press, exhale as the arm straightens.
content.rom_notes: Full range is the hand at shoulder height to a straight arm along the bar's angle. It is deliberately not a vertical lockout — record it as its own lift, not a light overhead press.
content.safety_notes: Make sure the pivot end cannot slide out, especially if you are wedging into a corner rather than using a landmine attachment. This is the pressing pattern to reach for first when a shoulder cannot tolerate full overhead lockout.

grip_variations.name: Single arm, half kneeling
grip_variations.effect: Most anti-rotation demand, removes leg drive entirely.

grip_variations.name: Single arm standing split stance
grip_variations.effect: Allows heavier loads with a little leg contribution.

grip_variations.name: Two hands on the bar end
grip_variations.effect: Symmetrical and much heavier, but loses the anti-rotation work.

content.summary: An overhead press seated on the floor with the legs straight out in front.
content.description: Sitting on the floor with straight legs removes every source of help — no leg drive, no back arch, no hip contribution — so the delts and the trunk are all that remain. It exposes exactly how much of an overhead press comes from the shoulders and how much came from leaning back, and it is unforgiving of poor thoracic or hip mobility. Loads are far lighter than a standing press and that is the point.
setup: Set a rack so the bar sits just above head height when you are seated on the floor.
Sit on the floor with the legs straight out in front, about hip width apart.
Sit tall on the sit bones rather than rolling back onto the tailbone.
Unrack the bar onto the front delts with the elbows slightly ahead of it.
Brace the trunk hard and press the heels into the floor.
execution: Breathe in and brace before the bar moves.
Press straight up, pulling the head back out of the bar's way.
Push the head back through the arms once the bar clears it.
Lock out with the bar over the middle of the shoulders.
Lower under control to the front delts without letting the torso rock back.
cues: Sit tall on the sit bones

common_mistakes.mistake: Rocking backwards to start each rep
common_mistakes.fix: Brace the trunk and hold the torso vertical; if you cannot press without the rock, the load is too heavy for this variation.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rolling back onto the tailbone with a rounded low back
common_mistakes.fix: Sit up on the sit bones, and if tight hamstrings pull you back, sit on a mat edge or bend the knees slightly until the mobility improves.

common_mistakes.mistake: Loading it like a standing press
common_mistakes.fix: Expect roughly 60 to 70 percent of your standing overhead press and log it as its own lift.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bar drifting forward because the head does not move
common_mistakes.fix: Pull the head back as the bar passes the face, then push it through the arms at lockout so the bar sits over the shoulders.

common_mistakes.mistake: Setting the rack too high and pressing from a standing unrack
common_mistakes.fix: Set the pins so the bar can be taken while already seated, or use dumbbells so no rack is needed.

content.breathing: Inhale and brace at the bottom, hold through the press, exhale at lockout. Reset the breath for every rep.
content.rom_notes: Full range is bar at the front delts to full overhead lockout with the head through. The seated straight-leg position is part of the exercise — any lean or rock voids the rep.
content.safety_notes: Set the rack pins so the bar can be taken and returned while seated, and never press with the bar starting above where you can safely bail it. Needs real hamstring and thoracic range to sit tall; use dumbbells or a bench if the low back rounds.

grip_variations.name: Barbell, shoulder width
grip_variations.effect: The standard, heaviest loading and strictest position.

grip_variations.name: Dumbbells
grip_variations.effect: Easier to bail out of and lets each arm find its own path.

grip_variations.name: Kettlebells in the rack position
grip_variations.effect: Adds a stability demand and keeps the wrists neutral.

content.summary: A push-up with the hips piked high, turning it into a bodyweight overhead press.
content.description: Walking the feet in until the hips stack over the shoulders tips the torso toward vertical, so the press runs overhead rather than horizontally and the delts take over from the chest. It needs no equipment and scales by raising the feet, which makes it the natural stepping stone between a push-up and a handstand push-up. How much load reaches the shoulders depends entirely on how vertical you get the torso.
setup: Start in a push-up position with the hands slightly wider than the shoulders.
Walk the feet in toward the hands until the hips are high and the body makes an inverted V.
Aim to get the torso as close to vertical as your hamstrings allow.
Straighten the arms and push the floor away so the shoulders are not shrugged.
Set the head in line with the arms, looking back between the feet.
execution: Breathe in and bend the elbows, letting them travel back and slightly out.
Lower the crown of the head toward the floor just ahead of the hands.
Stop when the head lightly touches or comes within an inch of the floor.
Press back up to straight arms, keeping the hips high the whole time.
Finish each rep with the shoulders pushed away from the ears.
cues: Head lands ahead of the hands
Push the floor away at the top

common_mistakes.mistake: Hips too low so it becomes a regular push-up
common_mistakes.fix: Walk the feet closer to the hands until the torso is near vertical — the height of the hips is what decides whether the delts work at all.

common_mistakes.mistake: Lowering the head straight down between the hands
common_mistakes.fix: Aim the crown of the head at a point just ahead of the hands so the press stays overhead rather than turning into a triceps extension.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bouncing the head off the floor
common_mistakes.fix: Stop an inch short and control the descent over three seconds; the head is not a rebound surface.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hips dropping as fatigue arrives
common_mistakes.fix: End the set when the pike collapses rather than grinding out reps in a flatter position.

common_mistakes.mistake: Staying flat-footed once it gets easy
common_mistakes.fix: Put the feet on a box or bench to raise the hips further and shift more bodyweight onto the shoulders.

content.breathing: Inhale on the way down, exhale on the press, keeping the trunk braced across the set.
content.rom_notes: Full range is head to the floor and full elbow lockout. Log the foot height with the set — feet on the floor and feet on a bench are very different loads.
content.safety_notes: Loaded wrist extension is the usual complaint; use push-up handles or parallettes if the wrists object. Keep the neck in line with the torso and never let the head take weight on the floor.

grip_variations.name: Shoulder width plus a hand, feet on the floor
grip_variations.effect: The standard entry point.

grip_variations.name: Feet elevated on a box
grip_variations.effect: More vertical torso, considerably more load on the delts.

grip_variations.name: Hands on parallettes
grip_variations.effect: Neutral wrists and a deeper range below hand level.

content.summary: An overhead press performed upside down, pressing your full bodyweight.
content.description: Inverted against a wall, the shoulders press close to your entire bodyweight through a full overhead range, which makes it one of the most demanding bodyweight movements there is. It asks for shoulder strength, overhead mobility and the balance to hold an inverted position under fatigue all at once. The wall version is the trainable one — free-standing adds a balance skill that has nothing to do with the pressing stimulus.
setup: Clear a wall and put a folded mat where the head will land.
Place the hands slightly wider than the shoulders, roughly a hand's length from the wall.
Kick up one leg at a time into a handstand with the heels resting on the wall.
Push the floor away hard so the shoulders are active, not sunk.
Squeeze the glutes and brace the trunk so the body makes one line.
execution: Breathe in and bend the elbows, letting them travel back and slightly out.
Lower until the crown of the head lightly touches the mat.
Keep the head landing just ahead of the hands so the three points make a triangle.
Press back up through the hands to straight arms.
Hold the top for a beat with the shoulders pushed away before the next rep.
cues: Head and hands make a triangle
Squeeze the glutes, one straight line
Push the floor away at the top
Come down before you fall down

common_mistakes.mistake: Attempting it before a solid wall handstand hold
common_mistakes.fix: Build to a 60 second wall handstand hold and clean feet-elevated pike push-ups first — the press comes after the position.

common_mistakes.mistake: Head landing in line with the hands
common_mistakes.fix: Set the head just ahead of the hands so the three contact points form a triangle; in line with them there is no base to press from.

common_mistakes.mistake: Back arching into a banana shape
common_mistakes.fix: Squeeze the glutes and pull the ribs down so the body holds one line from hands to heels.

common_mistakes.mistake: No mat or padding under the head
common_mistakes.fix: Fold a mat under the landing point every time — the last rep of a set is where the arms give out.

common_mistakes.mistake: Kipping the legs to finish a rep
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the legs still and end the set when a strict rep is no longer available, or use a band under the shoulders for assistance.

content.breathing: Inhale before lowering, hold the brace through the descent and press, exhale at lockout. Do not hold the breath for long strings of reps while inverted.
content.rom_notes: Full range is head to the mat and full elbow lockout. Deficit versions on parallettes go below hand level — log those separately.
content.safety_notes: Always work against a wall with padding under the head and a clear exit path — know how to cartwheel or bail sideways before kicking up. Skip inversions entirely if you have uncontrolled blood pressure, glaucoma, or a recent head or neck injury.

grip_variations.name: Hands slightly wider than shoulders
grip_variations.effect: The standard, strongest pressing position.

grip_variations.name: Hands on parallettes
grip_variations.effect: Neutral wrists and a deeper range below hand level.

grip_variations.name: Band assistance under the shoulders
grip_variations.effect: Takes a share of bodyweight so full reps can be built up.

content.summary: A pull-up with the palms facing you, sharing the work between lats and biceps.
content.description: Turning the hands to face you puts the biceps in a much stronger position than an overhand pull-up, so most people can do several more reps and load them heavier. The lats still lead the movement but the elbow flexors take a real share, which makes this the best single exercise for building pulling strength and arm size at the same time. It is usually the first strict bodyweight pull anyone manages.
setup: Take an underhand grip at roughly shoulder width.
Hang with the arms straight and the shoulders pulled down out of the ears.
Cross the ankles behind and squeeze the glutes so the body cannot swing.
Set the ribs down and brace the trunk.
Look straight ahead rather than up at the bar.
execution: Start by pulling the shoulder blades down and back before the elbows bend.
Drive the elbows down toward the ribs.
Pull until the chin clears the bar with the chest close to it.
Lower under control all the way to straight arms.
Pause briefly at the bottom without letting the shoulders shrug up.
cues: Shoulders down before the arms pull
All the way down every rep

common_mistakes.mistake: Kipping the hips to swing through the sticking point
common_mistakes.fix: Cross the ankles and squeeze the glutes so the body is one rigid line, and end the set when the swing appears.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stopping halfway down between reps
common_mistakes.fix: Return to straight arms every rep; the bottom of the range is where the lat gets its stretch and cutting it inflates the rep count.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leading with the arms and never using the back
common_mistakes.fix: Pull the shoulder blades down first and think of driving the elbows into the ribs rather than bending them.

common_mistakes.mistake: Shoulders left shrugged up at the bottom
common_mistakes.fix: At the bottom of each rep pull the shoulders away from the ears before starting the next pull.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbow pain from a fixed straight bar
common_mistakes.fix: Switch to rings or a neutral grip handle so the forearm can rotate as you pull rather than being locked supinated.

content.breathing: Exhale as you pull up, inhale on the way down. On heavy weighted sets, brace and hold through the pull.
content.rom_notes: Full range is straight arms at the bottom to chin clearly above the bar. Anything less is a partial — log it as such rather than counting it in the same set.
content.safety_notes: The fixed supinated grip loads the inner elbow, so switch to rings or neutral handles if the elbow starts complaining. Build up weighted chin-ups gradually and use a belt rather than holding a dumbbell between the feet.

grip_variations.name: Shoulder width underhand
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most biceps involvement.

grip_variations.name: Narrow underhand
grip_variations.effect: Even more biceps, harder on the wrists and elbows.

grip_variations.name: Rings
grip_variations.effect: The forearms rotate through the pull, much easier on the elbow.

content.summary: A pull-up on parallel handles with the palms facing each other.
content.description: With the palms facing each other the forearm sits in its most neutral position, which takes strain off both the wrist and the inner elbow and puts the brachialis to work alongside the biceps. Difficulty falls between an overhand pull-up and a chin-up. For anyone whose elbows or shoulders complain about the other two grips, this is usually the version that keeps vertical pulling in the programme.
setup: Find parallel handles, a v-bar over a straight bar, or rings turned to face each other.
Take the handles with the palms facing in and the arms straight.
Pull the shoulders down out of the ears before anything else moves.
Cross the ankles and squeeze the glutes so the body cannot swing.
Brace the trunk with the ribs down.
execution: Depress the shoulder blades first, then start bending the elbows.
Drive the elbows straight down toward the hips.
Pull until the chin clears the handles or the upper chest meets them.
Lean back very slightly at the top so the chest rather than the chin leads.
Lower all the way to straight arms under control.

common_mistakes.mistake: Kicking the legs to generate momentum
common_mistakes.fix: Cross the ankles and hold the body rigid; if the kip is needed, use the assisted machine and build strict reps instead.

common_mistakes.mistake: Cutting the bottom of the range short
common_mistakes.fix: Return to a full dead hang with straight arms on every rep and drop the reps rather than the range.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pulling with the arms while the shoulders stay shrugged
common_mistakes.fix: Begin every rep by pulling the shoulder blades down, then let the elbows follow.

common_mistakes.mistake: Grip failing before the back does
common_mistakes.fix: Use straps on the heavier sets so the lats are the limit, and train grip separately rather than letting it cap every pulling set.

common_mistakes.mistake: Handles set too wide apart
common_mistakes.fix: Use handles at roughly shoulder width; wider than that loses the neutral position that makes this variation worth doing.

content.breathing: Exhale through the pull, inhale on the descent, keeping the trunk braced throughout.
content.rom_notes: Full range is a dead hang with straight arms to the chin above the handles. Handle spacing changes the feel, so keep it consistent between sessions.
content.safety_notes: This is the most joint-friendly of the three pull-up grips and the one to reach for if the elbow or wrist objects to the others. Add weight with a belt rather than pinching a dumbbell between the feet.

grip_variations.name: Shoulder width parallel handles
grip_variations.effect: The standard, kindest on the wrist and elbow.

grip_variations.name: V-bar hooked over a straight bar
grip_variations.effect: Very narrow, more biceps and brachialis, shorter range.

grip_variations.name: Rings turned neutral
grip_variations.effect: The forearms can rotate freely through the pull, easiest on the joints.

content.summary: A pull-up machine that carries part of your bodyweight so reps can be built up.
content.description: A counterweighted pad under the knees or feet pushes upward, cancelling out whatever share of bodyweight you dial in. That converts the pull-up from a pass-or-fail movement into an adjustable one, so the pattern can be trained with proper volume and a full range long before an unassisted rep exists. Because the movement itself is unchanged, the strength built here transfers directly — unlike lat pulldowns, which never make you move your own bodyweight.
setup: Set the assistance weight — more on the stack means more help, the opposite of a normal machine.
Take the overhead bar at your chosen grip and width.
Step or kneel onto the pad and let it take your weight.
Hang with straight arms and the shoulders pulled down out of the ears.
Brace the trunk so the body does not sag on the pad.
execution: Pull the shoulder blades down before the elbows bend.
Drive the elbows down toward the ribs.
Pull until the chin clears the bar.
Lower under control all the way back to straight arms.
Keep the body rigid on the pad rather than letting it bounce.
cues: Blades down before the elbows bend

common_mistakes.mistake: Reading the stack backwards and adding weight as progress
common_mistakes.fix: The number is assistance — progress means taking plates off, so log it and work the number down over the weeks.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bouncing off the pad at the bottom of each rep
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds on the descent and pause at the hang; the pad is there to hold weight, not to spring you back up.

common_mistakes.mistake: Half reps that never reach a straight arm
common_mistakes.fix: Add assistance rather than cutting the range — a full range with more help beats a partial with less.

common_mistakes.mistake: Staying on the same assistance for months
common_mistakes.fix: Once you hit 10 clean reps, drop one plate and rebuild the reps from there.

common_mistakes.mistake: Never testing an unassisted rep
common_mistakes.fix: Try a strict rep off the bar every couple of weeks — the machine can flatter you and the bar tells the truth.

content.breathing: Exhale through the pull, inhale on the way down.
content.rom_notes: Full range is straight arms to chin above the bar. Log the assistance weight with every set, since the same reps at less assistance is the whole progression.
content.safety_notes: Check the pad is locked at the height you set before putting weight on it, and mount and dismount with the arms straight rather than stepping off mid rep.

grip_variations.name: Overhand shoulder width
grip_variations.effect: Trains the pull-up directly, most lat involvement.

grip_variations.name: Underhand
grip_variations.effect: More biceps, usually a few more reps at the same assistance.

grip_variations.name: Neutral handles
grip_variations.effect: Kindest on the elbow and wrist.

content.summary: A cable pulldown to the chest, the seated stand-in for a pull-up.
content.description: A cable and a thigh pad let you load a vertical pull at any weight, which makes it the most scalable back exercise in the gym — anyone can find a working load on their first session, and it can be pushed close to failure with no spotter and no bail-out. It builds the lats through a full range, though it never asks you to move your own bodyweight, so it complements pull-ups rather than replacing them.
setup: Set the thigh pad tight enough that you cannot lift off the seat under load.
Take the bar at roughly 1.5 times shoulder width, palms forward.
Sit down with the arms straight and the shoulders allowed to rise at the top.
Set the feet flat and lean the torso back roughly 15 to 20 degrees.
Brace the trunk and hold that lean for the whole set.
execution: Start by pulling the shoulder blades down and back.
Drive the elbows down and toward the ribs.
Pull the bar to the upper chest, not behind the neck.
Pause for a beat with the chest tall and the elbows beside the ribs.
Let the bar rise under control until the arms are straight and the shoulders reach up again.
cues: Let the shoulders rise at the top

common_mistakes.mistake: Pulling the bar behind the neck
common_mistakes.fix: Pull to the upper chest — the behind-neck version forces the shoulder to end range with no benefit the front version lacks.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rocking the torso back and forth to move the weight
common_mistakes.fix: Set a lean of 15 to 20 degrees and hold it; if the torso has to swing, lower the load.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pulling with the arms while the shoulders stay high
common_mistakes.fix: Depress the shoulder blades first and think of the hands as hooks rather than the movers.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stopping short at the top so the lats never stretch
common_mistakes.fix: Let the arms straighten fully and the shoulders rise between reps — the stretch at the top is where much of the growth stimulus lives.

common_mistakes.mistake: Thigh pad set loose so you lift off the seat
common_mistakes.fix: Tighten it until the thighs are pinned; a loose pad caps the load at your bodyweight.

content.breathing: Exhale as you pull down, inhale as the bar returns.
content.rom_notes: Full range is straight arms with the shoulders elevated to the bar at the upper chest. Behind-the-neck is a different and worse movement, not a range variation.
content.safety_notes: Set the thigh pad before loading — a heavy set with a loose pad will pull you off the seat. Never pull behind the neck, which loads the shoulder at end external rotation.

grip_variations.name: Wide overhand
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most lat involvement.

grip_variations.name: Underhand shoulder width
grip_variations.effect: More biceps and lower lat, usually heavier.

grip_variations.name: Neutral v-bar
grip_variations.effect: Kindest on the elbow and wrist, strong mid-back involvement.

content.summary: A pulldown on a narrow neutral or underhand grip, biased to the lower lat.
content.description: Bringing the hands close together lengthens the path the elbows travel and lets them finish tight against the ribs, which loads the lat through more of its range and brings the biceps in more strongly than a wide grip. Most people can also handle more weight here. The narrow neutral handle is easy on the elbow, which makes this a good default pulldown for anyone whose joints dislike a wide pronated bar.
setup: Attach a v-bar or close neutral handle, or take a straight bar underhand at shoulder width.
Set the thigh pad tight enough that you cannot lift off the seat.
Sit with the arms straight and the shoulders allowed to rise at the top.
Plant the feet flat and lean back roughly 15 degrees.
Brace the trunk and hold that angle for the set.
execution: Pull the shoulder blades down before the elbows bend.
Drive the elbows down and back until they are tight against the ribs.
Bring the handle to the upper chest and pause with the chest tall.
Squeeze for a beat at the bottom of the pull.
Return under control to straight arms with the shoulders rising again.
cues: Chest tall to meet the handle

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaning back further and further as the set goes on
common_mistakes.fix: Hold a fixed 15 degree lean; a growing lean turns the pulldown into a row halfway through the set.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows drifting wide instead of tight to the ribs
common_mistakes.fix: Keep them tracking straight down beside the torso — the close path is the reason to use this variation.

common_mistakes.mistake: Yanking with the biceps from the first inch
common_mistakes.fix: Start each rep by depressing the shoulder blades so the lat initiates and the arms finish.

common_mistakes.mistake: Cutting the top of the range short
common_mistakes.fix: Let the arms straighten and the shoulders travel up between reps to load the lat in its stretched position.

common_mistakes.mistake: Weight so heavy the hips lift off the seat
common_mistakes.fix: Tighten the thigh pad and cut the load until the torso stays still.

content.breathing: Exhale as the handle comes down, inhale as it returns.
content.rom_notes: Full range is straight arms with shoulders elevated to the handle at the upper chest and the elbows beside the ribs. Log the handle used, as v-bar and underhand are not the same lift.
content.safety_notes: Fix the thigh pad before loading heavy. If the inner elbow complains on an underhand straight bar, switch to the neutral v-bar and the symptom usually disappears.

grip_variations.name: Neutral v-bar
grip_variations.effect: The standard, easiest on the elbow, strong lower lat involvement.

grip_variations.name: Underhand shoulder width
grip_variations.effect: More biceps, usually the heaviest version.

grip_variations.name: Rope with a spread at the bottom
grip_variations.effect: Allows a longer finish and more lat squeeze at the expense of load.

content.summary: A one-arm cable pulldown, with a longer range and no stronger side to hide behind.
content.description: Pulling one arm at a time removes the bar that normally forces both hands to move together, so the shoulder can travel further overhead at the top and the elbow can finish further back at the bottom. The result is a noticeably longer lat range than a two-handed pulldown, and any strength difference between sides shows up immediately instead of being masked. The trunk also has to resist being pulled sideways on every rep.
setup: Attach a single handle to a high pulley.
Kneel, sit on the floor, or use a pulldown seat facing the stack.
Take the handle in one hand with the arm straight overhead.
Let the shoulder rise fully at the top so the lat is stretched.
Brace the trunk and square the hips so the torso does not rotate.
execution: Pull the shoulder blade down and back before the elbow bends.
Drive the elbow down and toward the hip.
Finish with the hand beside the ribs and the elbow behind the torso.
Hold the squeeze for a beat with the torso still facing forward.
Return under control until the arm is straight and the shoulder rises again.
cues: Reach up and let the shoulder rise

common_mistakes.mistake: Torso twisting toward the working side
common_mistakes.fix: Square the hips and shoulders and brace the trunk; resisting the rotation is part of what makes the single-arm version worth doing.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaning away from the stack to add leverage
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the torso vertical and drop the load — the lean makes it a row and removes the overhead stretch.

common_mistakes.mistake: Not letting the shoulder rise at the top
common_mistakes.fix: Allow the shoulder blade to travel up fully at the end of each rep; the extra range is the whole reason to use one arm.

common_mistakes.mistake: Doing more reps on the stronger side
common_mistakes.fix: Start each set with the weaker side and match its rep count exactly with the stronger one.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pulling with the biceps and never involving the lat
common_mistakes.fix: Begin the rep by pulling the shoulder blade down, and think of the hand as a hook attached to the elbow.

content.breathing: Exhale through the pull, inhale as the arm returns overhead.
content.rom_notes: Full range is a straight arm with the shoulder blade elevated overhead to the elbow behind the torso. This range is longer than a two-handed pulldown, so expect lighter loads.
content.safety_notes: Anchor yourself before the set — kneeling or seated with the trunk braced — so a heavy rep does not pull you sideways off balance. Keep the free hand off the thigh so it cannot help.

grip_variations.name: Neutral single handle
grip_variations.effect: The standard, kindest on the elbow.

grip_variations.name: Underhand rotation through the pull
grip_variations.effect: Adds biceps involvement and a stronger finish position.

grip_variations.name: Half kneeling
grip_variations.effect: Increases the anti-rotation demand and locks the hips in place.

content.summary: Climbing a vertical rope, the most grip-demanding pull there is.
content.description: Hauling your bodyweight up a rope combines vertical pulling with a grip challenge nothing else matches, since the hands have to hold and release under full load repeatedly. Using the legs to lock the rope turns it into a strength exercise anyone with pull-ups can learn; climbing legless makes it one of the hardest bodyweight pulls in existence. The descent matters as much as the ascent, and it is where most injuries happen.
setup: Check the rope, its anchor and the mat beneath it before every session.
Learn a leg lock on the ground first — hook the rope over one foot and clamp it with the other.
Stand close to the rope and take a high grip with both hands.
Brace the trunk and set the shoulders down away from the ears.
Pull the knees up to establish the first leg lock before leaving the floor.
execution: Pull with the arms while driving the feet down against the leg lock to stand up the rope.
Release the lock, bring the knees to the chest and re-clamp higher.
Reach one hand at a time to a new grip and repeat the cycle.
Descend by reversing it — lock the feet, lower the hands, then slide the lock down.
Keep the feet clamped throughout the descent rather than sliding down the rope.
cues: Feet lock, then stand up the rope

common_mistakes.mistake: Sliding down the rope instead of climbing down
common_mistakes.fix: Reverse the climb one lock at a time; sliding gives rope burns on the hands and legs and is how most rope injuries happen.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pulling purely with the arms and no leg lock
common_mistakes.fix: Learn the foot clamp on the ground first — the legs carry most of the load and legless climbing is a separate, far harder exercise.

common_mistakes.mistake: Climbing higher than you can safely descend
common_mistakes.fix: Set a height you can climb down from with control and only raise it once the descent is comfortable.

common_mistakes.mistake: Not checking the anchor and matting
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect the rope for fraying, confirm the anchor point, and put a mat underneath before the first ascent of every session.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating it as conditioning when grip is already fatigued
common_mistakes.fix: Place it early in the session while the hands are fresh, since a grip that fails halfway up a rope means a fall.

content.breathing: Breathe steadily through the climb rather than holding — this lasts long enough that a held breath will cut the ascent short.
content.rom_notes: Measured in ascents rather than reps. Log the rope height and whether the climb was legless, since those are completely different exercises.
content.safety_notes: Always climb over matting, check the rope and anchor before every session, and never climb higher than you can descend under control. Do not slide down. Skip it if grip is already fatigued from earlier work.

grip_variations.name: Standard climb with a foot lock
grip_variations.effect: The legs share the load, the trainable version for most people.

grip_variations.name: Legless climb
grip_variations.effect: The full bodyweight on the arms and grip, dramatically harder.

grip_variations.name: Seated legless from the floor
grip_variations.effect: Removes the height risk while keeping the arm and grip demand.

content.summary: A row with the chest on a pad, removing the low back from the equation.
content.description: Lying face down on an angled pad means the torso is held for you, so nothing can be gained by heaving with the hips or rounding the spine.
