The back muscles have to move the weight on their own, which makes this the most honest row in the gym and the one to reach for when the low back is fatigued from squats and deadlifts or simply cannot be loaded. What it gives up is the trunk bracing work that free rows demand.
setup: Set the pad height so the handles sit level with the mid chest when the arms hang straight.
Lie face down with the chest against the pad and the feet planted.
Let the arms hang straight down and allow the shoulder blades to spread at the bottom.
Take the handles with the wrists stacked.
Brace lightly so the ribs stay in contact with the pad.
execution: Start the pull by drawing the shoulder blades together.
Drive the elbows back past the ribs.
Pull until the handles reach the torso and pause for a beat.
Lower under control until the arms are straight and the blades spread again.
Keep the chest against the pad throughout rather than lifting off to finish a rep.
cues: Chest stays glued to the pad
Squeeze for a beat at the top
Let the blades spread at the bottom

common_mistakes.mistake: Chest peeling off the pad to finish the rep
common_mistakes.fix: Cut the load until the ribs stay in contact — lifting off reintroduces exactly the cheating the pad exists to prevent.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pulling purely with the arms
common_mistakes.fix: Begin each rep by squeezing the shoulder blades together, then let the elbows travel back.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stopping short at the bottom
common_mistakes.fix: Let the arms straighten fully and the shoulder blades spread apart before starting the next pull.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pad set too high or too low for the handles
common_mistakes.fix: Adjust the pad so the arms hang straight to the handles, otherwise the range is cut before the set begins.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows flared wide out to the sides
common_mistakes.fix: Keep them at roughly 45 degrees from the torso to bias the lats, or wide and high only if the upper back is the deliberate target.

content.breathing: Exhale as you pull, inhale as the weight returns. Breathing is easier here than on a free row since the chest is supported.
content.rom_notes: Full range is straight arms with the blades spread to the handles touching the pad or torso. Pad height determines the range, so set it before the first working set.
content.safety_notes: One of the safest rows for a fatigued or sensitive low back, since the spine carries no load. Check the pad and any pins are locked before loading the plates.

grip_variations.name: Neutral handles, elbows at 45 degrees
grip_variations.effect: The standard, balanced lat and mid-back.

grip_variations.name: Wide overhand, elbows high
grip_variations.effect: Biases the rear delts, rhomboids and mid traps.

grip_variations.name: Underhand close
grip_variations.effect: More lower lat and biceps, usually the heaviest version.

content.summary: A hinged-bar row with a neutral grip, allowing very heavy loading.
content.description: One end of the bar is anchored so the load travels on an arc rather than straight up, and the close neutral handles put the arms in a strong pulling position. That combination lets most people move more weight here than on any other row, which is why it earns its place for building mid-back thickness. The trade-off is that the torso is held in a hinge under heavy load, so the low back and the bracing have to hold up.
setup: Load the free end of a landmine bar or step onto the platform of a t-bar machine.
Straddle the bar with the feet about hip width.
Hinge at the hips to roughly 45 degrees with the knees softly bent.
Take the neutral handles and let the arms hang straight.
Set the chest up, the spine neutral, and brace hard before the bar leaves the floor.
execution: Pull the shoulder blades together to start the movement.
Drive the elbows back and up along the arc of the bar.
Pull until the handles reach the lower chest or upper stomach.
Pause for a beat with the blades squeezed.
Lower under control to straight arms without letting the back round.
cues: Pull to the bottom of the ribs

common_mistakes.mistake: Back rounding as the weight climbs
common_mistakes.fix: Brace hard, set the chest up, and cut the load the moment the spine loses its neutral position — this is the row where people load the most and brace the least.

common_mistakes.mistake: Standing up out of the hinge to start each rep
common_mistakes.fix: Fix the torso angle at 45 degrees and keep it there; if the hips have to rise, the weight is too heavy.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bouncing the plates off the floor between reps
common_mistakes.fix: Stop just short of the floor and keep tension on the back, or set the bar on a platform if the plates ground out too early.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pulling with the arms and never squeezing the blades
common_mistakes.fix: Start the rep by drawing the shoulder blades together and let the elbows follow that.

common_mistakes.mistake: Grip giving out before the back does
common_mistakes.fix: Use straps on the heavy sets so the back is the limiting factor, and train grip separately.

content.breathing: Take a breath and brace at the bottom, hold it through the pull, exhale at the top before resetting.
content.rom_notes: Full range is straight arms to the handles at the lower ribs. Large plates can ground out early — use smaller plates or a raised platform to keep the full range.
content.safety_notes: This row carries a loaded spinal position, so brace properly and stop the set when neutral spine goes rather than grinding out extra reps. Make sure the anchored end is secure in a landmine pivot or corner before loading.

grip_variations.name: Close neutral handles
grip_variations.effect: The standard, heaviest position, strong mid-back and lat.

grip_variations.name: Wide overhand on the bar
grip_variations.effect: Biases the rear delts and upper back, lighter loads.

grip_variations.name: Underhand on a straight bar over the pivot
grip_variations.effect: More lower lat and biceps.

content.summary: A seated row against a cable, with constant tension through the whole range.
content.description: A cable pulls with the same force at every point in the range, so unlike a free-weight row there is no easy portion where gravity does the work. The seat and foot plate take the low back largely out of it, and the attachment can be swapped in seconds to shift the emphasis between lat and mid-back. It is the most adjustable row available and the easiest to run high reps on without form falling apart.
setup: Attach a v-bar or a wide bar and sit facing the stack.
Plant both feet on the platform with the knees slightly bent.
Reach forward to take the handle, letting the shoulder blades spread.
Sit up tall with the torso vertical and the chest lifted.
Brace the trunk and hold that upright position for the set.
execution: Start the pull by drawing the shoulder blades back and down.
Drive the elbows back past the ribs.
Pull the handle to the stomach and pause with the chest tall.
Return under control, letting the arms straighten and the blades spread forward.
Keep the torso still throughout rather than rocking with the weight.
cues: Reach forward at the end of each rep

common_mistakes.mistake: Rocking the torso back and forth with the weight
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the torso upright and let only the arms and shoulder blades move; if the body has to swing, the load is too heavy.

common_mistakes.mistake: Low back rounding as you reach forward
common_mistakes.fix: Let the shoulder blades spread while the spine stays neutral — the reach comes from the shoulders, not from slumping the back.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pulling the handle to the chest instead of the stomach
common_mistakes.fix: Aim for the belly button with the elbows tight to the ribs; pulling high turns a lat row into a rear delt exercise by accident.

common_mistakes.mistake: Knees locking straight so the hamstrings pull you forward
common_mistakes.fix: Keep a soft bend in the knees and the feet planted flat on the platform.

common_mistakes.mistake: Letting the stack slam down between reps
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds on the return and stop just short of the stack touching.

content.breathing: Exhale as you pull, inhale as the handle returns.
content.rom_notes: Full range is arms straight with the blades spread forward to the handle at the stomach and the elbows behind the torso. Log the attachment used — a v-bar and a wide bar are not the same exercise.
content.safety_notes: Do not let the low back round to chase extra reach at the front. Reach forward with the shoulder blades while the spine stays neutral, and check the attachment is clipped in before the first rep.

grip_variations.name: Neutral v-bar
grip_variations.effect: The standard, balanced lat and mid-back.

grip_variations.name: Wide overhand bar
grip_variations.effect: Elbows travel higher, biases the rear delts and rhomboids.

grip_variations.name: Rope with a spread at the finish
grip_variations.effect: Longer finish and more mid-back squeeze at the cost of load.

content.summary: A one-arm row with the free hand braced, the workhorse dumbbell back exercise.
content.description: Bracing one hand on a bench takes the low back largely out of it while leaving the working side free to travel through a long range — the shoulder can reach well forward at the bottom and the elbow can finish well behind the ribs. Rowing one arm at a time also exposes any strength difference between sides immediately. It needs one dumbbell and one bench, which makes it the most available serious back exercise there is.
setup: Place one knee and the same-side hand on a bench, or brace the hand on a rack upright with the feet split.
Set the torso roughly parallel to the floor with the spine neutral.
Let the working arm hang straight down with the shoulder reaching toward the floor.
Square the hips and shoulders to the floor rather than opening to the side.
Brace the trunk and set the neck in line with the spine.
execution: Start by pulling the shoulder blade back and down.
Drive the elbow up and back toward the hip.
Pull until the dumbbell reaches the lower ribs and the elbow is behind the torso.
Pause for a beat with the blade squeezed.
Lower under control to a full stretch with the shoulder reaching down again.
cues: Hips stay square to the floor

common_mistakes.mistake: Torso rotating open to lift the weight higher
common_mistakes.fix: Keep both hips and shoulders facing the floor; the twist adds nothing to the lat and loads the lumbar spine in rotation.

common_mistakes.mistake: Yanking the weight up with the whole body
common_mistakes.fix: Fix the torso in place and let only the arm and shoulder blade move; if the body has to heave, cut the load.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rowing to the armpit rather than the hip
common_mistakes.fix: Drive the elbow back toward the hip so the lat does the work — pulling high turns it into a rear delt exercise.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stopping short at the bottom
common_mistakes.fix: Let the arm straighten and the shoulder reach toward the floor between reps to load the lat in its stretched position.

common_mistakes.mistake: Neck craned up to watch in the mirror
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the head in line with the spine and look at the floor a metre ahead.

content.breathing: Exhale as you pull, inhale as the weight lowers, keeping the trunk braced throughout.
content.rom_notes: Full range is a straight arm with the shoulder reaching down to the elbow behind the torso. The reach at the bottom is part of the rep, not a rest.
content.safety_notes: Keep the spine neutral and the hips square — the rotation is what turns this from a back-friendly row into a low-back problem. Use straps on heavy sets if grip fails before the lat does.

grip_variations.name: Neutral, palm facing in
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most lat involvement.

grip_variations.name: Underhand
grip_variations.effect: More lower lat and biceps, elbow tracks tighter to the ribs.

grip_variations.name: Braced on a rack with a split stance
grip_variations.effect: Allows a longer range and keeps both feet loaded.

content.summary: A guided seated row with a chest pad and a fixed path.
content.description: The chest pad holds the torso and the machine fixes the path, so the back muscles are the only thing deciding whether the weight moves. That makes it the easiest row to learn, the safest to push near failure alone, and a dependable choice when the low back is already spent from heavy hinging. Most machines offer both a high wide grip and a low close one, which covers mid-back and lat emphasis from the same seat.
setup: Set the seat height so the handles line up with the mid chest.
Adjust the chest pad so it touches the sternum with the arms reaching forward.
Sit with both feet flat and the spine tall against the seat.
Take the handles with the wrists stacked and the arms straight.
Let the shoulder blades spread forward at the start of each rep.
execution: Draw the shoulder blades back and down to begin the pull.
Drive the elbows back past the ribs.
Pull until the handles reach the torso and pause for a beat.
Return under control until the arms are straight and the blades spread again.
Keep the chest against the pad throughout.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaning back away from the chest pad to move the weight
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the sternum in contact with the pad and cut the load — the pad exists to stop exactly that.

common_mistakes.mistake: Seat set too low so the elbows travel upward
common_mistakes.fix: Raise the seat until the handles are level with the mid chest and the elbows can track straight back.

common_mistakes.mistake: Letting the stack slam down between reps
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds on the return and stop just short of the plates touching.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pulling with the arms and never moving the shoulder blades
common_mistakes.fix: Start each rep by squeezing the blades together, then let the elbows follow.

common_mistakes.mistake: Never changing the handle used
common_mistakes.fix: Alternate the wide high grip and the close low grip across the week so both mid-back and lat get worked.

content.breathing: Exhale as you pull, inhale as the handles return.
content.rom_notes: Full range is arms straight with the blades spread to the handles at the torso. The seat and pad settings define the range, so record them with the load.
content.safety_notes: One of the safest rows to take close to failure alone, since letting go of the handles ends the set. Check the seat pin is fully engaged before loading.

grip_variations.name: Close neutral handles
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most lat involvement.

grip_variations.name: Wide overhand, elbows high
grip_variations.effect: Biases the rear delts, rhomboids and mid traps.

grip_variations.name: One arm at a time
grip_variations.effect: Longer range and exposes side-to-side differences.

content.summary: A bodyweight row under a fixed bar, the horizontal counterpart to a pull-up.
content.description: Hanging under a bar and rowing the chest up to it trains the back with bodyweight alone, and it doubles as a plank because the trunk has to hold a straight line the whole time. Difficulty scales purely by bar height and foot position, which means it works for someone who cannot yet do a single pull-up and for someone strong enough to add a weight vest. It is also the most joint-friendly row available.
setup: Set a barbell in a rack at roughly hip height, or use a fixed low bar.
Lie underneath and take an overhand grip slightly wider than the shoulders.
Walk the feet out until the body hangs in a straight line from heels to head.
Squeeze the glutes and brace the trunk so the hips cannot sag.
Hang with straight arms and let the shoulder blades spread.
execution: Pull the shoulder blades back and down to start the rep.
Drive the elbows back and pull the chest toward the bar.
Touch the chest to the bar, or come as close as strength allows.
Hold the top for a beat with the body still in one line.
Lower under control to straight arms with the blades spreading again.
cues: Chest to the bar, not the chin
Squeeze the glutes the whole set

common_mistakes.mistake: Hips sagging toward the floor
common_mistakes.fix: Squeeze the glutes and brace before the first rep, and raise the bar until the line can be held for the full set.

common_mistakes.mistake: Chin reaching for the bar ahead of the chest
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the head neutral and judge the rep by the chest — a craned neck hides a partial.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bar set too high so the movement is barely loaded
common_mistakes.fix: Lower the bar so the body sits closer to horizontal; the angle is the only load setting this exercise has.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bending at the hips to shorten the lever
common_mistakes.fix: Hold the body rigid from heels to head; piking the hips is the same as cutting the load without logging it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Never progressing once the reps get easy
common_mistakes.fix: Elevate the feet on a box, then add a weight vest, rather than adding endless reps.

content.breathing: Exhale as you pull, inhale on the way down, keeping the trunk braced across the set.
content.rom_notes: Full range is straight arms to chest touching the bar. Log the bar height and whether the feet were elevated, since those set the difficulty entirely.
content.safety_notes: Confirm the bar is properly seated in the rack before loading it with bodyweight. The most joint-friendly row available, and a good option when the low back or shoulders cannot handle loaded rows.

grip_variations.name: Overhand, slightly wider than shoulders
grip_variations.effect: The standard, balanced mid-back and lat.

grip_variations.name: Underhand
grip_variations.effect: More lat and biceps, elbows travel tighter to the ribs.

grip_variations.name: Feet elevated on a box
grip_variations.effect: Shifts more bodyweight onto the arms, the main progression.

content.summary: A bodyweight row on suspension straps, adjustable by simply walking the feet.
content.description: Straps hanging from a single anchor let the handles rotate freely, so the wrists and shoulders find their own path in a way no fixed bar allows. Difficulty is set by how far you walk the feet forward, which means the load can be dialled up or down mid-set without touching a weight. The free-hanging handles also add a stability demand that a barbell removes, so the mid-back and trunk work harder at the same angle.
setup: Anchor the straps overhead and set the handles to roughly hip height.
Take a handle in each hand with the palms facing each other.
Walk the feet forward until the body leans back at your chosen angle.
Squeeze the glutes and brace so the body makes one line from heels to head.
Start with the arms straight and the shoulder blades allowed to spread.
execution: Pull the shoulder blades back and down before the elbows bend.
Drive the elbows back past the ribs.
Pull until the hands reach the lower ribs and the chest is level with the handles.
Pause for a beat with the body still in one line.
Lower under control to straight arms without letting the hips drop.
cues: Walk the feet to set the load

common_mistakes.mistake: Hips sagging so the body bends in the middle
common_mistakes.fix: Squeeze the glutes and brace hard; if the line still breaks, walk the feet back to reduce the angle.

common_mistakes.mistake: Straps swinging and jerking through the rep
common_mistakes.fix: Slow the tempo and keep constant tension — the wobble means momentum is doing part of the work.

common_mistakes.mistake: Standing too upright so there is barely any load
common_mistakes.fix: Walk the feet further forward until the torso is closer to horizontal; the angle is the only load setting here.

common_mistakes.mistake: Anchor not checked before the set
common_mistakes.fix: Test the anchor point with bodyweight before leaning into it, especially on a door mount or a rig you did not set up.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pulling with the arms and never squeezing the blades
common_mistakes.fix: Start each rep by drawing the shoulder blades together and let the elbows follow.

content.breathing: Exhale through the pull, inhale on the descent, holding the brace across the set.
content.rom_notes: Full range is straight arms to hands at the lower ribs. Record the foot position or body angle, since that sets the load entirely.
content.safety_notes: Test the anchor before every session and keep the straps clear of edges that could fray them. The rotating handles make this one of the kindest rows on a sore shoulder or wrist.

grip_variations.name: Neutral, palms facing each other
grip_variations.effect: The standard, kindest on wrist and shoulder.

grip_variations.name: Overhand with the elbows high
grip_variations.effect: Biases the rear delts and mid traps.

grip_variations.name: Feet elevated
grip_variations.effect: Shifts more bodyweight onto the arms, the main progression.

content.summary: A single-arm row on the end of a landmine bar, taken from a staggered stance.
content.description: Rowing the end of an angled bar from a side-on staggered stance puts the working shoulder in a deep stretch at the bottom and lets the elbow finish high and behind the ribs. The arc of the landmine changes the resistance through the range in a way a dumbbell cannot, and the offset stance means the trunk resists both rotation and side bend on every rep. It is a lat exercise that also asks a lot of the grip.
setup: Set one end of a barbell in a landmine pivot and load the free end.
Stand side-on to the bar with the feet staggered, the outside foot forward.
Hinge at the hips to roughly 45 degrees and brace the free forearm on the forward thigh.
Take the end of the bar in the outside hand with an overhand grip.
Set the spine neutral and let the working shoulder reach toward the floor.
execution: Pull the shoulder blade back and down to start.
Drive the elbow up and back, letting it travel high past the ribs.
Pull until the bar end reaches the lower ribs.
Pause briefly with the blade squeezed and the torso still.
Lower under control until the arm is straight and the shoulder reaches down again.
cues: Reach the shoulder to the floor

common_mistakes.mistake: Torso rotating open with the pull
common_mistakes.fix: Keep both hips facing forward and brace hard; the loaded rotation is what makes this row hard on the low back when it goes wrong.

common_mistakes.mistake: Free arm pushing off the thigh to help the pull
common_mistakes.fix: Rest it on the thigh for position only and let the working side carry the whole load so both sides can be compared.

common_mistakes.mistake: Back rounding as the load climbs
common_mistakes.fix: Set the chest up and the spine long, and stop the set when neutral spine goes rather than adding reps.

common_mistakes.mistake: Ignoring that the bar itself adds weight
common_mistakes.fix: Log the plate weight and the bar used — a bar in a pivot delivers roughly half its own weight to your hand.

common_mistakes.mistake: Grip failing before the lat does
common_mistakes.fix: Use a strap on the heavy sets so the back is the limiting factor rather than the fingers.

content.breathing: Inhale and brace at the bottom, exhale through the top of the pull.
content.rom_notes: Full range is a straight arm with the shoulder reaching down to the bar end at the lower ribs. The bar's arc means the resistance is not constant, which is part of the exercise.
content.safety_notes: Secure the pivot end before loading. This row holds the spine in a hinged and slightly offset position, so brace properly and stop when neutral spine goes. Not the first choice when the low back is already irritated.

grip_variations.name: Overhand on the bar sleeve
grip_variations.effect: The standard, elbow travels high, strong lat and mid-back.

grip_variations.name: Landmine row handle
grip_variations.effect: Neutral wrist and a more secure grip on heavy sets.

grip_variations.name: Underhand
grip_variations.effect: Elbow tracks tighter to the ribs, more lower lat and biceps.

content.summary: A barbell row lying face down on a raised bench, with the torso completely fixed.
content.description: Lying prone on a bench high enough for the bar to hang clear removes every trace of body English — no hip drive, no torso swing, no spinal load at all. What is left is the purest barbell row there is, and the numbers are humbling the first time. Because the low back carries nothing, it can be programmed on the same day as heavy deadlifts or squats without adding to the fatigue that matters.
setup: Raise a bench on blocks or use a dedicated seal row bench so the bar hangs clear of the floor.
Load the bar and lie face down with the chest on the pad.
Let the arms hang straight down and check the bar clears the ground at full stretch.
Take an overhand grip slightly wider than the shoulders.
Squeeze the bench with the legs and brace lightly so the body stays still.
execution: Pull the shoulder blades back and down to start the rep.
Drive the elbows up and back toward the ceiling.
Pull until the bar touches the underside of the bench or the lower chest.
Pause for a beat with the blades squeezed together.
Lower under control to a full hang with the blades spreading again.

common_mistakes.mistake: Chest lifting off the bench to finish the rep
common_mistakes.fix: Cut the load until the body stays flat — coming off the pad reintroduces exactly the cheating this row exists to remove.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bench set too low so the plates hit the floor
common_mistakes.fix: Raise the bench on blocks or use smaller plates so the bar can hang at a full stretch.

common_mistakes.mistake: Blocks that shift under the bench
common_mistakes.fix: Use a purpose-built seal row bench, or stable boxes with the bench feet fully seated, and test it before loading.

common_mistakes.mistake: Loading it like a bent-over barbell row
common_mistakes.fix: Expect noticeably less weight and log it separately; with no hip drive available the numbers simply are lower.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pulling with the arms and no blade movement
common_mistakes.fix: Start every rep by squeezing the shoulder blades together, then let the elbows travel.

content.breathing: Exhale as you pull, inhale as the bar lowers. Breathing is restricted lying on the chest, so avoid long breath holds.
content.rom_notes: Full range is a dead hang with straight arms to the bar touching the bench or chest. Bench height determines whether the full stretch is available, so set it before the first working set.
content.safety_notes: Make sure the bench and any blocks are stable before loading — a bench shifting under a loaded bar is the main risk here. Carries no spinal load, so it is a strong option when the low back is fatigued or sore.

grip_variations.name: Overhand, slightly wider than shoulders
grip_variations.effect: The standard, strong mid-back and rear delt.

grip_variations.name: Underhand
grip_variations.effect: More lat and biceps, elbows tighter to the ribs.

grip_variations.name: Dumbbells instead of a bar
grip_variations.effect: Longer range and each side works independently.

content.summary: A high cable pull to the face, training the rear delts and the rotator cuff.
content.description: Pulling a rope from head height toward the face while rotating the hands outward loads the rear delts, the mid traps and the external rotators of the shoulder all at once — the exact muscles that heavy pressing leaves behind. It is the most commonly prescribed shoulder health exercise for good reason, and it is almost always done far too heavy. Light weight, high reps and a genuine pause at the back is what makes it work.
setup: Attach a rope to a cable set at roughly head height.
Take one end in each hand with the thumbs pointing back toward you.
Step back until the cable is under tension with the arms straight.
Stand tall in a split stance or with the feet hip width, trunk braced.
Set the shoulders down away from the ears before starting.
execution: Pull the rope toward the face, leading with the elbows.
Let the elbows travel high and wide, roughly level with the shoulders.
As the rope reaches the face, rotate the hands so the knuckles point back and up.
Pause for a full beat with the hands beside the ears and the blades squeezed.
Return under control until the arms are straight and the shoulders reach forward.
cues: Pause at the back every rep

common_mistakes.mistake: Going far too heavy and turning it into a row
common_mistakes.fix: Cut the load until the elbows can stay high and the external rotation happens; this is a high-rep exercise, not a strength lift.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows dropping so the lats take over
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the elbows level with the shoulders through the whole pull — dropped elbows mean the rear delts have stopped working.

common_mistakes.mistake: No external rotation at the end
common_mistakes.fix: Finish with the knuckles pointing back and up beside the ears; without that turn the rotator cuff gets nothing.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaning back and using the whole body
common_mistakes.fix: Stand tall in a split stance with the trunk braced and let only the arms and shoulder blades move.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rushing through reps with no pause
common_mistakes.fix: Hold the back position for a full second on every rep — the pause is where the work actually happens.

content.breathing: Exhale as you pull, inhale as the rope returns. Breathe normally rather than bracing, since the loads are light.
content.rom_notes: Full range is straight arms with the shoulders reaching forward to the hands beside the ears with the knuckles turned back. Without the rotation it is not a face pull.
content.safety_notes: One of the safest exercises in the gym and among the few worth doing even when the shoulders are irritated, provided the load stays light. If anything pinches, lower the cable slightly so the pull runs more horizontally.

grip_variations.name: Rope, thumbs back
grip_variations.effect: The standard, allows the full external rotation at the end.

grip_variations.name: Rope with the cable set low, pulling upward
grip_variations.effect: Biases the mid and lower traps.

grip_variations.name: Band instead of a cable
grip_variations.effect: Portable and self-limiting, ideal as a warm-up before pressing.

content.summary: A chest fly between two cable stacks, with tension held all the way to the finish.
content.description: Two opposing cables pull outward for the entire rep, so unlike a dumbbell fly the resistance does not disappear as the hands come together — the chest is still working at the point where it is fully shortened. Setting the pulleys high, level or low shifts the emphasis down, across or up the chest. It is the most complete chest isolation available and the one most worth doing after pressing rather than instead of it.
setup: Set both pulleys to the same height — chest level to start, high or low to shift emphasis.
Take a handle in each hand and step forward into a split stance.
Lean the torso forward slightly and brace the trunk.
Set the elbows in a soft fixed bend, roughly 20 degrees, and keep it there.
Let the arms open until the chest feels a stretch without shoulder strain.
execution: Breathe in and bring the hands together in a wide arc.
Keep the elbow angle fixed — the movement happens at the shoulder, not the elbow.
Bring the hands past each other or until they touch in front of the chest.
Squeeze for a full beat at the finish.
Open the arms under control back to the stretch without letting the shoulders roll forward.
cues: Cross the hands at the finish

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbow angle opening and closing so it becomes a press
common_mistakes.fix: Lock a soft 20 degree bend and hold it for the whole rep; if the elbows have to straighten and bend, the load is too heavy.

common_mistakes.mistake: Opening so wide the shoulders roll forward
common_mistakes.fix: Stop at the point where the chest stretches and the front of the shoulder stays quiet, rather than chasing depth.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stopping with the hands a foot apart
common_mistakes.fix: Bring the hands together or past each other — the last few inches are where cables beat dumbbells and skipping them wastes the exercise.

common_mistakes.mistake: Standing upright so the cables pull you backwards
common_mistakes.fix: Step forward into a split stance and lean the torso slightly into the movement.

common_mistakes.mistake: Never changing the pulley height
common_mistakes.fix: Rotate between high, mid and low settings across the week to cover the upper, mid and lower chest.

content.breathing: Inhale as the arms open, exhale as they come together.
content.rom_notes: Full range is a chest stretch at the open position to the hands meeting or crossing in front. Log the pulley height, since high, mid and low flies are effectively different exercises.
content.safety_notes: The open position puts the shoulder at end range, so keep the load moderate and stop the stretch where the joint stays comfortable. Set both pins fully before starting.

grip_variations.name: Pulleys at chest height
grip_variations.effect: The standard, even chest involvement.

grip_variations.name: Pulleys high, arms sweeping down
grip_variations.effect: Biases the lower chest.

grip_variations.name: Pulleys low, arms sweeping up
grip_variations.effect: Biases the upper chest.

content.summary: A machine chest fly with a fixed arc and a back pad.
content.description: Arms mounted on a pivot mean the path is decided for you and the seat back holds the torso, so the chest can be worked to failure with almost nothing to think about. It is the easiest chest isolation to learn, the safest to push hard on alone, and a dependable finisher after pressing. Where cables let you choose the angle, the pec deck trades that flexibility for simplicity — the one setting that matters is seat height.
setup: Set the seat so the handles or pads sit level with the mid chest.
Sit with the whole back against the pad and both feet flat.
Set the start lever so the arms begin open but not pulled behind the torso.
Take the handles with a soft fixed bend in the elbows, or place the forearms on the pads.
Pull the shoulders down and back into the seat before the first rep.
execution: Breathe in and bring the arms together in a wide arc.
Keep the shoulders pinned back against the pad throughout.
Bring the handles until they nearly touch in front of the chest.
Squeeze for a full beat at the finish.
Open under control back to the stretch without letting the stack rest.
cues: Hold the finish for a beat

common_mistakes.mistake: Shoulders rolling forward as the hands come together
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the shoulder blades pinned to the back pad and let the chest do the closing rather than the shoulder girdle.

common_mistakes.mistake: Start position set so wide the shoulders are pulled behind the torso
common_mistakes.fix: Move the start lever in a notch so the arms begin level with the torso, not behind it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Letting the stack slam open between reps
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds on the opening phase and stop just short of the plates touching.

common_mistakes.mistake: Seat set too high or low for the chest
common_mistakes.fix: Adjust until the handles line up with the mid chest, so the arc runs across the chest rather than up or down.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bouncing through reps with no pause at the finish
common_mistakes.fix: Hold the closed position for a full second — the shortened squeeze is what this machine does better than free weights.

content.breathing: Inhale as the arms open, exhale as they close.
content.rom_notes: Full range is the open stretch position to the handles nearly touching. The machine's start lever sets the open position, so adjust that rather than reaching further back.
content.safety_notes: One of the safest chest exercises to take to failure alone. Set the start lever so the shoulders are not forced behind the torso at the open position, which is where end-range shoulder strain comes from.

grip_variations.name: Handles with a soft elbow bend
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most chest involvement.

grip_variations.name: Forearms on the pads
grip_variations.effect: Removes the grip entirely and keeps the elbow angle fixed.

grip_variations.name: One arm at a time
grip_variations.effect: Longer range across the body and exposes side-to-side differences.

content.summary: A chest fly lying on a bench with two dumbbells, loading the stretched position hardest.
content.description: With dumbbells the resistance is greatest when the arms are wide and the chest is fully stretched, and it falls away to almost nothing as the hands come together overhead. That makes it the mirror image of a cable fly: excellent at loading the lengthened position, which is a strong growth stimulus, and useless at the top. It also puts the shoulder at end range under load with no cable to help, which is why the weights stay moderate.
setup: Sit on a flat or slightly inclined bench with a dumbbell on each thigh.
Kick the weights up one knee at a time and lie back.
Set the shoulder blades back and down and plant both feet flat.
Press the dumbbells to arms length over the chest, palms facing each other.
Set a soft fixed bend of roughly 20 degrees in the elbows.
execution: Breathe in and open the arms out to the sides in a wide arc.
Keep the elbow angle fixed — nothing bends or straightens at the elbow.
Lower until the upper arms are roughly level with the torso and the chest is stretched.
Stop at the point where the stretch is strong and the shoulder stays comfortable.
Bring the arms back together over the chest, stopping short of the weights touching.
cues: Fixed elbows, movement at the shoulder
Stretch to torso level, no lower

common_mistakes.mistake: Going too heavy and turning it into a pressing motion
common_mistakes.fix: Use a weight that lets the elbow angle stay fixed for every rep; if the arms have to bend and straighten, it has become a bad bench press.

common_mistakes.mistake: Lowering far below torso level chasing a deeper stretch
common_mistakes.fix: Stop when the upper arms reach torso level — beyond that the load hangs on the front of the shoulder capsule with no extra chest work.

common_mistakes.mistake: Locking the elbows completely straight
common_mistakes.fix: Hold a soft 20 degree bend to spread the load; straight arms put the whole lever on the shoulder joint.

common_mistakes.mistake: Clanging the dumbbells together at the top
common_mistakes.fix: Stop a hand's width apart — there is no tension left up there anyway, and the collision can knock a weight off line.

common_mistakes.mistake: Doing flies before pressing
common_mistakes.fix: Place them after the presses; pre-fatiguing the chest with an end-range shoulder movement makes the heavy work less safe.

content.breathing: Inhale as the arms open, exhale as they come back together.
content.rom_notes: Full range is the upper arms level with the torso at the bottom to the arms nearly vertical at the top. The bottom half carries almost all the useful tension.
content.safety_notes: This is the chest exercise most likely to irritate a shoulder, since the load peaks at end range. Keep the weight moderate, stop at torso level, and switch to a cable or pec deck if the shoulder complains.

grip_variations.name: Flat bench, palms facing
grip_variations.effect: The standard, even chest involvement.

grip_variations.name: Incline bench
grip_variations.effect: Biases the upper chest, usually the most comfortable version.

grip_variations.name: Slight rotation at the finish
grip_variations.effect: Adds a little contraction at the top where tension is otherwise lost.

content.summary: A cable pulldown with locked elbows, isolating the lats without the biceps.
content.description: Keeping the arms straight removes the elbow joint entirely, so the biceps cannot contribute and the lat has to bring the arm down on its own. That makes it the one lat exercise that never has the arms fail first, which is useful both as a pre-exhaust before pulling and as a finisher after it. The long head of the triceps also works to hold the elbow straight against the cable.
setup: Set a cable at head height or above and attach a straight bar or rope.
Stand a step back from the stack with the feet hip width.
Take the attachment with the arms straight and overhead in front of you.
Hinge slightly at the hips so the torso leans forward a little.
Brace the trunk and let the shoulders reach up at the start.
execution: Keep the elbows locked straight — nothing bends for the whole rep.
Pull the bar down in a wide arc by driving the shoulders down and back.
Bring the bar to the thighs and squeeze the lats for a beat.
Let the bar rise under control back overhead.
Allow the shoulders to reach up fully at the top of each rep.
cues: Elbows locked, shoulders do the work
Sweep the bar down in an arc

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows bending so it becomes a pushdown
common_mistakes.fix: Lock them straight and cut the load; the moment the elbow bends, the triceps take over and the lat stops being isolated.

common_mistakes.mistake: Standing too upright so the arc is cut short
common_mistakes.fix: Take a step back and hinge slightly forward so the bar has room to travel from overhead to the thighs.

common_mistakes.mistake: Going heavy and heaving with the whole body
common_mistakes.fix: Use a load light enough that only the shoulders move; this is a high-rep isolation, not a strength lift.

common_mistakes.mistake: Not letting the shoulders rise at the top
common_mistakes.fix: Allow the shoulder blades to travel up between reps so the lat is loaded in its stretched position.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using it as the only lat exercise
common_mistakes.fix: Programme it around rows and pulldowns rather than in place of them — it isolates well but loads lightly.

content.breathing: Exhale as the bar comes down, inhale as it returns overhead.
content.rom_notes: Full range is arms overhead with the shoulders reaching up to the bar at the thighs. The arc is the range — a short pull with bent elbows is a different exercise.
content.safety_notes: Light loads and a locked elbow keep this easy on the joints. If the shoulder pinches overhead at the start, lower the pulley slightly so the arms begin below head height.

grip_variations.name: Straight bar overhand
grip_variations.effect: The standard, easiest to keep the elbows locked.

grip_variations.name: Rope
grip_variations.effect: Allows the hands to split at the bottom for a stronger squeeze.

grip_variations.name: Single handle, one arm
grip_variations.effect: Longer range and exposes side-to-side differences.

content.summary: A one-arm lateral raise on a low cable, with tension held at the bottom.
content.description: A cable pulls from the side rather than straight down, so the side delt is loaded at the bottom of the range where a dumbbell gives almost nothing. That changes where the hard part of the rep sits and lets the muscle work through more of its range. Doing one arm at a time also allows a lean away from the stack, lengthening the delt further. Loads are small and that is normal.
setup: Set a cable to the lowest pulley and attach a single handle.
Stand side-on with the working arm furthest from the stack.
Take the handle in the outside hand so the cable crosses in front of the body.
Hold the frame with the free hand and lean slightly away from the stack.
Set a soft fixed bend in the working elbow and keep it there.
execution: Raise the arm out to the side, leading with the elbow.
Keep the shoulder pressed down rather than shrugging toward the ear.
Stop at roughly shoulder height.
Pause for a beat at the top.
Lower slowly, resisting the cable all the way back down past the hip.
cues: Fight the cable on the way down

common_mistakes.mistake: Going too heavy and swinging the body
common_mistakes.fix: Halve the load — the side delt is small and the cable version is harder than the dumbbell one, not easier.

common_mistakes.mistake: Shrugging the trap to lift the arm
common_mistakes.fix: Press the shoulder down before each rep and lighten the weight until the trap stays quiet.

common_mistakes.mistake: Raising above shoulder height
common_mistakes.fix: Stop level with the shoulder; higher hands over to the traps and increases impingement risk with no extra delt work.

common_mistakes.mistake: Letting the arm snap back down
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds on the descent — the constant cable tension on the way down is the reason to choose this over dumbbells.

common_mistakes.mistake: Doing more reps on the stronger side
common_mistakes.fix: Start with the weaker arm and match its rep count on the other side.

content.breathing: Exhale as you raise, inhale as you lower.
content.rom_notes: Full range is the hand past the opposite hip at the bottom to the arm at shoulder height. The extra range below the hip is what the cable adds over a dumbbell.
content.safety_notes: If the shoulder has an impingement history, stop below shoulder height and turn the thumb slightly up. Do not lean so far from the stack that the free hand is carrying you.

grip_variations.name: Behind the back, cable crossing in front
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most tension at the bottom.

grip_variations.name: Cable in front of the body
grip_variations.effect: Slightly shorter range, easier on a sensitive shoulder.

grip_variations.name: Thumb turned slightly up
grip_variations.effect: Reduces impingement for shoulders that pinch at the top.

content.summary: A guided lateral raise with pads on the upper arms and a fixed arc.
content.description: Pads against the upper arms mean the hands carry nothing, so the grip cannot become the limit and the elbow angle cannot drift. The fixed arc removes the swinging that ruins most dumbbell lateral raises, which makes this the easiest way to take the side delt genuinely close to failure. It is also the version to reach for when the shoulder is fussy, since the path is predictable and the seat back stops any body English.
setup: Set the seat so the shoulder joint lines up with the machine's pivot.
Sit with the back against the pad and both feet flat.
Place the upper arms against the pads with the elbows leading.
Rest the hands lightly on the handles without gripping hard.
Set the shoulders down away from the ears before the first rep.
execution: Push the pads outward and upward by driving with the elbows.
Raise to roughly shoulder height, following the machine's arc.
Pause for a beat at the top with the shoulders still pressed down.
Lower slowly, resisting the whole way.
Stop just short of the stack touching so tension stays on the delt.
cues: Push with the elbows, not the hands

common_mistakes.mistake: Seat set so the shoulder does not line up with the pivot
common_mistakes.fix: Adjust until the shoulder joint sits level with the machine's axis, otherwise the arc fights the joint through the whole set.

common_mistakes.mistake: Gripping the handles hard and pulling with the arms
common_mistakes.fix: Rest the hands lightly and push through the upper arm pads; the hands are there for position, not for lifting.

common_mistakes.mistake: Shrugging the traps to complete the rep
common_mistakes.fix: Press the shoulders down and cut the load until they stay down for the whole set.

common_mistakes.mistake: Letting the stack slam between reps
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds on the descent and stop just short of the plates touching.

common_mistakes.mistake: Loading it heavy because it feels stable
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the reps in the twelve to twenty range — the side delt is small regardless of how secure the machine feels.

content.breathing: Exhale as you raise, inhale as you lower.
content.rom_notes: Full range is arms at the sides to roughly shoulder height along the machine's arc. Seat height determines whether that arc matches your shoulder, so set it first.
content.safety_notes: The most controlled lateral raise available and the best option for a shoulder with an impingement history, since the path cannot drift. Stop below shoulder height if anything pinches.

grip_variations.name: Upper arms on the pads
grip_variations.effect: The standard, removes the grip entirely.

grip_variations.name: Hands on the handles
grip_variations.effect: Slightly longer lever, more demanding at the same load.

grip_variations.name: One arm at a time
grip_variations.effect: Exposes side-to-side differences and allows a longer pause.

content.summary: A straight-arm raise to the front, isolating the front delt.
content.description: Raising a weight from the thighs to eye level with a locked elbow puts the load squarely on the anterior deltoid. It is the most commonly overused isolation in the gym, because the front delt already works hard in every press and every push-up — most people need less of this, not more. Where it earns a place is in a programme light on pressing, or when the front delt is a specific lagging point.
setup: Stand with a dumbbell in each hand resting on the front of the thighs.
Set the feet hip width with the knees soft.
Squeeze the glutes and brace so the trunk cannot swing.
Set a soft fixed bend in the elbows and hold it.
Turn the palms down, or neutral if that suits the shoulder better.
execution: Raise one or both arms forward in a controlled arc.
Keep the elbow angle fixed throughout the rep.
Stop at roughly eye level, or shoulder height if the shoulder is sensitive.
Pause for a beat at the top.
Lower slowly back to the thighs, resisting the whole way.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaning back and swinging the weight up
common_mistakes.fix: Squeeze the glutes, brace the trunk, and halve the load — the swing means the low back is doing what the delt should.

common_mistakes.mistake: Programming it alongside heavy pressing volume
common_mistakes.fix: Drop it if you already press two or three times a week; the front delt is rarely the muscle that needs more work.

common_mistakes.mistake: Raising well above eye level
common_mistakes.fix: Stop at eye level — beyond that the traps take over and the shoulder gets no additional benefit.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows bending and straightening through the rep
common_mistakes.fix: Hold a soft fixed bend; if the arms have to pump, the weight is too heavy for an isolation.

common_mistakes.mistake: Palms fully pronated on a sensitive shoulder
common_mistakes.fix: Turn the palms neutral so the thumbs point up, which usually clears the pinch at the top.

content.breathing: Exhale as you raise, inhale as you lower.
content.rom_notes: Full range is the thighs to roughly eye level. Higher than that shifts the work to the traps rather than extending the useful range.
content.safety_notes: The overhead end of this movement is where shoulders pinch. Stop at shoulder height with a neutral grip if you have an impingement history, or skip it entirely — nothing here is unavailable elsewhere.

grip_variations.name: Dumbbells, palms down
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most front delt involvement.

grip_variations.name: Neutral grip, thumbs up
grip_variations.effect: Kinder to the shoulder, brings the upper chest in slightly.

grip_variations.name: Alternating arms
grip_variations.effect: Allows a longer pause per side and reduces the urge to swing.

content.summary: A bent-over fly with dumbbells, isolating the rear delts.
content.description: Hinging forward and opening the arms out to the sides loads the posterior deltoid, the smallest of the three delt heads and the one that pressing never touches. It matters for shoulder balance as much as for appearance, since the rear delt and the mid-back are what hold the shoulder blade in position against a chest-heavy programme. The bent-over position means the low back holds a hinge, so the loads stay light.
setup: Take a light dumbbell in each hand and stand with the feet hip width.
Hinge at the hips until the torso is close to parallel with the floor.
Let the arms hang straight down with the palms facing each other.
Set a soft fixed bend in the elbows.
Brace the trunk and keep the spine neutral rather than rounded.
execution: Raise the arms out to the sides in a wide arc.
Lead with the elbows and keep the angle fixed.
Stop when the arms are level with the torso.
Squeeze the shoulder blades lightly and pause for a beat.
Lower slowly back to the hang, resisting the whole way.
cues: Chest toward the floor, back flat

common_mistakes.mistake: Standing up out of the hinge as the set goes on
common_mistakes.fix: Hold the torso close to parallel for every rep; standing up removes the angle that puts the load on the rear delt.

common_mistakes.mistake: Back rounding under the hinge
common_mistakes.fix: Set the chest and keep the spine neutral, and switch to the machine version if the low back cannot hold the position.

common_mistakes.mistake: Going far too heavy and rowing the weights up
common_mistakes.fix: Cut the load until the arms can travel in a wide arc; a bent elbow pulling back is a row, not a fly.

common_mistakes.mistake: Shrugging the traps at the top
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the shoulders pressed away from the ears and think about the elbows moving, not the shoulder blades pinching hard.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rushing the reps with no control on the way down
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds lowering — with a small muscle and light weight, the controlled descent is most of the stimulus.

content.breathing: Exhale as the arms rise, inhale as they lower. Breathe normally rather than bracing hard, since the loads are light.
content.rom_notes: Full range is arms hanging straight down to level with the torso. Raising higher than the torso brings the traps and rhomboids in rather than the rear delt.
content.safety_notes: The hinged position loads the low back, so keep the weights light and switch to the machine or a chest-supported version if the back is fatigued or sore.

grip_variations.name: Neutral, palms facing each other
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most rear delt involvement.

grip_variations.name: Palms down, thumbs in
grip_variations.effect: Slightly more mid-trap and rhomboid.

grip_variations.name: Chest supported on an incline bench
grip_variations.effect: Removes the low back entirely and stops any swinging.

content.summary: A reverse pec deck, isolating the rear delts with the chest supported.
content.description: Sitting with the chest against a pad and sweeping the arms backwards gives the rear delt a clean fixed arc and takes the low back out entirely. That solves the main problem with dumbbell rear delt work, where holding a bent-over hinge for twenty reps tires the back long before the delt. Because nothing can be cheated and nothing has to be balanced, this is the version to use when the aim is simply to fatigue the muscle.
setup: Set the seat so the handles line up with the shoulders.
Sit facing the pad with the chest against it and both feet flat.
Set the start levers so the arms begin in front of the body, not stretched around it.
Take the handles with a soft fixed bend in the elbows.
Press the shoulders down away from the ears.
execution: Sweep the arms outward and back in a wide arc.
Lead with the elbows and keep the angle fixed.
Stop when the arms are level with the torso.
Squeeze for a beat with the shoulders still pressed down.
Return slowly under control without letting the stack rest.

common_mistakes.mistake: Chest lifting off the pad to finish the rep
common_mistakes.fix: Cut the load until the sternum stays in contact — coming off the pad is the only way to cheat this machine and it removes its main advantage.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows bending and straightening through the rep
common_mistakes.fix: Hold a soft fixed bend so it stays a fly; a pumping elbow turns it into a row.

common_mistakes.mistake: Seat set too high or low for the shoulders
common_mistakes.fix: Adjust until the handles line up with the shoulder joints so the arc runs level rather than up or down.

common_mistakes.mistake: Shrugging the traps to move the weight
common_mistakes.fix: Press the shoulders down before each rep and lower the load until they stay down.

common_mistakes.mistake: Letting the stack slam back between reps
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds on the return and stop just short of the plates touching.

content.breathing: Exhale as the arms sweep back, inhale as they return.
content.rom_notes: Full range is arms in front of the body to level with the torso. The start levers set the front position — do not stretch the arms behind the shoulders to chase extra range.
content.safety_notes: One of the safest exercises available and a good choice when the low back rules out bent-over rear delt work. Take it to failure freely; releasing the handles ends the set.

grip_variations.name: Neutral handles, thumbs up
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most rear delt involvement.

grip_variations.name: Palms down on horizontal handles
grip_variations.effect: Elbows travel higher, brings in the mid traps and rhomboids.

grip_variations.name: One arm at a time
grip_variations.effect: Longer range and exposes side-to-side differences.

content.summary: A vertical pull to the collarbones, working the side delts and traps.
content.description: Pulling a bar straight up the front of the body loads the lateral delt and the upper traps together, and it allows heavier loading than a lateral raise. It also has the worst reputation of any common exercise, because a narrow grip pulled to the chin drives the shoulder into internal rotation at the top — the classic impingement position. A wider grip stopped at chest height removes most of that problem and keeps the benefit.
setup: Take a barbell or EZ bar with an overhand grip at roughly shoulder width or wider.
Stand with the feet hip width and the bar resting against the thighs.
Squeeze the glutes and brace so the trunk cannot swing.
Set the shoulders down away from the ears.
Let the arms hang straight with the wrists relaxed.
execution: Pull the bar up the front of the body by driving the elbows out and up.
Keep the bar close, brushing the shirt as it rises.
Stop when the upper arms reach roughly shoulder height, with the bar around chest level.
Pause briefly at the top with the elbows level with or just below the shoulders.
Lower under control back to the thighs.

common_mistakes.mistake: Narrow grip pulled all the way to the chin
common_mistakes.fix: Widen to shoulder width or beyond and stop at chest height — the narrow high version is the single most impingement-prone position in the gym.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows travelling above the shoulders
common_mistakes.fix: Stop the pull when the upper arms reach shoulder level; past that the shoulder is internally rotated at end range under load.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bouncing the bar off the thighs with hip drive
common_mistakes.fix: Brace the glutes and trunk and cut the load until only the arms and shoulders move.

common_mistakes.mistake: Wrists bent hard over the bar
common_mistakes.fix: Use an EZ bar or dumbbells so the wrists can angle naturally instead of being forced into flexion.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pushing through shoulder pain because it is a standard exercise
common_mistakes.fix: Swap to lateral raises and shrugs, which cover the same muscles with none of the risk.

content.breathing: Exhale as the bar rises, inhale as it lowers.
content.rom_notes: Full range here is deliberately capped — thighs to the bar at chest height with the elbows no higher than the shoulders. Pulling to the chin is not more range, it is a worse position.
content.safety_notes: The most impingement-prone common exercise when done narrow and high. Use a wide grip, stop at chest height, and drop it entirely if you have a shoulder history — lateral raises and shrugs together cover the same ground safely.

grip_variations.name: Wide overhand, stopping at chest height
grip_variations.effect: The safest version, most lateral delt involvement.

grip_variations.name: EZ bar at shoulder width
grip_variations.effect: Kinder on the wrists, slightly more trap.

grip_variations.name: Dumbbells or a cable rope
grip_variations.effect: Lets the hands travel apart, which clears most of the impingement position.

content.summary: A straight vertical shrug with a barbell, loading the upper traps heavily.
content.description: Holding a heavy bar and lifting the shoulders straight up is the most direct trap exercise there is, and the traps tolerate very heavy loading — this is often the heaviest isolation anyone does. The whole movement happens at the shoulder blade, which means a range of a few inches; the temptation is to add weight until the shoulders barely move at all. Grip usually gives out first, which is why straps belong here.
setup: Set a bar in a rack at mid-thigh height, or deadlift it into position.
Take an overhand grip just outside the hips.
Stand tall with the feet hip width and the arms hanging straight.
Set the chest up and the spine neutral, with the bar resting against the thighs.
Brace the trunk before the first rep.
execution: Lift the shoulders straight up toward the ears.
Keep the arms completely straight — the elbows never bend.
Pause for a full beat at the top with the shoulders as high as they will go.
Lower slowly and let the shoulders travel all the way down.
Feel a stretch at the bottom before starting the next rep.
cues: Let the shoulders drop at the bottom

common_mistakes.mistake: Rolling the shoulders in a circle
common_mistakes.fix: Move straight up and straight down; the rolling motion adds a loaded shoulder rotation with no benefit to the trap.

common_mistakes.mistake: Loading so heavy the shoulders barely move
common_mistakes.fix: Cut the weight until the full few inches of range happens with a pause at the top — an inch of movement is not a rep.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bending the elbows and turning it into a partial row
common_mistakes.fix: Lock the arms straight and treat the hands purely as hooks.

common_mistakes.mistake: Grip failing before the traps do
common_mistakes.fix: Use straps on the working sets so the traps are the limiting factor, and train grip separately.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bouncing at the bottom with no stretch
common_mistakes.fix: Let the shoulders travel fully down and pause briefly before lifting again.

content.breathing: Inhale and brace at the bottom, exhale at the top of the shrug.
content.rom_notes: Full range is the shoulders fully depressed at the bottom to fully elevated at the top — a few inches in total. That short range is the exercise, but it has to be the whole few inches.
content.safety_notes: The bar hangs from the shoulders and loads the spine axially, so keep the trunk braced and the spine neutral. Use straps rather than a hook grip on heavy sets, and set the bar in a rack rather than deadlifting it repeatedly.

grip_variations.name: Overhand outside the hips
grip_variations.effect: The standard, heaviest loading.

grip_variations.name: Bar behind the back
grip_variations.effect: Keeps the shoulders back, more mid-trap, harder to set up.

grip_variations.name: Trap bar
grip_variations.effect: Load sits beside the body rather than in front, the most comfortable version.

content.summary: A shrug with a dumbbell in each hand, the load hanging beside the body.
content.description: With dumbbells the weight sits beside the hips rather than in front of them, which lets the shoulders travel straight up without the bar pushing them forward. The range is slightly longer than a barbell shrug and the shoulders sit in a more natural position, at the cost of the very heaviest loads. Each side also works independently, so a stronger trap cannot carry a weaker one through the set.
setup: Take a dumbbell in each hand and stand tall with the feet hip width.
Let the arms hang straight down with the weights beside the thighs.
Set the palms facing in toward the body.
Set the chest up with the spine neutral and the head level.
Brace the trunk and let the shoulders drop fully before the first rep.
execution: Lift both shoulders straight up toward the ears.
Keep the elbows locked straight throughout.
Pause for a full beat at the top.
Lower slowly and let the shoulders travel all the way back down.
Feel a stretch at the bottom before the next rep.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rolling the shoulders backwards at the top
common_mistakes.fix: Move straight up and down; the roll loads the shoulder in rotation and does nothing extra for the trap.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bouncing at the knees to launch the weights
common_mistakes.fix: Stand tall with the legs still and cut the load until only the shoulders move.

common_mistakes.mistake: No pause at the top
common_mistakes.fix: Hold the shrugged position for a full second — with a range this short, the pause is most of the tension.

common_mistakes.mistake: Grip giving out first
common_mistakes.fix: Use straps on the heavier sets so the traps are the limit rather than the fingers.

common_mistakes.mistake: Head jutting forward as the shoulders rise
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the chin tucked lightly and the head stacked over the shoulders.

content.breathing: Inhale at the bottom, exhale at the top of the shrug.
content.rom_notes: Full range is shoulders fully depressed to fully elevated. The dumbbell position beside the body gives a slightly longer range than a barbell.
content.safety_notes: Easier on the shoulders than a barbell shrug since the weights hang beside rather than in front of the body. Use straps on heavy sets and pick the dumbbells up with a hinge rather than a rounded back.

grip_variations.name: Neutral, weights beside the thighs
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most natural shoulder position.

grip_variations.name: Straps on heavy sets
grip_variations.effect: Removes the grip as the limiting factor.

grip_variations.name: One arm at a time holding a rack
grip_variations.effect: Longer range per side and exposes differences between traps.

content.summary: A light cable rotation outward, training the rotator cuff directly.
content.description: Rotating the forearm away from the body against a cable trains the small external rotators of the shoulder — infraspinatus and teres minor — which nothing else in a normal programme loads directly. They are the muscles that hold the head of the humerus centred while the big pressing muscles pull it forward, so keeping them strong is genuine shoulder maintenance. The loads involved are tiny and that is exactly right.
setup: Set a cable to elbow height and attach a single handle.
Stand side-on with the working arm furthest from the stack.
Take the handle across the body with the elbow tucked against the ribs.
Bend the elbow to 90 degrees and keep it pinned to the side.
Roll a towel between the elbow and the ribs if the elbow tends to drift.
execution: Rotate the forearm outward, away from the body.
Keep the elbow glued to the ribs and the upper arm still.
Stop when the forearm points straight ahead or slightly beyond.
Pause for a beat at the end of the rotation.
Return slowly across the body, resisting the cable the whole way.

common_mistakes.mistake: Going far too heavy and rowing the elbow back
common_mistakes.fix: Drop to the lightest plate on the stack — these muscles are tiny, and if the elbow leaves the ribs it has become a bad row.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbow drifting away from the side
common_mistakes.fix: Hold a rolled towel between the elbow and the ribs so any drift is obvious immediately.

common_mistakes.mistake: Torso twisting to complete the rotation
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the hips and shoulders square and let only the forearm move; if the body turns, the load is too heavy.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rushing through reps
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds returning across the body — the controlled phase is where the cuff actually works.

common_mistakes.mistake: Skipping it because it feels like nothing
common_mistakes.fix: Treat it as maintenance and put it at the end of pressing days; the point is not fatigue, it is keeping the cuff able to do its job.

content.breathing: Exhale as you rotate out, inhale as the arm returns. Breathe normally throughout — no bracing needed at these loads.
content.rom_notes: Full range is the forearm across the stomach to pointing straight ahead or slightly past. The upper arm never moves; if it does, the range being measured is not rotation.
content.safety_notes: One of the few exercises worth doing while a shoulder is recovering, provided the load is light and the range is pain free. Stop at the point where the rotation is comfortable rather than forcing the end range.

grip_variations.name: Elbow at the side, cable at elbow height
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most direct cuff work.

grip_variations.name: Elbow raised on a pad to 90 degrees
grip_variations.effect: Trains the rotation in the overhead position used by pressing and throwing.

grip_variations.name: Band instead of a cable
grip_variations.effect: Portable and self-limiting, ideal as a warm-up before pressing.

content.summary: A band stretched apart at chest height, training the rear delts and mid-back.
content.description: Holding a band at arm's length and pulling the hands apart loads the rear delts and rhomboids through a clean horizontal arc with almost no joint stress. It costs nothing, packs into a bag, and is the most commonly used warm-up for pressing days because it wakes up the muscles that hold the shoulder blade in place. Because band tension rises as it stretches, the hardest point is exactly where the muscle is shortest.
setup: Hold a light band with both hands, palms down, roughly shoulder width apart.
Raise the arms straight out in front at chest height.
Set a soft fixed bend in the elbows, or lock them straight.
Stand tall with the feet hip width and the ribs down.
Take up the slack so there is light tension before the first rep.
execution: Pull the hands apart, sweeping the arms out to the sides.
Keep the arms level with the chest through the whole arc.
Continue until the band touches the chest and the arms are level with the torso.
Squeeze the shoulder blades together for a full beat.
Return slowly, resisting the band all the way back to the start.
cues: Pull to the chest, not the neck
Squeeze the blades for a beat
Fight the band on the way back

common_mistakes.mistake: Band too heavy so the elbows bend to finish
common_mistakes.fix: Use a lighter band — the elbow angle must stay fixed, and a bent arm turns the movement into a short row.

common_mistakes.mistake: Arms drifting up toward the neck
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the hands level with the sternum so the arc runs horizontally across the chest.

common_mistakes.mistake: Letting the band snap back
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds returning; the band pulls hardest at the end, and the controlled return is half the work.

common_mistakes.mistake: Shrugging the traps to open the arms
common_mistakes.fix: Press the shoulders down away from the ears and lighten the band until they stay there.

common_mistakes.mistake: Ribs flaring and back arching to help
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the ribs pulled down over the hips and let only the arms move.

content.breathing: Exhale as the hands pull apart, inhale as they return. Breathe normally throughout.
content.rom_notes: Full range is hands together at arm's length to the band touching the chest with the arms level with the torso. Log the band colour or thickness — that is the load setting.
content.safety_notes: About as safe as an exercise gets, and one of the few worth doing daily. Check the band for nicks or thin spots before each session, since a band that snaps at chest height snaps toward the face.

grip_variations.name: Palms down at chest height
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most rear delt and rhomboid.

grip_variations.name: Palms up
grip_variations.effect: Shifts the emphasis toward the lower traps.

grip_variations.name: Overhead diagonal pull
grip_variations.effect: Adds external rotation and works the lower traps in an overhead position.

content.summary: The standard two-handed biceps curl with a straight bar.
content.description: A straight bar lets both arms work together and allows the heaviest loading of any curl, which is why it remains the reference biceps exercise. The fixed straight grip holds the forearms fully supinated, the position where the biceps is strongest, but also the position that puts the most strain on the wrist and the inner elbow. Anyone whose elbows complain here usually finds the EZ bar solves it entirely.
setup: Take a barbell with an underhand grip at roughly shoulder width.
Stand tall with the feet hip width and the bar resting against the thighs.
Set the elbows lightly against the sides of the torso.
Squeeze the glutes and brace the trunk so the body cannot swing.
Set the shoulders down and back before the first rep.
execution: Curl the bar upward by bending only at the elbows.
Keep the upper arms still and pinned to the sides.
Bring the bar to roughly chest height and pause for a beat.
Lower slowly under control until the arms are fully straight.
Pause briefly at the bottom before the next rep.
cues: All the way straight at the bottom

common_mistakes.mistake: Swinging the bar up with the hips and low back
common_mistakes.fix: Squeeze the glutes, brace the trunk and cut the load until only the elbows move — the swing is the low back doing the biceps' job.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows drifting forward at the top
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the upper arms pinned to the sides; once the elbows travel forward the front delt takes over and the biceps stops working.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stopping short of straight arms at the bottom
common_mistakes.fix: Straighten the arms fully every rep — the lengthened position is a large part of the stimulus and cutting it inflates the rep count.

common_mistakes.mistake: Wrists bending back under the bar
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the wrists stacked in line with the forearms, and switch to an EZ bar if they will not stay there.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pushing through inner elbow pain
common_mistakes.fix: Move to the EZ bar or dumbbells, which let the forearm rotate slightly and usually clear the symptom in one session.

content.breathing: Exhale as you curl, inhale as you lower.
content.rom_notes: Full range is arms fully straight to the bar at chest height with the elbows still at the sides. Curling higher than that only moves the shoulders.
content.safety_notes: The fixed supinated grip loads the wrist and the inner elbow, which is where problems show up first. Switch to an EZ bar at the first sign of elbow discomfort rather than training through it.

grip_variations.name: Shoulder width underhand
grip_variations.effect: The standard, balanced biceps involvement.

grip_variations.name: Narrow grip
grip_variations.effect: Slightly more outer biceps, harder on the wrists.

grip_variations.name: Wide grip
grip_variations.effect: More inner biceps, often more comfortable for wide shoulders.

content.summary: A barbell curl on a cambered bar, easier on the wrists and elbows.
content.description: The bends in an EZ bar let the hands sit at a slight angle rather than fully supinated, which takes most of the strain off the wrist and the inner elbow while keeping nearly all of the biceps involvement. For most people it is simply a better barbell curl — the small loss in biceps leverage is more than repaid by being able to train the movement without joint pain. It is the default choice for anyone with cranky elbows.
setup: Take an EZ bar on the inner angled sections with an underhand grip.
Stand tall with the feet hip width and the bar against the thighs.
Set the elbows lightly against the sides of the torso.
Brace the trunk and squeeze the glutes so nothing can swing.
Check the wrists sit in line with the forearms.
execution: Curl the bar up by bending only at the elbows.
Keep the upper arms pinned to the sides throughout.
Bring the bar to chest height and pause for a beat.
Lower slowly until the arms are completely straight.
Hold the bottom briefly before the next rep.
cues: Wrists in line with the forearms

common_mistakes.mistake: Heaving the bar with the hips
common_mistakes.fix: Brace the trunk and drop the weight until only the elbows move; a strict curl looks boring and works better.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows sliding forward as the bar rises
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the upper arms still against the sides — elbows travelling forward hands the work to the front delt.

common_mistakes.mistake: Gripping the outer bends and losing the angle
common_mistakes.fix: Hold the inner angled sections so the wrists sit at the intended tilt, which is the whole point of the bar.

common_mistakes.mistake: Half reps at the bottom
common_mistakes.fix: Straighten the arms fully every rep and reduce the load rather than the range.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming it is a lighter exercise than the straight bar
common_mistakes.fix: Expect similar loads and log it separately, since grip angle changes leverage slightly.

content.breathing: Exhale on the way up, inhale on the way down.
content.rom_notes: Full range is straight arms to the bar at chest height with the elbows still at the sides.
content.safety_notes: The most joint-friendly barbell curl and the first swap to try when the wrist or inner elbow complains on a straight bar. If pain persists on the EZ bar too, move to dumbbells or a hammer curl.

grip_variations.name: Inner angled sections, underhand
grip_variations.effect: The standard, kindest on the wrist and elbow.

grip_variations.name: Wide on the outer bends
grip_variations.effect: Closer to a straight bar position, more inner biceps.

grip_variations.name: Overhand on the same bar
grip_variations.effect: Becomes a reverse curl, shifting the work to the forearm.

content.summary: A two-dumbbell curl with the wrists free to rotate.
content.description: With a dumbbell in each hand the forearm can start neutral and turn as it rises, which adds the supination the biceps performs alongside elbow flexion — the muscle does both, and a fixed bar only trains one. Each side also works independently, so a stronger arm cannot quietly carry a weaker one. It is the most adaptable curl: alternating, simultaneous, seated, standing, all from the same pair of weights.
setup: Stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand and the arms hanging at the sides.
Start with the palms facing in toward the thighs.
Set the elbows lightly against the sides of the torso.
Squeeze the glutes and brace the trunk.
Set the shoulders down and back.
execution: Curl one or both weights upward, bending only at the elbow.
Rotate the palm to face upward as the forearm passes halfway.
Bring the weight to shoulder height and squeeze for a beat with the palm fully turned up.
Lower slowly, reversing the rotation back to neutral.
Straighten the arm fully at the bottom before the next rep.
cues: Turn the palm up as you curl

common_mistakes.mistake: Swinging the torso to launch the weights
common_mistakes.fix: Brace hard and cut the load; if the body has to move, the weight is heavier than the biceps can curl.

common_mistakes.mistake: Never rotating the wrist
common_mistakes.fix: Turn the palm from neutral to fully up during the rep — the supination is what the dumbbell offers over a bar.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows drifting forward at the top
