common_mistakes.fix: Keep the upper arms pinned to the sides so the delt cannot take over.

common_mistakes.mistake: Curling both weights but only watching one
common_mistakes.fix: Alternate arms so each rep gets attention, or use a mirror to check both sides move at the same speed.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stopping halfway down between reps
common_mistakes.fix: Let the arm straighten completely each time to load the biceps in its lengthened position.

content.breathing: Exhale as you curl, inhale as you lower.
content.rom_notes: Full range is a straight arm with the palm neutral to the weight at shoulder height with the palm fully supinated. The rotation is part of the rep.
content.safety_notes: The free wrist makes this the most joint-friendly of the standing curls. If the elbow complains even here, switch to hammer curls, which remove the supination entirely.

grip_variations.name: Rotating from neutral to supinated
grip_variations.effect: The standard, trains both jobs of the biceps.

grip_variations.name: Palms up the whole way
grip_variations.effect: Closer to a barbell curl, slightly more inner elbow strain.

grip_variations.name: Alternating arms
grip_variations.effect: Allows a longer squeeze per side and reduces the urge to swing.

content.summary: A curl with the palms facing in throughout, targeting the brachialis and forearm.
content.description: Holding the dumbbells like hammers keeps the forearm neutral, which takes the biceps out of its strongest position and puts the brachialis and brachioradialis in charge. The brachialis sits underneath the biceps, so building it pushes the biceps upward and adds visible arm thickness that curls alone will not. The neutral grip is also the kindest position for the wrist and elbow, which makes this the curl that survives when others hurt.
setup: Stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand and the palms facing in.
Let the arms hang straight with the weights beside the thighs.
Set the elbows lightly against the sides of the torso.
Brace the trunk and squeeze the glutes.
Keep the wrists straight and firm.
execution: Curl the weight upward keeping the palm facing inward the whole time.
Bend only at the elbow, with the upper arm still.
Bring the dumbbell to shoulder height and pause for a beat.
Lower slowly to a completely straight arm.
Keep the wrist neutral throughout — no rotation at any point.

common_mistakes.mistake: Letting the palm rotate up as the weight rises
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the thumb pointing at the ceiling for the whole rep; any rotation hands the work back to the biceps.

common_mistakes.mistake: Swinging the weights with the body
common_mistakes.fix: Brace the trunk and reduce the load — the neutral grip allows more weight than a supinated curl, but not that much more.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows travelling forward at the top
common_mistakes.fix: Hold the upper arms against the sides so the shoulder cannot help.

common_mistakes.mistake: Wrists bending back under the load
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the wrist stacked in line with the forearm and grip firmly so the weight cannot tip it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating it as an optional extra
common_mistakes.fix: Programme it alongside supinated curls — the brachialis is a genuine contributor to arm size and nothing else trains it as directly.

content.breathing: Exhale as you curl, inhale as you lower.
content.rom_notes: Full range is a straight arm to the weight at shoulder height with the palm still facing in. Any supination means it has become a different exercise.
content.safety_notes: The most joint-friendly curl available, and the one to keep when the wrist or elbow rules out supinated curling. Cross-body hammer curls are an option if the shoulder prefers that path.

grip_variations.name: Neutral, straight up
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most brachialis and brachioradialis.

grip_variations.name: Cross-body toward the opposite shoulder
grip_variations.effect: More brachialis, often more comfortable for the shoulder.

grip_variations.name: Rope on a cable
grip_variations.effect: Constant tension throughout and a neutral wrist.

content.summary: A curl lying back on an incline bench, with the arms hanging behind the body.
content.description: Reclining the bench lets the arms hang behind the torso, which stretches the long head of the biceps before the rep even starts — that head crosses the shoulder, so it is only fully lengthened when the arm is behind the body. Loading a muscle in its stretched position is a strong growth stimulus, and no other curl reaches it. The trade-off is that the bottom of the rep is genuinely hard, so the weights drop.
setup: Set a bench to roughly 45 to 60 degrees.
Sit back with a dumbbell in each hand and the whole back against the pad.
Let the arms hang straight down behind the line of the torso.
Start with the palms facing forward or neutral.
Plant both feet flat and keep the shoulders back on the pad.
execution: Curl the weight upward bending only at the elbow.
Keep the upper arm hanging back — the elbow does not travel forward.
Rotate the palm fully up as the forearm rises, if starting neutral.
Squeeze at the top for a beat.
Lower slowly all the way back to the hanging stretch.
cues: Let the arms hang behind you
Elbows stay back the whole rep
Feel the stretch at the bottom

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows swinging forward to make the rep easier
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the upper arms hanging behind the torso; the moment they swing forward, the stretch that makes this exercise worth doing is gone.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bench set too upright
common_mistakes.fix: Recline to 45 to 60 degrees so the arms genuinely hang behind the body rather than straight down.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the same weight as a standing curl
common_mistakes.fix: Expect noticeably less — the stretched start position removes the easiest part of the range.

common_mistakes.mistake: Shoulders rolling forward off the pad
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the shoulder blades pinned to the bench so the stretch stays in the biceps rather than the shoulder.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rushing the descent
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds lowering into the stretch, which is where the stimulus concentrates.

content.breathing: Exhale as you curl, inhale as you lower into the stretch.
content.rom_notes: Full range is arms hanging behind the torso to the weights at shoulder height. Record the bench angle, since it determines how much stretch the start position gives.
content.safety_notes: The stretched start loads the biceps tendon at the shoulder, so build up gradually and keep the weights moderate. If the front of the shoulder complains, raise the bench angle a notch.

grip_variations.name: Supinated throughout
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most stretch on the long head.

grip_variations.name: Rotating from neutral
grip_variations.effect: Adds supination and is easier on the elbow at the bottom.

grip_variations.name: One arm at a time
grip_variations.effect: Allows a longer pause and exposes side-to-side differences.

content.summary: A curl with the upper arms fixed on an angled pad, removing all body English.
content.description: Resting the upper arms on a sloped pad locks the elbows in place, so nothing can swing and the shoulder cannot contribute — what moves the weight is the biceps or nothing. The pad angle also loads the bottom of the range hard, which makes the stretched position the difficult part rather than the easy one. It is the strictest curl there is and the most humbling in terms of weight used.
setup: Set the seat so the top of the pad sits under the armpits.
Rest the upper arms flat on the pad with the chest against the top edge.
Take an EZ bar or dumbbells with an underhand grip.
Let the arms straighten fully so the pad supports them throughout.
Plant both feet flat and sit tall.
execution: Curl the bar upward, bending only at the elbows.
Keep the upper arms flat against the pad for the whole rep.
Bring the bar up until the forearms are roughly vertical and squeeze.
Lower slowly and under full control.
Straighten the arms completely at the bottom without dropping the weight.
cues: Armpits on the top of the pad
Control the last inch at the bottom

common_mistakes.mistake: Letting the weight drop fast into the straight-arm position
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds on the descent — the bottom of a preacher curl is the most stretched and most vulnerable point for the biceps tendon.

common_mistakes.mistake: Lifting the upper arms off the pad to finish
common_mistakes.fix: Keep them flat and cut the load; peeling off the pad reintroduces exactly the cheating this bench removes.

common_mistakes.mistake: Seat set too low so the armpits sit above the pad
common_mistakes.fix: Raise the seat until the top edge is under the armpits and the chest rests against it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Loading it like a standing curl
common_mistakes.fix: Expect considerably less weight; with no swing and a hard bottom position, the numbers are simply lower.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stopping short of a straight arm
common_mistakes.fix: Straighten fully each rep under control — the full range is the reason to use this bench.

content.breathing: Exhale as you curl, inhale as you lower.
content.rom_notes: Full range is arms straight along the pad to the forearms roughly vertical. Curling past vertical unloads the biceps entirely and is just a rest.
content.safety_notes: The straight-arm bottom position under load is where biceps tendon strains happen. Never drop into it — control the last portion of every descent and warm up before heavy sets.

grip_variations.name: EZ bar, inner angled grip
grip_variations.effect: The standard, kindest on the wrists.

grip_variations.name: Straight bar
grip_variations.effect: Fully supinated, more biceps but harder on the elbows.

grip_variations.name: Single dumbbell, one arm at a time
grip_variations.effect: Allows a longer squeeze and exposes side-to-side differences.

content.summary: A biceps curl against a low cable, with tension held through the whole range.
content.description: A cable pulls with the same force at every point, so unlike a dumbbell there is no easy top position where the load falls off. The biceps stays under tension from the straight arm to the full squeeze, which makes this an efficient way to accumulate work without heavy loading. Swapping the attachment or the pulley height changes the angle in seconds, so one station covers several variations.
setup: Attach a straight bar, EZ bar or rope to the lowest pulley.
Stand a step back from the stack with the feet hip width.
Take the attachment with an underhand grip and let the arms hang straight.
Set the elbows lightly against the sides of the torso.
Brace the trunk so the body cannot lean back.
execution: Curl the attachment upward by bending only at the elbows.
Keep the upper arms still against the sides.
Bring the hands to chest height and squeeze for a beat.
Lower slowly, resisting the cable the whole way.
Straighten the arms fully at the bottom without letting the stack rest.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaning back so the cable pulls you into a row
common_mistakes.fix: Stand tall with the trunk braced and step closer to the stack; if the body has to lean, the load is too heavy.

common_mistakes.mistake: Letting the stack touch down between reps
common_mistakes.fix: Stop just short at the bottom so the constant tension — the main reason to use a cable — is not lost each rep.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows drifting forward at the top
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the upper arms at the sides so the front delt cannot take over.

common_mistakes.mistake: Standing too close so the cable goes slack at the bottom
common_mistakes.fix: Take a half step back until there is tension from the very first inch of the rep.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using only one attachment forever
common_mistakes.fix: Rotate between straight bar, EZ bar and rope so the wrist angle and emphasis vary across the week.

content.breathing: Exhale as you curl, inhale as you lower.
content.rom_notes: Full range is straight arms to the hands at chest height with the elbows still at the sides. Log the attachment used, since the wrist angle changes with each.
content.safety_notes: Light and joint-friendly, and a reasonable option when a wrist or elbow will not tolerate a fixed bar. Check the attachment is clipped in before the first rep.

grip_variations.name: Straight bar underhand
grip_variations.effect: The standard, fully supinated, most biceps.

grip_variations.name: EZ bar attachment
grip_variations.effect: Angled wrists, kinder on the elbows.

grip_variations.name: Rope, neutral grip
grip_variations.effect: Becomes a hammer-style curl, more brachialis.

content.summary: A seated one-arm curl with the elbow braced against the inner thigh.
content.description: Bracing the elbow on the inside of the thigh locks the upper arm completely, so the biceps works in total isolation with nothing else able to contribute. Working one arm at a time and being able to watch the whole rep makes it the easiest curl to feel and control, which is why it appears at the end of arm sessions rather than the start. Loads are small and the point is the squeeze, not the number.
setup: Sit on the end of a bench with the feet wide and flat.
Take a dumbbell in one hand and lean forward from the hips.
Brace the back of that upper arm against the inside of the same-side thigh.
Let the arm hang straight down with the palm facing forward.
Rest the free hand on the other thigh for support.
execution: Curl the weight upward, bending only at the elbow.
Keep the upper arm pressed into the thigh throughout.
Bring the dumbbell toward the opposite shoulder.
Squeeze hard at the top for a full beat.
Lower slowly all the way to a straight arm.
cues: Elbow stays welded to the thigh

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbow sliding up the thigh as the weight rises
common_mistakes.fix: Press the upper arm into the leg and cut the load; a sliding elbow means the shoulder has joined in.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rocking the torso to help each rep
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the free hand braced and the chest still, and lower the weight until only the forearm moves.

common_mistakes.mistake: Going heavy to match other curls
common_mistakes.fix: Use a much lighter dumbbell — this is a finisher built around the squeeze, not a loading exercise.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stopping short of a straight arm
common_mistakes.fix: Let the arm extend fully at the bottom of every rep before curling again.

common_mistakes.mistake: Doing more reps on the dominant arm
common_mistakes.fix: Start with the weaker arm and match its rep count exactly on the other side.

content.breathing: Exhale as you curl, inhale as you lower.
content.rom_notes: Full range is a straight arm to the dumbbell near the opposite shoulder, with the elbow fixed on the thigh throughout.
content.safety_notes: Very low risk given the light loads and the braced arm. Hinge from the hips rather than rounding the low back to reach the starting position.

grip_variations.name: Supinated, palm up
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most biceps peak involvement.

grip_variations.name: Rotating from neutral
grip_variations.effect: Adds supination through the rep.

grip_variations.name: Cable version standing
grip_variations.effect: Keeps constant tension and removes the need to brace on a thigh.

content.summary: A guided biceps curl with the arms on a pad and a fixed arc.
content.description: The pad holds the upper arms and the machine fixes the path, so the only variable left is how hard the biceps pulls. That makes it the simplest curl to learn, the safest to take to failure alone, and a sensible finisher when the grip and the rest of the body are already tired from heavier work. The cam on most machines also keeps the resistance more even through the range than a free weight manages.
setup: Set the seat so the elbows line up with the machine's pivot.
Sit with the chest against the top of the pad and both feet flat.
Rest the upper arms flat on the pad.
Take the handles with an underhand grip and the wrists stacked.
Let the arms straighten fully before the first rep.
execution: Curl the handles upward along the machine's arc.
Keep the upper arms flat on the pad throughout.
Squeeze for a beat at the top of the movement.
Lower slowly under control to straight arms.
Stop just short of the stack touching between reps.

common_mistakes.mistake: Seat set so the elbows sit off the machine's pivot
common_mistakes.fix: Adjust the seat until the elbow lines up with the axis, otherwise the arc fights the joint all set.

common_mistakes.mistake: Letting the stack slam down each rep
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds on the descent and stop just short of the plates touching.

common_mistakes.mistake: Lifting the upper arms off the pad
common_mistakes.fix: Keep them flat and reduce the load; peeling off the pad brings the shoulders in.

common_mistakes.mistake: Half reps at the bottom
common_mistakes.fix: Straighten the arms fully every rep and drop the weight rather than shortening the range.

common_mistakes.mistake: Gripping the handles so hard the forearms cramp
common_mistakes.fix: Hold firmly but not maximally; the machine guides the path so the grip does not have to stabilise.

content.breathing: Exhale as you curl, inhale as you lower.
content.rom_notes: Full range is straight arms to the handles at the top of the arc. Seat height determines whether that arc matches your elbow, so set it before loading.
content.safety_notes: One of the safest curls to take to failure alone, since releasing the handles ends the set. Check the seat pin is fully engaged before starting.

grip_variations.name: Underhand on the handles
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most biceps involvement.

grip_variations.name: Neutral handles where fitted
grip_variations.effect: More brachialis, kinder on the wrist.

grip_variations.name: One arm at a time
grip_variations.effect: Exposes side-to-side differences and allows a longer squeeze.

content.summary: A curl with an overhand grip, shifting the work to the forearm and brachioradialis.
content.description: Turning the hands over puts the biceps in its weakest position and hands the job to the brachioradialis, the muscle that runs along the thumb side of the forearm. It builds the part of the arm that shows between the elbow and the wrist, and it strengthens grip in a way supinated curls do not. Loads are much lighter than a normal curl and the wrists have to hold the bar against gravity throughout.
setup: Take a barbell or EZ bar with an overhand grip at roughly shoulder width.
Stand tall with the feet hip width and the bar resting against the thighs.
Set the elbows lightly against the sides of the torso.
Brace the trunk and squeeze the glutes so nothing can swing.
Set the wrists straight, in line with the forearms.
execution: Curl the bar upward by bending only at the elbows.
Keep the knuckles pointing up and the wrists locked straight.
Bring the bar to chest height and pause for a beat.
Lower slowly under control to fully straight arms.
Do not let the wrists collapse downward at any point.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the same weight as a supinated curl
common_mistakes.fix: Expect roughly half — the overhand grip removes the biceps' leverage and the forearm cannot make up the difference.

common_mistakes.mistake: Wrists dropping so the bar hangs below the knuckles
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the wrists locked in line with the forearms; a collapsed wrist takes the brachioradialis out and strains the joint.

common_mistakes.mistake: Swinging the bar with the body
common_mistakes.fix: Brace the trunk and cut the load until only the elbows move.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows drifting forward at the top
common_mistakes.fix: Hold the upper arms against the sides so the shoulders cannot contribute.

common_mistakes.mistake: Skipping it because the weights look small
common_mistakes.fix: Judge it by forearm fatigue rather than the number on the bar; this is the only common exercise that loads the brachioradialis directly.

content.breathing: Exhale as you curl, inhale as you lower.
content.rom_notes: Full range is straight arms to the bar at chest height with the wrists locked straight. A dropping wrist is not extra range, it is a lost rep.
content.safety_notes: The overhand grip loads the wrist in extension, so use an EZ bar if the wrists complain on a straight one. Keep the loads light — this is a forearm exercise, not a strength lift.

grip_variations.name: Straight bar overhand
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most brachioradialis involvement.

grip_variations.name: EZ bar overhand
grip_variations.effect: Angles the wrists slightly, much kinder on the joint.

grip_variations.name: Cable with a straight bar
grip_variations.effect: Constant tension and easier to keep the wrists locked.

content.summary: A cable pushdown on a rope, with the hands splitting apart at the bottom.
content.description: A rope lets the hands travel apart at the end of the rep, which allows a harder contraction than a fixed bar because the forearms can rotate outward as the elbow straightens. Constant cable tension means the triceps works from the top of the rep to the bottom with no easy portion. It is the most common triceps exercise for good reason — easy to set up, easy to control, and it can be pushed to failure without any risk.
setup: Attach a rope to a high pulley and set the weight.
Take an end in each hand with the palms facing each other.
Stand a half step back with the feet hip width and a slight forward lean.
Pin the elbows against the sides of the torso.
Brace the trunk so the body cannot rock.
execution: Push the rope down by straightening the elbows.
Keep the upper arms completely still against the sides.
As the arms straighten, pull the rope ends apart and slightly back.
Squeeze the triceps hard for a beat at full extension.
Let the rope rise under control until the forearms are past parallel.
cues: Split the rope at the bottom

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaning over the weight and pushing with the whole body
common_mistakes.fix: Stand tall with a slight lean and cut the load until only the elbows move; the body drop is the shoulders doing the work.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows drifting forward and down through the rep
common_mistakes.fix: Pin the upper arms to the sides — travelling elbows turn the pushdown into a partial press.

common_mistakes.mistake: Not splitting the rope at the bottom
common_mistakes.fix: Pull the ends apart as the arms straighten; that spread is the reason to choose a rope over a bar.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stopping the return at a right angle
common_mistakes.fix: Let the forearms rise past parallel each rep so the triceps is loaded through its full range.

common_mistakes.mistake: Doing only pushdowns for triceps
common_mistakes.fix: Add an overhead extension too — pushdowns keep the shoulder neutral, so the long head never gets a stretch.

content.breathing: Exhale as you push down, inhale as the rope returns.
content.rom_notes: Full range is forearms past parallel at the top to full elbow lockout with the hands split at the bottom. This never stretches the long head, which is what overhead work is for.
content.safety_notes: Among the lowest-risk exercises in the gym and safe to take to failure alone. If the elbow feels pinched at lockout, ease off the very end of the range slightly.

grip_variations.name: Rope, hands splitting at the bottom
grip_variations.effect: The standard, strongest contraction at lockout.

grip_variations.name: Straight bar overhand
grip_variations.effect: Allows more weight, less spread at the finish.

grip_variations.name: V-bar
grip_variations.effect: A middle ground, comfortable wrists and heavier loading than a rope.

content.summary: A triceps extension with the arms overhead, stretching the long head.
content.description: The long head of the triceps crosses the shoulder, so it is only fully stretched when the arm is raised overhead — a position no pushdown reaches. Extending from behind the head loads that stretched position directly, which is why overhead work belongs alongside pushdowns rather than instead of them. It asks for enough shoulder range to get the arms vertical without the ribs flaring, and the elbows have to stay narrow.
setup: Take a single dumbbell in both hands, or one in each hand.
Sit on an upright bench or stand with the feet hip width.
Press the weight overhead until the arms are straight.
Set the elbows pointing forward and close to the head.
Brace the trunk and pull the ribs down over the hips.
execution: Lower the weight behind the head by bending only at the elbows.
Keep the upper arms vertical and the elbows narrow throughout.
Descend until the forearms are past parallel and the triceps is stretched.
Press back up to straight arms without the elbows flaring out.
Squeeze at the top for a beat before the next rep.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows flaring wide as the weight lowers
common_mistakes.fix: Keep them pointing forward and close to the head; flared elbows shorten the range and shift the load off the long head.

common_mistakes.mistake: Low back arching to get the arms overhead
common_mistakes.fix: Pull the ribs down and brace, and sit with a back pad if the position cannot be held standing.

common_mistakes.mistake: Upper arms drifting forward so it becomes a press
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the upper arms vertical for the whole rep — only the forearms should travel.

common_mistakes.mistake: Going too heavy behind the head
common_mistakes.fix: Use a load you can control at the deepest point; the weight sits behind the skull and there is no safe way to bail.

common_mistakes.mistake: Skipping it because pushdowns feel easier
common_mistakes.fix: Keep one overhead movement in the week — without it the long head never trains in a stretched position.

content.breathing: Inhale as the weight lowers behind the head, exhale as you press up.
content.rom_notes: Full range is arms straight overhead to the forearms well past parallel behind the head. The deep stretch is the point of the exercise.
content.safety_notes: The weight travels behind the head, so use a load you can control at the bottom and have a spotter or use a cable if going heavy. Needs enough shoulder range to get the arms vertical — use a cable from a low pulley if not.

grip_variations.name: Single dumbbell in both hands
grip_variations.effect: The standard, easiest to keep the elbows narrow.

grip_variations.name: Rope on a low cable, facing away
grip_variations.effect: Constant tension and no need to control a weight behind the head.

grip_variations.name: One arm at a time
grip_variations.effect: Longer range and exposes side-to-side differences.

content.summary: A lying triceps extension where the bar lowers toward the forehead.
content.description: Lying on a bench with the arms angled slightly back puts the triceps under a strong stretch while still allowing decent loading, which makes it the best compromise between the deep range of overhead work and the heavy loading of a pushdown. It has a blunt reputation for elbow irritation, most of which comes from using a straight bar and from letting the bar drop rather than lowering it. An EZ bar solves most of it.
setup: Lie on a flat bench with an EZ bar held at arms length over the chest.
Take the inner angled sections with an overhand grip.
Plant both feet flat and set the shoulder blades back.
Angle the arms back slightly so the bar sits over the forehead rather than the chest.
Set the elbows at shoulder width and keep them there.
execution: Lower the bar by bending only at the elbows.
Bring it toward the forehead or just behind the head.
Keep the upper arms fixed at their angle — they do not travel.
Descend until the triceps is stretched, then press back to straight arms.
Stop just short of a hard lockout to keep tension on the muscle.
cues: Lower to the forehead, not the chest

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows flaring out as the bar lowers
common_mistakes.fix: Keep them at shoulder width; flaring makes it a close-grip press and takes the load off the triceps.

common_mistakes.mistake: Upper arms swinging back and forth
common_mistakes.fix: Fix the upper arm angle at the start and let only the forearms move, cutting the load if they will not stay put.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using a straight bar with sore elbows
common_mistakes.fix: Switch to an EZ bar or dumbbells so the wrists can angle slightly, which clears most elbow complaints.

common_mistakes.mistake: Lowering the bar to the chest
common_mistakes.fix: Aim for the forehead or just behind the head; a bar to the chest is a press and the triceps stops being isolated.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dropping fast into the bottom position
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds down — the bar is travelling toward your face and the stretched elbow is the vulnerable point.

content.breathing: Inhale as the bar lowers, exhale as you press back up.
content.rom_notes: Full range is straight arms to the bar at or just behind the forehead. Stopping just short of hard lockout keeps tension on the triceps.
content.safety_notes: The bar travels toward the head, so control the descent and use a spotter on heavy sets. Use an EZ bar or dumbbells rather than a straight bar if the elbows are sensitive, and never let the bar fall into the bottom.

grip_variations.name: EZ bar, inner angled grip
grip_variations.effect: The standard, kindest on the wrists and elbows.

grip_variations.name: Dumbbells, neutral grip
grip_variations.effect: Each arm works independently and the wrist is free.

grip_variations.name: Lowering behind the head instead of to the forehead
grip_variations.effect: Longer range and more stretch on the long head.

content.summary: A bodyweight dip with the hands behind you on a bench and the feet in front.
content.description: Sitting on the edge of a bench, sliding forward and lowering between the hands loads the triceps with bodyweight and needs nothing but a bench. It is genuinely accessible, which is its main virtue. It is also the most shoulder-unfriendly triceps exercise in common use, because the hands are fixed behind the body and the shoulder is forced into internal rotation and extension at the same time — a position that irritates a lot of shoulders.
setup: Sit on the edge of a bench and place the hands beside the hips, fingers forward.
Slide the hips forward off the bench so the weight is on the arms.
Set the feet flat on the floor with the knees bent for the easier version.
Keep the hips close to the bench rather than out in front.
Push the shoulders down away from the ears.
execution: Bend the elbows and lower the hips straight down.
Keep the elbows tracking straight back, not flaring out.
Descend until the upper arms are roughly parallel to the floor.
Stop at the depth where the shoulder stays comfortable.
Press back up to straight arms without shrugging.
cues: Hips brush the bench on the way down
Shoulders down away from the ears

common_mistakes.mistake: Dropping far below parallel
common_mistakes.fix: Stop when the upper arms reach parallel; deeper puts the shoulder in the position most likely to cause an impingement problem.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hips travelling forward away from the bench
common_mistakes.fix: Keep them brushing the edge so the load stays on the triceps rather than swinging on the shoulder.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows flaring out to the sides
common_mistakes.fix: Track them straight back behind you, which keeps the triceps loaded and the shoulder in a better position.

common_mistakes.mistake: Continuing when the front of the shoulder aches
common_mistakes.fix: Switch to a pushdown or a machine extension — this is the most replaceable exercise in the triceps list and nothing is lost by dropping it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Wrists complaining under the load
common_mistakes.fix: Grip the edge of the bench rather than pressing flat palms down, or use parallettes so the wrists stay neutral.

content.breathing: Inhale on the way down, exhale as you press up.
content.rom_notes: Full range stops at upper arms parallel to the floor. Depth beyond that is not extra range — it is where the shoulder problems come from. Log foot position, since straight legs or feet elevated change the load.
content.safety_notes: Loads the shoulder in internal rotation and extension simultaneously, the least forgiving position in common use. If there is any shoulder history, use a pushdown or a parallel bar dip instead. Wrists are also loaded in extension.

grip_variations.name: Knees bent, feet flat
grip_variations.effect: The easiest version, least load on the arms.

grip_variations.name: Legs straight out
grip_variations.effect: More bodyweight on the triceps.

grip_variations.name: Feet on a second bench
grip_variations.effect: The hardest version, and the hardest on the shoulder.

content.summary: A guided triceps extension with the arms fixed and a set path.
content.description: Pads or a seat fix the upper arms so the elbows cannot travel, which removes the single most common fault in triceps training. The path is decided, the load is easy to change, and the set ends the moment you let go — so this is the triceps exercise to take genuinely to failure. It gives up the overhead stretch, so it works best paired with an overhead extension somewhere in the week.
setup: Set the seat so the elbows line up with the machine's pivot.
Sit with the back against the pad and both feet flat.
Place the upper arms on the pad or against the rests.
Take the handles with the wrists stacked over the forearms.
Start with the elbows bent and the triceps under tension.
execution: Push the handles away by straightening the elbows.
Keep the upper arms flat on the pad throughout.
Extend to nearly straight without slamming into lockout.
Squeeze for a beat at full extension.
Return slowly under control until the elbows are fully bent.

common_mistakes.mistake: Seat set so the elbows sit off the machine's pivot
common_mistakes.fix: Adjust until the elbow lines up with the axis, otherwise the arc works against the joint for the whole set.

common_mistakes.mistake: Letting the stack slam back between reps
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds on the return and stop just short of the plates touching.

common_mistakes.mistake: Lifting the upper arms off the pad to finish
common_mistakes.fix: Keep them flat and reduce the load; peeling off brings the shoulders and chest into the movement.

common_mistakes.mistake: Half reps that never fully bend the elbow
common_mistakes.fix: Return until the elbows are fully flexed each rep and cut the weight rather than the range.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using it as the only triceps exercise
common_mistakes.fix: Pair it with an overhead extension so the long head gets trained in a stretched position too.

content.breathing: Exhale as you extend, inhale as the handles return.
content.rom_notes: Full range is elbows fully bent to nearly straight along the machine's arc. Seat height decides whether that arc matches your elbow, so set it before loading.
content.safety_notes: One of the safest exercises available and the best triceps movement to take to true failure, since releasing the handles ends the set immediately. Check the seat pin is engaged before starting.

grip_variations.name: Neutral handles
grip_variations.effect: The standard, kindest on the wrist.

grip_variations.name: Overhand where fitted
grip_variations.effect: Slightly different forearm angle, similar triceps involvement.

grip_variations.name: One arm at a time
grip_variations.effect: Exposes side-to-side differences and allows a longer squeeze.

content.summary: A one-arm triceps extension in a bent-over position, squeezing at lockout.
content.description: Hinging forward and extending the arm behind you loads the triceps hardest at full lockout, where the muscle is completely shortened. That is the opposite of an overhead extension and makes it a finishing movement rather than a builder — the loads are tiny and the range is short. Working one arm at a time and being able to watch the whole rep makes it easy to feel, which is most of its appeal.
setup: Place one knee and the same-side hand on a bench, or hinge forward with a split stance.
Set the torso roughly parallel to the floor with a neutral spine.
Take a light dumbbell in the working hand.
Raise the upper arm until it is parallel to the torso and pin it there.
Let the forearm hang straight down with the elbow bent to 90 degrees.
execution: Straighten the elbow, driving the weight back and up.
Keep the upper arm locked parallel to the torso the entire time.
Extend until the arm is completely straight.
Squeeze hard at lockout for a full beat.
Lower slowly back to 90 degrees without letting the elbow drop.

common_mistakes.mistake: Upper arm dropping as the set goes on
common_mistakes.fix: Hold it parallel to the torso for every rep; once the elbow drops, the shoulder swings the weight instead of the triceps extending it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Swinging the weight up with the shoulder
common_mistakes.fix: Use a much lighter dumbbell — this is a squeeze exercise and momentum removes the only thing it offers.

common_mistakes.mistake: Back rounding in the hinge
common_mistakes.fix: Set the chest and keep the spine neutral, or brace a hand on a bench so the low back is supported.

common_mistakes.mistake: Not fully straightening the arm
common_mistakes.fix: Extend completely and hold — the shortened lockout is where all the tension in this exercise lives.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using it as a main triceps exercise
common_mistakes.fix: Place it at the end of a session after pushdowns or extensions; it finishes well but builds little.

content.breathing: Exhale as you extend, inhale as the weight returns.
content.rom_notes: Full range is the elbow bent to 90 degrees to a completely straight arm, with the upper arm fixed parallel to the torso. Range is short by design.
content.safety_notes: The hinged position loads the low back lightly, so brace a hand on a bench if that is a concern. Loads are small enough that joint stress is minimal.

grip_variations.name: Neutral, palm facing in
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most comfortable wrist position.

grip_variations.name: Rotating to palm up at lockout
grip_variations.effect: Slightly stronger contraction at the finish.

grip_variations.name: Cable from a low pulley
grip_variations.effect: Constant tension rather than peak tension only at lockout.

content.summary: A kneeling crunch against a high cable, the loadable version of an ab exercise.
content.description: Kneeling below a rope and curling the spine down against the cable is the only common abdominal exercise that can be progressively loaded like any other lift. Because the resistance can climb week to week, the abs can be trained in the same eight to fifteen rep range as everything else rather than only for endless bodyweight reps. The movement is spinal flexion, so it belongs in a programme alongside bracing work, not instead of it.
setup: Attach a rope to a high pulley and kneel facing the stack.
Take an end of the rope in each hand and bring the hands beside the ears.
Kneel far enough back that the cable is under tension.
Sit the hips back slightly and keep them still for the whole set.
Set the elbows pointing down and the shoulders relaxed.
execution: Curl the spine downward, bringing the ribs toward the pelvis.
Round the upper back deliberately rather than hinging at the hips.
Continue until the elbows approach the thighs.
Squeeze the abs hard for a beat at the bottom.
Uncurl slowly back to an upright spine, resisting the cable.
cues: Curl the spine, don't bow at the hips

common_mistakes.mistake: Hinging at the hips instead of curling the spine
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the hips fixed and think about bringing the ribs to the pelvis; a hip hinge is a lat exercise with a rope attached.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pulling with the arms
common_mistakes.fix: Lock the hands beside the ears and let them travel only because the torso moves; if the arms pull, the load is too heavy.

common_mistakes.mistake: Going too heavy to curl at all
common_mistakes.fix: Cut the weight until the spine can visibly round; a rigid torso moving up and down trains nothing.

common_mistakes.mistake: Letting the stack pull you back up fast
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds uncurling; the controlled return is a large part of the work.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating it as the only core work
common_mistakes.fix: Pair it with anti-extension and anti-rotation work — this trains flexion, which is one job of several.

content.breathing: Exhale hard as you curl down, inhale as you return. The forced exhale helps the abs shorten fully.
content.rom_notes: Full range is an upright spine to a fully curled one with the elbows near the thighs. The hips do not move — any hip travel is outside the range.
content.safety_notes: This is loaded spinal flexion, so build the weight up gradually and skip it entirely if you have a disc history or your low back reacts to flexion. Anti-extension work like planks and rollouts is the alternative.

grip_variations.name: Rope beside the ears
grip_variations.effect: The standard, keeps the arms out of the movement.

grip_variations.name: Rope held at the forehead
grip_variations.effect: Shorter lever, easier to keep the arms passive.

grip_variations.name: Seated on a bench facing away
grip_variations.effect: Removes any hip hinge entirely and fixes the pelvis.

content.summary: A short-range spinal flexion on the floor, lifting the shoulders only.
content.description: Curling the ribs toward the pelvis and lifting only the shoulder blades trains the rectus abdominis through the range it actually works in, without bringing the hip flexors in the way a full sit-up does. It needs nothing but floor space and it is almost impossible to do dangerously. The main limitation is that bodyweight is the only load available, so progress means adding reps, tempo or a weight on the chest.
setup: Lie on your back with the knees bent and the feet flat on the floor.
Place the hands lightly beside the head or crossed over the chest.
Set the low back in light contact with the floor.
Tuck the chin slightly so the neck follows the spine.
Take a breath before the first rep.
execution: Curl the ribs toward the pelvis, lifting the shoulder blades off the floor.
Keep the low back in contact with the ground throughout.
Rise only until the shoulder blades clear the floor — no higher.
Squeeze the abs for a beat at the top.
Lower slowly until the shoulder blades touch down again.
cues: Shoulder blades just clear the floor
Chin off the chest, hands don't pull

common_mistakes.mistake: Hands pulling the head forward
common_mistakes.fix: Rest the fingertips beside the ears without gripping, or cross the arms over the chest so the neck cannot be yanked.

common_mistakes.mistake: Sitting all the way up
common_mistakes.fix: Stop once the shoulder blades clear the floor; going higher brings the hip flexors in and turns it into a sit-up.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bouncing off the floor between reps
common_mistakes.fix: Lower under control and pause briefly at the bottom rather than using the rebound.

common_mistakes.mistake: Chin jammed onto the chest
common_mistakes.fix: Keep a fist's gap between the chin and the chest so the neck stays neutral.

common_mistakes.mistake: Chasing hundreds of reps
common_mistakes.fix: Add a weight plate on the chest or slow the tempo instead; the abs respond to load like any other muscle.

content.breathing: Exhale as you curl up, inhale as you lower. The forced exhale helps the abs shorten fully.
content.rom_notes: Full range is shoulder blades on the floor to shoulder blades just clear of it. That short range is the exercise — sitting further up is a different movement.
content.safety_notes: Low risk, but it is still repeated spinal flexion, so limit the volume if your low back reacts badly to bending. Never pull on the head with the hands.

grip_variations.name: Arms crossed over the chest
grip_variations.effect: The standard, removes any temptation to pull on the neck.

grip_variations.name: Fingertips beside the ears
grip_variations.effect: Slightly harder lever, requires discipline not to pull.

grip_variations.name: Weight plate held on the chest
grip_variations.effect: Adds load so the reps can stay in a productive range.

content.summary: A full curl from lying to sitting, using the abs and the hip flexors together.
content.description: Coming all the way from the floor to a seated position takes the abs through their range and then hands over to the hip flexors to finish the movement. That makes it more of a whole-trunk exercise than a crunch, and it is the version used in fitness tests and military standards for that reason. The hip flexor involvement is also its main criticism, since those muscles attach to the lumbar spine and pull on it.
setup: Lie on your back with the knees bent and the feet flat on the floor.
Anchor the feet under something, or leave them free for a stricter version.
Cross the arms over the chest or place the fingertips beside the ears.
Tuck the chin slightly so the neck stays in line with the spine.
Set the low back in light contact with the floor.
execution: Curl the spine up one segment at a time, ribs toward the pelvis first.
Continue rising until the torso is upright over the hips.
Keep the movement controlled rather than throwing the torso up.
Lower back down under control, uncurling the spine in reverse.
Touch the shoulder blades to the floor before the next rep.
cues: Roll down one vertebra at a time

common_mistakes.mistake: Yanking the head forward with the hands
common_mistakes.fix: Cross the arms over the chest so the neck cannot be pulled, and lower the rep count if that makes the set harder.

common_mistakes.mistake: Throwing the torso up with momentum
common_mistakes.fix: Curl the spine deliberately and take at least two seconds on the way up; a thrown sit-up loads the low back and trains little.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hinging straight up with a flat back
common_mistakes.fix: Round the spine as you rise so the abs work before the hip flexors take over.

common_mistakes.mistake: High-rep sets when the low back is already sore
common_mistakes.fix: Switch to crunches or anti-extension work; the hip flexors pull on the lumbar spine and high volume here can make a sore back worse.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dropping flat between reps
common_mistakes.fix: Control the descent all the way down; the lowering phase is at least as valuable as the rise.

content.breathing: Exhale as you sit up, inhale as you lower.
content.rom_notes: Full range is flat on the floor to the torso upright over the hips. Anchoring the feet lets the hip flexors do more, so record whether the feet were held.
content.safety_notes: The hip flexors attach to the lumbar spine, so high-volume sit-ups can aggravate a sore low back. Use crunches or planks instead if that applies, and never pull on the head or neck.

grip_variations.name: Arms crossed over the chest
grip_variations.effect: The standard, safest for the neck.

grip_variations.name: Feet unanchored
grip_variations.effect: Reduces hip flexor contribution and makes the abs work harder.

grip_variations.name: Weight plate held on the chest
grip_variations.effect: Adds load so the reps stay in a productive range.

content.summary: A small-range curl at the wrist only, training the forearm flexors.
content.description: Resting the forearms on a bench and curling the hands upward isolates the muscles on the palm side of the forearm, the ones that close the fingers and hold onto a bar. They rarely fail before the back does on rows and pulls, but building them directly makes a difference to grip endurance and to forearm size, which curls alone barely touch. The range is a few inches and the loads are small.
setup: Sit on a bench with a dumbbell in each hand, or a light bar in both.
Rest the forearms flat along the thighs or on the bench.
Let the wrists hang just past the end of the support.
Turn the palms upward.
Let the weight roll down toward the fingertips at the start.
execution: Curl the weight back into the palm by closing the fingers.
Then curl the wrist upward as far as it will travel.
Keep the forearms flat on the support throughout — nothing else moves.
Squeeze at the top for a beat.
Lower slowly and let the weight roll open to the fingertips again.
cues: Let it roll to the fingertips
Close the fingers, then curl the wrist

common_mistakes.mistake: Lifting the forearms off the support
common_mistakes.fix: Press them down onto the bench or thighs; once they lift, the biceps has joined in and the forearm stops being isolated.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using far too much weight for a wrist joint
common_mistakes.fix: Start light enough that the full range happens — this is a small joint moving a few inches and it does not need heavy loading.

common_mistakes.mistake: Skipping the roll to the fingertips
common_mistakes.fix: Let the weight open the fingers at the bottom of every rep, which adds the finger flexors to the work.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bouncing quickly through reps
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds lowering; with a range this short, the controlled descent is most of the tension.

common_mistakes.mistake: Training flexors only
common_mistakes.fix: Pair it with reverse wrist curls so both sides of the forearm are balanced, which matters for elbow health.

content.breathing: Exhale as you curl up, inhale as you lower. Breathe normally throughout.
content.rom_notes: Full range is the weight rolled to the fingertips with the wrist extended to the wrist fully flexed. A few inches, but all of them.
content.safety_notes: Loads the wrist joint directly, so build the weight up slowly and stop if there is any sharp pain rather than a working burn. Skip it if you have a current wrist injury.

grip_variations.name: Dumbbells, one per hand
grip_variations.effect: The standard, each wrist works independently.

grip_variations.name: Barbell in both hands
grip_variations.effect: Allows more weight, both wrists locked to the same path.

grip_variations.name: Behind the back with a bar
grip_variations.effect: Standing version, easier on the elbows for some people.

content.summary: A wrist curl in the opposite direction, training the forearm extensors.
content.description: Curling the back of the hand upward trains the muscles along the top of the forearm, which almost nothing else in a normal programme touches. They matter more than their size suggests: weak extensors relative to the flexors are strongly associated with tennis elbow, and this is the direct fix. The loads are tiny, far lighter than the regular wrist curl, and that difference is normal rather than a sign of anything wrong.
setup: Sit on a bench with a light dumbbell in each hand, or a light bar in both.
Rest the forearms flat along the thighs or on the bench.
Let the wrists hang just past the end of the support.
Turn the palms downward.
Let the weight hang so the wrists are fully flexed at the start.
execution: Lift the back of the hand upward by extending the wrist.
Keep the forearms flat and still on the support.
Raise as far as the wrist will comfortably travel.
Squeeze at the top for a beat.
Lower slowly back to a full hang.

common_mistakes.mistake: Matching the weight used on regular wrist curls
common_mistakes.fix: Use roughly a third — the extensors are much smaller, and overloading them is how this exercise causes the problem it should prevent.

common_mistakes.mistake: Lifting the forearms to help
common_mistakes.fix: Press them flat into the bench so only the wrist moves.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rushing the reps
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds lowering; the eccentric is specifically what helps a tendon issue at the elbow.

common_mistakes.mistake: Only doing it when the elbow already hurts
common_mistakes.fix: Include it regularly as maintenance, especially if you grip hard on rows, deadlifts and pull-ups.

common_mistakes.mistake: Gripping the bar hard through the set
common_mistakes.fix: Hold it just firmly enough to control; a crushing grip brings the flexors in and works against the point.

content.breathing: Exhale as you lift, inhale as you lower. Breathe normally throughout.
content.rom_notes: Full range is the wrist fully flexed at the bottom to fully extended at the top. Range is small and the load should be too.
content.safety_notes: Commonly used in the rehabilitation of tennis elbow, but only at light loads with slow lowering. If the outer elbow is currently painful, keep the weight very light and stop short of any sharp sensation.

grip_variations.name: Dumbbells, one per hand
grip_variations.effect: The standard, each wrist works independently.

grip_variations.name: Light barbell or EZ bar
grip_variations.effect: Both wrists on the same path, easier to control tempo.

grip_variations.name: Slow eccentric only
grip_variations.effect: The version most used for tennis elbow rehabilitation.

content.summary: Hanging from a bar for time, training grip endurance and decompressing the shoulders.
content.description: Simply holding onto a bar with the full bodyweight is the most direct grip test there is, and it doubles as a shoulder position drill — hanging with the shoulders active teaches the same setup every pull-up needs. It is measured in seconds rather than reps, and it is one of the few exercises where doing nothing but holding on is the entire point. A minute is a reasonable target for most people.
setup: Find a bar you can hang from with the feet clear of the floor.
Take an overhand grip at roughly shoulder width.
Step or jump up and let the body hang straight.
Squeeze the glutes lightly so the legs do not swing.
Decide before starting whether to hang passive or active.
execution: Hang with straight arms and the body still.
For an active hang, pull the shoulders down away from the ears and hold that.
For a passive hang, let the shoulders rise and simply hold on.
Breathe steadily and keep the body from swinging.
Come down under control rather than dropping when the grip goes.
cues: Shoulders down for an active hang

common_mistakes.mistake: Swinging the legs to distract from the grip
common_mistakes.fix: Squeeze the glutes and hold the body still; the swing shortens the hang and makes the time recorded meaningless.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dropping off the bar when the hands give out
common_mistakes.fix: Set the bar low enough to step down, or bail before failure so the landing is controlled.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using straps
common_mistakes.fix: Hang without them — the grip is the exercise, and straps turn it into a shoulder stretch.

common_mistakes.mistake: Holding the breath through the hang
common_mistakes.fix: Breathe steadily; a held breath cuts the hang short well before the hands do.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hanging fully passive with a sore shoulder
common_mistakes.fix: Use the active version with the shoulders pulled down, which loads the muscles rather than the joint capsule.

content.breathing: Breathe steadily and normally throughout. Never hold the breath — the hang lasts long enough that it will end the set early.
content.rom_notes: Measured in seconds, not reps. Record whether the hang was active with the shoulders pulled down or passive, since they train different things.
content.safety_notes: Set the bar low enough that you can step down when the grip fails, and check it is secure before hanging. Use the active version if the shoulder is irritated, since a fully passive hang loads the joint capsule.

grip_variations.name: Overhand, shoulder width
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most grip demand.

grip_variations.name: One arm at a time
grip_variations.effect: Dramatically harder, builds toward one-arm hanging strength.

grip_variations.name: Fat bar or towel over the bar
grip_variations.effect: Much greater grip demand at a shorter duration.

content.summary: A controlled backward nod against resistance, training the muscles behind the neck.
content.description: Lying face down and lifting the head against a light weight or harness trains the extensors that hold the head up all day. They matter for anyone in a contact sport, and for people who spend hours at a desk with the head drifting forward. The neck is not a muscle group to be casual with: the loads are tiny, the tempo is deliberately slow, and the range stops well short of the end.
setup: Lie face down on a bench with the head and neck hanging past the end.
Start with no weight at all for the first few sessions.
Once ready, hold a light plate on the back of the head with a towel between, or use a head harness.
Set the shoulders down and the upper back flat on the bench.
Lower the chin toward the chest to begin.
execution: Lift the head slowly, extending the neck backward.
Move only at the neck — the shoulders and upper back stay still.
Stop when the head is roughly in line with the torso.
Hold for a beat at the top.
Lower slowly back to a chin-toward-chest position.
cues: No weight for the first weeks

common_mistakes.mistake: Adding weight before bodyweight reps are easy
common_mistakes.fix: Spend the first two to four weeks with no load at all; the neck adapts slowly and the tissue does not forgive being rushed.

common_mistakes.mistake: Extending far past the line of the torso
common_mistakes.fix: Stop when the head is level with the body — end-range neck extension under load is the position to avoid entirely.

common_mistakes.mistake: Moving fast or bouncing
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds in each direction and pause at both ends; speed is what turns a neck exercise into a neck injury.

common_mistakes.mistake: Resting a plate directly on the skull
common_mistakes.fix: Put a folded towel between the plate and the head, and keep a hand on the plate throughout.

common_mistakes.mistake: Training extension without flexion
common_mistakes.fix: Pair it with neck flexion so both sides develop together rather than pulling the head out of balance.

content.breathing: Breathe steadily throughout, exhaling as the head lifts. Never brace hard or hold the breath during neck work.
content.rom_notes: Full range is chin toward the chest to the head level with the torso. Extending past that line is outside the working range, not extra range.
content.safety_notes: Start with no weight and progress slowly over weeks. Stop immediately for any dizziness, tingling, or pain travelling into the arms, and skip neck training entirely with any history of neck injury or disc problems unless cleared by a clinician.

grip_variations.name: Bodyweight only, face down
grip_variations.effect: The correct starting point for everyone.

grip_variations.name: Light plate with a towel
grip_variations.effect: The usual progression once bodyweight reps are comfortable.

grip_variations.name: Head harness
grip_variations.effect: Easier to load in small increments and keeps the hands free.

content.summary: A controlled forward nod against resistance, training the muscles at the front of the neck.
content.description: Lying face up and lifting the head against light resistance trains the deep flexors at the front of the neck, which are usually the weaker side of the pair in anyone who sits at a desk. Balanced neck strength matters for contact sports and for holding the head over the shoulders rather than in front of them. As with extension, the weights are tiny, the tempo is slow, and there is no reason ever to rush it.
setup: Lie face up on a bench with the head and neck hanging past the end.
Start with no weight for the first several sessions.
Once ready, hold a light plate on the forehead with a towel between, or use a head harness.
Keep the shoulders down and the upper back flat on the bench.
Let the head lower gently so the neck starts extended.
execution: Tuck the chin and lift the head slowly toward the chest.
Move only at the neck — the shoulders stay on the bench.
Continue until the chin approaches the chest.
Hold for a beat at the top.
Lower slowly back to the start without letting the head drop.
cues: No load for the first weeks

common_mistakes.mistake: Jutting the chin forward instead of tucking it
common_mistakes.fix: Lead with a chin tuck so the deep flexors work; a jutting chin uses the superficial muscles that are already overactive.

common_mistakes.mistake: Adding weight too early
common_mistakes.fix: Use bodyweight alone for the first two to four weeks; the neck adapts slowly and there is nothing to gain from hurrying.

common_mistakes.mistake: Letting the head fall at the end of the rep
common_mistakes.fix: Control the descent over three seconds — an uncontrolled drop into extension is the riskiest moment in the movement.

common_mistakes.mistake: Plate resting directly on the forehead
common_mistakes.fix: Use a folded towel between plate and skin, and keep a hand on the plate for the whole set.

common_mistakes.mistake: Training flexion alone
common_mistakes.fix: Pair it with neck extension so the front and back develop together.

content.breathing: Breathe steadily, exhaling as the head lifts. Never hold the breath or brace hard during neck work.
content.rom_notes: Full range is a gently extended neck to the chin near the chest. Do not chase extra range at the extended end.
content.safety_notes: Begin with no weight and progress over weeks, not sessions. Stop immediately for dizziness, tingling, or any pain travelling into the arms, and avoid neck training entirely with a history of neck injury or disc problems unless cleared by a clinician.

grip_variations.name: Bodyweight only, face up
grip_variations.effect: The correct starting point for everyone.

grip_variations.name: Light plate with a towel
grip_variations.effect: The usual progression once bodyweight is comfortable.

grip_variations.name: Head harness
grip_variations.effect: Allows small increments and keeps the hands free.

content.summary: A prone machine curl, bending the knee against a pad on the ankles.
content.description: Lying face down and curling the heels toward the glutes trains the hamstrings at the knee, which is one of their two jobs — the other, extending the hip, is what deadlifts and Romanian deadlifts cover. A complete hamstring programme needs both, and this is the simplest way to get the knee half. The prone position leaves the hip roughly straight, so the hamstring works in a shorter position than the seated version.
setup: Set the ankle pad so it sits just above the heels, on the achilles.
Lie face down with the knees just past the edge of the pad.
Take the handles and press the hips into the bench.
Point the toes or flex them depending on the emphasis you want.
Start with the legs straight but not locked.
execution: Curl the heels toward the glutes by bending the knees.
Keep the hips pressed down into the pad throughout.
Curl as far as the machine and the hamstring allow.
Squeeze for a beat at the top.
Lower slowly to straight legs without letting the stack rest.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hips lifting off the bench to finish the curl
common_mistakes.fix: Press them down and cut the load; lifting the hips shortens the hamstring at both ends and removes the tension.

common_mistakes.mistake: Ankle pad set too high on the calf
common_mistakes.fix: Move it down to just above the heels so the lever is right and the calf is not being crushed.

common_mistakes.mistake: Letting the stack slam down between reps
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds lowering and stop just short of the plates touching.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bouncing out of the straight-leg position
common_mistakes.fix: Pause briefly at the bottom; the hamstring is stretched there and a bounce is where strains happen.

common_mistakes.mistake: Doing only leg curls for hamstrings
common_mistakes.fix: Pair them with a hip hinge such as a Romanian deadlift — the hamstring has two jobs and curls only train one.

content.breathing: Exhale as you curl, inhale as the legs straighten.
content.rom_notes: Full range is legs straight to the heels as close to the glutes as the machine allows. Pad position determines whether that full range is available.
content.safety_notes: Warm up before heavy sets and avoid bouncing out of the stretched position — hamstring strains happen at the bottom. Stop just short of locking the knees at full extension.

grip_variations.name: Toes pointed away
grip_variations.effect: The standard, takes the calf out of the movement.

grip_variations.name: Toes pulled toward the shins
grip_variations.effect: Brings the calf in slightly, often feels stronger.

grip_variations.name: One leg at a time
grip_variations.effect: Exposes side-to-side differences, useful after an injury.

content.summary: A seated machine curl with the hips bent, stretching the hamstring further.
content.description: Sitting with the hips flexed lengthens the hamstring before the rep begins, because the muscle crosses both the hip and the knee. Curling from that stretched position produces noticeably more hamstring growth than the lying version in most comparisons, and the seated setup also braces the torso so nothing can be cheated. If only one machine curl fits in the session, this is generally the one to pick.
setup: Set the back pad so the knees line up with the machine's pivot.
Sit with the back flat against the pad and the thighs under the lap restraint.
Set the ankle pad just above the heels.
Tighten the lap pad so the thighs cannot lift.
Start with the legs extended but not locked.
execution: Curl the heels down and back by bending the knees.
Keep the back flat against the pad and the thighs pinned.
Curl as far as the machine allows.
Squeeze for a beat at the bottom of the curl.
Return slowly to extended legs without letting the stack rest.

common_mistakes.mistake: Lap pad left loose so the thighs lift
common_mistakes.fix: Tighten it until the thighs cannot move; a loose pad lets the hips help and removes the stretch the seated version provides.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaning back away from the pad
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the whole back in contact — leaning back reduces the hip flexion that makes this variation better than the lying one.

common_mistakes.mistake: Knees not lined up with the pivot
common_mistakes.fix: Adjust the back pad until the knee sits on the machine's axis, otherwise the arc fights the joint all set.

common_mistakes.mistake: Letting the stack pull the legs straight quickly
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds returning; the stretched end of the range is where the growth stimulus concentrates.

common_mistakes.mistake: Skipping hip hinge work because curls feel effective
common_mistakes.fix: Keep a Romanian deadlift or good morning in the week — the hamstring extends the hip as well as bending the knee.

content.breathing: Exhale as you curl, inhale as the legs extend.
content.rom_notes: Full range is legs extended to the heels curled as far under as the machine allows. Knee alignment with the pivot decides whether the full range is usable.
content.safety_notes: Warm up before heavy sets and control the return rather than letting the stack straighten the legs. Stop just short of a hard knee lockout at the extended end.

grip_variations.name: Toes pointed away
grip_variations.effect: The standard, isolates the hamstring from the calf.

grip_variations.name: Toes pulled toward the shins
grip_variations.effect: Brings the calf in, often feels stronger.

grip_variations.name: One leg at a time
grip_variations.effect: Exposes side-to-side differences, useful after a hamstring injury.

content.summary: A calf raise with the knees straight, biasing the gastrocnemius.
content.description: The gastrocnemius crosses the knee as well as the ankle, so it only contributes fully when the leg is straight — which is exactly what a standing calf raise provides. It is the larger and more visible of the two calf muscles, and the one that produces the shape people are usually after. Range matters more than load here: most people bounce through a few inches and wonder why nothing changes.
setup: Set the shoulder pads so you stand tall with the knees straight but not locked.
Place the balls of the feet on the platform with the heels hanging free.
Set the feet hip width with the toes pointing forward.
Stand up to take the weight and let the heels drop below the platform.
Brace the trunk and keep the knees straight throughout.
execution: Push through the balls of the feet and rise as high as possible.
Keep the knees straight — no bending to help the movement.
Pause for a full beat at the top with the calves fully contracted.
Lower slowly until the heels are well below the platform.
Hold the stretch briefly at the bottom before the next rep.
cues: All the way up, all the way down

common_mistakes.mistake: Bouncing through a few inches of range
common_mistakes.fix: Take the heels well below the platform and rise onto the toes fully; the calf tendon is springy and a bounce lets it do all the work.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bending the knees to push the weight up
common_mistakes.fix: Keep them straight for the whole set — a bent knee shifts the load to the soleus and makes this a seated calf raise standing up.

common_mistakes.mistake: Loading heavy and skipping the pause
common_mistakes.fix: Cut the weight and hold the top for a full second; the calves respond to time under tension more than to load.

common_mistakes.mistake: Heels dropping fast into the stretch
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds lowering and control the bottom rather than dropping into it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Training only the standing version
common_mistakes.fix: Add a seated calf raise as well so the soleus, which works with the knee bent, gets trained too.

content.breathing: Exhale as you rise, inhale as the heels lower.
content.rom_notes: Full range is heels well below the platform to fully up on the toes. The full stretch and the full contraction are both part of the rep.
content.safety_notes: The shoulder pads load the spine axially, so keep the trunk braced and the spine neutral. If the low back is sensitive, use the leg press calf raise instead, which loads nothing through the spine.

grip_variations.name: Toes pointing forward
grip_variations.effect: The standard, even calf involvement.

grip_variations.name: Toes turned slightly out
grip_variations.effect: Shifts emphasis toward the inner head.

grip_variations.name: Toes turned slightly in
grip_variations.effect: Shifts emphasis toward the outer head.

content.summary: A calf raise with the knees bent, targeting the soleus underneath.
content.description: Bending the knees takes the gastrocnemius largely out of the movement, because it crosses the knee and goes slack when the leg is folded. What is left is the soleus, the flatter muscle underneath that does most of the work in walking and running and adds thickness to the lower leg. It responds well to higher reps, and it is the half of the calf that standing raises never properly reach.
setup: Set the thigh pad so it sits snugly across the lower thighs, just above the knees.
Sit with the balls of the feet on the platform and the heels hanging free.
Set the feet hip width with the toes pointing forward.
Release the safety lever and let the heels drop below the platform.
Sit tall with the back straight.
execution: Push through the balls of the feet and raise the heels as high as possible.
Keep the thighs pressed into the pad throughout.
Pause for a full beat at the top.
Lower slowly until the heels are well below the platform.
Hold the stretch briefly before the next rep.
cues: All the way up onto the toes
Pause and squeeze at the top

common_mistakes.mistake: Short bouncing reps
common_mistakes.fix: Use the full range from a deep stretch to a full contraction; the soleus is dense and only responds to real range and time under tension.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pushing down on the pad with the hands
common_mistakes.fix: Rest the hands lightly and let the calf lift the weight; pressing down adds load the log does not record.

common_mistakes.mistake: Thigh pad set too far up the leg
common_mistakes.fix: Position it just above the knees so the force goes through the lower leg rather than the quads.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating it as interchangeable with standing raises
common_mistakes.fix: Programme both — the bent knee here targets the soleus, which the standing version largely misses.

common_mistakes.mistake: Low reps with heavy weight
common_mistakes.fix: Work in the fifteen to twenty-five range; the soleus is built for endurance and responds accordingly.

content.breathing: Exhale as the heels rise, inhale as they lower.
content.rom_notes: Full range is heels well below the platform to fully up on the toes with the knees bent throughout. Knee angle is what makes this a soleus exercise.
content.safety_notes: Loads nothing through the spine, which makes it a good calf option when the low back cannot handle a standing raise. Release the safety lever carefully so the pad does not drop onto the thighs.

grip_variations.name: Toes pointing forward
grip_variations.effect: The standard, even soleus involvement.

grip_variations.name: Toes turned slightly out
grip_variations.effect: Shifts emphasis toward the inner lower leg.

grip_variations.name: One leg at a time
grip_variations.effect: Exposes side-to-side differences and allows a longer pause.

content.summary: A calf raise done on the leg press sled, with no load on the spine.
content.description: Pushing the sled with the balls of the feet while the legs stay straight trains the gastrocnemius exactly as a standing raise does, but with the body seated and the spine carrying nothing. That makes it the calf exercise of choice on a heavy leg day, when the low back is already tired, or when no dedicated calf machine is free. It also allows very heavy loading, since the leg press stack is usually the largest in the gym.
setup: Sit in the leg press and place the balls of the feet at the bottom edge of the platform.
Set the feet hip width with the heels hanging off the plate.
Press the sled out until the legs are straight but not locked.
Release the safety catches.
Keep the hips and back flat against the seat.
execution: Push the sled by rising onto the toes, extending the ankles fully.
Keep the knees straight — do not bend them to help.
Pause for a beat at the top.
Let the ankles flex slowly so the heels drop and the calves stretch.
Control the bottom rather than letting the sled push the feet back.
cues: Push through the balls of the feet
Control the stretch at the bottom

common_mistakes.mistake: Feet placed too far up the platform
common_mistakes.fix: Set the balls of the feet right at the bottom edge so the heels can drop below it and the full range is available.

common_mistakes.mistake: Knees bending as the calves fatigue
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the legs straight throughout; a bending knee shifts the load to the soleus and disguises how tired the calves are.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaving the safety catches engaged
common_mistakes.fix: Release them before starting, and re-engage before taking the feet off the platform at the end of the set.

common_mistakes.mistake: Short reps with a very heavy sled
common_mistakes.fix: Cut the load until the heels can drop fully below the platform and you can pause at the top.

common_mistakes.mistake: Feet sliding toward the edge of the platform
common_mistakes.fix: Reset the feet between sets and stop immediately if they start to creep — a foot slipping off a loaded sled is the real risk here.

content.breathing: Exhale as you push the sled, inhale as the heels lower.
content.rom_notes: Full range is heels dropped below the platform edge to full ankle extension. Foot placement decides whether that range exists at all.
content.safety_notes: Keep the feet firmly placed and stop the set if they begin to slide — a foot coming off a loaded sled is the main danger. Re-engage the safety catches before removing the feet, and never fully lock the knees.

grip_variations.name: Toes forward, hip width
grip_variations.effect: The standard, even calf involvement.

grip_variations.name: Toes turned slightly out or in
grip_variations.effect: Shifts emphasis between the inner and outer heads.

grip_variations.name: One leg at a time
grip_variations.effect: Exposes side-to-side differences and halves the load needed.

content.summary: A seated machine that pushes the knees apart, training the outer glute.
content.description: Pressing the knees outward against pads loads the gluteus medius, the muscle on the side of the hip that stops the pelvis dropping when you stand on one leg. It is a small muscle that squats and deadlifts train only indirectly, and weakness there shows up as a knee falling inward under load or a hip that aches after running. The machine is the most direct way to work it, and it is nearly impossible to do badly.
setup: Set the start width so the knees begin close together but not forced.
Sit with the whole back against the pad and both feet flat on the rests.
Place the outside of the knees against the pads.
Hold the handles lightly and sit tall.
Choose an upright torso for the upper glute or a forward lean for the lower fibres.
execution: Push the knees apart against the pads.
Open as far as the machine allows without the hips shifting on the seat.
Hold the open position for a full beat.
Return slowly, resisting the pads on the way in.
Stop just short of the stack touching between reps.
cues: Push through the knees, not the feet
Sit tall or lean forward, then hold it
Slow on the way back in

common_mistakes.mistake: Bouncing the knees open and shut
common_mistakes.fix: Hold the open position for a second and take three seconds returning; the glute medius responds to controlled tension, not speed.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaning back and shifting the hips to force it open
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the back flat on the pad and the hips still, cutting the load until they stay put.

common_mistakes.mistake: Changing torso angle mid-set without noticing
common_mistakes.fix: Pick upright or leaned forward before the set and hold it, since the two hit different parts of the glute.

common_mistakes.mistake: Letting the stack slam closed
common_mistakes.fix: Stop just short of the plates touching so tension stays on the muscle between reps.

common_mistakes.mistake: Skipping it because it looks like a small exercise
common_mistakes.fix: Keep it in if your knees drift inward when you squat or your hips ache after running — it addresses that directly.

content.breathing: Exhale as the knees push apart, inhale as they return.
content.rom_notes: Full range is knees together to as wide as the machine allows without the hips shifting. Record the torso angle, since upright and leaning forward emphasise different fibres.
content.safety_notes: One of the safest machines in the gym and commonly used in hip and knee rehabilitation. Set the start width so the hips are not forced open before the set begins.

grip_variations.name: Upright torso
grip_variations.effect: The standard, emphasises the upper glute fibres.

grip_variations.name: Leaning forward from the hips
grip_variations.effect: Shifts the work toward the lower glute medius and maximus.

grip_variations.name: Band walks as a free-weight alternative
grip_variations.effect: Same muscle, adds a standing balance demand.
