content.summary: A seated machine that squeezes the knees together, training the inner thigh.
content.description: Drawing the knees together against pads loads the adductors, the group running down the inside of the thigh. They contribute more to squatting than most people realise and they are one of the most commonly strained muscle groups in sport, particularly in anything involving sudden changes of direction. Training them directly through a full range is the best insurance against that, and this machine is the simplest way to do it.
setup: Set the start width so the legs open to a comfortable stretch, not a forced one.
Sit with the whole back against the pad and both feet on the rests.
Place the inside of the knees against the pads.
Hold the handles lightly and sit tall.
Check the stretch at the start position before releasing the safety.
execution: Squeeze the knees together against the pads.
Bring them fully together and hold for a beat.
Keep the back flat and the hips still on the seat.
Return slowly, resisting the pads as the legs open.
Stop at the same stretched position each rep without letting the stack rest.

common_mistakes.mistake: Start width set too wide on the first session
common_mistakes.fix: Begin with a modest opening and increase it over weeks; a forced stretch under load is how adductor strains happen.

common_mistakes.mistake: Letting the pads snap the legs open
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds on the opening phase — the lengthened position is exactly where the strain risk sits.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bouncing at the closed position
common_mistakes.fix: Hold the squeeze for a full second rather than pulsing through reps.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rounding the low back to push harder
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the back flat against the pad and lower the weight until it stays there.

common_mistakes.mistake: Only training abduction and skipping this
common_mistakes.fix: Do both — the outer and inner hip work as a pair, and the adductors are the more commonly injured of the two.

content.breathing: Exhale as the knees squeeze together, inhale as they open.
content.rom_notes: Full range is a comfortable stretch at the open position to the knees fully together. Log the start width, since that setting is what changes over time.
content.safety_notes: Increase the starting stretch gradually rather than setting it wide on day one. Anyone with a history of groin strain should build the range slowly and control every opening phase.

grip_variations.name: Moderate start width
grip_variations.effect: The standard, safe working range for most people.

grip_variations.name: Wider start over time
grip_variations.effect: Loads the adductor in a longer position, useful for injury resilience.

grip_variations.name: Copenhagen plank as a free-weight alternative
grip_variations.effect: Same muscle group, held isometrically at bodyweight.

content.summary: A one-leg hip extension against a low cable, isolating the glute.
content.description: Driving one leg back against a cable trains hip extension without the hamstrings and low back sharing the load the way they do in a hinge. Because it is done one side at a time, it exposes a weaker glute immediately, which matters after any hip or knee problem. The range is short and the loads are small — this is a movement to feel and squeeze rather than one to load heavily.
setup: Attach an ankle strap to a low cable and fasten it around one ankle.
Face the stack and hold the frame with both hands for balance.
Stand on the other leg with a soft bend in that knee.
Hinge forward slightly at the hips with a neutral spine.
Bring the working leg forward so the cable is under tension at the start.
execution: Drive the working leg back and slightly up by extending the hip.
Keep the knee at a fixed angle — the leg does not kick straight.
Stop when the thigh is roughly in line with the torso.
Squeeze the glute hard for a full beat.
Return slowly to the start without letting the stack rest.
cues: Drive from the hip, not the knee
Stop in line with the torso
Squeeze the glute at the top
Hips stay square to the stack

common_mistakes.mistake: Arching the low back to swing the leg higher
common_mistakes.fix: Stop when the thigh is in line with the torso; extra height comes from the spine, not the hip, and it loads the low back.

common_mistakes.mistake: Torso rotating open with each rep
common_mistakes.fix: Keep both hips square to the stack and hold the frame firmly; if the body twists, the load is too heavy.

common_mistakes.mistake: Kicking the leg straight at the top
common_mistakes.fix: Hold a fixed knee angle so the hip does the work rather than the hamstring finishing the rep.

common_mistakes.mistake: Going heavy and swinging the leg
common_mistakes.fix: Cut the load until the movement is controlled in both directions; this is a squeeze exercise and momentum removes the point.

common_mistakes.mistake: Doing more reps on the stronger side
common_mistakes.fix: Start with the weaker leg and match its rep count on the other side.

content.breathing: Exhale as the leg drives back, inhale as it returns.
content.rom_notes: Full range is the thigh forward under tension to the thigh in line with the torso. Anything past that line comes from arching the low back.
content.safety_notes: Low risk provided the low back does not arch to add range. Hold the frame for balance and keep the standing knee soft rather than locked.

grip_variations.name: Ankle strap, knee fixed
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most glute isolation.

grip_variations.name: Bent knee driving the heel up
grip_variations.effect: Shortens the lever, easier to feel the glute working.

grip_variations.name: Standing further from the stack
grip_variations.effect: Longer range and a stronger stretch at the start.

content.summary: Lifting the toes against resistance, training the muscle along the shin.
content.description: The tibialis anterior runs down the front of the shin and lifts the foot with every step. Almost nothing in a normal gym programme trains it, because calf raises work the opposite side of the lower leg — and that imbalance is a large part of why shin splints are so common in runners. It needs no equipment in its simplest form, and a few sets a week is usually enough to notice.
setup: Stand with the back against a wall and the heels roughly a foot's length out from it.
Keep the legs straight and the back flat on the wall.
Rest the weight on the heels with the toes free to lift.
For a loaded version, hook a weight over the toes seated, or use a tib bar.
Set the feet hip width and pointing forward.
execution: Lift the toes and forefoot toward the shins as far as they will travel.
Keep the heels planted and the legs straight.
Hold the top position for a beat.
Lower the toes slowly back toward the floor.
Stop just short of the toes resting before the next rep.
cues: Pull the toes to the shins

common_mistakes.mistake: Standing too close to the wall
common_mistakes.fix: Step the heels out about a foot's length so the shin has to work against real leverage.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bending the knees to make it easier
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the legs straight for the whole set and stop when they start to bend.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rushing the reps
common_mistakes.fix: Hold the top for a second and take two to three seconds lowering; the shin cramps easily and speed makes it worse.

common_mistakes.mistake: Doing only calf raises for the lower leg
common_mistakes.fix: Add this to balance the front and back of the shin — that imbalance is a common contributor to shin splints.

common_mistakes.mistake: Adding load before the bodyweight version is easy
common_mistakes.fix: Build to twenty-five clean wall reps first, then use a tib bar or a weight hooked over the toes.

content.breathing: Exhale as the toes lift, inhale as they lower. Breathe normally throughout.
content.rom_notes: Full range is toes near the floor to lifted as high as the ankle allows. Record whether it was the wall version or loaded, since they are not comparable.
content.safety_notes: Very low risk. The shin cramps easily when it is untrained, so start with fewer reps than feel possible and build up over a few weeks.

grip_variations.name: Standing against a wall
grip_variations.effect: The standard bodyweight version, no equipment needed.

grip_variations.name: Seated with a weight over the toes
grip_variations.effect: Allows progressive loading in small increments.

grip_variations.name: Tib bar
grip_variations.effect: The dedicated tool, easiest to load and to track.

content.summary: A rollout on a wheel, resisting the spine extending as the arms reach away.
content.description: Rolling the wheel forward lengthens the lever between the hands and the hips, and the abs have to stop the low back sagging into extension the whole way out. It is the most demanding anti-extension exercise in common use — far harder than a plank, and unforgiving of a core that cannot hold position. Done from the knees with a short range it is manageable; done badly it is a straightforward way to irritate a low back.
setup: Kneel on a mat with the wheel on the floor directly under the shoulders.
Grip the handles with the arms straight.
Squeeze the glutes and tuck the pelvis so the low back is slightly rounded, not arched.
Brace the trunk hard before the wheel moves.
Set a target distance you can reach and return from cleanly.
execution: Roll the wheel forward slowly, letting the body extend.
Keep the glutes squeezed and the pelvis tucked the entire way out.
Stop at the furthest point where the low back has not started to arch.
Pause briefly at the end position.
Pull back by drawing the hips and ribs together, not by yanking with the arms.
cues: Ribs and hips draw together on the way back
Short and clean beats long and sagging

common_mistakes.mistake: Rolling out further than the core can hold
common_mistakes.fix: Stop at the point where the low back would start to arch; distance means nothing if the spine is doing the extending instead of the abs resisting it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Low back arching and hips sagging at the end range
common_mistakes.fix: Squeeze the glutes and tuck the pelvis throughout, and shorten the rollout until that position can be held.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pulling back with the arms and lats
common_mistakes.fix: Return by drawing the ribs toward the hips so the abs do the work; arm-pulling turns it into a straight-arm pulldown.

common_mistakes.mistake: Attempting standing rollouts too early
common_mistakes.fix: Master full kneeling rollouts first — standing is a large jump and the failure mode is falling flat with a loaded spine.

common_mistakes.mistake: Doing it with a low back that already hurts
common_mistakes.fix: Use dead bugs or planks instead; this is the least forgiving core exercise for a sensitive spine.

content.breathing: Inhale before rolling out, hold the brace through the movement, exhale on the way back. Do not release the brace at the end range.
content.rom_notes: Range is however far you can go without the low back arching, and that is the honest measure. Log the distance or a marker on the floor rather than just the rep count.
content.safety_notes: The end position loads the spine near full extension, which is where this goes wrong. Never roll out past the point the core can hold, and skip it entirely in favour of planks or dead bugs if the low back is sensitive.

grip_variations.name: Kneeling, short range
grip_variations.effect: The entry point, safest way to learn the position.

grip_variations.name: Kneeling, full range to the floor
grip_variations.effect: The standard target, considerably harder.

grip_variations.name: Standing rollout
grip_variations.effect: The advanced version, only after full kneeling reps are easy.

content.summary: A supine drill lowering opposite limbs while the low back stays flat.
content.description: Lying on your back and lowering an opposite arm and leg while keeping the low back pressed to the floor teaches the core to hold position while the limbs move — which is what it does all day. It is the gentlest anti-extension exercise available, works with almost any back complaint, and is the standard first drill in rehabilitation for exactly that reason. Slow and controlled beats fast every time here.
setup: Lie on your back with the arms pointing straight up at the ceiling.
Lift the knees so the hips and knees are both bent to 90 degrees.
Press the low back flat into the floor and hold it there.
Exhale fully so the ribs settle down over the hips.
Brace the trunk lightly before moving anything.
execution: Lower one arm overhead and the opposite leg toward the floor together.
Move slowly and keep the low back pressed flat throughout.
Stop at the point just before the back would start to lift.
Return both limbs to the start under control.
Alternate sides, keeping the trunk completely still.
cues: Low back glued to the floor

common_mistakes.mistake: Low back arching off the floor as the limbs lower
common_mistakes.fix: Shorten the range and stop before the gap appears; the whole exercise is the back staying flat, not how far the limbs travel.

common_mistakes.mistake: Moving fast and treating it as cardio
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds lowering and three returning — speed hides exactly the fault this drill exists to correct.

common_mistakes.mistake: Holding the breath through the reps
common_mistakes.fix: Exhale as the limbs lower; the exhale is what keeps the ribs down and the back flat.

common_mistakes.mistake: Moving the same-side arm and leg
common_mistakes.fix: Use opposite limbs, which is what creates the diagonal challenge the core has to resist.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dismissing it as too easy
common_mistakes.fix: Slow the tempo, lower closer to the floor, or add a light weight in the hands before moving on.

content.breathing: Exhale as the limbs lower, inhale as they return. The exhale is part of the technique, not just a rhythm.
content.rom_notes: Range is however far the limbs can travel while the low back stays flat on the floor. That distance is the measure of progress, not the rep count.
content.safety_notes: Among the safest core exercises there is and a common starting point in low back rehabilitation. If the back lifts, shorten the range rather than pushing through.

grip_variations.name: Opposite arm and leg
grip_variations.effect: The standard, full diagonal challenge.

grip_variations.name: Legs only, arms held still
grip_variations.effect: An easier version for a very sensitive back.

grip_variations.name: Light weights in the hands
grip_variations.effect: Adds load once the standard version is comfortable.

content.summary: Raising the legs while hanging from a bar, working the abs and hip flexors.
content.description: Hanging from a bar and lifting the legs asks the abs to curl the pelvis upward while the hip flexors bring the thighs, and it does so with nothing supporting the torso. The grip becomes a limiting factor long before the abs do for most people. Done properly the pelvis tucks at the top; done as a straight leg swing it becomes a hip flexor exercise with the low back taking the strain.
setup: Hang from a bar with an overhand grip at shoulder width.
Pull the shoulders down away from the ears into an active hang.
Squeeze the glutes lightly so the body does not swing.
Start with the legs straight down and still.
Decide before starting whether to raise bent knees or straight legs.
execution: Raise the legs by curling the pelvis upward first.
Bring the knees or feet up toward the chest.
Continue until the pelvis has tucked and the lower back rounds slightly.
Pause for a beat at the top.
Lower slowly under control without letting the body swing.
cues: Curl the pelvis, don't just lift the legs

common_mistakes.mistake: Swinging the body to throw the legs up
common_mistakes.fix: Pause at the bottom of every rep until the swing stops; momentum turns the whole set into a grip hold.

common_mistakes.mistake: Lifting the legs without tucking the pelvis
common_mistakes.fix: Curl the pelvis up at the top — without it the hip flexors do everything and the abs barely work.

common_mistakes.mistake: Starting with straight legs before bent knees are easy
common_mistakes.fix: Build to fifteen clean knee raises first, then progress to straight legs.

common_mistakes.mistake: Grip failing halfway through the set
common_mistakes.fix: Use straps or hanging arm slings so the abs are the limit, or use the captain's chair instead.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dropping the legs fast at the end of each rep
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds lowering; the drop is where the low back gets pulled into extension.

content.breathing: Exhale as the legs rise, inhale as they lower. The exhale helps the pelvis tuck at the top.
content.rom_notes: Full range is a straight hang to the pelvis tucked with the knees or feet high. A rep without the pelvic tuck is a hip flexor rep, not an ab rep.
content.safety_notes: The grip and the shoulders both take load here, so use an active hang and come down before the hands fail. Anyone whose low back reacts to loaded flexion should use dead bugs or planks instead.

grip_variations.name: Bent knees
grip_variations.effect: The standard entry point, shorter lever.

grip_variations.name: Straight legs to horizontal
grip_variations.effect: Much harder, considerably more ab and hip flexor demand.

grip_variations.name: Toes to bar
grip_variations.effect: The full range version, requires strong lats as well.

content.summary: A knee raise with the forearms supported, removing the grip from the equation.
content.description: Padded arm rests take the bodyweight through the forearms rather than the hands, so the grip never becomes the limit and the torso cannot swing the way it does hanging from a bar. That makes it the version where the abs actually get to work to failure. It is the sensible starting point for anyone building toward hanging leg raises, and a reliable finisher when the hands are already spent from pulling.
setup: Step up onto the frame and place the forearms on the pads.
Grip the handles and press the back against the back pad.
Let the legs hang straight down with the feet clear of the floor.
Push the shoulders down away from the ears.
Brace the trunk before the first rep.
execution: Raise the knees by curling the pelvis upward first.
Bring the knees toward the chest.
Continue until the pelvis has tucked and the low back presses into the pad.
Pause for a beat at the top.
Lower slowly under control back to hanging legs.
cues: Curl the pelvis, then the knees

common_mistakes.mistake: Lifting the knees without curling the pelvis
common_mistakes.fix: Tuck the pelvis at the top of every rep; without it the hip flexors do the work and the abs are barely involved.

common_mistakes.mistake: Swinging the legs and using momentum
common_mistakes.fix: Pause with the legs still at the bottom of each rep and slow the tempo down.

common_mistakes.mistake: Shoulders shrugging up around the ears
common_mistakes.fix: Push down through the forearms so the shoulders stay low, which keeps the load off the shoulder joint.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dropping the legs at the end of the rep
common_mistakes.fix: Take three seconds lowering — the uncontrolled drop is what pulls the low back into extension.

common_mistakes.mistake: Staying on knee raises indefinitely
common_mistakes.fix: Progress to straight legs, or move to hanging leg raises once fifteen clean knee raises are easy.

content.breathing: Exhale as the knees rise, inhale as they lower.
content.rom_notes: Full range is legs hanging straight to the pelvis tucked with the knees high. The pelvic tuck is what makes the rep count as ab work.
content.safety_notes: Very low risk and a good option when grip is fatigued or a bar hang irritates the shoulder. Keep the shoulders pressed down rather than hanging from the pads.

grip_variations.name: Bent knees
grip_variations.effect: The standard, shortest lever.

grip_variations.name: Straight legs
grip_variations.effect: Much harder, longer lever and more ab demand.

grip_variations.name: Adding a twist at the top
grip_variations.effect: Brings the obliques in alongside the abs.

content.summary: A cable press held away from the body, resisting rotation rather than creating it.
content.description: Standing side-on to a cable and pressing the handle straight out means the cable is constantly trying to turn you toward the stack, and the job is simply not to let it. The further the hands travel from the chest, the harder that becomes. It trains the trunk to stay square under a rotational load, which is what it does in almost every sport and every carry, and it does so with no spinal movement at all.
setup: Set a cable to roughly chest height and attach a single handle.
Stand side-on to the stack and take the handle in both hands.
Step away until the cable is under tension.
Set the feet shoulder width, or half kneeling for a stricter version.
Hold the handle at the sternum with the hips and shoulders square.
execution: Press the handle straight out in front of the chest until the arms are extended.
Resist the pull that wants to turn the torso toward the stack.
Hold the extended position for two to three seconds.
Return the handle to the chest under control.
Keep the hips and shoulders square for the entire set.
cues: Press straight out from the sternum

common_mistakes.mistake: Torso rotating toward the stack as the arms extend
common_mistakes.fix: Cut the load until the hips and shoulders can stay square; letting the twist happen removes the entire purpose.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaning away from the cable to counterbalance
common_mistakes.fix: Stand tall with the ribs down over the hips and reduce the weight rather than using body position to cheat.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pressing fast with no hold
common_mistakes.fix: Hold the extended position for two to three seconds; that hold is where the anti-rotation work actually happens.

common_mistakes.mistake: Cable set too high or too low
common_mistakes.fix: Use chest height so the pull runs horizontally, which is the direction the trunk has to resist.

common_mistakes.mistake: Doing only one side
common_mistakes.fix: Complete matched sets facing both directions, since the trunk resists rotation in both.

content.breathing: Exhale as you press out, breathe steadily through the hold, inhale as the hands return. Do not hold the breath through the isometric.
content.rom_notes: Range is handle at the sternum to arms fully extended. The hold at extension is the working part; a fast press and return trains very little.
content.safety_notes: Among the safest core exercises available, with no spinal movement under load, which makes it a good option for a back that reacts to flexion or rotation.

grip_variations.name: Standing, feet shoulder width
grip_variations.effect: The standard, allows the heaviest loads.

grip_variations.name: Half kneeling
grip_variations.effect: Removes leg contribution and increases the demand on the trunk.

grip_variations.name: Pressing overhead at the end of the rep
grip_variations.effect: Longer lever, adds a shoulder and lat challenge.

content.summary: An opposite arm and leg reach from all fours, keeping the trunk still.
content.description: Extending one arm and the opposite leg from hands and knees creates a diagonal load the trunk has to resist, both against rotating and against the low back sagging. It needs no equipment, can be done with almost any back complaint, and is one of the standard drills in low back rehabilitation. The whole exercise is what does not move — if the hips rock as the leg goes back, the point has been missed.
setup: Kneel on all fours with the hands under the shoulders and the knees under the hips.
Set the spine neutral, neither arched nor rounded.
Tuck the chin slightly so the neck follows the spine.
Brace the trunk lightly and squeeze the glutes.
Spread the fingers and push the floor away so the upper back is broad.
execution: Extend one arm forward and the opposite leg back at the same time.
Reach until both limbs are roughly level with the torso, no higher.
Keep the hips completely square to the floor throughout.
Hold the extended position for two to five seconds.
Return both limbs under control and repeat on the other side.
cues: Hips stay level, like a tray on the low back

common_mistakes.mistake: Hips rotating open as the leg extends
common_mistakes.fix: Keep both hips square to the floor and lower the reach; the resistance to that rotation is the entire exercise.

common_mistakes.mistake: Lifting the leg higher than the torso
common_mistakes.fix: Stop level with the body — extra height comes from arching the low back, not from the hip.

common_mistakes.mistake: Flicking through reps quickly
common_mistakes.fix: Hold the extended position for two to five seconds so the trunk actually has to stabilise.

common_mistakes.mistake: Low back sagging toward the floor
common_mistakes.fix: Brace lightly and squeeze the glutes before extending, and shorten the reach until the position holds.

common_mistakes.mistake: Head lifting to look forward
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the chin tucked and the eyes on the floor so the neck stays in line with the spine.

content.breathing: Breathe steadily through the hold rather than bracing hard. Exhale as the limbs extend.
content.rom_notes: Range is limbs tucked to reaching level with the torso. Reaching higher is not more range — it is the low back extending.
content.safety_notes: One of the safest exercises there is and a standard drill in low back rehabilitation. Shorten the reach rather than pushing through if the position cannot be held.

grip_variations.name: Opposite arm and leg
grip_variations.effect: The standard, full diagonal challenge.

grip_variations.name: Leg only, hands staying down
grip_variations.effect: An easier version for a very sensitive back.

grip_variations.name: Balancing a light object on the low back
grip_variations.effect: Gives immediate feedback if the hips or spine move.

content.summary: A hold on one forearm and the side of the feet, resisting the hips dropping.
content.description: Supporting the body sideways means the obliques on the down side have to stop the hips sagging toward the floor, and the glute medius has to hold the pelvis level. It is the simplest way to train the trunk against side bending, needs nothing at all, and is gentle enough to use with most back complaints. Time held is the measure, and holding a clean position for thirty seconds beats a sagging minute.
setup: Lie on one side with the forearm on the floor and the elbow under the shoulder.
Stack the feet, or stagger them for more stability.
Set the body in one straight line from the head to the heels.
Push the floor away so the down shoulder is not sinking.
Squeeze the glutes and brace the trunk before lifting.
execution: Lift the hips off the floor until the body makes one straight line.
Hold with the hips level and stacked over each other.
Keep the top shoulder stacked over the bottom one — no rolling forward or back.
Breathe steadily throughout rather than holding the breath.
Lower under control when the position starts to break.
cues: Push the floor away with the elbow
End the set when the hips drop

common_mistakes.mistake: Hips sagging toward the floor as the hold goes on
common_mistakes.fix: End the set when the line breaks; a sagging side plank trains nothing and the recorded time stops meaning anything.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rolling the top shoulder forward
common_mistakes.fix: Stack the shoulders and hips vertically so the obliques work against side bending rather than the position collapsing into a plank.

common_mistakes.mistake: Sinking into the down shoulder
common_mistakes.fix: Push the forearm into the floor so the shoulder blade stays set and the joint is not hanging.

common_mistakes.mistake: Holding the breath through the set
common_mistakes.fix: Breathe steadily; a held breath ends the hold well before the obliques do.

common_mistakes.mistake: Chasing longer and longer holds
common_mistakes.fix: Once you can hold sixty clean seconds, raise the top leg or add a weight on the hip rather than adding time.

content.breathing: Breathe steadily and normally throughout. Never hold the breath during an isometric hold.
content.rom_notes: Measured in seconds per side. Record whether the knees or the feet were down, since the two versions are not comparable.
content.safety_notes: Very low risk and usable with most back complaints. Drop to the knees version if the full hold cannot be held cleanly, and stop the set when the hips drop rather than grinding out extra seconds.

grip_variations.name: Forearm and feet
grip_variations.effect: The standard, full length lever.

grip_variations.name: Forearm and knees
grip_variations.effect: Shorter lever, the entry point for most people.

grip_variations.name: Top leg raised, or a weight on the hip
grip_variations.effect: Progression once sixty clean seconds is comfortable.

content.summary: A side plank with the top leg on a bench, loading the inner thigh hard.
content.description: Resting the top leg on a bench and lifting the hips means the adductors of that leg have to hold the whole body up. It is the most effective adductor exercise there is, and the evidence for it reducing groin injuries in field sports is stronger than for almost any other single movement. It is also genuinely hard — the short-lever version with the knee on the bench is where nearly everyone should start.
setup: Lie on one side beside a bench with the forearm on the floor, elbow under the shoulder.
Place the inside of the top knee on the bench for the short-lever version.
For the full version, place the inside of the top ankle on the bench instead.
Let the bottom leg hang below the bench.
Brace the trunk and set the body in one line before lifting.
execution: Press down through the top leg and lift the hips off the floor.
Raise until the body makes one straight line from head to heel.
Squeeze the bottom leg up toward the bench if you can.
Hold with the hips level and the shoulders stacked.
Lower under control when the position starts to break.
cues: Press down through the top leg
Start with the knee, not the ankle

common_mistakes.mistake: Starting with the ankle on the bench
common_mistakes.fix: Use the knee version first — the long lever more than doubles the load on the adductor and it is the classic way to strain one here.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hips sagging through the hold
common_mistakes.fix: End the set when the line breaks; time spent sagging does nothing for the adductor.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rolling the chest toward the floor
common_mistakes.fix: Stack the shoulders and hips vertically so the load stays on the inner thigh rather than on the front of the shoulder.

common_mistakes.mistake: Adding it in the middle of a heavy training block
common_mistakes.fix: Introduce it gradually — soreness after the first few sessions is substantial, and jumping in cold is how the groin gets strained.

common_mistakes.mistake: Skipping it because it is uncomfortable
common_mistakes.fix: Keep it if you play any sport with sprinting or changes of direction; it is the single best insurance against groin strain.

content.breathing: Breathe steadily throughout. Do not hold the breath during the hold.
content.rom_notes: Measured in seconds per side. Record whether the knee or the ankle was on the bench — those are effectively different exercises.
content.safety_notes: Loads the adductor at long lengths, which is exactly why it works and why it must be introduced gradually. Always start with the knee version, and stop immediately for any sharp groin sensation rather than a working burn.

grip_variations.name: Top knee on the bench
grip_variations.effect: The short-lever entry version, correct starting point for everyone.

grip_variations.name: Top ankle on the bench
grip_variations.effect: The full version, dramatically harder on the adductor.

grip_variations.name: Adding a lift of the bottom leg
grip_variations.effect: Brings both adductors in and increases the demand further.

content.summary: A seated twist from side to side with the feet off the floor.
content.description: Sitting leaned back and rotating the torso side to side works the obliques through rotation while the hip flexors hold the position. It needs nothing and it is easy to do anywhere, which explains its popularity. It also combines loaded spinal rotation with loaded flexion, the two positions a sensitive low back likes least, so it is worth knowing when to reach for a Pallof press instead.
setup: Sit on the floor with the knees bent and the heels lightly touching down.
Lean the torso back to roughly 45 degrees with the spine long, not slumped.
Hold the hands together in front of the chest, or a light weight.
Lift the feet slightly if the position can be held without the back rounding.
Brace the trunk before the first rep.
execution: Rotate the torso to one side, turning the shoulders rather than just the arms.
Keep the hips and knees facing forward throughout.
Pause briefly at the end of the rotation.
Return through the middle and rotate to the other side.
Keep the torso angle constant — do not sit up between reps.
cues: Turn the shoulders, not the hands

common_mistakes.mistake: Swinging the arms while the torso stays still
common_mistakes.fix: Turn from the ribs so the shoulders travel with the hands; waving the arms trains nothing.

common_mistakes.mistake: Low back rounding into a slump
common_mistakes.fix: Sit tall with a long spine at 45 degrees, and put the feet down until that position can be held.

common_mistakes.mistake: Racing through reps for a count
common_mistakes.fix: Pause at the end of each rotation and control the return; speed here is what turns it into a low back exercise.

common_mistakes.mistake: Doing it with a low back that reacts to bending or twisting
common_mistakes.fix: Use a Pallof press instead — this combines loaded flexion and rotation, and that combination is the one to avoid.

common_mistakes.mistake: Adding a heavy weight to make it harder
common_mistakes.fix: Slow the tempo or straighten the legs instead; heavy load in a twisted, flexed position is not a good trade.

content.breathing: Exhale as you rotate, inhale through the middle. Keep breathing rather than bracing hard.
content.rom_notes: Full range is a comfortable rotation to each side with the hips staying square. Chasing extra rotation comes from the lumbar spine, which is not where the movement should happen.
content.safety_notes: Combines loaded spinal rotation with loaded flexion, so skip it if the low back has a disc history or reacts to either. Anti-rotation work such as the Pallof press gives most of the benefit with none of that.

grip_variations.name: Hands together, heels down
grip_variations.effect: The standard entry version.

grip_variations.name: Feet lifted off the floor
grip_variations.effect: Adds hip flexor demand and makes the position harder to hold.

grip_variations.name: Light plate or medicine ball
grip_variations.effect: Adds load; keep it light given the spinal position.

content.summary: A diagonal cable pull across the body, training rotation under load.
content.description: Pulling a cable from high on one side to low on the other trains the obliques through a rotation that most of sport actually uses — the power comes from the hips turning and the trunk transmitting it, not from the arms. Because the resistance is constant and adjustable, it is the most controllable way to load rotation. The hips should lead and the spine should turn very little; that distinction is what keeps it safe.
setup: Set a cable high and attach a rope or a single handle.
Stand side-on to the stack with the feet slightly wider than the shoulders.
Take the handle in both hands and step away until the cable is tensioned.
Set the knees soft and the trunk braced.
Start with the hands high on the side nearest the stack.
execution: Pull the handle down and across the body toward the opposite hip.
Let the back foot pivot and the hips turn as the hands travel.
Keep the arms fairly straight so the torso does the work, not the elbows.
Finish with the hands past the far hip and the hips facing away from the stack.
Return slowly under control to the high starting position.

common_mistakes.mistake: Keeping the feet planted and twisting the spine alone
common_mistakes.fix: Let the back foot pivot so the hips can rotate; forcing all the turn through the lumbar spine is where this becomes a problem.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bending the elbows and pulling with the arms
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the arms fairly straight so the rotation comes from the torso rather than turning into a one-arm row.

common_mistakes.mistake: Going heavy and letting the weight yank you back up
common_mistakes.fix: Cut the load and take three seconds returning; the controlled return is where the obliques do their work.

common_mistakes.mistake: Only working one direction
common_mistakes.fix: Do matched sets on both sides, and rotate between high-to-low and low-to-high across the week.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rounding the back at the finish position
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the spine long and let the hips and knees absorb the movement rather than folding the torso down.

content.breathing: Exhale as you pull across, inhale as the handle returns.
content.rom_notes: Full range is hands high on one side to past the opposite hip with the hips turned. Log the pulley height and direction, since high-to-low and low-to-high are different exercises.
content.safety_notes: Rotation under load is safe when the hips lead and risky when the lumbar spine does all the turning. Let the back foot pivot, keep the loads moderate, and skip it if the back has a disc history.

grip_variations.name: High to low
grip_variations.effect: The standard chopping direction, most oblique involvement.

grip_variations.name: Low to high
grip_variations.effect: Reverses the pattern and brings the upper obliques in more.

grip_variations.name: Half kneeling
grip_variations.effect: Removes the leg drive and isolates the trunk rotation.

content.summary: An explosive throw of a medicine ball into a wall, rotating through the hips.
content.description: Throwing a ball sideways into a wall as hard as possible is the one rotational exercise done at real speed, and speed is the point — every sporting rotation, from a swing to a punch to a change of direction, happens far faster than a cable can be moved. Because the ball leaves the hands, there is no eccentric to control, which makes it surprisingly easy on the body despite the effort involved.
setup: Find a solid wall that will take repeated impact and a ball that will not bounce back hard.
Stand side-on a couple of metres from the wall.
Hold the ball at chest height with both hands.
Set the feet slightly wider than the shoulders with the knees soft.
Load slightly onto the back leg by turning away from the wall.
execution: Drive from the back foot and turn the hips toward the wall.
Let the torso follow the hips and the arms follow the torso.
Release the ball explosively at the point the chest faces the wall.
Catch or collect the ball and reset fully before the next throw.
Throw every rep at full intent — this is a power exercise, not a conditioning one.
cues: Arms are the last link, not the first

common_mistakes.mistake: Throwing with the arms while the hips stay still
common_mistakes.fix: Start the movement with the back foot and hip turn; the arms should be the last thing to move, not the first.

common_mistakes.mistake: High rep sets treated as conditioning
common_mistakes.fix: Keep sets to three to six throws with full rest — once speed drops, the training effect is gone and it is just cardio with a ball.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using a ball that bounces back hard
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dead-bounce medicine ball or slam ball, and check the wall can take repeated impact.

common_mistakes.mistake: Holding back on the throw
common_mistakes.fix: Throw at genuine full effort; a submaximal power exercise trains nothing that a cable would not do better.

common_mistakes.mistake: No reset between throws
common_mistakes.fix: Return to the loaded starting position and settle before each throw so every rep starts from the same place.

content.breathing: Exhale sharply on the throw. Breathe freely between reps rather than bracing continuously.
content.rom_notes: Measured in throws, not reps under tension. Log the ball weight and whether the throws stayed fast — quality drops long before fatigue feels obvious.
content.safety_notes: Check the wall and the ball before starting, and make sure nobody is standing in the rebound path. Warm up the hips and trunk first; this is a maximal-effort rotation and it should not be the first thing done cold.

grip_variations.name: Standing side-on
grip_variations.effect: The standard, full hip and trunk sequence.

grip_variations.name: Half kneeling
grip_variations.effect: Removes the leg drive so the trunk has to generate the speed.

grip_variations.name: Step-behind approach
grip_variations.effect: Adds a movement step, closest to a sporting rotation.

content.summary: Walking with a heavy weight in each hand, loading grip, traps and trunk.
content.description: Picking up two heavy weights and walking is about as close to a whole-body exercise as anything gets: the grip holds, the traps and upper back support the shoulders, the trunk stops the ribs collapsing, and the legs do the walking. It carries over directly to real-world lifting in a way few gym movements do, and it builds grip strength faster than any dedicated forearm exercise.
setup: Set a heavy dumbbell, kettlebell or farmer's handle on each side of you.
Plan the route before picking anything up — distance and turning points.
Stand between the weights with the feet hip width.
Hinge at the hips with a neutral spine and take a firm grip on both.
Stand up by driving through the legs, keeping the chest up.
execution: Stand tall with the shoulders pulled back and down.
Brace the trunk and keep the ribs down over the hips.
Walk with short, controlled steps rather than long strides.
Keep the weights from swinging into the legs.
Set the weights down with a hinge, not by dropping or rounding the back.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rounding the back to pick the weights up or set them down
common_mistakes.fix: Hinge at the hips with a neutral spine at both ends — the pickup and the put-down are where backs get hurt, not the walk.

common_mistakes.mistake: Shoulders rolling forward under the load
common_mistakes.fix: Pull them back and down and hold that; a collapsed posture is the whole thing this exercise is meant to train against.

common_mistakes.mistake: Long strides and a swinging gait
common_mistakes.fix: Take short controlled steps so the load stays stable and the trunk keeps working.

common_mistakes.mistake: Not planning the route
common_mistakes.fix: Decide the distance and turning points before lifting; running out of floor with heavy weights is how they get dropped badly.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using straps every set
common_mistakes.fix: Go strapless most of the time so the grip gets trained, and save straps for the heaviest carries only.

content.breathing: Breathe steadily in short breaths through the carry while keeping light trunk tension. Do not hold one long breath.
content.rom_notes: Measured in distance or time under load rather than reps. Log the weight per hand and the distance together — either number alone means nothing.
content.safety_notes: The pickup and the put-down carry the real risk, so hinge properly at both ends. Keep a clear route, and set the weights down early rather than fighting a failing grip.

grip_variations.name: Dumbbells or kettlebells
grip_variations.effect: The standard, available anywhere.

grip_variations.name: Farmer's handles
grip_variations.effect: Allows much heavier loading and a longer walk.

grip_variations.name: Fat grips or a towel wrap
grip_variations.effect: Dramatically increases grip demand at a lighter weight.

content.summary: A carry with weight in one hand only, resisting the lean toward that side.
content.description: Loading only one side turns a carry into an anti-side-bend exercise: the obliques and quadratus lumborum on the opposite side have to work continuously to keep the torso upright. It is the walking equivalent of a side plank, with the added grip demand, and it exposes a weak side immediately. Half the load of a farmer's carry per hand feels considerably harder for the trunk.
setup: Place a single heavy dumbbell or kettlebell on one side of you.
Plan the route before picking it up.
Stand beside it with the feet hip width.
Hinge at the hips with a neutral spine and take a firm grip.
Stand up by driving through the legs with the chest up.
execution: Stand tall with both shoulders level, resisting the pull to one side.
Brace the trunk and keep the ribs down over the hips.
Walk with short, controlled steps.
Keep the free arm hanging naturally rather than reaching out to counterbalance.
Set the weight down with a hinge and repeat on the other side.
cues: Don't lean away from the weight

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaning away from the weight to counterbalance
common_mistakes.fix: Stand tall with both shoulders level and lower the load; the lean removes exactly the work this carry exists to create.

common_mistakes.mistake: Sticking the free arm out to the side
common_mistakes.fix: Let it hang naturally so the trunk does the balancing rather than the arm.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using a farmer's carry weight in one hand
common_mistakes.fix: Start considerably lighter — half the total load in one hand is much harder for the trunk than the same total split across two.

common_mistakes.mistake: Doing unequal distance on each side
common_mistakes.fix: Match the distance and the weight on both sides, starting with the weaker one.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rounding the back to set the weight down
common_mistakes.fix: Hinge at the hips to place it, especially at the end of a carry when the trunk is already fatigued.

content.breathing: Breathe steadily in short breaths while keeping light trunk tension throughout the carry.
content.rom_notes: Measured in distance or time per side. Log the weight and the distance together, and keep both sides matched.
content.safety_notes: The offset load asks the trunk to resist side bending, which is exactly the point, but it also means a fatigued trunk lets the spine bend under load. Stop the carry when the torso starts to lean rather than pushing to a distance target.

grip_variations.name: Single dumbbell or kettlebell
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most anti-side-bend demand.

grip_variations.name: Offset carry, heavier in one hand
grip_variations.effect: A middle ground between a farmer's and a suitcase carry.

grip_variations.name: Fat grip on the handle
grip_variations.effect: Increases the grip demand at a lighter weight.

content.summary: A carry with the weight held at the shoulders, loading the trunk and upper back.
content.description: Holding kettlebells or a barbell at the shoulders puts the load in front of the body's centre line, so the trunk has to work hard to stop the ribs flaring and the back arching. The upper back and shoulders have to hold the rack position while the legs walk. It is the carry that most directly builds the bracing needed for front squats and cleans, and the position becomes the limiting factor long before the legs do.
setup: Clean two kettlebells to the shoulders, or take a barbell into a front rack.
Plan the route before picking anything up.
Set the elbows in front of and slightly below the hands for kettlebells.
Pull the ribs down over the hips and brace the trunk.
Stand tall with the shoulders pulled back.
execution: Walk with short, controlled steps.
Keep the ribs down and the low back from arching under the front load.
Hold the elbows up rather than letting them drift down.
Breathe in short breaths without releasing the brace.
Return the weights to the shoulders and lower them under control at the end.

common_mistakes.mistake: Low back arching under the front load
common_mistakes.fix: Pull the ribs down over the hips and brace; the arch is the trunk giving up and it is what this carry is meant to train against.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbows dropping through the walk
common_mistakes.fix: Hold them up in the rack position and end the set when they fall rather than carrying on with a collapsed position.

common_mistakes.mistake: Holding one long breath
common_mistakes.fix: Take short breaths while maintaining trunk tension; a single held breath cuts the carry short and spikes blood pressure.

common_mistakes.mistake: Wrists bent back hard under kettlebells
common_mistakes.fix: Set the bells so they rest against the forearms with the wrists straight, or use a barbell instead.

common_mistakes.mistake: Loading it like a farmer's carry
common_mistakes.fix: Start much lighter; the front rack position fails long before the grip or legs would.

content.breathing: Take short breaths while keeping trunk tension throughout. Never hold one long breath through a loaded carry.
content.rom_notes: Measured in distance or time under load. Log the total weight and the distance, and note whether kettlebells or a barbell were used since the rack positions differ.
content.safety_notes: The front load pulls the spine into extension, so brace properly and stop when the ribs start to flare. Getting the weight into the rack position is its own skill — learn the clean first if using kettlebells.

grip_variations.name: Two kettlebells in the rack
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most trunk and upper back demand.

grip_variations.name: Barbell front rack
grip_variations.effect: Allows heavier loading, needs wrist and shoulder mobility.

grip_variations.name: Single kettlebell
grip_variations.effect: Adds an anti-rotation demand alongside the anti-extension.

content.summary: A walk with the weight locked out overhead, holding the shoulder in position.
content.description: Carrying a weight overhead demands that the shoulder stay stable in its least stable position while the trunk stops the ribs flaring and the back arching. Done with one arm it also resists side bending. It is the most demanding carry per kilo of anything on this list and the one that needs the most shoulder range, which is why the loads look small next to a farmer's carry.
setup: Plan a clear route with nothing overhead and nobody nearby.
Clean and press a kettlebell or dumbbell to lockout in one hand.
Lock the elbow fully and set the arm beside the ear, not in front of the face.
Pull the ribs down and squeeze the glutes.
Set the shoulder down away from the ear rather than shrugged.
execution: Walk with short, controlled steps and the eyes forward.
Keep the weight stacked directly over the shoulder throughout.
Hold the ribs down so the low back does not arch.
Resist the pull toward the loaded side if carrying one arm.
Lower the weight under control at the end rather than dropping it.
cues: Arm beside the ear, elbow locked

common_mistakes.mistake: Low back arching to get the arm vertical
common_mistakes.fix: Pull the ribs down and squeeze the glutes; if the arm still cannot reach vertical, the shoulder range is not there yet and a front rack carry is the better choice.

common_mistakes.mistake: Weight drifting forward over the face
common_mistakes.fix: Keep it stacked over the shoulder joint — in front of the line, the shoulder is holding a lever rather than supporting a load.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbow softening through the walk
common_mistakes.fix: Lock it fully and end the carry the moment it bends, since a bending elbow overhead is the failure point.

common_mistakes.mistake: Walking under low ceilings or near people
common_mistakes.fix: Clear the route first — a weight coming down overhead has nowhere safe to go if there is anything in the way.

common_mistakes.mistake: Loading it like a front rack carry
common_mistakes.fix: Start much lighter; overhead is the least stable position and the weights should reflect that.

content.breathing: Take short steady breaths while keeping trunk tension. Do not hold one long breath with the weight overhead.
content.rom_notes: Measured in distance or time per side. Log the weight and distance together, and note whether it was single or double arm.
content.safety_notes: Needs enough shoulder range to lock out without arching the low back — use a front rack carry instead if that is not available. Clear the route overhead, and bail sideways rather than forward if the arm gives out.

grip_variations.name: Single arm
grip_variations.effect: The standard, adds an anti-side-bend demand.

grip_variations.name: Both arms overhead
grip_variations.effect: Symmetrical and heavier, purely an anti-extension challenge.

grip_variations.name: Bottoms-up kettlebell
grip_variations.effect: Dramatically more grip and shoulder stability demand at a much lighter weight.

content.summary: A slow rise from lying to standing with a weight held overhead throughout.
content.description: Getting from flat on your back to standing while keeping a kettlebell locked out overhead is a sequence of positions rather than a single movement, and every one of them asks the shoulder to stay stable while the rest of the body changes shape underneath it. It takes a minute per rep, it exposes every weak link, and it is the reason coaches use it as both a strength exercise and an assessment.
setup: Learn the whole sequence with a shoe on the fist before ever using a weight.
Lie on your back and roll the kettlebell into position with both hands.
Press it to lockout with one arm, elbow straight and the shoulder packed.
Bend the knee on the same side as the weight, foot flat on the floor.
Set the other arm and leg out at roughly 45 degrees.
execution: Roll onto the free elbow, then press up onto that hand.
Drive through the planted foot and lift the hips into a bridge.
Sweep the straight leg back underneath into a half kneeling position.
Come up to kneeling, then stand, keeping the weight locked overhead throughout.
Reverse the entire sequence step by step to return to lying.
cues: Eyes on the weight until standing
One position at a time, no rushing
Reverse it exactly as you came up

common_mistakes.mistake: Loading it before the sequence is learned
common_mistakes.fix: Practise the full get-up with a shoe balanced on the fist until every position is automatic, then add a light bell.

common_mistakes.mistake: Elbow bending at any point
common_mistakes.fix: Keep it locked throughout and abandon the rep if it softens; a bending arm overhead mid-sequence is the main injury risk.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rushing between positions
common_mistakes.fix: Pause at each step — the exercise is the positions, and a rep should take close to a minute.

common_mistakes.mistake: Looking away from the weight too early
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the eyes on it until you are standing, then look forward, and find it again on the way back down.

common_mistakes.mistake: Doing it for high reps or for conditioning
common_mistakes.fix: Keep sets to one to five reps per side; quality collapses quickly and a sloppy get-up under load is not worth doing.

content.breathing: Breathe steadily throughout, exhaling on each transition. The rep lasts too long to hold a single breath.
content.rom_notes: One rep is a full sequence from lying to standing and back down. Log the weight and reps per side, and treat a half get-up as a separate exercise.
content.safety_notes: Learn it unloaded first and always bail by letting the bell go away from the body rather than trying to save a failing rep. Needs full overhead shoulder range — skip it if that is not available, and never rush a transition.

grip_variations.name: Kettlebell overhead
grip_variations.effect: The standard, the bell rests on the forearm and is easier to hold.

grip_variations.name: Dumbbell
grip_variations.effect: Harder to balance overhead through the transitions.

grip_variations.name: Half get-up, stopping at the bridge
grip_variations.effect: Trains the hardest early positions without the standing phase.

content.summary: A barbell pulled explosively from the floor and caught on the shoulders.
content.description: The power clean takes a bar from the floor to the front rack in one movement, which means generating enough hip and leg power to send it upward and then dropping under it fast enough to catch it. It is the standard way athletes train explosive hip extension, and it develops rate of force production in a way no grinding lift does. It is also a genuine skill and needs coaching rather than imitation.
setup: Set the bar over the middle of the feet with a stance about hip width.
Take an overhand grip just outside the knees, ideally with a hook grip.
Drop the hips until the shoulders sit slightly ahead of the bar.
Set the chest up, the back flat and the arms straight and relaxed.
Take a breath and brace before the bar leaves the floor.
execution: Push the floor away with the legs, keeping the back angle constant as the bar passes the knees.
As the bar reaches the thighs, extend the hips and knees violently.
Shrug and let the elbows travel up and out as the bar rises.
Pull under the bar, whipping the elbows through to catch it on the front delts.
Receive in a partial squat with the elbows high, then stand up.
cues: Bar stays close to the body
Arms are ropes until the hips finish

common_mistakes.mistake: Pulling with the arms early
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the elbows straight until the hips have fully extended; bending early kills the power the legs generated.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bar swinging out away from the body
common_mistakes.fix: Keep it brushing the thighs the whole way up — a bar out in front cannot be caught in a good rack position.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hips shooting up first so the back angle changes
common_mistakes.fix: Push the floor away with the legs and hold the torso angle until the bar is past the knees.

common_mistakes.mistake: Catching with low elbows and rounded wrists
common_mistakes.fix: Drive the elbows high and forward in the catch so the bar rests on the delts rather than hanging on the hands.

common_mistakes.mistake: Learning it from videos with a loaded bar
common_mistakes.fix: Start with a broomstick or empty bar and get coaching; this is a technical lift and load hides nothing.

content.breathing: Take a breath and brace before the pull, hold it through the pull and catch, exhale after standing. Reset the breath every rep.
content.rom_notes: One rep is floor to a caught front rack and standing. Power cleans catch above parallel; full squat cleans are a separate lift and should be logged separately.
content.safety_notes: Use bumper plates on a platform so a failed rep can be dumped forward safely. Never try to save a bar that has drifted — let it go. Learn the sequence unloaded, and skip it entirely if the low back cannot hold a neutral position under speed.

grip_variations.name: Hook grip, just outside the knees
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most secure under speed.

grip_variations.name: Straps
grip_variations.effect: Removes grip as the limit but makes bailing dangerous — not for maximal work.

grip_variations.name: Clean from blocks
grip_variations.effect: Removes the floor portion so the second pull can be trained alone.

content.summary: A clean starting from the thighs rather than the floor.
content.description: Starting with the bar already at the thighs removes the first pull from the floor and leaves only the explosive part — the hip extension and the drop under the bar. That makes it markedly easier to learn than a full clean, easier on the low back because there is no long pull from the floor, and the usual first step in teaching the movement. It also lets an athlete train the power portion without accumulating pulling fatigue.
setup: Take the bar from a rack or deadlift it up to standing.
Grip overhand just outside the knees, hook grip if you can.
Stand tall with the bar resting against the thighs.
Set the feet hip width and brace the trunk.
Hinge back to lower the bar to mid-thigh or just above the knee.
execution: From the hang position, extend the hips and knees violently.
Keep the arms straight until the hips have finished.
Shrug and let the elbows travel up and out.
Pull under the bar and whip the elbows through to catch it on the front delts.
Receive in a partial squat with the elbows high, then stand.
cues: Hinge back, then jump the bar up
Arms straight until the hips finish

common_mistakes.mistake: Bending the arms to pull the bar up
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the elbows locked until the hips fully extend; early arm bend is the single most common fault in any clean.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hanging with a rounded back
common_mistakes.fix: Set the chest up and hinge from the hips so the spine stays neutral in the start position.

common_mistakes.mistake: Catching with the elbows pointing down
common_mistakes.fix: Drive them high and forward so the bar sits on the shoulders rather than in the hands.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hanging too low, near the floor
common_mistakes.fix: Start at mid-thigh or just above the knee; hanging much lower reintroduces the first pull without the floor to reset from.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating it as a lighter power clean
common_mistakes.fix: Log it as its own lift — the shorter pull changes the numbers, usually downward.

content.breathing: Breathe and brace in the standing position, hold through the pull and catch, exhale after standing. Reset every rep.
content.rom_notes: One rep is from the hang at mid-thigh to a caught front rack and standing. Record the hang height, since mid-thigh and below-knee are different lifts.
content.safety_notes: Use bumper plates so a missed rep can be dumped forward. Easier on the low back than a floor clean, but the hang position still needs a neutral spine held under speed.

grip_variations.name: Hook grip, hang at mid-thigh
grip_variations.effect: The standard teaching position.

grip_variations.name: Hang below the knee
grip_variations.effect: Longer pull, closer to a full clean, harder on the back.

grip_variations.name: Dumbbells instead of a bar
grip_variations.effect: Each side works independently and a miss is easy to bail.

content.summary: A wide-grip barbell pulled from the floor to overhead in one movement.
content.description: The snatch sends a bar from the floor to locked out overhead without stopping, which makes it the fastest lift in the gym and the one that demands the most from every joint at once. The wide grip shortens the distance the bar must travel but puts the shoulders at their end range in the catch. It develops explosive power better than almost anything, and it is unquestionably the most technical lift on this list.
setup: Set the bar over the middle of the feet with a stance about hip width.
Take a wide grip — roughly where the bar sits in the hip crease when standing.
Use a hook grip; at snatch speed a normal grip will slip.
Drop the hips with the shoulders slightly ahead of the bar and the back flat.
Brace hard before the bar moves.
execution: Push the floor away, keeping the back angle constant as the bar passes the knees.
As the bar reaches the hips, extend violently and let it brush the hip crease.
Shrug and pull the elbows high and outside.
Pull under the bar and punch the arms into a locked-out overhead position.
Receive in a partial squat with the bar over the shoulders, then stand.
cues: Bar brushes the hips, not the thighs
Arms stay long until the hips finish

common_mistakes.mistake: Pulling early with the arms
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the elbows straight until the hips have finished extending; every bit of early arm bend costs bar speed.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bar looping out in front on the way up
common_mistakes.fix: Keep it close and let it contact the hip crease — a looping bar cannot be caught overhead in a stable position.

common_mistakes.mistake: Catching with the bar in front of the head
common_mistakes.fix: Punch straight up and push the head through so the bar finishes over the shoulders and the mid foot.

common_mistakes.mistake: Attempting it without the shoulder and thoracic range to lock out overhead
common_mistakes.fix: Test an overhead squat with an empty bar first; without that position the catch cannot be safe at any weight.

common_mistakes.mistake: Learning it unsupervised
common_mistakes.fix: Get coaching and spend weeks with a broomstick or empty bar; this is the least forgiving lift in the gym to self-teach.

content.breathing: Breathe and brace before the pull, hold through the pull and catch, exhale once standing. Reset every rep.
content.rom_notes: One rep is floor to locked out overhead and standing. Power snatches catch above parallel; full squat snatches are a separate lift.
content.safety_notes: Use bumper plates on a platform with clear space front and back, and always drop a failed rep rather than trying to save it. Requires full overhead shoulder range — do not attempt without it. Coaching is not optional here.

grip_variations.name: Wide hook grip
grip_variations.effect: The standard, shortest bar path to overhead.

grip_variations.name: Snatch from blocks or the hang
grip_variations.effect: Removes the floor pull to train the explosive portion alone.

grip_variations.name: Dumbbell or kettlebell snatch
grip_variations.effect: Far lower skill demand and much easier to bail.

content.summary: A clean to the shoulders followed by a jerk overhead, the heaviest overhead lift.
content.description: Two movements in sequence: the bar is cleaned to the front rack, then driven overhead with a dip, a drive and a drop under. Splitting the work in two is why more weight can be put overhead this way than by any other means, and why it is the second contested lift in weightlifting. It demands everything the clean does plus a jerk on top, at the point when the legs are already tired.
setup: Set up exactly as for a power clean, bar over the middle of the feet.
Grip overhand just outside the knees with a hook grip.
Chest up, back flat, arms straight and relaxed.
Decide in advance whether the jerk will be a split or a push jerk.
Brace hard before the bar leaves the floor.
execution: Clean the bar to the front rack and stand up fully.
Reset the feet, the grip and the breath before the jerk.
Dip a few inches by bending the knees with the torso vertical.
Drive the bar upward and drop under it, splitting or pushing into the receive.
Recover the feet and stand with the bar locked overhead.
cues: Stand up and reset before the jerk

common_mistakes.mistake: Rushing into the jerk while still off balance from the clean
common_mistakes.fix: Stand fully, reset the feet and take a fresh breath; the jerk is a separate lift and treating it as a continuation loses both.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dipping forward so the bar leaves the shoulders early
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the torso vertical through the dip and the weight through the mid foot.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pressing the bar out with the arms instead of dropping under
common_mistakes.fix: Drive with the legs and move the feet fast; the jerk is about getting under the bar, not pressing it up.

common_mistakes.mistake: Attempting the full lift before both halves are solid
common_mistakes.fix: Train cleans and jerks separately until each is reliable, then combine them.

common_mistakes.mistake: Learning it without coaching
common_mistakes.fix: Get a coach and start with an empty bar; two technical lifts stacked is not something to reverse-engineer from video.

content.breathing: Brace before the clean and hold through it, reset the breath in the rack position, then brace again for the jerk.
content.rom_notes: One rep is floor to locked out overhead with a stand between the two halves. Log it as a single lift, and jerks done alone from a rack as a separate one.
content.safety_notes: Use bumper plates on a platform with clear space in every direction, and drop a failed lift rather than trying to save it. Heavy overhead work with a hard brace spikes blood pressure — factor that in if relevant to you.

grip_variations.name: Split jerk
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most stable receiving position and the heaviest loads.

grip_variations.name: Push jerk, feet staying parallel
grip_variations.effect: Simpler to learn, less depth available under the bar.

grip_variations.name: Jerk from a rack
grip_variations.effect: Trains the overhead half alone without clean fatigue.

content.summary: An explosive pull to chest height, training the power phase without the catch.
content.description: A high pull is a clean without the turnover: the bar is driven upward by the hips and allowed to rise to chest height, then lowered. Removing the catch removes most of the technical difficulty while keeping the hip extension that makes the Olympic lifts valuable, which makes it the usual entry point for athletes who need the power but not the sport. The one caution is the top of the pull, which resembles an upright row.
setup: Set the bar over the middle of the feet, or start from a hang at mid-thigh.
Grip overhand just outside the knees.
Set the chest up, back flat and arms straight.
Brace the trunk before the bar moves.
Decide the finish height in advance — chest, not chin.
execution: Push the floor away, keeping the back angle constant as the bar passes the knees.
Extend the hips and knees violently as the bar reaches the thighs.
Shrug hard and let the elbows travel up and outside.
Let the bar rise to roughly chest height with the elbows above the hands.
Lower the bar under control back to the start.
cues: Legs and hips first, arms last
Finish at the chest, not the chin

common_mistakes.mistake: Pulling with the arms from the start
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the elbows straight until the hips have finished; the arms are there to guide the bar, not to lift it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pulling all the way to the chin
common_mistakes.fix: Stop at chest height with the elbows no higher than the shoulders — the high finish is the same impingement position as an upright row.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating it as a heavy shrug
common_mistakes.fix: Use a weight light enough that the bar genuinely accelerates; if it grinds, the power element is gone.

common_mistakes.mistake: Back rounding as the load climbs
common_mistakes.fix: Set the chest up and brace, and cut the weight the moment neutral spine goes under speed.

common_mistakes.mistake: Continuing when the shoulder pinches at the top
common_mistakes.fix: Lower the finish height or switch to a clean pull, which stops before the elbows rise at all.

content.breathing: Brace before the pull, hold through it, exhale as the bar lowers. Reset the breath every rep.
content.rom_notes: One rep is from the floor or hang to the bar at chest height with the elbows above the hands. Log the start position, since floor and hang versions differ.
content.safety_notes: The top of the pull puts the shoulder in the same internally rotated position as an upright row, so keep the finish at chest height and skip it if you have a shoulder history. Bumper plates and a platform if pulling from the floor.

grip_variations.name: Clean grip, just outside the knees
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most transferable to the clean.

grip_variations.name: Snatch-width grip
grip_variations.effect: Higher finish, more trap involvement, more shoulder stress.

grip_variations.name: Clean pull, no elbow bend at all
grip_variations.effect: Removes the impingement position entirely while keeping the hip drive.

content.summary: A kettlebell swung and rotated up into the rack position at the shoulder.
content.description: Cleaning a kettlebell means driving it up with the hips and then guiding it around the hand into the rack, rather than catching it. The difference between a good clean and a bruised forearm is entirely in that rotation — the bell should roll around the wrist, not flip over and bang down. It teaches explosive hip extension with far less technical risk than a barbell clean, and one bell is all that is needed.
setup: Stand behind a kettlebell with the feet slightly wider than the hips.
Hinge at the hips and take the handle with one hand, thumb pointing back.
Set the chest up, the back flat and the shoulder pulled into the socket.
Hike the bell back between the legs like a rugby pass.
Keep the working arm relaxed and close to the body.
execution: Drive the hips forward explosively to send the bell up.
Keep the elbow close to the ribs so the bell travels up the body, not out.
As it rises, spear the hand through the handle so the bell rotates around the wrist.
Receive it in the rack with the bell resting on the forearm and the elbow tucked in.
Guide it back down by hinging and letting it swing between the legs.
cues: Elbow stays close to the ribs
Spear the hand through, don't flip it

common_mistakes.mistake: Bell flipping over and banging the forearm
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the elbow tight to the ribs and spear the hand through the handle as it rises; a bruised forearm always means the bell travelled out and over.

common_mistakes.mistake: Curling the bell up with the arm
common_mistakes.fix: Drive with the hips and let the arm guide only; if the biceps is working, the load is being lifted rather than thrown.

common_mistakes.mistake: Swinging the bell out in front like a kettlebell swing
common_mistakes.fix: Keep it close and travelling up the body — the clean path is vertical, not an arc out front.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rounding the back in the hike
common_mistakes.fix: Hinge at the hips with a flat back and the chest up; the hike is a hinge, not a squat or a bend.

common_mistakes.mistake: Learning it with a heavy bell
common_mistakes.fix: Start light enough that the rotation is smooth and quiet, then add weight.

content.breathing: Exhale sharply as the hips drive, inhale as the bell descends. Keep the rhythm with the movement.
content.rom_notes: One rep is from the hike position to the bell resting in the rack. Log reps per side and the bell weight together.
content.safety_notes: The most common injury here is a bruised forearm from a flipping bell, which is a technique signal rather than bad luck. Keep clear space in front, and let a bad rep go forward rather than trying to save it.

grip_variations.name: Single bell, one arm
grip_variations.effect: The standard, adds an anti-rotation demand.

grip_variations.name: Double kettlebell clean
grip_variations.effect: Symmetrical and heavier, no rotation to resist.

grip_variations.name: Dead-stop clean from the floor each rep
grip_variations.effect: Removes the swing rhythm and makes each rep start fresh.

content.summary: A kettlebell driven from between the legs to locked out overhead in one movement.
content.description: The kettlebell snatch sends the bell from a hike straight to overhead without stopping at the shoulder. Like the barbell version it trains explosive hip extension, but the bail-out is far simpler — a bad rep just gets dropped. It is the standard test in kettlebell sport for exactly that reason, and the same forearm-bruising rotation problem as the clean applies, just at a higher and faster point in the arc.
setup: Stand behind a kettlebell with the feet slightly wider than the hips.
Hinge and take the handle with one hand, thumb pointing back.
Set the chest up, back flat and the shoulder packed down.
Hike the bell back between the legs.
Keep the working arm relaxed and the grip loose enough to rotate.
execution: Drive the hips forward explosively to send the bell upward.
Guide it up close to the body with the elbow leading slightly.
As it passes chest height, spear the hand through the handle and punch upward.
Lock out overhead with the bell resting on the back of the forearm.
Lower by letting the bell fall into a swing and hinging to absorb it.
cues: Hips throw it, arm steers it
Punch the hand through at the top
Lock out with the bell on the forearm
Absorb the drop with a hinge

common_mistakes.mistake: Bell flipping over and slapping the forearm at lockout
common_mistakes.fix: Punch the hand through the handle as the bell passes the head rather than letting it swing over the top.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bell arcing out in front like a swing
common_mistakes.fix: Keep it travelling close to the body so the path to overhead is short and vertical.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pressing the last portion with the arm
common_mistakes.fix: Drive harder with the hips so the bell is weightless at the top; a press means the hip drive was not enough.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rounding the back catching the bell on the way down
common_mistakes.fix: Hinge at the hips to absorb the descent, keeping the chest up and the spine neutral.

common_mistakes.mistake: Attempting it before the swing and clean are solid
common_mistakes.fix: Build the hinge with swings and the rotation with cleans first; the snatch combines both at speed.

content.breathing: Exhale sharply on the hip drive, inhale as the bell descends. Keep breathing with the rhythm rather than holding.
content.rom_notes: One rep is from the hike to a locked out overhead position. Log reps per side with the bell weight; sets are often measured by time in kettlebell sport.
content.safety_notes: Needs full overhead shoulder range to lock out safely. Keep clear space around you and let a bad rep drop forward rather than fighting it. Build the swing and clean first.

grip_variations.name: Single bell, one arm
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most common version.

grip_variations.name: Dead-stop from the floor each rep
grip_variations.effect: Removes the swing rhythm so each rep starts from scratch.

grip_variations.name: Half snatch, returning to the rack
grip_variations.effect: Lowers to the shoulder instead of the swing, easier on the grip.

content.summary: A front squat straight into an overhead press, done as one continuous movement.
content.description: A thruster takes a weight from the shoulders down into a squat and then drives it overhead in one motion, using the leg drive to launch the press. It is the most efficient way to fatigue nearly the whole body with a single movement, which is why it appears in almost every conditioning workout ever written. It also means a tired press happens on tired legs, so the loads should stay well short of what either lift could handle alone.
setup: Clean one or two kettlebells to the rack position at the shoulders.
Set the feet shoulder width with the toes turned slightly out.
Keep the elbows tucked in and the bells resting on the forearms.
Pull the ribs down and brace the trunk.
Set the chest up and the weight through the mid foot.
execution: Squat down by pushing the hips back and the knees out.
Descend to at least parallel with the chest staying up.
Drive out of the bottom explosively through the legs.
Let the leg drive carry into the press and punch the bells overhead.
Lock out overhead, then lower back to the rack and straight into the next rep.
cues: Elbows in, chest up in the squat
Let the legs launch the press
Lock out fully before the next rep

common_mistakes.mistake: Pausing at the top of the squat before pressing
common_mistakes.fix: Blend the two — the whole point is the leg drive carrying into the press, and a pause throws that away.
