common_mistakes.mistake: Chest collapsing forward in the squat
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the elbows up and the chest tall; a dropped chest means the bells travel forward and the press cannot start.

common_mistakes.mistake: Loading it like a front squat
common_mistakes.fix: Use a weight limited by the press, not the squat; the overhead half always fails first.

common_mistakes.mistake: Low back arching at the overhead lockout
common_mistakes.fix: Pull the ribs down and squeeze the glutes at the top, and lighten the load if the arch persists.

common_mistakes.mistake: Grinding out reps as a conditioning finisher
common_mistakes.fix: Stop the set when the lockout gets sloppy; a failing overhead press under fatigue is not a rep worth having.

content.breathing: Inhale at the rack, brace through the squat, exhale forcefully through the press and lockout.
content.rom_notes: One rep is rack position to squat at or below parallel to a full overhead lockout. A rep without full lockout does not count.
content.safety_notes: Needs enough shoulder range to lock out overhead without arching the low back, and enough ankle and hip range to squat to parallel. Under fatigue the technique degrades fast — end the set on quality, not on a rep target.

grip_variations.name: Two kettlebells in the rack
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most load and most demand.

grip_variations.name: Single kettlebell
grip_variations.effect: Adds an anti-rotation demand and halves the load.

grip_variations.name: Goblet position, one bell in both hands
grip_variations.effect: The easiest version to learn, keeps the chest upright in the squat.

content.summary: Driving a loaded sled forward, a leg workout with no eccentric at all.
content.description: Pushing a sled loads the legs hard while producing almost no muscle damage, because there is no lowering phase — the muscles only ever shorten. That means it can be done heavy without the soreness that follows squats, which makes it uniquely useful for conditioning, for building work capacity, and for training legs on days when recovery matters. It is also about as safe as loaded exercise gets, with nothing overhead and nothing to drop.
setup: Load the sled and check the surface will let it move.
Plan the distance before starting.
Take the high handles for an upright push or the low ones for a driving push.
Set the arms straight and lean the body into the sled.
Brace the trunk and set the back foot ready to drive.
execution: Drive through the legs with short, powerful steps.
Keep the arms straight and the body in one line from head to heel.
Extend each leg fully behind you before the next step.
Keep the head neutral and the eyes a few metres ahead.
Slow down under control at the end rather than stopping dead.
cues: Arms straight, body in one line
Drive each leg all the way back
Lean into it, don't bend at the waist

common_mistakes.mistake: Bending at the waist instead of leaning the whole body
common_mistakes.fix: Keep a straight line from head to heel and lean from the ankles; folding at the hips puts the load on the low back.

common_mistakes.mistake: Arms bending and absorbing the push
common_mistakes.fix: Lock them straight so the force goes from the legs through to the sled.

common_mistakes.mistake: Long strides
common_mistakes.fix: Take short powerful steps; long strides mean the leg is pushing at its weakest angle.

common_mistakes.mistake: Loading it so heavy the sled barely moves
common_mistakes.fix: Pick a weight that lets you keep moving for the whole distance unless a heavy grind is deliberately the goal.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using it as a warm-up for heavy squats
common_mistakes.fix: Place it after the main work; even without eccentric damage it fatigues the legs considerably.

content.breathing: Breathe steadily and hard throughout. Do not hold the breath — these efforts last long enough that it will cut them short.
content.rom_notes: Measured in distance and load rather than reps. Log the sled weight and the distance together, and note the surface since it changes the effort substantially.
content.safety_notes: One of the safest loaded exercises there is — nothing overhead, nothing to drop, and no eccentric. Check the path is clear and the surface is suitable before loading.

grip_variations.name: Low handles
grip_variations.effect: The standard driving position, most leg drive.

grip_variations.name: High handles, upright torso
grip_variations.effect: More quad emphasis and easier on the low back.

grip_variations.name: Heavy short distance
grip_variations.effect: Becomes a strength effort rather than conditioning.

content.summary: Pulling a loaded sled behind or in front of you with a harness or straps.
content.description: Dragging a sled loads the legs through a different range than pushing does, and the direction changes the emphasis entirely — walking forward works the glutes and hamstrings, walking backward hammers the quads and is widely used for knee rehabilitation. Like the push it has no eccentric, so it builds work capacity without soreness. Backward dragging in particular is one of the few loaded knee exercises that most sore knees tolerate well.
setup: Attach a harness, a belt, or take two straps in the hands.
Load the sled and plan the distance and direction.
For a forward drag, face away from the sled and lean slightly forward.
For a backward drag, face the sled and lean slightly back.
Brace the trunk and take up the slack before the first step.
execution: Walk with short, deliberate steps.
For a forward drag, drive through the hips and extend each leg fully behind.
For a backward drag, reach with the heel and straighten the knee as you pull.
Keep the trunk braced and the spine neutral throughout.
Come to a controlled stop at the end of the distance.
cues: Backward: reach with the heel, straighten the knee

common_mistakes.mistake: Rounding the back to lean into the drag
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the spine neutral and lean from the ankles rather than folding at the waist.

common_mistakes.mistake: Backward dragging without straightening the knee
common_mistakes.fix: Reach the heel out and extend the knee fully on each step; the knee extension is exactly what makes the backward drag useful.

common_mistakes.mistake: Loading it so heavy the walk becomes a stagger
common_mistakes.fix: Choose a weight that allows a steady rhythm, especially when using it for knee rehabilitation.

common_mistakes.mistake: Only dragging in one direction
common_mistakes.fix: Alternate forward and backward across the week — they train opposite sides of the leg.

common_mistakes.mistake: Not checking behind you on a backward drag
common_mistakes.fix: Clear the route first and glance over the shoulder periodically; you are walking blind.

content.breathing: Breathe steadily and hard throughout rather than holding the breath.
content.rom_notes: Measured in distance and load. Log the weight, the distance and the direction — forward and backward drags are effectively different exercises.
content.safety_notes: Very safe with no eccentric loading and nothing to drop. Backward dragging is a common knee rehabilitation tool, but the route must be clear since you cannot see where you are going.

grip_variations.name: Backward drag with straps
grip_variations.effect: Quad emphasis, the version used for knee rehabilitation.

grip_variations.name: Forward drag with a harness
grip_variations.effect: Glutes and hamstrings, allows the heaviest loads.

grip_variations.name: Lateral drag
grip_variations.effect: Works the glute medius and adductors.

content.summary: Running on a treadmill, the most direct cardiovascular training there is.
content.description: Running trains the heart and lungs harder per minute than almost anything else, and a treadmill lets the pace and incline be set exactly rather than drifting. That makes intervals precise and steady efforts honest. The cost is impact: each stride lands with several times bodyweight through the knees, hips and ankles, which is why it suits some people and rules others out entirely.
setup: Clip the safety key to your clothing before starting the belt.
Start the belt slow and step on once it is moving steadily.
Set the incline to at least one percent to approximate outdoor running.
Stand tall with the eyes forward rather than down at the display.
Decide the session — steady pace or intervals — before you start.
execution: Run with a tall posture and the shoulders relaxed.
Land with the foot under the body rather than reaching out in front.
Aim for short, quick strides rather than long ones.
Keep the arms swinging forward and back, not across the body.
Step onto the side rails to stop rather than jumping off a moving belt.

common_mistakes.mistake: Holding the handrails while running
common_mistakes.fix: Let go — holding on takes weight off the legs, distorts the stride and makes the calorie and pace readings meaningless.

common_mistakes.mistake: Overstriding with the foot landing well in front
common_mistakes.fix: Shorten the stride and increase the cadence so the foot lands under the hips, which cuts the braking force through the knee.

common_mistakes.mistake: Running at zero incline and calling it outdoor equivalent
common_mistakes.fix: Set one to two percent; a flat belt is easier than road running because there is no air resistance.

common_mistakes.mistake: Skipping the safety clip
common_mistakes.fix: Attach it every time — a trip at speed on a moving belt causes far worse than a fall outdoors.

common_mistakes.mistake: Adding running volume quickly on top of heavy leg training
common_mistakes.fix: Build the mileage by no more than about ten percent a week, and separate hard runs from heavy squat days.

content.breathing: Breathe rhythmically and deeply, settling into a pattern with the stride. Nose or mouth is a matter of comfort rather than technique.
content.rom_notes: Measured in distance, time and pace rather than reps. Log the incline alongside the speed, since the two together define the effort.
content.safety_notes: Always use the safety clip. Impact loads the knees, hips and ankles repeatedly, so build volume gradually and switch to a bike, elliptical or incline walk if joints are complaining.

grip_variations.name: Steady pace
grip_variations.effect: The standard, builds aerobic base.

grip_variations.name: Intervals with speed changes
grip_variations.effect: Higher intensity in less time, considerably more fatiguing.

grip_variations.name: Incline running
grip_variations.effect: More glute and calf involvement, lower impact at the same effort.

content.summary: Walking at a steep incline, a hard cardio effort with no impact at all.
content.description: Raising the treadmill to a steep gradient and walking briskly produces a heart rate close to a run while both feet stay in contact with the ground, so there is no landing impact whatsoever. It loads the glutes and calves noticeably more than flat walking. That combination — real cardiovascular work with joint stress close to zero — makes it the default cardio choice for anyone whose knees, hips or back rule out running.
setup: Clip the safety key to your clothing.
Start the belt at a walking pace on a flat setting.
Raise the incline gradually to somewhere between ten and fifteen percent.
Adjust the speed so the pace stays brisk but sustainable.
Stand tall with the eyes forward.
execution: Walk with a tall posture and a normal stride length.
Let the heel land first and push off through the whole foot.
Drive the hips forward rather than leaning into the belt.
Keep the hands off the rails and let the arms swing naturally.
Lower the incline before reducing speed at the end.
cues: Incline sets the effort, not speed

common_mistakes.mistake: Gripping the handrails to survive a steeper incline
common_mistakes.fix: Let go and lower the incline until you can walk unsupported — holding on removes most of the work and all of the honesty from the numbers.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaning forward into the belt
common_mistakes.fix: Stand tall with the hips under the shoulders; leaning turns it into an assisted walk.

common_mistakes.mistake: Going too fast at a steep incline
common_mistakes.fix: Set the incline first, then find the fastest speed you can hold with good posture for the whole session.

common_mistakes.mistake: Walking on tiptoes at high inclines
common_mistakes.fix: Let the heel make contact each step so the glutes and hamstrings work rather than the calves alone.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dismissing it as too easy to count
common_mistakes.fix: Check your heart rate — at ten to fifteen percent it sits close to an easy run with none of the impact.

content.breathing: Breathe deeply and steadily. You should be able to talk in short sentences but not hold a conversation comfortably.
content.rom_notes: Measured in time, distance and incline. The incline is the variable that matters most — log it every session or the numbers are not comparable.
content.safety_notes: The lowest-impact way to get a genuine cardiovascular effort, which makes it the first choice when knees, hips or the low back rule out running. Use the safety clip and lower the incline before stepping off.

grip_variations.name: Ten to fifteen percent, brisk walk
grip_variations.effect: The standard, hard effort with no impact.

grip_variations.name: Maximum incline, slower pace
grip_variations.effect: More glute and calf involvement, closer to hill climbing.

grip_variations.name: Carrying dumbbells
grip_variations.effect: Adds load and grip demand; keep the posture tall.

content.summary: A full-body cardio machine driven mostly by the legs, not the arms.
content.description: Rowing works close to the whole body at once, and roughly sixty percent of the power comes from the legs — which is the single thing most people get wrong, pulling with the arms and wondering why their back aches. Done properly it is one of the best cardio options available, low impact and scalable from easy to brutal. Done as an arm exercise it is an efficient way to irritate a low back.
setup: Set the damper between three and five for most people, not ten.
Strap the feet in with the straps across the widest part of the foot.
Sit tall and take the handle with an overhand grip.
Slide forward to the catch with the shins vertical and the arms straight.
Set the back long and hinged slightly forward from the hips.
execution: Drive with the legs first, keeping the arms straight and the back angle fixed.
As the legs finish, swing the torso back to roughly eleven o'clock.
Finally pull the handle to the bottom of the ribs with the arms.
Reverse the order on the recovery — arms away, then body, then legs.
Slide forward under control and set up for the next stroke.
cues: Legs, body, arms — in that order
Arms away first on the recovery
Handle to the bottom of the ribs

common_mistakes.mistake: Pulling with the arms before the legs have driven
common_mistakes.fix: Push the legs flat first with straight arms; legs, then body, then arms is the whole technique and reversing it is why backs get sore.

common_mistakes.mistake: Setting the damper to ten
common_mistakes.fix: Use three to five — a high damper is not more resistance, it just makes each stroke slower and heavier, like rowing a barge.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rounding the back at the catch
common_mistakes.fix: Hinge from the hips with a long spine, and shorten the slide if tight hamstrings pull the back round.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rushing the recovery
common_mistakes.fix: Take roughly twice as long coming forward as going back; a fast slide forward wastes energy and jars the catch.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaning back too far at the finish
common_mistakes.fix: Stop at about eleven o'clock; leaning further loads the low back and adds nothing to the stroke.

content.breathing: Exhale on the drive, inhale on the recovery. At higher rates one breath per stroke, at lower rates two.
content.rom_notes: Measured in distance, time and split rather than reps. Log the damper setting with the split, since the same split at different dampers is different work.
content.safety_notes: The low back takes the load whenever the sequence goes wrong or the catch rounds. Keep the spine long, drive with the legs, and stop the piece if the back rather than the legs and lungs is what is failing.

grip_variations.name: Standard overhand, damper three to five
grip_variations.effect: The standard, best balance of rate and power.

grip_variations.name: Higher damper, lower rate
grip_variations.effect: More strength-like, heavier per stroke.

grip_variations.name: Interval pieces
grip_variations.effect: Much higher intensity, shorter total volume.

content.summary: A fan bike with moving handles, where resistance rises with your own effort.
content.description: A large fan provides the resistance, so the harder you push the harder it pushes back — there is no setting to hide behind and no coasting. Because the arms and legs both drive, the whole body contributes and the heart rate climbs faster than on almost any other machine. It is famously unpleasant at high intensity and famously effective, and it is completely low impact, which is why it appears in so many programmes.
setup: Set the seat height so the knee is slightly bent at the bottom of the pedal stroke.
Sit with the back upright and take the handles at chest height.
Place the feet flat on the pedals with the straps snug if fitted.
Decide the interval structure or the target time before starting.
Start pedalling easily for thirty seconds before pushing.
execution: Drive with the legs and push and pull the handles in rhythm.
Keep the torso upright rather than hunching over the handles.
Push through the whole foot rather than the toes.
Keep the pace steady rather than surging and fading.
Ease off gradually at the end rather than stopping dead.
cues: The fan gives back what you give it

common_mistakes.mistake: Starting an interval at a pace you cannot hold
common_mistakes.fix: Pick a sustainable output for the whole interval; the fan punishes surging harder than any other machine.

common_mistakes.mistake: Seat set too low
common_mistakes.fix: Raise it until the knee is only slightly bent at the bottom, which stops the knees taking a cramped, repetitive load.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hunching over the handles
common_mistakes.fix: Sit tall so the trunk can transmit the arm work and breathing is not restricted.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using only the legs and letting the arms coast
common_mistakes.fix: Drive the handles actively; the arms are roughly a third of the output and coasting turns it into a worse stationary bike.

common_mistakes.mistake: Comparing calorie numbers between machines
common_mistakes.fix: Compare only against your own previous efforts on the same bike; the readouts are not standardised across brands.

content.breathing: Breathe hard and rhythmically. At high intensity, breathing is usually the limiting factor before the legs are.
content.rom_notes: Measured in calories, distance or time rather than reps. Log the machine as well as the numbers, since readouts differ between brands.
content.safety_notes: Very low impact and safe on the joints. The main caution is intensity — this machine can take an untrained person to their limit within a minute, so build the intervals up gradually.

grip_variations.name: Arms and legs together
grip_variations.effect: The standard, full body output.

grip_variations.name: Legs only, arms resting
grip_variations.effect: Isolates the legs, useful when the shoulders are fatigued.

grip_variations.name: Short hard intervals
grip_variations.effect: The classic use, highest intensity available with no impact.

content.summary: A seated bike, the gentlest sustained cardio option in the gym.
content.description: Cycling seated takes bodyweight off the joints entirely, which makes it the easiest cardio to do for a long time and the one most people can use through almost any lower body complaint. Resistance is adjustable in fine increments, so it scales from a recovery spin to a genuinely hard interval session. It works the quads more than anything else and asks very little of the upper body.
setup: Set the seat height so the knee has a slight bend at the bottom of the stroke.
Adjust the seat forward or back so the knee sits over the pedal at the front.
Set the handlebars at a height that lets the back stay comfortable.
Place the balls of the feet over the pedal axles.
Start with light resistance for the first few minutes.
execution: Pedal in smooth circles rather than stamping down.
Keep the knees tracking forward, not splaying out or falling in.
Sit tall or lean lightly on the bars without hunching.
Maintain a cadence somewhere around eighty to ninety revolutions per minute.
Ease the resistance down for a few minutes at the end.
cues: Slight knee bend at the bottom

common_mistakes.mistake: Seat set too low
common_mistakes.fix: Raise it until the knee is only slightly bent at the bottom; a low seat is the most common cause of knee pain on a bike.

common_mistakes.mistake: Grinding a very heavy resistance slowly
common_mistakes.fix: Lower the resistance and raise the cadence toward eighty to ninety; heavy grinding loads the knees without improving fitness faster.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hunching over the bars
common_mistakes.fix: Raise the handlebars or sit taller so the low back and neck are not held in a slump for half an hour.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reading and pedalling at no real effort
common_mistakes.fix: Set an intensity target — a heart rate or a resistance level — so the session is training rather than time spent.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pedalling with the arch or heel on the pedal
common_mistakes.fix: Place the ball of the foot over the axle so the ankle can contribute to the stroke.

content.breathing: Breathe steadily in rhythm with the pedal stroke. Effort should dictate the breathing rather than the other way round.
content.rom_notes: Measured in time, distance and resistance level. Log the resistance with the time, since duration alone says nothing about the effort.
content.safety_notes: The gentlest cardio option available and usable through most lower body injuries. Seat height is the one setting that causes problems — too low is the usual source of knee pain.

grip_variations.name: Upright bike
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most similar to outdoor cycling.

grip_variations.name: Recumbent bike
grip_variations.effect: Full back support, the easiest option for a sore low back.

grip_variations.name: Interval sprints
grip_variations.effect: Much higher intensity in a shorter session.

content.summary: A standing machine pulled from overhead down to the hips, driven by the lats and trunk.
content.description: Modelled on cross-country skiing, the ski erg is pulled from overhead down past the hips using the lats, triceps and trunk, with the legs contributing a hinge rather than a drive. It is the only common cardio machine that loads the upper body as the primary mover, which makes it a genuinely useful option when a lower body injury rules out the bike, the treadmill and the stair climber.
setup: Stand facing the machine with the feet hip width, a step back from the frame.
Reach up and take the handles at roughly head height or above.
Set the damper between four and six.
Soften the knees and hinge slightly at the hips.
Set the shoulders down and the trunk braced.
execution: Pull the handles down by driving the elbows toward the hips.
Let the trunk crunch forward and the hips hinge back as the handles descend.
Finish with the hands past the hips and the torso folded forward.
Stand up and reach the arms back overhead in one motion.
Keep a rhythm rather than pausing at either end.
cues: Pull with the lats, not the arms

common_mistakes.mistake: Pulling with the arms alone
common_mistakes.fix: Drive the elbows down and let the lats and trunk do the work; the arms fatigue in under a minute if they lead.

common_mistakes.mistake: Squatting instead of hinging
common_mistakes.fix: Push the hips back with soft knees; the legs contribute a hinge, not a squat, and squatting shortens the pull.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rounding the low back at the finish
common_mistakes.fix: Let the crunch come from the ribs while the spine stays long, rather than folding the lumbar spine under load.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stopping the pull at the thighs
common_mistakes.fix: Finish with the hands past the hips — the last portion is where most of the lat work happens.

common_mistakes.mistake: Overlooking it when the legs are injured
common_mistakes.fix: Keep it in mind as the upper body cardio option; almost every other machine needs working legs.

content.breathing: Exhale on the pull, inhale on the reach back up. One breath per stroke at pace, two when going easier.
content.rom_notes: Measured in distance, time and split. Log the damper alongside the split, since they interact.
content.safety_notes: The finish position involves trunk flexion under load, so keep the spine long and let the ribs do the crunching. Skip it or shorten the finish if the low back reacts to repeated bending.

grip_variations.name: Double pull, both handles together
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most power and the usual version.

grip_variations.name: Alternating single arm
grip_variations.effect: Closer to actual skiing, adds a rotation demand.

grip_variations.name: Seated on a box
grip_variations.effect: Removes the legs entirely, purely upper body cardio.

content.summary: A revolving staircase, loading the glutes and quads with every step.
content.description: Climbing a moving staircase asks for hip and knee extension over and over against bodyweight, which loads the glutes and quads far more than flat walking and keeps the heart rate high without any landing impact. It sits between the bike and the treadmill in demand, and it is one of the few cardio machines where the legs usually fatigue before the lungs do.
setup: Step on carefully while the stairs are stationary or moving slowly.
Start at a slow speed and build up over the first minute.
Stand tall with the eyes forward and the hands resting lightly on the rails.
Set the feet fully on each step rather than just the toes.
Decide the duration or interval structure before starting.
execution: Step up with the whole foot landing on the stair.
Drive through the heel to extend the hip and knee.
Stand tall rather than leaning on the handrails.
Keep a steady rhythm rather than rushing and coasting.
Slow the machine down before stepping off.
cues: Stand tall, rails for balance only

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaning heavily on the handrails
common_mistakes.fix: Rest the hands lightly for balance only — leaning takes a large share of bodyweight off the legs and makes the readout meaningless.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stepping on the toes only
common_mistakes.fix: Land the whole foot and drive through the heel so the glutes work rather than the calves doing everything.

common_mistakes.mistake: Skipping steps at a fast setting
common_mistakes.fix: Slow the machine to a speed you can take every step at, unless double steps are a deliberate variation.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hunching forward over the console
common_mistakes.fix: Stand tall with the hips under the shoulders; leaning forward shifts work off the glutes.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stepping on or off while it is moving fast
common_mistakes.fix: Slow it right down at both ends of the session — most stair climber injuries happen getting on or off.

content.breathing: Breathe deeply and steadily. Expect the legs to fatigue before the breathing does at moderate speeds.
content.rom_notes: Measured in time, floors or steps rather than reps. Log the speed setting alongside the duration.
content.safety_notes: No impact, but the moving stairs are a trip hazard — step on and off at low speed and keep a hand near the rail. Skip it if balance is a concern.

grip_variations.name: Single steps, hands light on the rails
grip_variations.effect: The standard, steady glute and quad work.

grip_variations.name: Double steps
grip_variations.effect: More glute involvement and a longer range per step.

grip_variations.name: Carrying dumbbells
grip_variations.effect: Adds load; only at a slow, controlled speed.

content.summary: A machine where the feet follow a fixed oval path and never leave the pedals.
content.description: Because the feet stay on the pedals throughout, there is no landing and no impact at all, while the movement pattern still resembles walking or running. Most machines add moving handles so the arms contribute too. It is the gentlest way to accumulate cardio minutes, and the usual honest criticism is that it is very easy to do at almost no effort without noticing.
setup: Step onto the pedals with the machine stationary and hold the fixed rails.
Set the resistance and incline before building up speed.
Take the moving handles if you want the arms to contribute.
Stand tall with the weight through the middle of the feet.
Start slowly for the first minute.
execution: Drive the pedals in a smooth oval motion.
Push and pull the handles in rhythm with the legs.
Keep the torso upright rather than hanging on the rails.
Push through the whole foot rather than the toes.
Slow down gradually before stepping off.

common_mistakes.mistake: Coasting at almost no resistance
common_mistakes.fix: Set a resistance that requires real effort and check the heart rate; momentum makes it very easy to move fast and work barely at all.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaning on the fixed rails
common_mistakes.fix: Stand tall and use the moving handles or let the arms swing; leaning transfers work away from the legs.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pushing only through the toes
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the whole foot on the pedal and drive through the mid foot to avoid calf cramping.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using it for months without progressing anything
common_mistakes.fix: Increase the resistance or the incline over time rather than only the duration.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stepping on or off while the pedals are moving
common_mistakes.fix: Wait for them to stop and hold the fixed rails; the pedals carry momentum.

content.breathing: Breathe steadily in rhythm with the stride. Effort should be high enough that breathing is noticeably deeper than at rest.
content.rom_notes: Measured in time, distance and resistance. Log the resistance and incline together with the duration, or the session cannot be compared.
content.safety_notes: Zero impact and among the safest machines available, suitable through most lower body complaints. Step on and off only when the pedals are stationary.

grip_variations.name: Moving handles, arms and legs
grip_variations.effect: The standard, full body involvement.

grip_variations.name: Fixed rails, legs only
grip_variations.effect: Isolates the legs, useful when shoulders are fatigued.

grip_variations.name: High incline setting
grip_variations.effect: More glute involvement, closer to climbing.

content.summary: Skipping for time, training calves, coordination and conditioning at once.
content.description: Skipping raises the heart rate quickly, trains the calves and achilles to absorb and return force, and demands a rhythm that takes real practice to hold. It packs into a bag and needs a few square feet of floor. It is genuinely high impact — every skip lands on the forefoot — so it builds resilient lower legs in someone who tolerates it and aggravates shins and achilles in someone who does too much too soon.
setup: Size the rope by standing on the middle — the handles should reach roughly to the armpits.
Find a floor with some give rather than concrete if possible.
Hold the handles at hip height with the elbows close to the ribs.
Stand tall with the feet together and the knees soft.
Start with short sets while the technique is still forming.
execution: Turn the rope with the wrists, not the arms or shoulders.
Jump just high enough to clear the rope, a couple of centimetres.
Land on the balls of the feet with soft knees and ankles.
Keep the torso tall and the eyes forward.
Keep a steady rhythm rather than jumping high and pausing.
cues: Jump low, just clear the rope

common_mistakes.mistake: Turning the rope with the whole arm
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the elbows tucked and turn from the wrists; big arm circles tire the shoulders and make the rhythm impossible to hold.

common_mistakes.mistake: Jumping far higher than needed
common_mistakes.fix: Clear the rope by a couple of centimetres — high jumping multiplies the landing impact for no benefit.

common_mistakes.mistake: Landing flat-footed or on the heels
common_mistakes.fix: Land on the balls of the feet with soft ankles and knees so the calf absorbs the landing.

common_mistakes.mistake: Doing long sessions in the first weeks
common_mistakes.fix: Build up gradually with short sets; achilles and shin problems come from volume added too fast, not from the technique.

common_mistakes.mistake: Skipping on concrete in worn shoes
common_mistakes.fix: Find a floor with some give and use shoes with intact cushioning; the surface matters more here than in most exercises.

content.breathing: Breathe steadily and rhythmically with the skips rather than holding the breath through a set.
content.rom_notes: Measured in time or unbroken skips. Log both the total time and the longest unbroken set, since coordination and conditioning improve separately.
content.safety_notes: High impact through the forefoot, achilles and shins. Build volume slowly, use a forgiving surface, and stop if the achilles or shins start to ache rather than pushing through.

grip_variations.name: Basic two-foot bounce
grip_variations.effect: The standard, lowest coordination demand.

grip_variations.name: Alternating feet
grip_variations.effect: Closer to running, slightly less impact per foot.

grip_variations.name: Double unders
grip_variations.effect: Much higher intensity and coordination demand.

content.summary: Driving the knees alternately toward the chest from a push-up position.
content.description: Holding a push-up position and running the knees in toward the chest combines a plank with a fast leg drive, so the trunk has to stop the hips rising or sagging while the hip flexors work continuously. It needs no equipment and raises the heart rate within seconds, which is why it appears in every bodyweight circuit ever written. The trade-off is that the shoulders and wrists carry bodyweight the whole time.
setup: Start in a push-up position with the hands under the shoulders.
Set the body in one straight line from the head to the heels.
Push the floor away so the upper back is broad rather than sunk.
Squeeze the glutes and brace the trunk.
Set the feet hip width with the weight on the balls of the feet.
execution: Drive one knee toward the chest while the other leg stays straight.
Return that foot and drive the other knee forward.
Keep the hips low and level — they should not rise with each step.
Keep the shoulders stacked over the hands throughout.
Maintain a steady pace rather than starting fast and collapsing.
cues: Drive the knee, don't bounce the hips

common_mistakes.mistake: Hips bouncing up with every knee drive
common_mistakes.fix: Slow down and keep the hips level; a rising and falling hip means the trunk has stopped holding position.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hips sagging toward the floor
common_mistakes.fix: Squeeze the glutes and brace before starting, and end the set when the line breaks.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hands creeping forward so the shoulders sit behind them
common_mistakes.fix: Reset the hands under the shoulders; shoulders behind the hands puts the load on the joint rather than the muscles.

common_mistakes.mistake: Going as fast as possible from the first second
common_mistakes.fix: Pick a pace you can hold for the whole interval — speed with a broken position trains very little.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pushing through wrist pain
common_mistakes.fix: Use push-up handles or dumbbells to keep the wrists neutral, or swap to a bike or rope if that does not help.

content.breathing: Breathe steadily and rhythmically throughout. Do not hold the brace as a single breath — these intervals last too long.
content.rom_notes: Measured in time or total knee drives. Log the interval length rather than a rep count, since pace varies more than reps do.
content.safety_notes: The wrists are loaded in extension for the whole set, which is the usual complaint. Use handles or dumbbells if that bothers you, and stop when the hips start to sag rather than continuing.

grip_variations.name: Hands on the floor
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most demand on the shoulders and wrists.

grip_variations.name: Hands elevated on a bench
grip_variations.effect: Easier on the shoulders and wrists, simpler to hold the line.

grip_variations.name: Cross-body knee drives
grip_variations.effect: Brings the obliques in alongside the hip flexors.

content.summary: A two-footed jump onto a raised box, training explosive leg power.
content.description: Jumping onto a box trains the legs to produce force fast, which is a different quality from producing force heavily and one that squats alone do not develop. Landing on a raised surface means the drop is much shorter than jumping and landing on the floor, so the impact is far lower than the height suggests. The single biggest mistake is treating box height as the score — a tucked landing on a tall box proves flexibility, not power.
setup: Choose a box height you can land on with the hips above parallel.
Check the box is stable and will not slide or tip.
Stand a comfortable distance back with the feet hip to shoulder width.
Set the arms free to swing.
Clear the floor around and behind the box.
execution: Dip quickly into a quarter squat, swinging the arms back.
Drive the arms up and extend the hips, knees and ankles explosively.
Land softly on the box with both feet flat and the knees bent.
Stand up fully on the box to complete the rep.
Step down one foot at a time rather than jumping back down.
cues: Stand up to finish the rep

common_mistakes.mistake: Jumping back down off the box
common_mistakes.fix: Step down one foot at a time — the landing from the box is a far bigger impact than the jump up, and it is where achilles injuries happen.

common_mistakes.mistake: Choosing a box so tall you land in a deep tuck
common_mistakes.fix: Use a height you can land on with the hips above parallel; tucking the knees to the chest measures hip flexibility, not jump power.

common_mistakes.mistake: Landing hard and noisily
common_mistakes.fix: Absorb through the ankles, knees and hips so the landing is quiet; a loud landing means nothing is absorbing it.

common_mistakes.mistake: High rep sets for conditioning
common_mistakes.fix: Keep sets to three to five jumps with full rest — this is a power exercise and tired jumps are both slower and riskier.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using a box that slides on the floor
common_mistakes.fix: Test it with bodyweight first, and use a soft plyo box if there is any chance of catching a shin.

content.breathing: Exhale on the jump and breathe freely between reps. There is no need to brace continuously across a set.
content.rom_notes: Measured in reps at a given box height. Log the height with the reps, and note that the honest measure is landing with the hips above parallel.
content.safety_notes: Step down between reps rather than jumping down — the descent is the risky part. Use a soft box if available, keep the area clear, and stop the set once the jumps slow down.

grip_variations.name: Two-footed jump, step down
grip_variations.effect: The standard, safest and most repeatable.

grip_variations.name: Seated start on a bench
grip_variations.effect: Removes the countermovement so pure starting strength is trained.

grip_variations.name: Single leg step-up jump
grip_variations.effect: Lower load, exposes side-to-side differences.

content.summary: A two-footed jump forward for distance, training horizontal power.
content.description: Jumping forward rather than upward trains hip extension in the direction sprinting and change of direction actually use, which makes it more transferable to field sport than a vertical jump. It also produces a hard flat landing with nothing to step onto, so it demands the ability to absorb force as well as produce it. Distance is easy to measure honestly, which makes it one of the better simple tests of lower body power.
setup: Find a clear run of floor with a forgiving surface if possible.
Mark the starting line and clear the landing area.
Stand with the feet hip to shoulder width behind the line.
Set the arms free to swing.
Decide the number of jumps before starting — this is a low-rep exercise.
execution: Swing the arms back and dip into a quarter squat.
Drive the arms forward and extend the hips explosively forward and up.
Reach the legs forward as you travel through the air.
Land on both feet with the knees and hips bending to absorb.
Stick the landing under control rather than stumbling forward.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stumbling or stepping forward on landing
common_mistakes.fix: Jump a distance you can stick — if the landing cannot be controlled, the jump was longer than the legs can absorb.

common_mistakes.mistake: Landing stiff-legged
common_mistakes.fix: Bend the knees and hips on contact; a flat landing takes several times bodyweight and the joints have to absorb it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Doing them for high reps as conditioning
common_mistakes.fix: Keep sets to three to five jumps with full rest; the landings accumulate and tired jumping is when things go wrong.

common_mistakes.mistake: Jumping onto a hard slick surface
common_mistakes.fix: Use rubber flooring or grass — a landing on concrete or a slippery floor is the main hazard here.

common_mistakes.mistake: Only ever training vertical jumps
common_mistakes.fix: Include horizontal jumping too; it transfers more directly to sprinting and changing direction.

content.breathing: Exhale on the jump and breathe freely between reps.
content.rom_notes: Measured in reps and distance jumped. Log the distance for the best jump, since that is the number that reflects power output.
content.safety_notes: The landing carries the risk here, not the jump — it is flat, hard and unassisted. Use a forgiving surface, jump only as far as you can stick, and stop when the landings stop being controlled.

grip_variations.name: Single jump for distance
grip_variations.effect: The standard, a clean power test.

grip_variations.name: Repeat broad jumps
grip_variations.effect: Adds a rebound element and much more landing volume.

grip_variations.name: Standing start with no arm swing
grip_variations.effect: Removes the arm contribution to isolate the legs.

content.summary: A drop to the floor, a push-up and a jump, repeated for reps or time.
content.description: A burpee moves the body from standing to lying to standing again with a jump on the end, which raises the heart rate faster than almost any other bodyweight movement. It needs no equipment and a square metre of floor. It is also a full push-up and a jump landing repeated dozens of times, so the wrists, shoulders and shins accumulate a great deal of work in a set that feels like cardio rather than lifting.
setup: Find a clear square of floor with some give if possible.
Stand with the feet hip width.
Decide the rep count or the interval length before starting.
Decide whether the chest touches the floor or a push-up is performed.
Set a pace you can hold rather than sprinting the first ten.
execution: Squat down and place the hands on the floor in front of the feet.
Jump or step the feet back into a push-up position.
Lower the chest to the floor, or perform a full push-up.
Jump or step the feet back in under the hips.
Stand and jump, clapping overhead, then go straight into the next rep.
cues: Steady pace beats a fast start
Step it back if the form goes

common_mistakes.mistake: Hips sagging in the bottom position
common_mistakes.fix: Brace the trunk and squeeze the glutes as the feet land back; a sagging middle repeated forty times is what makes backs sore afterwards.

common_mistakes.mistake: Sprinting the first ten reps
common_mistakes.fix: Pick a pace you can hold for the whole set — burpees punish a fast start more than almost anything.

common_mistakes.mistake: Landing hard on every jump
common_mistakes.fix: Land through the whole foot with soft knees; the landings add up quickly across a long set.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pushing through wrist pain
common_mistakes.fix: Use push-up handles or step back rather than jumping, or swap to mountain climbers if that does not help.

common_mistakes.mistake: Keeping the jump when tired
common_mistakes.fix: Step the feet back and forward and drop the jump once the position degrades; a slow clean burpee beats a fast broken one.

content.breathing: Breathe continuously and rhythmically. Holding the breath through reps is the fastest way to end the set early.
content.rom_notes: One rep is chest to the floor and a jump with the hands overhead. Log whether the chest touched and whether the jump was included, since versions vary widely.
content.safety_notes: The wrists take repeated loading in extension and each jump is an impact. Step the feet rather than jumping them if the wrists or shins complain, and drop the jump before dropping the standards.

grip_variations.name: Full burpee with chest to floor and jump
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most demanding version.

grip_variations.name: Step-back burpee, no jump
grip_variations.effect: Removes the impact entirely, much easier on wrists and shins.

grip_variations.name: Burpee with a pull-up or box jump added
grip_variations.effect: Considerably harder, common in conditioning workouts.

content.summary: Waving two heavy ropes for time, an upper body conditioning tool.
content.description: Whipping heavy ropes raises the heart rate through the shoulders and arms rather than the legs, which makes it one of the few conditioning options available when the lower body is injured or already fatigued. The grip gives out fast and the shoulders burn within thirty seconds. It is entirely low impact, requires no coordination to speak of, and the intensity is set purely by how hard you choose to move.
setup: Anchor the ropes securely and check the anchor point before starting.
Take an end in each hand and walk back until there is slight slack.
Set the feet shoulder width with the knees soft.
Hinge slightly at the hips with the chest up and the trunk braced.
Decide the interval length before starting — thirty seconds is plenty.
execution: Drive the arms up and down alternately to send waves down the ropes.
Keep the waves reaching all the way to the anchor.
Stay in an athletic stance with the knees soft and the trunk braced.
Breathe continuously rather than holding through the interval.
Stop when the waves shorten rather than at a fixed time.

common_mistakes.mistake: Small waves that die halfway down the rope
common_mistakes.fix: Drive the arms through a full range so the wave reaches the anchor; short flicks look busy and do very little.

common_mistakes.mistake: Standing up straight and locking the knees
common_mistakes.fix: Stay in an athletic stance with the knees soft so the whole body can absorb and contribute.

common_mistakes.mistake: Holding the breath through the interval
common_mistakes.fix: Breathe continuously; thirty seconds of hard rope work is long enough that a held breath ends it early.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rounding the back and hunching over
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the chest up and the trunk braced rather than folding forward as fatigue arrives.

common_mistakes.mistake: Overlooking it when the legs are injured
common_mistakes.fix: Keep it in mind alongside the ski erg — these are the two conditioning options that need almost nothing from the lower body.

content.breathing: Breathe hard and continuously throughout the interval rather than bracing and holding.
content.rom_notes: Measured in time rather than reps. Log the interval length and note when the waves started to shorten, which is the real end of the working set.
content.safety_notes: Very low risk and completely low impact. Check the anchor before each session, and keep the rope path clear of anyone walking past.

grip_variations.name: Alternating waves
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most sustainable and the usual version.

grip_variations.name: Double waves, both arms together
grip_variations.effect: More trunk involvement, harder to sustain.

grip_variations.name: Slams or side-to-side waves
grip_variations.effect: Brings the lats and obliques in more strongly.

content.summary: A front squat into a throw at a wall target, caught and repeated.
content.description: Squatting with a medicine ball and using the leg drive to throw it at a target above head height combines a squat and a press into one continuous movement, with a catch on the way down that loads the eccentric too. It is a staple of conditioning workouts because it fatigues the legs, shoulders and lungs simultaneously. The catch is what people underestimate — receiving a ball overhead repeatedly while already tired.
setup: Pick a wall with a target height, typically around three metres.
Choose a ball weight you can throw to the target when tired, not just when fresh.
Stand roughly an arm's length from the wall with the feet shoulder width.
Hold the ball at chest height with the elbows tucked in.
Brace the trunk and set the chest up.
execution: Squat down to at least parallel with the ball held at the chest.
Drive up explosively through the legs.
Let the leg drive carry into the throw and release the ball at the target.
Catch the ball as it returns, absorbing it into the next squat.
Continue in a rhythm rather than resetting between reps.
cues: Legs throw the ball, not the arms
Catch soft into the next squat

common_mistakes.mistake: Squatting shallower as the set goes on
common_mistakes.fix: Hit at least parallel on every rep; the depth is the first thing to disappear and the reps stop counting when it does.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pressing the ball with the arms
common_mistakes.fix: Drive hard with the legs so the ball is almost weightless at the top; an arm press means the timing is off.

common_mistakes.mistake: Catching the ball with straight arms
common_mistakes.fix: Receive it with the elbows bending and absorb straight into the squat; a stiff catch jars the shoulders and wrists.

common_mistakes.mistake: Picking a ball that is too heavy
common_mistakes.fix: Choose a weight you can still hit the target with at the end of the set, not one that works only for the first five reps.

common_mistakes.mistake: Standing too far from the wall
common_mistakes.fix: Stay about an arm's length away so the ball comes straight back down rather than out toward you.

content.breathing: Exhale sharply on the throw, inhale as the ball descends. Breathe every rep rather than holding across several.
content.rom_notes: One rep is a squat to at least parallel plus a throw that hits the target. Log the ball weight and the target height with the reps.
content.safety_notes: Keep the eyes on the ball throughout and make sure nobody is standing beside or behind you. Needs enough shoulder range to throw overhead and enough ankle and hip range to squat to parallel.

grip_variations.name: Standard weight and target
grip_variations.effect: The standard conditioning version.

grip_variations.name: Heavier ball, lower target
grip_variations.effect: More of a strength effort, less cardiovascular.

grip_variations.name: Throwing without catching, resetting each rep
grip_variations.effect: Removes the eccentric catch, easier on the shoulders.

content.summary: Throwing a medicine ball hard into the floor, driven by the lats and trunk.
content.description: Raising a ball overhead and slamming it into the floor trains the lats and trunk to produce force fast in the one direction most gym exercises never load — downward and forward. Because the ball leaves the hands there is no eccentric to control, which makes it far easier on the joints than the effort suggests. It is also one of the more satisfying exercises in any gym, which counts for something in adherence.
setup: Use a dead-bounce slam ball, not a bouncy medicine ball.
Stand on a solid floor with the feet shoulder width.
Check nobody is standing close by.
Hold the ball at chest height with both hands.
Brace the trunk and set the knees soft.
execution: Reach the ball overhead, extending the hips and rising onto the toes.
Drive the ball down hard by pulling with the lats and crunching the trunk.
Hinge at the hips as the ball travels down rather than folding the low back.
Release at roughly knee height so the ball hits the floor in front of the feet.
Pick it up with a hinge and reset for the next rep.
cues: Pull with the lats, not the arms
Pick it up with a hinge too

common_mistakes.mistake: Using a bouncy medicine ball
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dead-bounce slam ball — a bouncing ball comes straight back at your face at the speed you threw it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rounding the low back to follow the ball down
common_mistakes.fix: Hinge at the hips with a long spine; the crunch should come from the ribs, not from folding the lumbar spine at speed.

common_mistakes.mistake: Bending over to pick the ball up between reps
common_mistakes.fix: Hinge to collect it, especially late in a set — that pickup is repeated dozens of times and it is where backs get tweaked.

common_mistakes.mistake: Slamming at half effort for high reps
common_mistakes.fix: Throw every rep at full intent and keep the sets short; a soft slam is neither power training nor useful conditioning.

common_mistakes.mistake: Slamming near other people or on a fragile floor
common_mistakes.fix: Clear the space and check the surface — slam balls split and floors crack.

content.breathing: Exhale sharply on the slam. Breathe freely between reps rather than bracing continuously.
content.rom_notes: One rep is a full overhead reach to a slam released around knee height. Log the ball weight with the reps.
content.safety_notes: Only use a dead-bounce slam ball. Keep the area clear, check the ball for splits before each session, and hinge rather than bending to pick it up — the repeated pickup is the real risk, not the slam.

grip_variations.name: Overhead slam straight down
grip_variations.effect: The standard, most lat and trunk involvement.

grip_variations.name: Rotational slam to one side
grip_variations.effect: Brings the obliques in, closer to a rotational throw.

grip_variations.name: Slam into a squat catch
grip_variations.effect: Adds a leg element and makes it more conditioning than power.
